XS.2 is 33B parameters, one of the most competitive models for its size on coding and agentic coding specifically.
data.description: Previewed and not yet public: Laguna S — 118B total / 8B active parameters, 30 trillion tokens, 4,000 GPUs, also to be released open weights. Base-model evals (caveated as pre-post-training): S beats XS.2 and the much larger M.1 on MultiPL-E / LiveCodeBench / BigCodeBench, beats GLM 4.5 Air, a recent Qwen model, and the larger DeepSeek V4 Flash Max; competitive-but-not-top on BIG-Bench Hard, close on EvalPlus; best of every model tested on SWE-bench Multilingual (agentless); behind Nemotron and DeepSeek on MMLU Pro knowledge, which poolside attributes to a data gap it deprioritized in favour of coding.

data.name: 13% of Laguna XS.2's 6T-token pre-training mix is synthetic
data.brief: Quantified synthetic-data share from a frontier lab: 13% of the Laguna XS.2 pre-training mix is synthetic (pre-training stages only, before any post-training), drawn from a corpus that now stands at 6 trillion tokens and is continuously growing in multiple directions.
data.description: Stated position: synthetic data is not a replacement for organic data in the current state of the world, but a complement — organic data hides a great deal implicitly and often presents it sub-optimally, and synthetic generation is the mechanism for extracting those features and projecting them onto new planes (exposing implicit rationale, implicit planning, implicit structure), filling gaps, and regularizing both how tokens are presented and how the model is taught.

data.name: Running out of unique high-quality tokens saturated poolside's models early
data.brief: Named scaling failure that forced the synthetic pivot: poolside began at small scale optimizing quality over quantity maybe a little too much; when the models and the training budget scaled, the high-quality corpus ran out of unique tokens, producing non-optimal repetition that saturated the model too early.
data.description: The fix was rephrasing — regenerating seeds into fresh phrasings to restore token uniqueness — with ablations showing a consistent gap between seeds-with-repetition and repetition-reduced mixes (numbers presented with an explicit take-them-with-a-grain-of-salt caveat). Two specialized rephrasing pipelines were built beyond the generic one: math to code and text, and STEM documents.

data.name: A single broken GPU silently corrupted a training run, caught by replica hashing
data.brief: Previously unpublished failure account: two training runs with identical model configuration, training data and implementation produced visibly different loss curves — one spiky, with huge gradient norms — and the only difference was that one run had drawn a broken GPU, which caused silent data corruption.
data.description: The class of failure is invisible in the usual telemetry and was caught only because cross-replica weight hashes diverged when they are mathematically required to match.

data.name: BF16 accumulation at the unembedding stopped Laguna M.1 converging at 50k steps
data.brief: Second previously unpublished account, and the crisper one: the initial Laguna M.1 run stopped converging at roughly 50,000 steps — the loss flattened outright. Cause: activations immediately before the LM head (the unembedding) grew steadily during training, and the tensor-parallel accumulation there ran in BF16 by default, which eventually had insufficient numerical precision to be accurate, so the model could no longer learn.
data.description: Because of where it sits, the error back-propagates into the entire model trunk. Fix: resume from the pre-divergence checkpoint with the accumulation moved to FP32; the model converged again and the gradient norm reversed from an increasing to a decreasing trend. Emphasized as observable only at scale.

data.name: A DeepGEMM FP8 race condition silently randomized ~0.5% of gradients
data.brief: Third failure account, on the Laguna S run: adding FP8 training on DeepSeek's open-source DeepGEMM FP8 kernels introduced a race condition, visible as illegal memory accesses and NaNs in the gradients, and — the unobservable part — roughly 0.5% of gradient values silently replaced with random values.
data.description: poolside traced it back to the kernels and has a fix in a public PR that is not yet merged upstream. The finding doubles as the limit case for their own defence: replica hashing cannot catch it, because real runs carry no two replicas holding the same weights and the same data, so forward/backward equivalence is never checkable; a dry-run hash checker is in progress.

data.name: At scale the dangerous training failures are the silent ones
data.brief: At hundreds of billions of parameters across thousands of GPUs, the dangerous failures are the silent ones: a broken GPU corrupting data, a default BF16 accumulation quietly running out of precision, an open-source kernel randomizing half a percent of your gradients. None announces itself; each is only visible as a shape in a loss curve or a gradient norm you happened to be watching, and each can cost a training run.
data.description: The team's stance — we don't trust anything — turns into engineering by hunting checkable invariants (replica weights must be identical; gradient norms should trend down) and crashing the run the moment one breaks. The corollary the talk is honest about is that the invariant set is incomplete: what has no redundancy in a real run cannot be checked, so the verification layer itself has to be extended (dry-run redundant hashing) rather than trusted.

data.name: Synthetic data is re-projection of implicit structure, not volume
data.brief: The case for synthetic data here is not volume, it is re-projection: organic data already contains the rationale, the planning and the structure you want the model to learn, but implicitly and in a form that is often not the most teachable. Synthetic generation extracts those features and projects them onto new planes, which is simultaneously a way to fill gaps and to regularize how the model is taught rather than merely what it is shown.
data.description: Two consequences follow. First, ambition is bounded by difficulty, not by the teacher model: if the task is too hard for your model, your model will fall on its face — lose correctness, lose diversity — so you decompose until each step is easy, which is precisely how orchestrated pipelines escape the ceiling of what a single teacher model can produce. Second, because pipelines decompose into the same six parts, complexity becomes a dial you set per data class — cheap seed-heavy generation with small models for bulk, expensive orchestration only where the data is worth it.

data.name: Compose synthetic pipelines from six parts and four shapes
guidelines: Treat every pipeline as the same six components — seeds, primary inputs, metadata, secondary inputs, a generator function (prompt template or tool-using agent), and supplementary functions (filters, validators) — then pick a point on the complexity axis per data class: cheap, seed-heavy, small-model pipelines for bulk (where output quality rides almost entirely on seed quality, so invest there), orchestrated multi-agent workflows only where the data justifies the cost. Four shapes cover most of it: rephrasing (break token repetition

ablate against the repeated-seed baseline), multi-stage decomposition (don't generate the novel — generate setting, characters, styles, plot and twists first, then the chapters), cross-domain porting (translate between modes — code to another language, math problems into code), and multi-turn loops (two agents in conversation, or a judge and an evolver alternating for k rounds). Governing rule of thumb: if a task is too hard for the generating model it loses both correctness and diversity — break it down and make each step simpler, which is what frees you from the ceiling of whatever the teacher model can do in one shot. Run it on infrastructure that makes this configurable: a queue of agents with per-agent prompt/parameters/model and entry, exit and frequency rules, orchestrators between agents to impose hierarchy, rewrite the next agent's instructions and route or skip agents, and a supervisor with a global view policing the orchestrator

data.name: Assume the training stack is lying to you, and instrument invariants
guidelines: Treat data quality and training-codebase correctness as one problem, not two — if you've got data that sucks you can't train a good model

if you've got a training code base that sucks, you also can't. Then find invariants you can actually check and enforce them: under distributed data parallel every replica must hold identical weights, so hash the weights per replica, compare periodically, and crash the run on any mismatch rather than letting it continue — that is what surfaces silent data corruption from a single bad GPU. Watch gradient norms next to the loss, not the loss alone: a run that flattens with a rising gradient norm is a numerics story, and the specific one to check is accumulation precision at the unembedding — activations grow during training, BF16 accumulation under tensor parallelism eventually runs out of precision, and the fix is to move that accumulation to FP32 and resume from the last good checkpoint. Audit third-party kernels the same way: FP8 GEMM kernels produced illegal memory accesses, NaN gradients, and a silent ~0.5% random-value gradient corruption. Know your blind spot — real runs have no replicas sharing both weights and data, so forward/backward equivalence and kernel race conditions escape the hash check entirely
build a redundant dry-run checker to cover it

data.name: Loop Engineering from First Principles (Kyle Mistele, HumanLayer — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Kyle Mistele
Agentic control loop
data.brief: An agent loop built to the control-theory template instead of while true: a set point (desired end state of the codebase with respect to one property), a sensor that measures current state (deterministic — ast-grep, ESLint rules, Packwerk — or non-deterministic — an agent plus a skill and natural-language rules — or a pipeline mixing both), the measured error (the violation list), a controller that turns that error into a control signal about one incremental change, and an actuator that applies it, all while the system takes disturbances (teammates shipping). Because the components are agents, the lines blur in practice: a hybrid sensor+controller or a merged controller+actuator are both normal. The controller is the load-bearing part — without a well-tuned one the loop makes too large a change or the wrong change, repeatedly. Precedents named as existing control loops: thermostats, Kubernetes autoscaling, infrastructure-as-code, Postgres autovacuum, React's virtual DOM.

data.name: ast-grep
data.brief: Language-agnostic structural code search and lint used as a deterministic loop sensor: a rule matches the unmigrated code pattern, granular include/exclude paths scope it, extra rules layer on over time for other patterns to remove, and it works across a multilingual monorepo. Explicitly chosen over an agent, ripgrep or TypeScript-native tooling because it is out of band from tsconfig and ESLint — the config an agent will happily disable with an inline comment. Raw output is ~50 keys per violation, filtered to ~4 and sorted deterministically before it reaches the controller.

data.name: Golden patterns
data.brief: Idiomatic reference implementations written by hand, by humans, before the loop is turned on, and shipped inside the actuator's skill. Rationale: agents are pattern replicators, so without golden patterns the loop reproduces whatever is in the docs or in the model's memory of the internet rather than your house style. The skill should also carry a response template; expect to iterate the skill from what actually works rather than front-loading it.

data.name: Loop flow control
data.brief: Adaptive throttling that keeps a loop from outrunning human review: every loop labels the PRs it creates, and before doing any work the workflow checks whether any PR carrying its label is still open — if so it shuts down immediately, before checkout and dependency install. Invariant: at most one open PR per loop, no stacking, no duplicated work, few conflicts. The reasoning is explicitly about review capacity, not compute: an open PR means no human has reviewed the loop's last output, so there is no reason to manufacture more.

data.name: Loop feedback file
data.brief: A markdown file tracked in version control that is deterministically loaded into the actuator agent's context on every run (after the controller). An /iterate comment on one of the loop's own labelled PRs triggers the workflow to load the PR context — diff, comments, review comments, description — alongside the skill and instruct the agent both to fix the code and to update the feedback file. Turns re-steering from a checkout-edit-commit-push chore into a PR comment, and makes the steering history diffable and revertible.

data.name: CI as the loop runtime
data.brief: Running agent loops on the CI system you already have (GitHub Actions, GitLab, CircleCI) rather than new infrastructure: it already holds code access, secrets, and dispatch plus scheduling primitives. One workflow run equals one loop iteration (sense, control, actuate, open PR), scheduled daily so the team walks in to one small, low-risk PR. We don't need a new cluster for this.

data.name: Loop-maximal codebases ship the visibly worse outcomes
data.brief: HumanLayer's second public critique of loops-maxing, argued from shipped outcomes rather than theory: the discourse is hype and really not helpful; six code-review agents still leave you with 40,000-line PRs nobody wants to read.
data.description: The most loop-maximal codebases have the visible quality problems — Claude Code's terminal flicker took six months to fix while the OpenCode team wrote a renderer in a fraction of that; OpenClaw notoriously has stability issues — and the whole configuration is affordable only with a frontier lab's unlimited token budget, while, per Matt Pocock, bad code is more expensive in the age of agents than it has ever been.

data.name: Agent loops should be built to the control-theory template
data.brief: The counter-program: model the loop on control theory — set point, sensor, measured error, controller, actuator, disturbances — because control loops change a system incrementally instead of jumping to the end state and blowing it up, which avoids over-steering and minimises risk.
data.description: Loops are appropriate exactly when you have a system you want to change, a property you can measure, and a way to get feedback on the change (what good software engineers have always been taught to do). Stated scope beyond code cleanup: conforming an API to someone else's OpenAPI spec, tracking the MCP specification version, mirroring a project from Python to TypeScript, maintaining a fork against upstream.

data.name: HumanLayer migrates 150 RPC procedures to Effect with a production control loop
data.brief: The production loop, end to end: HumanLayer is incrementally migrating ~150 RPC procedures to Effect. Sensor equals an ast-grep rule finding unmigrated procedures (out of band from tsconfig/ESLint, multilingual-monorepo-safe), output filtered from ~50 keys to 4 and deterministically sorted.
data.description: Before migrating anything they stop the bleeding: one full scan on main, violations committed to version control, and every new PR checked for added violations — a disturbance dampener against teammates shipping unmigrated code. Controller equals deterministically pick the first (or, cleverer, the smallest) violation via bash/jq or ast-grep — never send an agent to do deterministic code's job — optionally enriched with telemetry so the control signal names the procedures with the most errors, least instrumentation, or APM gaps, letting the actuator improve the code rather than doing a 1:1 translation. Actuator equals CLI coding agent plus a skill with hand-written golden patterns and a response template; then a deterministic commit, push and PR whose description is the agent's final message.

data.name: Loop flow control and a feedback file fix the two failure modes found in production
data.brief: Two failure modes found by running the loop for real, and their fixes. (1) Re-steering was so high-friction — check out the branch, change the skill, change the code, commit, push — that they turned the loop off; fixed with a version-controlled markdown feedback file loaded into the agent's context every run plus an /iterate PR-comment trigger that loads the diff, comments and description and instructs the agent to fix the code and update the feedback file, so steering is diffable and revertible.
data.description: (2) A week at a customer site left every loop's PRs stacked, duplicated and conflicting — the loop's work is important, but it's not that important; fixed by labelling each loop's PRs and having the workflow exit immediately if its previous PR is still open, since an open PR means no human reviewed the last output.

data.name: Loop engineering needs an old theory: the controller is the load-bearing part
data.brief: Loop engineering doesn't need new theory, it needs an old one. What separates a loop you can run on a real codebase from a blind one is whether you can name its set point, sensor, measured error, controller and actuator — and above all whether the controller exists and is tuned, because a loop with no controller makes too large a change or the wrong change and then repeats it.
data.description: The payoff is not only safety: an incremental, well-instrumented loop produces diffs small enough that humans keep reading the code, and a control signal carrying telemetry makes the loop improve the code it touches instead of transliterating it.

data.name: Human review capacity, not tokens, is the scarce resource governing a loop
data.brief: The scarce resource governing an agent loop is human review capacity, not tokens or compute. If nobody has reviewed the loop's last PR, another iteration only manufactures work nobody wants — so the loop should read its own labels and refuse to run.
data.description: Scaling then happens along axes that respect that constraint: batch 3-5 items per run with a separate implementation phase (and context window) each — cheaper and more reliable — or run the workflow N times and hand one PR to each of N teammates, rather than letting one loop stack N PRs on one reviewer.

data.name: Build the loop as a control loop
guidelines: Ask three qualifying questions first: can you measure the thing, can you apply changes incrementally, can you get feedback on change quality? Then: define the set point (desired end state with respect to one property of the codebase)

build the sensor deterministically wherever possible (ast-grep, ESLint, Packwerk) and out of band from config the agent can disable with an inline comment — an agent plus skill sensor is legitimate where determinism isn't
filter and deterministically sort the violation list
stop the bleeding before migrating — full scan on main, commit the violation baseline to version control, and check every PR for newly added violations (the disturbance dampener)
design the controller explicitly — first violation, or smallest violation to minimise risk, chosen by bash/jq or ast-grep, and never by an agent doing deterministic code's job
enrich the control signal with the data the change is meant to fix (error rates, missing instrumentation, APM gaps) so the actuator improves the code rather than transliterating it
make the actuator an agent plus skill and end the run with a deterministic commit, push, and PR whose body is the agent's final message

data.name: Operate loops on the CI you already have
guidelines: Use GitHub Actions / GitLab / CircleCI — they already have code access, secrets, and dispatch plus scheduling primitives

no new cluster. One workflow run equals one iteration (sense, control, actuate, PR), scheduled daily so the team arrives to one small low-risk PR. Label every PR a loop creates so each workflow can identify its own work when several loops run. Add a comment trigger (/iterate) that deterministically loads PR diff, comments, review comments and description into the agent's context alongside the skill. Keep a version-controlled markdown feedback file, load it every run after the controller, and have the /iterate handler update it as well as the code, so steering accumulates in git. Gate the whole workflow on whether any PR with my label is still open, and exit before checkout if so. Scale velocity by having the controller pick 3-5 items with a separate implementation phase per item, or by running the workflow N times for N reviewers

data.name: Hand-write golden patterns before turning the loop on
guidelines: Agents are pattern replicators — without idiomatic hand-written examples in the skill you get what's in the docs or what the model absorbed from the internet, not your house style. Write the golden patterns by hand first, put them in the actuator's skill along with a response template, and spend real time on the skill — but not all of it up front: iterate it from what the loop actually produces, and let the /iterate feedback file carry the corrections between skill revisions

data.name: Evals-Driven Development for a Mental Health AI Coach (Akele Reed & Dave Revere, SonderMind — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Akele Reed
Dave Revere
SonderMind
data.brief: Mental-health care company: matches individuals with human therapists and psychiatrists nationwide, has served over a million people, partners named on stage include Headspace, Aetna and Anthem. Stated north star is access and outcomes — people get better faster. Builds and operates Sonder, a clinically grounded AI coach, and has open-sourced its guardrail evaluation datasets.

data.name: Guardrail sandwich (separate-call input/output guardrails)
data.brief: Safety implemented as independent LLM-as-judge calls that sandwich the core agent rather than as rules inside its prompt. The input guardrail inspects the incoming user message and decides whether intervention is required before the core responds; the output guardrail inspects the AI response and the conversation as a whole, and can intervene to keep the conversation on track. Three stated reasons for keeping them as separate calls: modularity (the core can be iterated without compromising user safety), robustness (separate calls are harder to prompt-engineer around and harder to jailbreak by conversationally driving the model off the rails), and evaluability. The latency and cost cost is explicitly accepted as warranted by the sensitivity of the use case.

data.name: Coded risk disclosure (the sentence underneath the sentence)
data.brief: The engineering problem statement of clinical safety: the words are not the message. The worked example — I packed a box today, just to feel what it would be like to be gone — is a real scenario contributed by a clinician from patient experience, and it reads as risk to a clinician while defeating every naive detector: regex lists of self-harm words and phrases, safety rules buried in verbose prompt instructions, and broad third-party moderation APIs. The signal is the implication, the context, and the position in the conversation, not any one word.

data.name: Guardrail over-calibration
data.brief: The failure mode on the other side of safety: general-purpose LLM guardrails are far too conservative, and an inappropriate trigger on someone in a vulnerable moment is a door slam to the face that leaves them more isolated and can prevent them from getting care. The design objective is therefore stated as not more triggers, more correct triggers. Three calibrated response tiers are demonstrated: present-tense danger, surface local resources and disengage; past-tense disclosure, surface resources and continue if the user is comfortable; no risk indicator, silent pass-through where the user never knows the guardrails are there.

data.name: Clinician-annotated typed evals
data.brief: The pipeline that puts an accountable licensed expert, not the engineering team, in charge of correct. Every conversation is traced; a flagged edge-case moment goes into the clinician's annotation queue with a small rubric — expected result, expected observation (which becomes the eval's assertion), turn index (which lets the conversation be replayed up to the point where the guardrail should have fired), category metadata, and a note that tells the engineer how to categorize the scenario. An annotation-extraction script triages the flagged traces into a report for discussion and normalizes the same annotations into the eval schema as typed evals. Once committed, a clinician's judgment is living in CI: every prompt change, model change and guardrail change is scored against what the clinician taught the system.

data.name: Sonder (clinically grounded AI coach)
data.brief: SonderMind's purpose-built mental-health AI coach: conversational with voice capability, available 24/7, helping users reflect on their lives, track progress on goals, and practise evidence-informed grounding exercises and tools — positioned for people seeking support who aren't ready for therapy yet or are between sessions, and as a front door into SonderMind's human provider network when a human is the right next step. Architecture: input guardrails, Sonder core (memory, personalization), output guardrails, with analytics and alerting alongside.

data.name: Open guardrail scenario datasets
data.brief: SonderMind's open-sourced evaluation corpus: 200 input-guardrail scenarios and 100 output-guardrail scenarios, every one clinically reviewed and calibrated against real conversation patterns, single- and multi-turn, spanning the spectrum of mental health. Released as a shared baseline for anyone building in the space, with an explicit caveat that it is not a replacement for building your own learning loop — there might be real hurting people depending on your learning curve.

data.name: SonderMind sandwiches its coach with separate input and output guardrail calls
data.brief: Production safety architecture for a mental-health coach serving a company that has cared for over a million people: input and output guardrails as separate LLM-judge calls sandwiching the core agent — the input guardrail decides whether the user's message needs intervention before the core responds; the output guardrail reads the response and the whole conversation and can intervene.
data.description: Stated design reasons: modularity (iterate the core without compromising safety), jailbreak resistance (separate calls are harder to prompt-engineer around than in-prompt rules and resist conversational drift attacks), and evaluability. The latency and cost trade-off is accepted explicitly because of the use case's sensitivity, and every architectural decision was made with safety as a primary objective.

data.name: SonderMind turned off provider guardrails as unfit for mental-health care
data.brief: Vertical builders are ripping out the frontier providers' safety layer: SonderMind turned off the built-in guardrails on day one because running their own clinical datasets through them would just filter everything. General-purpose LLMs are over-calibrated — described as a compassionate choice by the model providers — and are not built for mental-health care, a gap the speakers tie to tragic events now in the news and the courts.
data.description: Market context given: an American Psychological Association survey found 77% of psychologists say their patients are using AI for mental-health support of some kind, and mental-health support is among the top use cases for AI today. The design objective that replaces the provider default is not more triggers, more correct triggers, because an inappropriate guardrail on someone in a vulnerable moment is a door slammed in their face.

data.name: A licensed clinician, not the system, defines correct in clinical edge cases
data.brief: The learning loop, stated as a design principle: our system isn't deciding what correct is in a clinical edge case — a licensed professional is. Conversations are traced; flagged edge cases go to a clinician's annotation queue with a small rubric (expected result, expected observation, turn index, category, note).
data.description: An extraction script both triages flagged traces into a report for discussion and normalizes the annotations into typed evals in the team's eval schema; committed, a clinician's judgment is living in CI and every prompt, model and guardrail change is scored against it. The scenarios themselves come from the clinician's real patient experience — she knows the type of people our system is going to meet before we meet them — and the payoff is categorical: not one sentence fixed, the entire self-harm category lifted.

data.name: Clinician-labeled scenarios become evals that gate every release
data.brief: Calibration made executable through three stated design choices: (1) the clinical team owns the definition of good — vibes don't count here, an accountable judgment from a licensed expert does; (2) labeled scenarios ask concrete questions — did the expected observation fire, did the right category trigger, did it happen at the right point in the conversation, did the output evaluator catch the issue type; (3) those scenarios become evals that gate releases.
data.description: The declared philosophy is explicitly not benchmark maximization: we're not pursuing perfection with these benchmarks, because that can cause us to drift our focus away from the human those benchmarks are supposed to protect — real ambiguity exists in the edge cases, so the goal is benchmarks built from real failure modes in real data, counting false positives, false negatives, category and timing.

data.name: SonderMind open-sources 300 clinically reviewed guardrail scenarios
data.brief: SonderMind open-sourced its guardrail evaluation corpus at the talk: 200 input-guardrail scenarios and 100 output-guardrail scenarios, each clinically reviewed and calibrated against real conversation patterns, single- and multi-turn, across the spectrum of mental health.
data.description: Rationale: the problems SonderMind is facing are not unique to us — anyone working in this space is going to face some version of these, so a shared baseline matters even though it cannot replace a team's own learning loop, because there might be real hurting people depending on your learning curve. A safety-critical vertical treating its eval assets as a public good rather than a moat.

data.name: In care settings over-triggering is its own class of harm
data.brief: In a care setting, false positives are not the conservative default — they are a distinct class of harm. Refusing someone at their lowest point isolates them and can prevent them from getting care, which means precision of intervention is itself a safety property, not a UX nicety.
data.description: That reframing has an organisational consequence: the accountable definition of correct cannot come from the engineering team's judgment or from the model provider's global calibration, it has to come from the licensed professional who owns the clinical outcome — safety is helping to define the capability.

data.name: An eval gate does not make a system safe; a learning loop can
data.brief: A simple eval gate does not make a system safe. A learning loop can. The durable artifact is not the passing test or the one edge case that got fixed — it is the pipeline that converts a traced production moment into an expert annotation, the annotation into a typed eval with a replayable turn index, and the eval into a CI gate.
data.description: That is what makes an entire risk category lift at once and every subsequent prompt, model and guardrail change get scored against accumulated expert judgment. The corollary the speakers draw is against benchmark maximization: chasing a perfect score drifts attention away from the humans the benchmark exists to protect.

data.name: Build safety as separate calls, not prompt rules
guidelines: Put an input guardrail in front of the core agent (does this message require intervention before we respond?) and an output guardrail behind it that reads the response and the conversation as a whole and has the authority to intervene and steer the conversation back. Keep both as their own LLM-judge calls rather than rules inside the core prompt: they are harder to prompt-engineer around, harder to jailbreak by conversationally driving the model off the rails, independently evaluable, and they let you iterate the core without touching safety — accept the latency and cost if the use case warrants it. Tier the responses instead of using one trigger: present-tense danger, surface local resources and disengage
past-tense disclosure with no active risk, surface resources and continue if the user is comfortable

no risk indicator, silent pass-through. Turn off the provider's built-in guardrails only if you are replacing them with your own domain-calibrated layer. Wire analytics and alerting alongside so you find out when something goes wrong

data.name: Run the expert-annotation to typed-eval to CI loop
guidelines: Trace every conversation so the moment is capturable after the fact. Route flagged edge cases into a domain expert's annotation queue with a small rubric whose fields are load-bearing: expected result, expected observation (this is the eval's assertion), turn index (so the conversation can be replayed to the exact point the guardrail should have fired), category metadata, and a free-text note telling the engineer how to categorize the scenario. Run an extraction script that does double duty — triage all flagged traces into a report for team discussion, and normalize the annotations into your eval schema as typed evals. Commit them alongside any calibration changes so the expert's judgment gates every prompt, model and guardrail change from then on. Source the hardest scenarios from the expert's real practice rather than from your imagination of failure — the people who know what your system will meet have met them already

data.name: Calibrate the gate; don't maximize the benchmark
guidelines: Give the accountable domain team — not engineering, not the model provider — ownership of the definition of good

vibes don't count. Turn each labeled scenario into concrete questions (did the expected observation fire, did the right category trigger, at the right point in the conversation, did the output evaluator catch the issue type) and gate releases on them. Count false positives and false negatives, plus category and timing, as first-class costs — in a care setting over-triggering is its own harm, so the aim is to shrink the margin rather than to pick a preferred failure direction. Do not pursue benchmark perfection: real ambiguity exists in edge cases, and chasing the number drifts focus away from the humans the benchmark protects — build benchmarks from real failure modes in real data instead. Where the domain has collective stakes, publish a clinically reviewed baseline set so other builders don't learn on live users

data.name: Why Large? Tiny LMs & Agents on Edge/Robotics (Cormac Brick, Google — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Cormac Brick
Apple
data.brief: Coined on reference: carries FastVLM, its 0.5B vision-language model; also named as shipping a small model with Apple Intelligence, and as the platform for the local-dictation app.

data.name: Tiny language models
data.brief: The sub-billion tier, defined operationally against the small tier: roughly 50M-500M parameters, under ~2 GB of RAM (often far less), shippable natively with an application, and fast enough for real-time loops. The playbook differs from small models in kind, not degree — small models are used by zero-shot prompting, tiny models generally require either an off-the-shelf fixed-task model (ASR, vision, embeddings) or a task-specific fine-tune. Reach is the point: they run on older laptops, lower-tier web browsers, IoT boards and consumer robots that the 1-4B tier cannot touch, and they are small enough to be one tiny thing in a corner running while the rest of the system runs.

data.name: LiteRT / LiteRT-LM / MediaPipe
data.brief: Google AI Edge's open-source on-device runtime stack for deploying models to edge devices — the toolchain behind every throughput number in the talk, spanning CPU, GPU and NPU backends across phones, single-board computers and IoT modules. Carries the memory work (mixed 2/4/8-bit quantization, per-layer embeddings) and multi-token prediction. Developed first-party for Google products, then released so the wider world can build the same class of thing.

data.name: Gemma (open model family)
data.brief: Google's open model family as the on-device workhorse, with the talk's measured numbers. The ~2B E2B variant reasons on par with a much larger Gemma from ~12 months earlier; quantized to a mix of 2-, 4- and 8-bit with per-layer embeddings it reaches ~2.9 bits per weight, 841 MB of weights for a text-only model, ~2 GB active RAM once runtime and KV cache are added, hence the ~4 GB DRAM rule of thumb for shipping this grade of model on a device. Vision tokenization: a medium-resolution image is about 500 tokens, high-resolution about 1,120 tokens. Tiny variants start around 270M.

data.name: Function Gemma
data.brief: Gemma variant carrying extra pre-training on function-calling patterns, used as the fine-tuning base when the target task is free text in, structured call out. Distinguished in the talk from general-purpose Gemma at the same parameter count; the open mobile actions dataset exists so the demo can be reproduced by fine-tuning Function Gemma from scratch.

data.name: Voice-to-function-calling
data.brief: The interaction pattern the team calls the key capability for IoT and edge devices: a small ASR model in front of a fine-tuned tiny action model that maps arbitrary free-text input to one of a fixed set of device functions. Demonstrated with a mobile actions model covering ~10 output functions at over 86% reliability on arbitrary text — schedule a calendar event, turn Wi-Fi on or off — entirely on device. The motivation is interface, not novelty: small devices push their capabilities into settings menus, which are a genuine accessibility barrier, and speaking the desired outcome replaces the menu.

data.name: Synthetic-data fine-tuning playbook
data.brief: The stated recipe for getting a tiny model into production: pick a base model; check that its latency and memory footprint are inside your device budget; if no off-the-shelf fixed-task model does the job, synthetically generate training data — 10,000 to 10 million samples is the range found sufficient — and fine-tune for the single task. Result claimed across function calling, summarization and proofreading: quality equal to or better than a 2-4B general model on that one task, at a fraction of the size and latency and across a much wider device set. The open-sourced mobile actions dataset on Hugging Face is the worked example; the named remaining friction is dataset creation, with agent-generated data as the intended fix.

data.name: On-device dictation (subscription-free)
data.brief: Shipping example of the tiny-model playbook: a voice-dictation app whose entire backbone is two fine-tuned tiny Gemma models in the low hundreds of millions of parameters — an ASR engine plus a text-policing engine that cleans up ums and ahs and biases recognition toward the user's personal vocabulary and names. Everything runs locally on device, on iOS, with no subscription — displacing what had been a server-only, subscription-gated capability at very good quality.

data.name: FastVLM
data.brief: Apple's 0.5B-parameter vision-language model, shown running fast on an Android device with hardware acceleration. Cited as the exemplar of the off-the-shelf fixed-task tier — ASR, vision and embedding models that are stock features needing no fine-tuning — and as the cheapest way to add a first level of visual awareness to an edge or IoT device.

data.name: DRAM cost is the binding constraint on edge AI and it is rising
data.brief: The binding constraint on edge AI is now DRAM cost, and it is moving the wrong way: some mobile-phone manufacturers are putting less DRAM into this year's devices than last year's, and a 6 GB Raspberry Pi has risen in price by roughly 2.5x since launch.
data.description: That single constraint casts a shadow over the rest of the talk — it is why aggressive quantization and choosing the smallest model that clears the task are mandatory rather than optional. Two compounding challenges named: a much wider pool of target devices than cloud deployment ever has, and the fact that most LLM research hours go into the large end, leaving the low end of the spectrum comparatively understudied.

data.name: A 2B Gemma quantizes to 2.9 bits per weight and fits the 4GB device tier
data.brief: Measured state of the small tier from the team that ships it: the ~2B Gemma E2B reasons on par with a much larger Gemma from ~12 months earlier, and quantizes (mixed 2/4/8-bit plus per-layer embeddings) to ~2.9 bits per weight — 841 MB of weights, ~2 GB active RAM with runtime and KV cache, giving the ~4 GB DRAM device rule of thumb.
data.description: Decode throughput on Google's own runtime: ~7.6 tok/s on a Raspberry Pi (roughly 2x with multi-token prediction), ~24 tok/s on a Jetson Orin Nano (faster still on NVIDIA's own toolchain), and on a Qualcomm IoT board popular in higher-end robotics ~4,000 tok/s prefill and 31 tok/s decode on the NPU — fast enough to push about three frames per second of high-resolution image tokens (1,120 tokens per image) through a VLM while keeping decode usable.

data.name: Below 1B parameters the playbook flips from prompting to fine-tuning
data.brief: Below roughly 1B parameters the deployment playbook flips from prompting to fine-tuning, and Google's edge team reports it works at production quality: synthetically generate 10K-10M samples for one task and fine-tune a 270M-500M base (general Gemma, or Function Gemma where the task is function-call-shaped), and you get quality equal to or better than a 2-4B general model on that task — proven on function calling, summarization and proofreading — while reaching a far wider device set and running far more responsively.
data.description: The mechanism is memory bandwidth: on the same Raspberry Pi, decode goes from mid-single-digit to ~45 tok/s because there is less to read from memory each step.

data.name: Voice-to-function-calling hits 86% reliability on a fine-tuned tiny model
data.brief: Voice-to-function-calling is now robust on tiny models: a fine-tuned mobile actions model does text in / function call out, knows about 10 output functions, and calls them at over 86% reliability from arbitrary free text (schedule a calendar event, toggle Wi-Fi), with an ASR model chained in front to make it voice-driven — all on device.
data.description: Framed as a key capability rather than a demo because small devices bury their functionality in settings menus that are genuinely hard for many people to navigate. The corresponding mobile actions dataset is open-sourced on Hugging Face so the result is reproducible, and generalizing the pattern — ideally with an agent generating the synthetic data — is named as the team's next goal.

data.name: Tiny on-device models displace subscription-gated server features
data.brief: Tiny models are taking capabilities back off the server: a shipped iOS voice-dictation app runs entirely locally on two fine-tuned tiny Gemma models in the low hundreds of millions of parameters — an ASR engine plus a text-policing engine that strips ums and ahs and biases toward the user's own vocabulary and names — delivering what used to be a server-only, subscription-gated feature at very good quality with no subscription.
data.description: Same mechanism inside the browser: Chrome's developer-preview built-in summarization and proofreading APIs are delivered by tiny models, which is what lets the Chrome team ship them to a far wider set of users than a server-backed implementation could reach.

data.name: Cheap boards still miss real-time interaction requirements for robots
data.brief: Honest capability gap from the platform team, measured on hardware: a DeepMind engineer's hobby build put the same open-source OpenDog Mini v2 robot stack on two boards — the Jetson-based robot achieves genuinely real-time interaction (reads signs, reacts, nods, takes both voice and image input) while the Raspberry Pi one works but is a lot slower.
data.description: Verdict: for some interaction types even today's best small models do not meet user-interaction requirements on the cheap device class. Named open frontiers: faster vision models covering a wider set of tasks such as segmentation.

data.name: Edge engineering asks for the smallest model that clears the task
data.brief: Edge engineering inverts the frontier question. You do not ask what the best model can do; you ask what the smallest model that clears this specific task is, because DRAM is the budget and weights, KV cache, runtime, render headroom and the operating system are all charged against it — and DRAM is getting more expensive, not less.
data.description: The corollary that decides most real designs: the model is usually not the product. It is one tiny thing in a corner that needs to run while everything else in the system is running, so system health caps the footprint long before quality does.

data.name: A fine-tune on synthetic data buys an entire device class
data.brief: For a single task, a synthetic dataset plus a fine-tune does not buy a few points of accuracy — it buys an entire device class. A 270M-500M model fine-tuned on 10K-10M synthetic samples matches or beats a 2-4B general model on that task while reaching older laptops, low-tier browsers, IoT boards and consumer robots that the small tier cannot run on at all, and while being several times more responsive because there is less to read from memory per step.
data.description: The remaining friction is the dataset, not the model — which is why having an agent generate the synthetic data for you is the stated route to making this playbook available to far more people.

data.name: Size the model to the device before anything else
guidelines: Start from the four reasons to be on-device at all — latency (fast and consistent), privacy (data stays on the device), offline availability (the feature still works with no reception), and cost (cheap tokens multiplied by app-scale user interaction adds up quickly). Then budget memory first: ~4 GB+ DRAM for a 1-4B model (a 2B quantized to ~2.9 bits/weight is ~841 MB of weights and ~2 GB active once runtime and KV cache are counted), under ~2 GB for the tiny tier, and remember the OS and the rest of the app are charged against the same budget. Use mixed-precision quantization (2/4/8-bit per layer) and per-layer embeddings rather than uniform quantization. Check whether an NPU path exists for your target — an NPU took an IoT board to ~4,000 tok/s prefill — and turn on multi-token prediction where supported (~2x decode). For fixed tasks (ASR, vision, embeddings) take an off-the-shelf model before fine-tuning anything. Try candidates on the real hardware early: the AI Edge Gallery app on iOS and Android runs these models on your own phone and is fully open source, including the runtime

data.name: Fine-tune one tiny model per task
guidelines: Confirm first that no off-the-shelf fixed-task model (ASR, vision, embeddings) already does the job — that tier is stock and works well. Otherwise: pick a base model in the 270M-500M range, choose Function Gemma over a general model when the task is free-text-in / structured-call-out, and verify latency and memory footprint on target hardware before investing. Synthesize the training data — 10,000 to 10 million samples is the range that reliably works — and fine-tune for the single task
expect single-task quality at or above a 2-4B general model with much wider device reach and several times the responsiveness. Chain a small ASR model in front when the interface should be voice

that combination is what makes voice-to-function-calling work on device. Reuse or publish datasets rather than regenerating them (mobile actions is on Hugging Face as a complete worked example), and treat agent-generated synthetic data as the way to scale this beyond specialist teams

data.name: Forward Deployed Engineering 101 (Kevin Bai, Anthropic — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Kevin Bai
Palantir
data.brief: Load-bearing subject of the forward-deployed-engineering track rather than a passing reference: Foundry, the FDE origin story and the average-contract-value numbers. Founded around 2004-05 per the talk; the origin institution of the FDE discipline.

data.name: Palantir Foundry
data.brief: App-building data platform: centralizes an organization of arbitrary size's data in one place and builds an "ontology" — proper nouns out of data, so instead of table one/two/three there is a single source-of-truth warehouses table — then lets the company build applications on top. Because value is gated on the customer's ability to build with it (a licence cost plus a training tax), Foundry is sold with engineers attached rather than as software alone.

data.name: Outcome as the product
data.brief: Selling products and services as one combined thing: the customer buys neither a software licence nor someone's time, they buy a business outcome (shelf placement, sales throughput). Industry buyers do not care how the data is organized — "that's an implementation detail" — so the vendor absorbs the implementation and is paid for the result.

data.name: Shared-primitive platform (the FDE precondition)
data.brief: The line between an FDE function and a dev shop: FDEs assemble solutions from a shared set of platform primitives and never write software from scratch. Without it, per-customer bespoke code compounds into unmaintainable sprawl ("55 repos"), maintenance costs "eat your P&L alive", and the engineers quit. Primitive granularity is a function of customer breadth — some platforms ship apps 60% built with 40% customized, others (AWS/DynamoDB) offer extremely granular primitives to serve a broad swath.

data.name: FDE answers one quadrant: a technical product sold to a non-technical buyer
data.brief: Anthropic applied-AI engineer (ex-Palantir, ex-Rippling) gives the track's definitional framing: FDE is not a general upgrade to go-to-market, it is the answer to one quadrant of {how technical is what you sell} x {how technical is who buys it}.
data.description: Technical product + technical buyer (GitHub, Datadog) leads to DevRel/developer engagement; simple-or-configurable product + non-technical buyer (Rippling, Jira, Slack) leads to sales-led SaaS; only a technical product sold to a non-technical buyer (Foundry into a Fortune 500 oil-and-gas company whose "pipelines are not data pipelines") needs FDE.

data.name: Palantir tops public SaaS average contract value at ~$4M, more than 3x the next vendor
data.brief: Numbers offered as evidence the motion works: among public SaaS companies in the Fortune 500 ranked by average contract value, Palantir is first at ~$4M ACV, ServiceNow next at ~$1.2M, Workday ~$600K, and no other public SaaS company cracks half a million — reached at only a few thousand headcount.

data.name: FDE is design partnership at enterprise scale, built on shared platform primitives
data.brief: FDE defined as the early-startup design partnership ("give me your context, I'll build you a really good solution" — how most B2B startups find PMF) scaled up into the enterprise, with one non-negotiable condition: if each FDE builds from scratch you do not have an FDE function, you have a dev shop. The differentiator is building on top of a platform of shared primitives.

data.name: Every platform is now agentic and therefore customizable, so nearly every vendor needs FDE
data.brief: The 2026 thesis, stated as personal hypothesis: what changed since Palantir's 2004-era motion is not that the industry recognized it was a good idea — it is that nearly every platform is now agentic, therefore nearly every platform is customizable, therefore nearly every vendor now has customers who "have no idea what the heck it is that you actually do". Leaving success to the customer's ability to implement makes up-market, horizontal and vertical expansion fail.

data.name: Customers buy an outcome; the software is an implementation detail
data.brief: Selling only technology fails at the last mile: you have organized the buyer's data, but the buyer asks "what does that do for my actual business?" Selling only services is a dev shop.
data.description: The working configuration is both at once — smart engineers who learn the customer's business and assemble a solution on the vendor's platform — so what changes hands is an outcome, with the software as implementation detail. The fine-dining analogy: the waiter caters to your every need and figures out the problem for you.

data.name: Ask whether you need an FDE function, not whether you want one
data.brief: The advice Bai gives everyone considering FDE: ask whether you need one, not whether you want one — it is easy to want what is in vogue. Two qualifying questions: do you have to sell something technically complicated to a non-technical buyer, and do you have (or will you invest in) a platform of shared primitives for FDEs to build on?
data.description: A "no" to either means DevRel or a sales-led motion instead; a "yes" to the first and "no" to the second guarantees a maintenance burden that outruns the revenue.

data.name: Qualify (and platform-back) an FDE function before you build one
guidelines: Need, not want: only build FDE if you must GTM a technically complicated product to a non-technical buyer — otherwise run DevRel (technical buyer) or sales-led SaaS (simple product). Second gate: have a platform, or commit to building one

FDEs must assemble from shared primitives, never write from scratch. Set primitive granularity by customer breadth — some domains tolerate apps that ship 60% built with 40% customization, others need extremely granular configuration and tooling (AWS is the reference point). Keep anything bespoke to a single customer with that customer
generalize anything generalizable over time. Expect thin primitives at the start — that is fine, FDE also scouts which products to build next

data.name: Staff FDEs as customer-facing software engineers
guidelines: The whole profile in one line: "an FDE is nothing more than a customer-facing software engineer" — someone you would hire as a software engineer on your team and trust in front of a customer

the rest is figured out as you go. Do not run one FDE per account: multiple FDEs on a project is an encouraged pattern because bespoke customer work otherwise creates a single point of failure (one person holds all the context, goes on vacation, you are stuck). Cross-company FDE collaboration works like any contractor relationship — establish who the contractor is

data.name: How Forward Deployed Engineering is done at Factory (Eno Reyes — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Eno Reyes
Factory
data.brief: Builds autonomous software-engineering agents for enterprise teams; product is Droid (a model-independent agent harness) plus workflows, observability, cost controls and enterprise governance. The deployed-engineer role is publicly titled "engineer, deployed".

data.name: Software factory
data.brief: The implicit signal-to-deploy loop every organization already sits on top of, made explicit and instrumented: signals flow in (customer conversations, bug reports, internal Slack/Teams, an executive mandate — with different weights), humans triage/prioritize/plan, plans become changes to a source of truth (codebase, engineering system), changes pass a validation stage (code review, QA, security assessment, SAST, linters, type checkers), then ship — and deployed software emits new signals. Transforming each stage with AI yields a flow from signal to deploy uninterrupted by a human; humans still engineer, evolve and scale the system, they just stop manipulating the software directly. "Built, not bought" — it requires organizational investment, not a purchase.

data.name: Droid
data.brief: Factory's agent harness, sold as the canonical model-independent building block for a software factory: the customer owns every trace and every piece of data flowing through it, with centralized governance and control at the enterprise layer dictating what information goes where. Air-gappable — finance, healthcare and government partners run entirely contained software factories ("you could run Droid in a submarine"). Ships with workflows, observability, cost controls, auto model routing and SDLC-stage products (code review, incident response, QA, testing — each argued to be a billion-dollar business).

data.name: Agent readiness
data.brief: A property of a codebase measured by how many deterministic validation loops it contains — linters, type checkers, security scans, end-to-end tests: things that pass or fail with no judgment. Density of these loops sets how long agents can run on how complex a task without human intervention; the quality of a long-running harness's output is directly proportional to how far its work can be validated. Explicitly analogized to post-training: models need dense reward, and these verification signals are that reward over long-horizon goal-directed work. Consequence for deployments: the investment is "less solving the problem, more preparing the environment for verification of the problem".

data.name: Missions
data.brief: Factory's long-running harness for hard, validatable knowledge work: an extremely bounded task with an explicit definition of "complete", after which inference is pushed like a lever until the task is done, with human involvement only at the planning stage. Presented as the end-game of the agent era (pre-software-factory): if a problem can be framed as the set of verification systems that must validate it, it is solvable with AI today. Cited runs: fully autonomous migrations of 30-50M+ line codebases, deep-learning work in biomed/healthcare, equity-research modelling at financial institutions.

data.name: Autonomy ratio
data.brief: Factory's internal autonomy instrumentation: the ratio of actions taken by AI systems to actions taken by humans before an interruption. Factory reports ~15-20% "autonomy" with an autonomy ratio in the upper 80s for its own codebase; some customer codebases score higher because they operate under more constrained conditions; its internal legal-workflow droid is ~100% autonomously maintained while its own terminal harness is not — visual defects like flickering have no verifier. The 15-20% vs upper-80% figures are as-spoken and internally ambiguous.

data.name: Frontier labs are building massive FDE teams, a practice pioneered by Palantir
data.brief: Track-intro framing (MC, unnamed): forward deployed engineering is "one of the hottest topics in AI" and "the most important companies on the planet are building out massive FDE teams — think OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind"; the practice was pioneered by Palantir years ago to embed strong engineers directly in customer orgs and customize the platform around the nuances of the real world. An entire conference track now exists for it, with speakers from Anthropic, Cursor, Factory, Ramp, Decagon "and many more".

data.name: Factory refuses professional services: deployed engineers are the tip of the product spear
data.brief: Factory's positional claim: it explicitly refuses professional-services work — asked to run a codebase modernization the customer has already price-quoted from consulting firms, the answer is no, even when the work would use Factory's own product, because it does not make the product better and "is not the way you scale a business out enormously".
data.description: Deployed engineers are instead "the tip of the spear of the product": the information stream from the largest, most critical customers' engineering leadership and on-the-ground engineers, flowing back to rapidly adjust the product to fit the customer's environment. The product must then self-assemble — at 45,000 people, hundreds of thousands of engineers and tens of thousands of codebases, manual installation is not available.

data.name: Agent readiness — the density of deterministic validation loops — gates how far agents run
data.brief: The gating claim of the talk: "if your codebase isn't agent ready you won't see any of the success of the most capable AI systems in the world today". Agent readiness = density of deterministic validation loops; introduce validation at scale and you introduce autonomy at scale, because long-running-harness output quality is directly proportional to validatability. Framed with the post-training parallel — dense reward keeps models on track over long-horizon goals, and these verification signals are that reward.

data.name: A software factory is built, not bought, and must be model-independent
data.brief: Enterprise requirements Factory reports from the field: a software factory built on a vendor-locked, single-model solution is both expensive and strategically exposed ("what is the role of the model provider in dictating what you can or cannot build with your software factory?"), and not owning the traces and data flowing through it blocks later evolution. Hence model independence, full data access, centralized enterprise governance, and air-gapped operation for finance/healthcare/gov partners. And the factory itself is "built, not bought" — an organizational investment, not a purchase.

data.name: Engineers move from manipulating software to managing the system that builds it
data.brief: Role-shift claim: engineers go from directly manipulating software to maintaining and managing the system that builds software, and that jump in abstraction level is "actually very difficult" — most people, even very thoughtful software engineers, face a real learning curve.
data.description: Best-suited profiles are DevEx people already thinking about enabling other developers, product managers willing to become very technical very fast, and anyone from a team where high-quality dev environments were a priority. Blocker observed across customers: "most organizations do not have an autonomy maturity model" — no roadmap, no conception of what an autonomous software organization means.

data.name: Autonomy is unevenly distributed per codebase, and verification is the binding blocker
data.brief: Field observation with numbers: "the future is here, it's just not evenly distributed" — at the level of individual codebases, not companies. Factory's own codebase is fairly agent-ready with an autonomy ratio in the upper 80s; some customer codebases are more autonomous because they operate under tighter constraints; the most likely first 100%-autonomy targets are contained internal tools (Factory's legal droid is ~100% autonomously maintained).
data.description: The blocker on its own core harness is verification, not capability: flickering and other hard visual problems of a terminal-based harness have no validator, so the loop cannot close — building that verifier is itself an engineering task, and human visual/context advantages are what supply the remaining work.

data.name: Verification supply, not model capability, throttles autonomous work
data.brief: Autonomy is not bought from a model vendor, it is unlocked by verification supply: the amount of autonomous work an organization can absorb equals the amount of work it can automatically validate. This reframes an AI deployment as an environment-preparation project — build the deterministic loops first, and capability you already have becomes usable.
data.description: It also explains the uneven frontier: constrained internal tooling hits full autonomy before core products do, because verifiability, not difficulty, is the binding constraint.

data.name: Calibrate reference implementations so customers copy them rather than dismiss them
data.brief: Deployment change-management heuristic, via Walt Disney's Epcot — conceived as a master-planned exemplary city, landed as a theme park, yet real cities still copied its transit ideas. A reference implementation has to be advanced enough that people say "let's bring that to my part of the codebase", but not so advanced that they say "that's a theme park, that has nothing to do with how we work".
data.description: Building two or three exemplars at that calibration and letting the customer's own team scale them out is the transformation mechanism; overshooting triggers cost-of-change panic instead of adoption.

data.name: Prepare the environment for verification before scaling agents
guidelines: Scan the codebase for deterministic validation loops (linters, type checkers, security scans, end-to-end tests) and treat their density as the readiness score. About 30-40% is low-hanging fruit an agent fixes on request

the other 60% needs workflow change — humans are not used to the nitpickiness of automated systems, so introduce stricter validation without interrupting their dev flow and address their concerns explicitly. Frame every candidate task as "what set of verification systems must validate this?" — if you can frame it, you can solve it today. Where no verifier exists (hard visual problems, terminal flicker), building the verifier is the engineering task, not a reason to hand the work back to humans

data.name: Run deployed engineering as the tip of the spear, not a services arm
guidelines: Refuse professional-services engagements even when profitable — they do not improve the product and do not scale. Require an outcome/ROI story from the beginning that chains to core business goals (every change getting AI review, QA and security analysis is ~87% less likely to hit a bug, so bug rate down X, customer satisfaction up Y, revenue/growth), which needs both engineering and business knowledge. Make the product self-assemble into the customer environment

manual install does not survive enterprise scale. Teach the model: hand the customer an autonomy roadmap they do not have, prove it in a couple of places, then let their team scale it. Route everything learned in the field back into the product surface — enterprise controls, harness quality, workflows, observability, cost controls, model routing are all improvement opportunities discovered in diverse orgs. Hire former founders, fluent technical communicators with executive presence, and systems thinkers who like closing loops

data.name: How Forward Deployed Engineering is done at Cognition (Jia Wu — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Jia Wu
Devin
data.brief: Cognition's autonomous software-engineering agent. Debuted 2024 at ~13% on SWE-bench — "we're so back / we're so cooked" — then widely dismissed within a week as something you'd use only if desperate and out of ideas; Cognition ran with the joke in its SF ad campaign ("we're actually good now"). Today's surface area spans Devin Cloud (the cloud agent it is known for) plus a CLI and an IDE, the latter inherited from the Windsurf side. Positioned against "single-point tools that are just CLIs or just IDEs" on the claim that only an agent harness can lift a whole organization rather than individual engineers.

data.name: Token maxing
data.brief: Deploying agents with no specific direction so that consumption becomes the de-facto KPI. Described as the first era of deployed engineering (~1.5-2 years ago) when budgets were subsidized, nobody worried about spend, and maximizing token usage was the target; now an anti-pattern — "you're wasting tokens, burning spend, not getting any tangible outcomes" — as large regulated enterprises ask whether they are getting value or just burning tokens. Shared vocabulary across this FDE set: Ramp's failure mode for an unscoped agent pipeline is "a token maxing slop cannon".

data.name: Session-derived engineering hours
data.brief: Cognition's ROI instrumentation: one agent trace/trajectory is a "session", and metrics derive from sessions how many engineering hours were generated and how many were productive. Rolled up into three customer-facing deltas measured before vs after deploying the agent — headcount equivalent, delivery-timeline compression, and raw merged-PR counts — as the counter to the objection that session counts are just token maxing with extra steps.

data.name: Cognition shipped nearly an order of magnitude more PRs in six months using its own agent
data.brief: Cognition dogfooding number: over the last six months, "for better or worse we might have been behind on hiring", the org shipped almost an order of magnitude more good-quality robust PRs by deploying its own agent — described as a step-function increase in engineering leverage rather than an incremental one. Enterprise-side consumption of the agent described as parabolic growth in adoption and use cases.

data.name: Coding is mostly solved; testing, review, deploy and maintenance are the remaining 80%
data.brief: Cognition's problem framing: coding itself is "a mostly solved problem" — models are good enough that with enough context engineering you get the code blocks you care about — and writing code faster is only ~20% of the problem. The remaining 80% is testing, reviewing, deploying and maintaining code across the enterprise, on real legacy rather than zero-to-one prompting, in languages nobody learns anymore (COBOL, JCL).

data.name: Deployed engineering's KPI shifted from token maxing to measured ROI
data.brief: The KPI shift in deployed engineering, dated by a practitioner: a year and a half to two years ago the target was maximizing token usage — budgets were subsidized, "you could just run anything you wanted"; now the largest and most regulated enterprises ask whether they are getting true value or burning tokens, and the problem "has really shifted into the delivery space". ROI measurement for agents is stated outright as an unsolved problem — "the company that will solve this will be a $5 trillion market cap".

data.name: The unlock is making an organization 10x faster, not individual engineers
data.brief: Stated core differentiator: making individual engineers 10x faster is fine and still valuable, but the unlock is making an organization 10x faster — "including every single person that might be technical or non-technical across the company". Single-point tools that are just CLIs or just IDEs are argued to structurally fail at this, which is why the deployment is sold as a partnership rather than a seat.

data.name: Cognition reports +150% headcount equivalent and ~82% delivery-timeline reduction
data.brief: Deployment proof points offered on stage (anonymized case studies plus public ones): a 3-month embed delivering the equivalent of "+150% headcount"; ~82% reduction in delivery timelines measured on the customer's own pre/post agile metrics; roughly double the PR throughput versus single-point tools before an agent harness.
data.description: Also cited: Nubank's ETL migration, staffed with 50 engineers, delivered in about a third of the timeline autonomously; a large Latin American bank's tax-identification-system migration at half the required effort; and a public customer reporting ~10x weekly engineering output ("10x per week worth of engineering talent").

data.name: The deployed-engineering org is the vendor's highest-fidelity evaluation set
data.brief: The deployed-engineering org is the vendor's best evaluation set: "we have the highest fidelity evaluation set that comes back from our customers — we are in the field every single day". Solving the customer's problem completely is only half the equation; the other half is carrying that context back so the product moves toward the customers' problems, maximizing the overlap of the two circles (what we build x what they need).
data.description: Enterprise engineering challenges arrive "in similar shapes", so the field job is classification — is this challenge common across the enterprise or unique to this user, and should this workaround, hack or bug become a feature? — and the payoff is a de-risked roadmap where you know what to build for which revenue. The feedback is "half of the loop that makes the next deployment better than the previous deployment".

data.name: Hire deployed engineers as T-shaped generalists with genuine spikes
data.brief: The FDE persona is deliberately undefined by title — "are you a sales engineer? are you a solutions architect? what are you?" — and hired as a T with genuine spikes: wide across people, business, process, customer and technology skill, deep in at least one.
data.description: Cognition hires from product management (because if the cost of software engineering goes to zero, knowing how to design a product that makes sense is the scarce skill — "you can just prompt it"), from founders, and from spiky engineers: weak business sense can be taught, being the technical expert in the room while on the job cannot. Good deployed engineers do all of it; great ones add relentless curiosity about why this problem matters to the business, and relentless tie-in to the customer.

data.name: Map agent capabilities onto named customer problems, then measure
guidelines: Never deploy agents into a complex SDLC with no specific direction — that is token maxing. Split the day roughly 50/50 between customer calls and hands-on-keyboard work

use the calls to learn which strategic initiatives are highest-leverage for the business. Aim the agent at the specific inventory every enterprise has: the backlog nobody gets to, remediations, delayed code that never ships, tests nobody writes, alert triage. Then automate yourself out of the loop — set the agent up to fire on specific alerts and events rather than being manually triggered. Instrument from day one: sessions to engineering hours to productive hours, plus timeline and PR deltas against a pre-deployment baseline, because ROI measurement is the open problem and the customer will ask

data.name: Treat the field as the eval set and close the loop into the roadmap
guidelines: Take the highest-fidelity signal you have — daily customer contact — and route it back to product deliberately, not incidentally. For each challenge, ask whether it is common across the enterprise or unique to one user, and whether a workaround, hack or bug should become a feature. Always ask why the problem matters to the business as a whole and whether it can be communicated back in a way that improves things for every other customer

the goal is a de-risked roadmap. Flag engineering practices that need fixing with no ego attached — "we are all in the same boat". Treat every role as go-to-market: the target is customer success at all costs, and everybody owns it

data.name: How Forward Deployed Engineering is done at Ramp (Leo Mehr — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Leo Mehr
Always be scoping
data.brief: Ramp's first FDE principle, against the belief that an FDE's job is to say yes to the customer: you want to find a way to say yes, but you have to deliver good software and build the right thing. Practically it is a context-gathering interrogation before any build — what is actually driving the urgency (an end-of-quarter sales rep chasing quota is not the customer), who will use this, have all workarounds been exhausted, is there a manual stopgap, does the customer have technical resources to hit the API instead — and, most important, does anyone else in the pipeline or customer base benefit. Validate even the most basic assumptions ("horses with rockets strapped to their legs" is what saying yes without scoping builds).

data.name: Scale with tokens
data.brief: Ramp's second FDE principle: unless you are scaling with model capabilities you fall behind, so jobs must be reinvented continuously — whatever knowledge work you do today, figure out how models and agents do it for you. Applied to FDE it means taking the whole lifecycle (gather context, scope the request, write the spec, implement the feature) and replacing each stage with agents. Daunting whole, tractable in pieces: the first stage and the last stage are largely solved (intake agents; frontier models one-shot medium-size features), the middle is "gnarly, unformed and difficult" and is where the investment goes.

data.name: FDE request intake agent
data.brief: Ramp's internal agent on the #fde-requests channel, where account managers, solutions and sales reps post any prospect/customer blocker large enough to escalate; the underlying Notion workflow holds the detail. The problem it attacks is variance — some submitters write a thorough customer-sourced request, others write one line ("we need this SAP integration") — which previously forced FDEs to read, interpret, check what already exists in the product, and run manual back-and-forth. The V1, built with Notion agents, only read the request and asked a couple of questions; the current version runs several rounds of questioning with the submitter until it judges the request ready to become a spec (with a penguin persona to make it approachable). Results reported after a couple of weeks: reply latency from hours or days down to seconds, reps engaging with the agent directly, and roughly 20% of scoping time saved.

data.name: At Ramp, FDE lives inside the engineering organization, not in go-to-market
data.brief: Counter-framing from a non-vendor FDE org: the meme that FDE is "the final evolution / boss mode of technical go-to-market roles" is called "totally wrong" for Ramp. FDE there lives inside the engineering organization, its goal is to help Ramp win up-market, and the work is the core product plus new agentic features made to work well for the largest enterprise customers. Growth trajectory: 2 engineers ~2.5 years ago to ~30 engineers today across forward deployed, developer API and a new AI-services business. Opening admission: "no one knows what FDE is" — a running theme of the track.

data.name: Two Ramp field stories show scoping discipline beats saying yes
data.brief: Two field stories as the evidence for scoping discipline. (1) Friday night, an enterprise sales rep says a strategic logo only closes if Ramp builds an SAP S/4HANA integration; the default engineering reflex is to go find the SAP API docs, the trained FDE reflex is to ask what is driving the urgency — often the rep's end-of-quarter quota rather than the customer.
data.description: (2) The painful one: a large enterprise needed a mobile reimbursement feature, the mobile team was swamped, two FDEs taught themselves iOS and Android and shipped both in a couple of weeks — then the customer revealed it mandates iOS devices for all employees. The Android half was wasted because the most basic assumption went unvalidated.

data.name: Ramp is agentifying its own FDE lifecycle stage by stage
data.brief: An FDE org agentifying its own job function, stage by stage. Shipped: the request-intake agent (hours/days to seconds, ~20% of scoping time saved, reps now talk to it directly). Already easy: spec to working software, because frontier models one-shot medium-size features. The remaining middle of the pipeline is "super gnarly and unformed" and is where the team is investing.
