data.description: Mehr's 6-12-month projection of what FDE at Ramp is: applied-AI problems — keeping the agent harness running each stage smooth, keeping per-stage output quality good with evals, rubrics and human feedback, and the biggest challenge, getting the agent the right context (a product manager's head-knowledge; Notion docs, knowledge base and help articles only go so far; skills, memories, tools).

data.name: Without scoping discipline the agent factory becomes a token maxing slop cannon
data.brief: The talk's closing claim, stated as a two-way failure mode: build the agent factory without scoping discipline and you get "a token maxing slop cannon"; keep the scoping discipline without investing in the factory and "your agent-native competitors are just going to overtake you and outcompete" — "it's going to be over for you". Both principles are required, and the throughline that survives the automation is that the FDE still owns taste and judgment over the final output.

data.name: Scoping discipline and the agent factory multiply rather than add
data.brief: The two principles are a product, not a sum: scoping without an agent factory loses to agent-native competitors on speed; an agent factory without scoping industrializes building the wrong thing. Automating an unexamined intake pipeline does not produce leverage, it produces volume — the same failure the iOS/Android story produced by hand, at machine scale. Which is why Ramp put its first agent on the scoping stage rather than the implementation stage.

data.name: Taste and judgment over the output are what survive the job's own automation
data.brief: When every stage of your own job — context gathering, scoping, spec writing, implementation — is being handed to agents, what remains is responsibility for taste and judgment over the final output; that is the throughline of the role, and the reason the job description survives its own automation. The corollary is that the FDE's future work is applied-AI work: harness smoothness, per-stage output quality via evals/rubrics/human feedback, and the context-supply problem of getting a product manager's head-knowledge into an agent.

data.name: Interrogate an inbound customer request before building anything
guidelines: Do not treat "yes" as the job. Before touching the integration docs, ask: what is actually driving the urgency, and is it the customer or the rep's quarter? Who will use this? Have we exhausted the workarounds? Is there something manual we can do in the meantime? Does the customer have technical resources — can they hit our API so we don't build this at all? Then look past the request: which other prospects in the pipeline and existing customers benefit, so what you build is generalizable rather than bespoke. Validate the basics explicitly — platform, user list, mandated devices — before committing engineering weeks
the assumption you never thought to check is the one that wastes the sprint

data.name: Replace your own job stage by stage with agents
guidelines: Break the lifecycle into stages (gather context, scope, spec, implement) and attack them one at a time

whole-pipeline replacement looks daunting and is tractable in pieces. Start where variance and latency are worst — request intake — and ship a trivial V1 (read the request, ask a couple of questions) rather than the full design

the latency drop alone changes behaviour, and submitters start engaging with the agent directly. Iterate to multi-round questioning until the agent can judge a request spec-ready. Measure it (reply latency, share of scoping time saved). Expect the last stage to be nearly free (frontier models one-shot medium features) and budget your effort for the gnarly middle. Wrap each stage with evals, rubrics and human feedback for output quality, and treat context supply — the product knowledge in a PM's head that Notion docs and help articles don't capture — as the hard problem, addressed with skills, memories and tools. Keep taste and judgment over the final output as a human responsibility

data.name: The Dirty Secret of Forward Deployed Engineering (Natalie Meurer, Sierra — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Natalie Meurer
FDE vintage
data.brief: Meurer's taxonomy of forward deployed engineering as five cumulative eras rather than a single job: 2008 platform stability / DevOps ("hints of panic" — the onboarding project was deploying the software on an EC2 instance; the 2 a.m. "someone unplugged the instance again" email), 2012 data integration (integrating a customer's data out of 20 places and modelling it into Palantir's ontology — "data integration software without integrated data is a movie theatre playing nothing"), 2016 custom solutions (Slate dashboards mapping page components to data sources), 2020 customer enablement (platform era: training thousands of customer engineers to do FDE work themselves), 2024+ all of the above plus agent building. Jobs-to-be-done accumulated over time instead of rotating out, which is why the title now means everything and nothing; proposed as an interview question — "what vintage of FDE are you?"

data.name: Outcome-based pricing
data.brief: Pricing software for the value it delivers rather than for seats or tokens, positioned on a 2x2 of outcome attributability x agency/autonomy to achieve the outcome: seat-based when the outcome is barely attributable to the product (how software has been priced for decades), usage-based when autonomy exists but attribution is weak (what buyers pay OpenAI/Anthropic), outcome-based when the agent has both agency and an attributable result (was the inquiry resolved, was the sale made). Sierra's model since founding; claim is that most pricing in this market converges here — and that pricing outcomes structurally requires someone accountable for guaranteeing them.

data.name: Agent engineering
data.brief: Meurer's July-2024 coinage: a subdiscipline of AI engineering carrying FDE-grade customer accountability but constituted as its own domain (she joined Sierra's "deployment team" and disliked the name). Her 2026 revision: agent engineering was not a peer discipline but a flavour of forward deployed engineering, heavily focused on outcomes — and harness engineering has since appeared as a further subdiscipline underneath it.

data.name: Forward deployed engineering has lost its referent while being the hottest job in AI
data.brief: The talk's titular claim, from someone who has hired for the role for 2.5 years: forward deployed engineering "doesn't exist" — the term is asked to describe DevOps, data integration, custom solutioning, enablement, agent building and product engineering at once, so it means nothing while simultaneously being "the hottest job in AI".
data.description: Evidence offered: Palantir's 2016 postings led with location (on-prem deployments meant literally sitting with the customer), while a 2026 composite of current FDE postings reads "staff engineer for eight years + six years direct sales experience + four years as a solution architect (teaching experience helps)". The single continuity across every vintage is accountability to the customer.

data.name: Google and OpenAI stand up FDE units at hyperscaler and frontier-lab scale
data.brief: Dated market build-out: Google announced a GCP effort to hire customer engineers / FDEs, OpenAI created a new unit with a massive investment to aid its corporate AI push, and operators including Aaron Levie are amplifying the function's importance publicly — i.e. the embedded-delivery function is now being staffed at hyperscaler and frontier-lab scale, not just by application startups. Corroborates the batch-5 Cursor signal from the demand side.

data.name: Cheap code makes FDE and product engineering converge and stack rather than narrow
data.brief: What cheap code does to the function: FDEs used to translate customer signal back into the product (stability, data integration); now they can build end-to-end solutions with coding agents themselves, and simultaneously — observed at Sierra — product engineering is becoming client-facing. The role is not narrowing but converging and stacking: product, infra and agent engineers are absorbing DevOps and deployment concerns while FDEs absorb product development.

data.name: Software pricing moves from seats through usage to outcomes, and outcomes need a guarantor
data.brief: Pricing-model claim, sourced to Emergence Capital's framework plus a post by Sierra's head of go-to-market ops (Elliot Greenwald): as code becomes cheap, the way software is sold changes — seat-based (weak outcome attribution) to usage-based (foundation-model APIs, where autonomy is high but attribution is weak) to outcome-based (customer-experience AI: was the inquiry resolved, was the sale made).
data.description: Prediction: most pricing in this market moves to outcome-based. The load-bearing consequence for this cluster: if you sell the outcome, you need a function accountable for guaranteeing it — "and that really is forward deployed engineering".

data.name: Every adjacent engineering discipline is converging on forward deployed engineering
data.brief: Her closing thesis: product engineering, agent engineering, AI engineering, solutions engineering and customer engineering are all trending toward forward deployed engineering, because enablement, DevOps, solution building, data integration and shipping an agent into production are all ultimately performed on behalf of a customer and should be priced against the outcome they produce. The discipline's incoherent definition is therefore not a problem to fix but the sign of a merge — "forward deployed engineering is dead; long live forward deployed engineering".

data.name: Asking which vintage of FDE someone is resolves a title that otherwise conveys nothing
data.brief: Because the role's jobs-to-be-done accumulated rather than rotated, "what vintage of FDE are you?" resolves a title that otherwise conveys nothing — a 2008-vintage FDE (platform stability) and a 2024-vintage FDE (agent building against customer outcomes) share only customer accountability. The same accumulation explains the Palantir alumni founder pipeline: the role is generalist training across every layer of delivering software to a customer, which is exactly the profile the market now bids for.

data.name: Hire and scope against a vintage, not a title
guidelines: Never accept "forward deployed engineer" as a specification — decide which vintage the work actually is: platform stability/DevOps (2008), data integration and data modelling into your ontology (2012), custom solutioning on top of integrated data (2016), customer enablement so thousands of their engineers do the work (2020), or end-to-end agent building against a contracted outcome (2024+). Ask the candidate which vintage they are and check it against the vintage you need

expect the eras to be additive rather than exclusive, so a real posting stacks skills instead of trading them. Treat the composite mega-posting (staff engineer + direct sales + solution architect + teaching) as a symptom of skipping this step

data.name: Place the product on the attribution x autonomy grid before choosing a pricing model
guidelines: Score two axes: how attributable the outcome is to your product, and how much agency/autonomy your product has to achieve it. Weak attribution means seat-based (the historical default). High autonomy with weak attribution means usage-based (the foundation-model API shape). High on both — a resolved support inquiry, a completed sale — means outcome-based, which is where agentic products belong and where the market is heading. Two consequences to plan for: outcome pricing is not always available, so be honest about which quadrant you are in
and once you price the outcome you must staff a function accountable for guaranteeing it, which is the structural reason vendors are building FDE orgs at all

data.name: How Forward Deployed Engineering is done at Decagon (Sunny Rekhi — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Sunny Rekhi
Decagon agent
data.brief: 24/7 AI customer-service agent replacing IVR trees and multi-day email queues with human-like phone and email response; multilingual and omni-channel (phone, email, text, WhatsApp). Deployment shape: land on the complex inbound support workflows that today must go to humans, then expand into revenue-generating outbound once the back-end integrations exist (stated example: Hertz, where the same integrations now drive proactive lease renewal/extension outreach). Design constraint that governs the whole FDE motion: the agent is configured in natural language and owned by the customer, so it must never become "a black box of prompts and patches" — brittle for the vendor and worse for the customer.

data.name: FDE role specialization (agent builder / agent software engineer)
data.brief: The org split that hypergrowth forced: the original generalist "agent software engineer" — who configured the agent brain beside the customer, built back-end integrations and upstreamed platform work — divides into two lanes. Agent builders are product experts with intuition for the models underneath, working in the UI wherever possible and flagging what must go off-UI; agent software engineers are the front line for customer product asks, responsible for getting them into the platform. Staffed on top with vertical expert pools — the people who ran financial-services customers A, B and C get staffed on D — so domain lingo, credibility and success criteria compound instead of being relearned per logo.

data.name: Custom becomes self-serve
data.brief: Decagon's stated guiding ethos for the field-to-product funnel: every manual or bespoke thing an FDE does is a defect to be upstreamed until the customer (or the agent-building team) can do it themselves. Canonical instance: custom CRM integrations were hand-built one at a time until roughly the 25th, when "enough is enough" produced a self-serve integration builder, moving work that required an engineer writing custom code to configuration. Generalized rule: solve enterprise A's ask so that B, C, D and E inherit the solution before they ask — which happens "with stunning regularity".

data.name: At Decagon, forward deployed engineering is identical to product engineering
data.brief: Stated as the talk's most important point ("so important I wish I had a slide for it"): at Decagon forward deployed engineering is identical to product engineering — same hiring bar, same reporting structure, often the same team, reflected in the org chart. Rationale: when a Fortune 20 customer expresses a pain point in a call, that is a product feature that has to be built and prioritized, so the delineation between "forward deployed person" and "person who works on the product" is "gone". Independent corroboration of the Sierra observation that the lines are blurring, from a vendor that has already restructured around it.

data.name: 50 to 500 people in a year split the generalist FDE role into two specialized lanes
data.brief: Org-scaling data point with dates: 50 to 500 people in a year (and not slowing) forced the generalist agent-software-engineer role to split into two specialized lanes — agent builder (configures the agent brain in the UI: tonality, literal voice, user intents to hand off to a human, back-end actions like password resets) and agent software engineer (upstreams customer asks into the platform) — plus vertical expert staffing so knowledge compounds across logos in a vertical and every deployment is faster than the last.

data.name: With AI coding this good, exercising restraint is the scarce skill
data.brief: Direct claim about what coding agents changed: "the scarce skill now that AI coding is so good is exercising restraint." The temptation is to prompt Codex or Claude Code to satisfy an important customer's ASAP request; the FDE's job is to refuse the one-off and architect the fix so future customers benefit — reinforced by the product ethos that agents are owned by the customer, so a pile of one-off prompts and patches is "far too brittle" for both sides.

data.name: Cheap code pushes more effort up front into written requirements gathering
data.brief: Counterintuitive second-order effect of cheap code, offered as a "really good learning": because starting is now nearly free, more effort has to move up front into requirements gathering — narrowing what success means (which metrics, which channels, which pain point, what the ideal outcome is), ideally in writing at deal-scoping time so there is no miscommunication later. Paired with a fast time-to-value discipline: a Fortune 500 will hand you the entire kitchen sink, so prove value immediately and expand within what is expected to be a multi-year partnership.

data.name: Cross-customer vantage makes the FDE an advisor, not just an executor
data.brief: The vendor-side information asymmetry, stated as a deliberate practice: Decagon ingests a customer's historical support data and tells them which workflows to automate first for the highest ROI — "and sometimes that's not actually what the customer had reached out about". Because an FDE sees the same problems repeat across every customer in a vertical, the role is "an advisor rather than just an executor" (it is both), and that earned advisory position is named as one of three reasons the company won its market position.

data.name: An embedded delivery motion only scales if the field is a funnel into the product
data.brief: An embedded delivery motion only scales if the field is a funnel into the product, not a queue of bespoke work: every manual FDE action is a defect, repeats are the signal (25 hand-built CRM integrations produce the integration builder), and the destination is configuration in natural language by the customer or the agent-building team. Measured this way, the health of an FDE org is the rate at which custom becomes self-serve — and the compounding runs in both directions, since knowledge shared across deployments improves the agent for customer B every time it meets customer A.

data.name: Seniority in a forward deployed org is measured in refusals and generalization
data.brief: When coding agents make the one-off fix nearly free, the binding constraint moves from writing the code to deciding whether it should exist. Seniority in a forward deployed org is therefore measured in refusals and in generalization — architecting one customer's ask so the next four inherit it — and in front-loaded requirements work that would have been wasted effort when implementation was the expensive step. The failure mode is not slowness but a brittle per-customer black box that neither side can own.

data.name: Scope on written success criteria, then prove value before you expand
guidelines: Define success in the first conversations, not after kickoff: which metrics, which channels (phone, email, text, WhatsApp), what the pain point is, what the ideal outcome looks like — and get it in writing so there is no miscommunication later. Resist the urge to start building

with cheap code the up-front alignment is now the expensive, valuable part. Assume a Fortune 500 will hand you the whole kitchen sink, so pick the narrowest thing that demonstrates value fast rather than accepting a multi-month time-to-value

land on deflecting the complex inbound work humans do today, then expand into revenue-generating workflows once your integrations are in place. Staff industry experts who have already delivered in that vertical so the customer hears their own lingo and the ramp is short
target every deployment being faster than the last

data.name: Run the field as a funnel into the product, and exercise restraint at its mouth
guidelines: Treat every manual action an FDE takes as something that must be upstreamed

count repeats and act on them (after ~25 hand-built CRM integrations, build the self-serve integration builder instead of the 26th). When a customer asks for something now, do not hand it to a coding agent as a one-off — ask how it scales to the customers who will ask in two weeks, and architect so they inherit it

a black box of prompts and patches is too brittle for a product the customer is supposed to own. Push the endpoint toward configuration in natural language so the rest of the business, not only engineers, can serve the ask. Share knowledge across deployments rigorously so the agent compounds with every customer interaction, and use the cross-customer vantage to advise (ingest historical support data, tell them what to automate first for ROI) rather than only execute

data.name: How Forward Deployed Engineering is done at Kepler (Vinoo Ganesh — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Vinoo Ganesh
Kepler
data.brief: The speaker's current company, where he is standing up the forward deployed engineering function on the Project Frontline model with a founding engineer. The talk says almost nothing else about it — no product, market or stage — so the node is thin and exists to carry the affiliation and the "what Kepler is doing" claim.

data.name: FDE as product strategy
data.brief: The talk's thesis and its explicit inversion of the go-to-market framing: "this is not a role, this is a product strategy" — an FDE is judged by their ability to be an extension of the product team, to identify areas of opportunity inside a customer and to generalize product solutions out of them, not by contract size or customer satisfaction. Attributed to Palantir's CTO (the person who named the discipline) in a statement made days before the talk. Corollaries stated: the field work is an input to a generalizable product rather than the deliverable being sold; making customers successful is a solutions architect's job, not an FDE's; and running FDE as a go-to-market extension is a luxury affordable only to a company with twenty years and unlimited money.

data.name: Project Frontline
data.brief: Palantir's rotation and training program, built by the speaker, that converted software engineers into forward deployed engineers — ~350 engineers went through it, and its alumni now staff FDE functions at OpenAI, Anthropic and xAI. Curriculum condensed to a cheat sheet: redefine the problem rather than take requirements, get badged on site, ship the fix before leaving to win goodwill, own the fix end to end inside the product ecosystem, convert fixes into product leverage, and be the person who gets the call when it breaks. Rebuilt afterwards at Citadel and now at Kepler; contrasted with the common failure mode of running the function as product-management plus customer-success process (requirements intake, scheduled user research, insight decks) with no mechanism for steering the product.

data.name: Linguistic lock-in
data.brief: The strategic reading of ontology work: every organization is made of nouns (entities) and verbs (operations), and the same entity is named differently per function — sales says customers, ops says clients, finance says billing entities, engineering says org IDs — which breaks integrations, corrupts data quality and stalls pipelines. Canonicalizing that vocabulary inside the product means users adopt your language along with your software, and "if you become the linguistic foundation, you're locked in". Palantir "tripped into" its ontology this way, not by schematizing everything into search. Live 2026 examples offered of vocabulary capture in progress: skills, and MCPs used to mean function calls with prompts. Diagnostic checklist: which terms are overloaded, where the integration points and translation layers are, which systems of record can never be swapped out, and what words people use when describing failures ("my agent keeps failing" — what is an agent?).

data.name: FDE is a product strategy, not a role and not a go-to-market extension
data.brief: The cluster's dissent, from the builder of Palantir's FDE training program (~350 engineers; alumni now at OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI): "the first fundamental truth of FDE is that this is not a role, this is a product strategy" — quoted from Palantir's current CTO days before the talk — and an FDE is judged by their ability to be an extension of the product team and generalize solutions, not by contract size, customer success or sales support.
data.description: Explicitly rejects the framings in the two preceding talks: FDE-as-go-to-market is what Palantir became after twenty years and unlimited money, not what built Foundry; "when people say FDEs are customer-facing software engineers whose job is to make the customer successful — that's not true"; closes with "please don't treat FDEs as go-to-market extensions".

data.name: Palantir's Phoenix store, built in isolation from customers, died on real data
data.brief: The origin story, with numbers: circa 2013 Palantir built a transaction store ("Phoenix") in complete isolation from customers — designed perfectly for assumed conditions, "crashed and burned" on real data. At a large financial customer, blank values defaulted to the 1970 epoch, and a 10-minute-bucketed retention strategy therefore generated ~2.3 million key spaces; at Cassandra's ~5 MB per file handle that meant ~14 TB of RAM just to start the server — dead on arrival, with no one else to call. Stated diagnosis: the gap was not missing user research, it was the absence of ownership from co-building the software while embedded with the customer.

data.name: A 47-page requirements doc collapsed into a four-hour Slack alert on site
data.brief: Requirements-versus-reality war story: a dispatching/shipping customer's VP of operations produced a 47-page requirements document for a custom BI tool — 14 metrics, drill-downs, alerts — scoped at three months, and the team spent four months scoping it remotely before anyone went on site. One on-site question ("what's the first thing you do with this information Monday morning?") produced the real workflow — check whether trucks are late, then call the dispatcher — which shipped as a trivial Slack alert in four hours. Rule: customers describe solutions, not problems, and don't know what happens after the solution exists; whoever defines the problem owns the solution, which is the actual reason FDEs are valuable in early sales.

data.name: A year-long Parquet migration block was unlocked by an overnight file viewer
data.brief: A data-quality engineer blocked a CSV-to-Parquet migration for about a year ("Parquet is way worse, it doesn't work"), with no articulable reason, while the daily ~1 TB CSV drop to S3 strained the pipelines. Watching her work on site revealed the cause: she downloaded CSVs to a Windows machine and double-clicked them to spot-check quality, and Parquet had no native viewer.
data.description: An overnight Parquet viewer got the migration approved in two days; pipeline execution fell from ~17 hours to ~2. Generalized tells that an FDE should watch for on site: any task done more than once, copy-paste between tools, tool or tab switching, phone-out mid-task, and visceral exasperation ("well, I have to").

data.name: Every temporary forward-deployed hack goes to production and stays there
data.brief: A "temporary" Groovy retention script, hacked together to unblock one customer and never productized, was still running 12 months later across a ~100,000-person customer in multiple places and became a company nickname (colleagues wore venue.groovy shirts to his wedding). Rules: "the most dangerous words in forward deployed engineering are 'this is just temporary'"; if it solves a problem it is permanent; ship everything as though it will run for 18 months, because it probably will.
data.description: Four calibration questions before shipping: will I get a 2 a.m. call about this in six months; what is the trade-off for the product as a whole versus this customer's pain point; who do I hand it to when I leave the site; what happens when it breaks and am I responsible.

data.name: Canonicalizing an enterprise's vocabulary is a competitive lock-in position
data.brief: Ontology reframed as a competitive position rather than a data-modelling exercise: because every function names the same entity differently (customers / clients / billing entities / org IDs) and terms like DAU mean different things to product and infosec, canonicalizing the vocabulary inside the platform means enterprises adopt your language when they adopt your product — "if you become the linguistic foundation, you're locked in". Palantir's ontology is described as an accidental discovery of this, and the enabling substrate for Foundry and everything built on it. Named as happening right now in AI vocabulary: skills, and MCPs used loosely to mean function calls with prompts.

data.name: Whoever defines the problem owns the solution
data.brief: The leverage in embedded work is not proximity to the customer but control of the problem statement: customers describe solutions, so an FDE who redefines the problem, ships the small real fix before leaving the site and then articulates what comes next permanently owns the system and the narrative around it. Trust bought with bite-sized solved problems is what buys access to the real problem — which is the raw material for generalization (Foundry as the general product informed by tens of thousands of hours of exactly this). This, not social skill, is why FDEs matter in early sales.

data.name: The durable position is the noun-and-verb layer, not the feature set
data.brief: When a customer adopts your vocabulary, they adopt your model of their own business — so the durable position is not the feature set but the noun-and-verb layer everything else is expressed in. Definitional ambiguity is a feature of how humans work in their own domains, not a bug to be schematized away; the winning move is to canonicalize it inside the platform so every later question, integration and tool is phrased in your terms. The corollary for AI vendors is immediate: whoever fixes what skill, MCP and agent mean occupies the same position Palantir's ontology did.

data.name: Get badged on site — residents get the truth
guidelines: The most valuable intel is never in documentation, and you cannot survey your way to it: your site badge and contractor email address are your data-mining permits, and being a forward deployed engineer in name from a conference room in New York is not the job. Before building anything, establish three things: what the customer is trying to accomplish, what happens after the solution exists, and how they solve it today. Then observe rather than interview — actions speak louder than words. Watch for any task done more than once (per hour, per day, per week), copy-paste between tools, tool or tab switching, phones coming out mid-task, and exasperation phrased as obligation ("well, I have to"). Open with "what's the most annoying part of your morning?" and aim to make their tomorrow different from their today. If the fix is under a day of work, just build it, ship it and close the loop — don't escalate it into a product initiative with PMs attached

data.name: Ship fast, but build as if it runs for 18 months
guidelines: Every hack that makes someone's life easier goes to production and stays there — you will support it in perpetuity, so treat "this is just temporary" as the most dangerous sentence in the job. Before shipping, answer four questions: will this generate a 2 a.m. call in six months
is this trade-off right for the product as a whole or only for this customer's pain point (small win now, negative compounding later)
who inherits it when I leave the site — the customer, another FDE, another institution
and what happens, and who is blamed, when it breaks. Decide explicitly whether each solution folds into the core offering or gets discarded quickly
a hack that wins goodwill but doesn't move product strategy is solutions-architect work, not FDE work

data.name: Map the nouns and verbs before you map the data
guidelines: Treat vocabulary as the first deliverable. Inventory which terms are overloaded — the same entity called customers, clients, billing entities and org IDs by four teams

DAU meaning quality-weighted actives to product and raw logins to infosec. Locate the integration points between systems (Snowflake to Databricks, platform to Tableau, model provider to ERP) and the translation layers where one term becomes another. Identify the system boundaries: which systems of record will never be swapped out. Listen to the words people use when describing failures, and interrogate the loose ones ("my agent keeps failing" — is an agent a prompt, a series of steps?). Then canonicalize: pick the terms, encode them in the platform as entities and operations, and get customers answering questions in your vocabulary — that is what makes you the foundation later tools are built on

data.name: AI Tools for Forward Deployed Engineering (Vasuman Moza + JD Puit, Varick Agents — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Vasuman Moza
JD Puit
Varick Agents
data.brief: AI transformation firm doing department-wide agentic re-engineering for large enterprises: begins every engagement with an on-site audit by forward deployed engineers/strategists, then implements agents on its own platform layered on top of the customer's existing systems of record. Explicitly positions itself as not a traditional consultancy (its own tooling is what keeps headcount sublinear) and not a product company ("what we're building for cannot be solved with just a product").

data.name: FD agent (forward-deployed-engineering agent)
data.brief: Varick's in-house "Codex for our FDEs", built because forward deployed engineers were uploading ~150 pages of client documentation to Claude, waiting ~2 minutes and getting verbose, incorrect analysis. Three stages, the third still unbuilt: (1) engagement agent — the FDE's assistant, ingesting Granola meeting notes, documentation and PowerPoint decks, answering the questions FDEs actually ask all day ("who is responsible for this process?", "the Sarah in this email and the Sarah in this Slack message — are these the same person?"); (2) workflow agent — the same agent embedded inside the platform while the FDE builds a workflow, flagging missed edge cases and process ownership so the built workflow actually shadows the real process, running alongside whichever coding agent the engineer uses; (3) autonomous agent (in development) — receives client change requests by email, queries the existing model of the company, and ships the workflow change without the FDE, reserving human time for on-site interviews and process discovery.

data.name: Varick OS
data.brief: The delivery platform: spin up and monitor agents with governance and evals built in, deliberately layered on top of the customer's existing systems of record (NetSuite, Dynamics, SAP, Salesforce) rather than requiring migration off them — the stated wedge for enterprises "too large to move". Hosts the workflows FDEs build and, increasingly, the FD agent that helps build them.

data.name: Process dependency graph
data.brief: The single source of truth for how a company actually functions, used as the substrate the FD agent reasons over. Claim about shape: enterprise workflows are "remarkably linear, they just have a lot of cycles in them", and process owners want them dependency-driven (person C should not act before A and B have approved) — so a dependency graph fits better than a document store, and the storage choice is deliberately un-opinionated ("five companies downstairs will sell you a graph DB; you can just use Postgres — it doesn't really matter"). What it must capture beyond the documented golden path: the exception routes ("Sarah in AP handles it this way, but when it breaks she sends it to Chris, who takes four days to reconcile a PO against an invoice"), which are unique per company and are the stated reason agents can't yet run end-to-end. Hard part is traversal, not storage.

data.name: Execution is solved; understanding a specific business is the next bottleneck
data.brief: The talk's thesis, stated as a before/after: in 2024, asking a room whether AI had completed an end-to-end task for them would have drawn almost no hands; in 2026 everyone's hand goes up. Models plus harnesses (browser-use tooling, API tooling, robust MCPs) have moved past the execution bottleneck — "knowledge work is almost entirely solved" — so the next bottleneck is how deeply you can understand a specific business and re-engineer its work around AI without scaling headcount exponentially. Supporting observation: a healthcare company's sales department operates nothing like a SaaS company's, and extracting that context out of employees into a model call is the part that breaks.

data.name: ~95% of generative-AI pilots fail because AI is layered on broken processes
data.brief: External statistics deployed as the market diagnosis: the MIT figure that ~95% of generative-AI pilots fail to reach production, and a second (~87%) that most pilots produce no measurable ROI — both attributed to AI being slapped on top of broken processes rather than to model capability. Amplifying claim: even engineers with goal loops and current tooling can't say "refactor this codebase" and walk away, so handing the same tooling to non-technical operators in finance, sales, marketing, procurement and logistics cannot produce an engineer's ROI. Consequence: the deliverable has to be the re-engineered process, not the tool.

data.name: Enterprises will not migrate again, so agents must be built on their systems of record
data.brief: Enterprise-reality constraint with a quoted number: enterprises are married to their systems of record — NetSuite, Dynamics, SAP, Salesforce — and one client is quoted as having spent $5 million and 5 years migrating to NetSuite. Pitching AI that lives separate from those systems means "they'll tell you to get out"; there is no appetite for another migration. Varick's answer is to build agents on top of the systems of record, with governance and evals in its own platform — "that is where enterprise needs AI the most, because they're too large to move".

data.name: Varick built an in-house FD agent to automate its own forward deployed function
data.brief: A vendor building tooling to automate its own forward deployed function, with the failure it was built from: the platform team was "hanging out with Codex and Claude" while the FDE side of the office was sleep-deprived and miserable, uploading ~150 pages of documentation to Claude per engagement and getting verbose, incorrect output two minutes later.
data.description: The FD agent's stated goal is one FDE or strategist covering several client engagements — clients emailing 24/7, every process lead (AP relies on AR relies on reconciliation relies on FP&A) pulling in a different direction — without hiring 50 people, which is what separates the model from a traditional consultancy. Third stage (autonomous change-shipping) explicitly not built yet.

data.name: Frontier models are too verbose for FDE analysis, forcing open-model post-training
data.brief: Concrete negative result on frontier models: asked whether extracted context yields high-quality FDE analysis out of Claude, the answer is "honestly no, which is kind of surprising" — frontier models are extremely verbose for long analysis and have no concept of which detail the client actually cares about, which is precisely the consultant's skill ("I only started believing in consultants once we started hiring them").
data.description: Response: post-train open-source models for the detail/clarity balance (they name a Kimi K2-series model as a favourite), and separately train graph-traversal tools in an RL environment — entity resolution across the many "Sarahs" in a company, plus detection of redundancy cycles and DAG violations in the knowledge graph — because reliably extracting the right context from the graph is the second half of the problem.

data.name: Department-wide re-engineering beats point solutions on ROI
data.brief: Point solutions cap out: automating prospecting inside sales, or AP inside finance, returns ~5-10% for that function, which is why so much deployed AI shows no measurable ROI. Transforming a whole department at once — classifying each step of an 8-step process as fully autonomous, human-in-the-loop, or human-only (risk too high, or too bespoke for an agent to add value) — is what produces the 25/50/75% numbers, denominated in the same three currencies the Cursor talk named: revenue uplift, cost savings, risk mitigation.
data.description: The binding design constraint is adoption, not capability: the new process must differ enough to capture the ROI but not so much that operators can't recognize it (replacing an 11-step workflow with one step gets handed back).

data.name: The undocumented exception paths are the context enterprise agents lack
data.brief: Enterprise documentation describes the golden path and maybe one edge case; the operational truth is the exception route — who it goes to when it breaks and how many days that costs — and it is different at every company. That undocumented layer, not model capability, is why agents can't run enterprise processes end to end, which makes "what happens when things go wrong?" the highest-yield question an FDE asks and makes the resulting dependency graph (with its cycles and its real owners) the actual deliverable of the discovery phase. Storage is incidental; reliable traversal is the hard problem, and it is worth an RL environment of its own.

data.name: Audit first, re-engineer the process, then deploy agents
guidelines: Start every engagement with an audit, not an install: embed forward deployed engineers/strategists on site and scope to a single department rather than the whole enterprise. Interview every process lead in it (in finance: AP, AR, card reconciliation, banking, billing, FP&A) and ask about both the documented golden path and — the part that matters — what happens when things go wrong, by name and by cycle time. Then re-engineer around AI step by step: mark each step fully autonomous, human-in-the-loop, or human-only where risk is too high or the work is too bespoke for an agent to add value. Keep the redesigned process recognizable — different enough to capture ROI, not so different that adoption collapses. Deploy on top of the systems of record the customer already paid millions to adopt
never make migration a precondition. Report value in revenue uplift, cost savings and risk mitigation, and target department-wide rather than single-workflow numbers

data.name: Build the assistant your forward deployed engineers actually need
guidelines: Watch the FDE side of your own office before building: the symptom is a 150-page document dump into a chat model and a verbose, wrong answer two minutes later. Ingest what they really work from — meeting notes, documentation, slide decks, email, Slack — and answer the questions they really ask (who owns this process
are these two mentions the same person). Represent the company as a dependency graph as the single source of truth

don't over-think the store (a graph DB and Postgres both work), because the hard part is traversal. Expect frontier models to be too verbose and to have no sense of what a client cares about, so post-train an open-source model for that balance, and train the traversal tools in an RL environment — entity resolution across duplicate names, redundancy-cycle and DAG-violation detection. Embed the assistant where the workflow is actually built so it flags missed edge cases and ownership in place, and let it run beside whatever coding agent the engineer already uses. Automate the routine client minutiae (a mailed request to reroute a report) last, so human time goes to on-site interviews and process design

data.name: Serving 2 Million Models Without Melting: Scaling the Hugging Face Hub (Arek Borucki, Hugging Face — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Arek Borucki
Hugging Face Hub
data.brief: The model/dataset hosting platform itself, treated here as a distributed system rather than a community: 3M public models, 1M datasets, 50,000 organizations, 14M users, with metadata in MongoDB Atlas and artifacts in cloud object storage, fronted by a Kubernetes-hosted Hub API. Growth is release-driven — "every big release like Llama or DeepSeek generates thousands of new models on top" — so the infrastructure problem is set by the derivative-model long tail, not by any single large model.

data.name: Metadata / artifact separation
data.brief: The Hub's foundational split: the database stores everything about the models (users, repositories, model and dataset records, bucket/space information, configuration, billing, access control) and never the models themselves; weights, tokenizer files, model-card assets and config files live in cloud object storage (AWS S3). Consequence: metadata, binary storage and compute scale — and get optimized — independently of each other.

data.name: Insert-time search tokenization
data.brief: Pay the tokenization cost on write, never on query: a model name (meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B) is split into small tokens at insert time and stored as an array on the document, in a denormalized read-only copy of the main repo collection built purely for reads and listings. Query-side becomes an autocomplete lookup over the token array, sorted by a trending score recomputed every 5 minutes from the last ~7 days of downloads and likes.

data.name: MongoDB Atlas Search (Lucene-backed full-text)
data.brief: Full-text search delivered by a separate mongot process wrapping Apache Lucene alongside the MongoDB server (core MongoDB provides no full-text engine); transparent to the caller — the same unified query API, with a $search stage in an aggregation pipeline naming the Lucene index. Adopted at the Hub to replace regex matching over the token array, which "doesn't scale well" and produced the latency problems that appeared as the dataset grew.

data.name: Replica-set read routing
data.brief: Workload placement across a 7-node MongoDB replica set as an explicit engineering discipline rather than a driver default: all writes and only strong-consistency reads on the primary; everything tolerating slight staleness on secondaries; heavy aggregation pipelines (large scans, sorts, groups, transforms) and change streams (cache invalidation, sync to Redshift, event-driven workloads) off the primary; and one hidden analytics node — invisible to the driver, still replicating from the primary, connected to directly for reporting and ad-hoc/experimental queries so they never touch production traffic. Stated rule: "primary should focus on what only primary can do".

data.name: Horizontal database sharding
data.brief: The next rung once a single replica set stops being enough: cut the dataset into pieces and give each shard its own replica set (primary + secondaries), letting a balancer distribute data across shards — replication multiplied rather than replaced. Scales CPU, memory, storage, reads and writes together, at the cost of choosing a shard key ("not a trivial operation"). Named as in-flight future work at Hugging Face, not yet shipped.

data.name: Two-layer Kubernetes autoscaling
data.brief: Pod layer plus node layer. Pod layer: horizontal pod autoscaler scaling the Hub deployment from 10 to 500 pods on CPU/memory thresholds — with a planned migration to KEDA (event-driven autoscaling) because HPA cannot see application-level signals like requests per second or event-loop utilization, and "a pod can have low CPU but a high request queue". Node layer: CAST AI adds cluster nodes when pods are pending because the scheduler has no capacity. Explicit goal is elasticity without overprovisioning — cost control as well as availability.

data.name: Hugging Face Hub reaches 14M users, 3M public models and 1M datasets
data.brief: First-party Hub numbers as of 2026-07: 14M users ("growing very fast, especially in the last couple of months"), 3M public models, 1M datasets, 50,000 organizations, and more than 30% of the Fortune 500 using Hugging Face as part of their AI workflows. Growth framing: ~20,000 models a few years ago to 3M today, ~150x, driven by derivative uploads — "every big release like Llama or DeepSeek generates thousands of new models on top" — which is the load the infrastructure is designed around. The talk title says 2M models while the speaker says 3M throughout.

data.name: Hugging Face datasets went from 10K in 2022 to 1M in 2026, doubling in the last year
data.brief: Dated dataset-count series from the platform owner: 10K in 2022, 100K in 2024, 500K less than a year ago, 1M today (2026-07) — i.e. the count doubled inside the last year after 5x the year before. Stated consequence: "all this data must be stored, indexed, and also must be searchable, and that's the hardest part" — the dataset curve, not the model curve, is what forced the search rewrite.

data.name: The Hub replaced regex search with Lucene-backed Atlas Search at 3M models
data.brief: Search rearchitecture at the Hub, with the reasoning stated: at 20,000 models any query is fast even without an index and "no one would notice"; at 3M the same approach breaks. The old path — a MongoDB find with a regex operator over a search-token array, sorted by trending score — stopped scaling as the dataset grew and produced user-visible latency.
data.description: The new path precomputes tokens at insert time into a denormalized read-only collection and queries Atlas Search / Apache Lucene autocomplete via a $search aggregation stage, still sorted by a trending score recomputed every 5 minutes over ~7 days of downloads and likes. Reported outcome: "we don't have any more latency issues in our search bar." The stated design target is P99, explicitly over P50, because at 14M users even 1% of traffic is 140,000 people hitting a slow search — and the competing hub is one click away.

data.name: A 7-node replica set carries the Hub, and sharding is the next rung
data.brief: How a 3M-model AI platform actually distributes database load: a 7-node replica set with writes and strong-consistency reads pinned to the primary, stale-tolerant reads spread across secondaries, heavy aggregations and change streams (cache invalidation, sync to AWS Redshift, event-driven workloads) deliberately kept off the primary, and a hidden analytics node — invisible to the MongoDB driver, still tailing the oplog — reserved for reporting and ad-hoc heavy queries. Named as insufficient going forward: "with 14 million users, 3 million models and our growth, soon a single MongoDB replica set will not be enough", so sharding is the next step, with shard-key selection called out as the hard, unfinished decision.

data.name: The Hub autoscales 10 to 500 pods plus nodes, and is moving from HPA to KEDA
data.brief: Two independent elasticity layers keep the Hub up without overprovisioning: the Hub deployment scales 10 to 500 pods on the Kubernetes horizontal pod autoscaler, and CAST AI adds nodes underneath when pods go pending because the scheduler has no capacity. Announced migration: HPA to KEDA, on the grounds that CPU/memory thresholds are the wrong signal for this workload — "a pod can have low CPU but a high request queue" — so scaling should be driven by requests per second and event-loop utilization instead of resource utilization.

data.name: The world's largest model host stores no models: metadata is the workload
data.brief: The surprising fact about the world's largest model host is that its database holds no models. Hosting weights is an object-storage problem and effectively solved; making 3M of them findable, listable, billable and access-controlled is a metadata problem, and that is where the engineering lives. Separating the two lets metadata, binaries and compute be scaled and tuned independently — and it means the platform's growth pressure shows up first as query latency and read distribution, not as storage cost.

data.name: At platform scale the P99 tail is the product
data.brief: At platform scale the tail is the product: 1% of 14M users is 140,000 people, so P99 matters more than P50, and a slow search bar simply sends developers elsewhere. The generalizable move is to shift work from query time to write time and from the primary to everywhere else — precompute tokens on insert, keep a denormalized read-only copy, refresh ranking on a 5-minute cadence, and route anything that can tolerate staleness away from the one node that cannot be replicated around. The user-facing goal is invisibility: "you never have to think about it… keeping the user experience simple no matter how complex it gets under the hood".

data.name: Scale an AI hub's metadata layer, not its blob layer
guidelines: Keep model artifacts (weights, tokenizers, cards, configs) in object storage and put only metadata in the database, so the two scale independently. For search: maintain a denormalized read-only copy of the main collection purely for reads and listings
tokenize names at insert time into an array rather than matching at query time
move off regex find to a Lucene-backed full-text index ($search in an aggregation pipeline) before the dataset makes regex latency user-visible

precompute the ranking signal on a cadence (trending score every 5 minutes over ~7 days of downloads and likes) instead of computing it per query. Optimize for P99, not P50 — at 14M users, 1% is 140,000 people. For read scaling: pin only writes and strong-consistency reads to the primary and audit that list continuously
push stale-tolerant reads, heavy aggregations and change streams to secondaries
keep a hidden analytics member for reporting and ad-hoc queries so they never touch production traffic
and plan sharding (with a deliberately chosen shard key) as the next rung when a single replica set runs out

data.name: Autoscale at both the pod and the node layer, on the right signal
guidelines: Run two layers, because the pod autoscaler is useless when the cluster has no free nodes: deployment-level autoscaling (the Hub runs 10-500 pods) plus infrastructure-level node autoscaling (CAST AI) that provisions capacity when pods go pending. Treat this as a cost control as much as an availability control — the point is handling spikes without permanent overprovisioning. Scale on application signals, not resource utilization: CPU and memory miss the case of a pod with low CPU and a deep request queue, so move from HPA to event-driven autoscaling (KEDA) driven by requests per second or event-loop utilization

data.name: AI Agents for Performance: Ship Faster, Pay Less (Rajat Shah, Netflix — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Rajat Shah
Netflix
data.brief: Streaming/media company, appearing as an enterprise building its own agent tooling rather than as an AI vendor: an internal AI Platform org hosting ML models at scale, and the performance-engineering agent playbook in this talk.

data.name: Performance pattern / anti-pattern catalog
data.brief: A central, ever-growing, cross-team catalog of code patterns and anti-patterns kept as markdown in a Git repo — deliberately not a vector database. Framed as the memory half of a two-part system: "a stateful catalog and a stateless LLM together become a full fleet-wide memory for a coding agent". Entry shape: query hints and a list of symbols, the services where the pattern was confirmed, a confidence level that rises as more services confirm it, and both the anti-pattern and its good-pattern counterpart. Written by agents from production findings and by humans building new frameworks; generalized across languages where the pattern is universal (an O(N^2) loop is). Must be hierarchically structured and indexed so an agent navigates to the relevant entry instead of loading the catalog into context. Bootstrapping sources named: Jeff Dean's C++ optimization blog post, PyTorch's torchfix anti-pattern repo, and the organization's existing performance playbooks — though "there is no harm in a catalog that is just empty in the beginning".

data.name: Profiling output as agent-readable context
data.brief: The talk's founding assumption: every profiler speaks the same language. Whatever the service's language or runtime (Java, Python, Go), a profiler run against a single production instance emits the same well-structured artifact — the call stack plus self CPU and inclusive CPU per method, sampled at high frequency — which is "very well-structured for an LLM agent to use" even though it is poor for humans (raw JSON of call stacks, needing a flame-graph visualizer and a real learning curve). The second half of the assumption is the model side: common inefficiency patterns (O(N^2) loops, loop invariants, repeated object allocation in hot paths, contention fixable by batching) are already in a good coding model's training data, so the agent can identify a bad pattern purely from the call stack, before looking at the code base.

data.name: Canary as the agent's ground truth
data.brief: The verification primitive that gates an agent-authored performance fix: two instances, one running the old code and one the candidate optimization, receiving the same traffic for ~10 minutes, producing a comparison report of CPU reduction, latency change and error rate. The agent reads the report and decides whether the change is worth a human's attention — a rise in error rate is a "red signal" that it broke business logic while optimizing. Mental model as stated: "profiler gives the estimate, canary gives ground truth, an engineer makes the decision." Explicitly not an AI problem — observability, canary and verification logic are standard pre-AI infrastructure that the agent only needs to know how to invoke and read.

data.name: Shift-left performance loop
data.brief: The staged migration of performance work from reactive to proactive, with the catalog as the vehicle. Stage 1 (reactive): production profiling, agent finds and fixes, code review; the right place to start, and how the catalog gets populated. Stage 2 (review time): a reviewer agent looks up the catalog against an incoming diff and leaves an inline comment ("based on the pattern catalog and observed profiling data, this is an anti-pattern — can you rewrite this?"). Stage 3 (authoring time): the catalog is hooked into the coding agent itself so it consults known anti-patterns before emitting tokens and writes the optimal code first. Stated cost of stage 3: slower generation and more tokens consumed — which is exactly why the catalog must be navigable rather than loadable.

data.name: Agents author code ~10x faster and compute cost is rising at a similar pace
data.brief: The premise, from a large-scale platform team: engineers now author code ~10x faster with coding agents, and compute cost is rising at a similar pace ("slight exaggeration", but stated as the reason the work exists) — agents are tuned to ship code fast, not fast code. The counter-argument that better models will fix it is rejected outright: an agent "doesn't know specific details about your platforms, your frameworks and your internal code base patterns", so it reproduces patterns from other code bases or invents new patterns in your code base that you did not anticipate an engineer to use with your framework.
data.description: Performance engineering is simultaneously the thing that scales worst: it is manual, has a real learning curve, and consequently "is done very rarely" — typically only when someone is woken at 2 a.m. by unbearable CPU.

data.name: A Netflix agent found and fixed an 8.8% CPU hot path end to end in under five minutes
data.brief: Netflix's first result, on live production services: fed profiling data, a coding agent identified an immutable-map copy inside a tensor-merge call path consuming 8.8% of CPU time during the profiling window, recognized it as quadratic rather than linear from the call stack alone — not from reading the code base — then, given instructions as a skill or prompt, checked the Git repo out at the exact commit running in production, located the implementation, traced the call path and opened a code review, end to end in under 5 minutes on a very large code base.
data.description: Baseline it replaces: ~20 minutes of a human engineer's time just to identify hot paths in a flame-graph visualizer, before any fix. Real production CPU and latency savings were measured for the optimized reimplementation, with figures shown on slide only and never spoken.

data.name: One anti-pattern found in 7 Netflix services, with 0.5-4.6% of CPU cycles recoverable
data.brief: The second and larger result — one finding amplified across the fleet. A Spectator metrics counter object being allocated on every iteration of a hot path was found in one service; via cross-repo code search the agent then found the same anti-pattern in 7 different services, with an estimated 0.5-4.6% of CPU cycles recoverable if fixed across all of them. The generalization is the point: a human fixes the instance, an agent fixes the class — and the finding it produced (an O(N^2) implementation) was noted as language-independent, so the catalog entry transfers across languages and frameworks.

data.name: Netflix's fleet-wide agent memory is markdown in a central Git repo, not a vector database
data.brief: Long-term agent memory at Netflix is markdown files in a central Git repo, explicitly chosen over "very fancy vector search or a vector database": "a stateful catalog and a stateless LLM together become a full fleet-wide memory". Entries carry symbols/query hints, the services where the pattern was confirmed, a rising confidence level, and both the anti-pattern and the good pattern.
data.description: Deliberately central rather than team- or product-specific, so a pattern discovered by one service's profiling run is available to every future agent profiling a different service "without having to redo all the exercise that the first agent did". Git-repo-by-design so humans and agents can both read and author it — including humans writing entries at framework-build time, when the context is freshest. Bootstrap sources named: Jeff Dean's C++ optimization blog post, PyTorch's torchfix repo, and internal performance playbooks.

data.name: Netflix stops at level-2 autonomy: the performance agent never pushes to production
data.brief: A large-scale platform team stating an autonomy ceiling and its reasoning. Netflix runs at level 2 — a fixed, predefined workflow (trigger profiler, download, analyze, canary, suggest fix) with tools, integrations, harnesses and hooks, on a weekly scheduled run per service so regressions are caught close to when the code was written.
data.description: The agent never pushes to production: "I'm still keeping the confidence bar to just send a code review, and that's by intent", because "you're modifying an existing code that is running just fine in production in order to optimize it, which is very risky" — without business context and test coverage you break things. Level 3 (agent plans, reasons and acts) is described as available but gated on heavy investment in evaluation and sandboxing, "because prompt injection and other security attacks a typical agent infrastructure currently cannot always solve for". Guidance: start at level 1, move to level 2, "and you get maximum benefits".

data.name: Profiler gives the estimate, canary gives ground truth, the engineer decides
data.brief: The three-part mental model that makes an autonomous performance agent safe: the profiler gives an estimate, the canary gives ground truth, the engineer makes the decision. Everything load-bearing here predates AI — rock-solid unit and integration tests with business logic properly encoded, excellent canary automation, and observability reporting CPU, latency and error rate.
data.description: The agent's job is only to know how to invoke canary and where to read the report, then make a judgment call on it. The inversion worth keeping: teams reach for AI first and foundations later, but without the foundations "it will just cause more friction and more bugs in production" — the AI is the cheapest part of an agentic performance loop, and the prerequisite investment is the expensive part.

data.name: The catalog, not the agent, is the compounding asset that earns the shift left
data.brief: Every step the anti-pattern check moves left removes a whole layer of overhead — production fix (risky, needs a canary), then a review comment (cheap, still a rewrite), then authoring time (no rewrite at all, the bad code is never written). But you cannot start at the left: the catalog has to be earned from reactive production findings before it is trustworthy enough to steer code generation.
data.description: That makes the reactive path the on-ramp rather than the failure mode, and it makes the catalog — not the agent — the compounding asset: one service's profiling run permanently upgrades every future agent's starting position, and the catalog's confidence levels are what let a later agent skip the discovery work entirely. The binding constraint at the far left is context, not capability: consulting the catalog before every token costs latency and tokens, so the catalog's structure and index are what decide whether shift-left is affordable.

data.name: Wire a performance agent into an existing profiling stack
guidelines: Build the integration points before introducing an LLM, and ask of each one whether an agent could drive it: can it trigger profiling on a production instance automatically, download the profiling data, feed it to the model, clone the Git repo at the exact commit running in production, run the test suite, invoke a canary and read the resulting report? Then let the agent do the four steps that used to be manual: identify the hot path from the call stack (it does not need the code base for this), find the implementation via code search, trace the call path skipping internal library frames, and propose the fix. Gate the output before it costs a human anything: functional tests first (the agent runs them itself to prove it did not break business logic), then a canary — two instances, old code and new, same traffic for ~10 minutes, comparing CPU, latency and error rate, with any error-rate increase treated as a stop signal. Keep human approval for the merge: you are changing code that already works, and without business context or coverage you will break it. Start reactive, then schedule the loop weekly per service so regressions surface near the commit that caused them. Expand the fix from the instance to the class — cross-repo code search for every other place the same anti-pattern appears

data.name: Build the anti-pattern catalog as fleet-wide agent memory
guidelines: Keep it as markdown in one central Git repo — not a vector store — so it is both human- and agent-readable and authorable, and keep it central: team- or product-scoped catalogs lose the whole benefit, which is that a pattern confirmed by one service's profiling run is free for every other service's agent. Give each entry query hints and symbols, the services where it was confirmed, a confidence level that rises with each confirmation (higher confidence means more willingness to open a code review), and both the anti-pattern and its good-pattern counterpart. Starting empty is fine

bootstrapping is faster — Jeff Dean's C++ optimization notes, PyTorch's torchfix catalog, and your own existing performance playbooks. Generalize entries across languages and frameworks where the underlying problem is universal (quadratic loops, loop invariants, per-iteration allocation, batchable contention). Let humans author entries too, especially while building new frameworks and platform components, when they have the most context. Structure and index it hierarchically so an agent navigates to the relevant entry instead of loading the catalog into its context window — this is what makes it usable at authoring time rather than only at review time

data.name: When Will The Benchmaxxing Plague End? (Nick Heiner, Surge AI — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Nick Heiner
Benchmaxxing
data.brief: Labs training too hard on benchmarks in ways that diverge from what people actually care about; restated at the end as "the exploitation of misalignments between benchmarks and human preference". Explicitly a two-sided phenomenon: construction antipatterns on the benchmark-builder side and gaming plays on the lab side. The term's existence is itself the evidence that "we have a sense that benchmarks don't always equal reality".

data.name: LMArena (crowd-vote model leaderboard)
data.brief: The talk's canonical bad-but-dominant benchmark: millions of dollars wagered on prediction markets over its outcomes while industry leaders openly brag about gaming it; Karpathy's observation that teams optimize LMArena models (nested bullets, emojis) rather than better models; no filtering of its voting workforce, so a crowdsourced army can be hired to vote and a watermark in the model's output tells them which response is yours; a published paper on its dynamics documents overfitting and undisclosed multi-model testing. Captioned "Elm Marina" throughout.

data.name: IFEval
data.brief: Instruction-following benchmark cited on many model cards, used here as the taste antipattern: built by mashing together arbitrary constraint prompts no user has ever asked in earnest ("do not use any commas", "use the letter T at most once"), so its value rests entirely on an unargued generalization claim. Contains fully unsolvable tasks (repeat this verbatim and translate it into Hindi; a riddle with exactly one bullet point and a few bullet points), a sentence splitter that doesn't match how humans split sentences, and unverified prompts — "write a story" is graded only on the count of the ASCII letter i, so every response scores full marks, including one that reward-hacks with the
data.description: Cyrillic homoglyph.

data.name: APEX (RAG benchmark)
data.brief: RAG benchmark (agent is given files and asked questions about them), used as the operational ability antipattern: in some tasks the file contents and the rubric's expected answer contradict each other, so an agent that faithfully follows the ground truth scores negative; and much of the data is visibly synthetic — placeholder values, dates and places that don't exist — which both pushes the model toward eval awareness and takes the task out of distribution from real-world data. Name from captions ("Apex").

data.name: AutomationBench
data.brief: Enterprise tool-calling benchmark used as the ambition antipattern: verifiers are hard-coded string matches, e.g. one arbitrary phone-number format among many acceptable ones, and the prompt never says which. Result: Haiku and Fable both score 20% — Haiku by making mistakes, Fable by getting it right 80% of the time and formatting differently. A task that cannot separate those two models measures nothing, and a hard-coded string match cannot be the instrument that tells us when AI is ready to remake an industry. Name from captions.

data.name: Hemingway Bench (Surge)
data.brief: Surge's writing benchmark, built on the premise that writing is too rich, deep, nuanced and human to score mechanically — and that LLM-as-judge fails here because LLMs don't have good taste in writing. Implementation: a workforce of thousands of paid professional writers across domains (technical writers, poets, journalists, editors) doing blind model comparisons, aggregated into a leaderboard. Deliberately expensive: "our goal is to maximize quality, not to minimize costs".

data.name: Benchmark build economics (the cost wall)
data.brief: Worked arithmetic for why benchmarks are built badly: 1,000 tasks x 60 expert-hours per task, at a software engineer costing $500k/year, is roughly $15M to build an agentic coding benchmark — plus roughly a third of tasks washed away every year by model progress, roughly $5M/year to replace. Out of budget for most projects, so builders reach for the workarounds (heavy AI assistance, cheap labor) that produce every antipattern downstream. The causal root of the talk.

data.name: You can't push the frontier from within the frontier
data.brief: Load-bearing constraint invoked twice: AI assistance cannot author frontier-grade benchmark tasks, and LLM-as-judge cannot grade domains where the models themselves lack taste. Both require injecting external human expertise — and it has to be good expertise; "if you try to use cheap labor, you're going to get what you pay for". The economic justification for expensive human workforces in benchmark construction and evaluation.

data.name: Benchmark/human-eval divergence
data.brief: Human eval is the actual target ("AI exists to serve humans"), but it's expensive, so benchmarks distill human preference into something scalable and hope the distillation stays faithful. Past some point, hill-climbing the benchmark leaves human eval flat — and can be pushed further until human eval declines. Illustration: for the prompt "what time is it?", a response no human evaluator would ever choose sits at the top of the LMArena leaderboard. If you're benchmaxxing, you simply stop caring about the divergence.

data.name: Two-way prompt/verifier alignment
data.brief: Construction rule: verifiers must check everything the prompt asks for, and everything the prompt asks for must be covered by the verifiers. Misalignment on either side is unfair to models and injects random noise into scores. Corollary drawn in the talk: reward design must be treated adversarially against a maximally lazy agent — "gradient descent is water flowing downhill looking for the path of least resistance".

data.name: Buyers cannot assess benchmark validity, so they assess popularity instead
data.brief: The demand-side mechanism that keeps bad benchmarks dominant: AI is aimed at everyone, everyone needs some tool to pick a model, and benchmarks are what exists — but almost nobody can assess whether a benchmark is good, so they assess what's popular, creating an avalanche in which the conversation is driven by incumbency and marketing rather than real-world value (the speaker includes himself: "unless I actually look at a benchmark in a fair amount of detail, I don't have an opinion on it").
data.description: Evidence that this survives insider disclosure: millions of dollars wagered on prediction markets over LMArena outcomes while industry leaders openly brag about gaming it and Karpathy publicly notes the rankings don't match the models he thinks are best.

data.name: Opus memorized SWE-bench Verified and the model card never discloses it
data.brief: Contamination measured, then not disclosed: given the first part of a SWE-bench Verified prompt, Opus verbatim completes the rest — questions and answers — and a Surge study comparing memorization of SWE-bench-Verified content against the rest of the same repositories found "very clear evidence" Opus had memorized a lot of it. Opus 4.8's model card reports its SWE score without disclosing this, and the industry has no disclosure habit at all, so benchmark consumers are simply missing the information.
data.description: Framing that generalizes the finding: contamination is not mainly labs training on the test set — it is "the default outcome unless you are very, very good", because public questions and answers on the internet get memorized to some extent no matter how hard labs work to hold the flood back.

data.name: A $15M build cost and $5M/yr upkeep push benchmark builders into shortcuts
data.brief: Costed root cause: a 1,000-task agentic coding benchmark at 60 expert-hours per task and $500k per software engineer per year is roughly $15M to build and roughly $5M/year to maintain (about a third of tasks obsoleted annually by model progress) — "out of budget for most projects". The workarounds are what produce broken benchmarks: heavy AI assistance in authoring (which cannot work — "you can't push the frontier forward from within the frontier") and cheap labor ("you're going to get what you pay for"). Surge's counter-position, stated as a differentiator: don't minimize cost, maximize quality, and in 2026 models are past the point where anything less than the best workers suffices.

data.name: Hard-coded string-match verifiers collapse a strong and a weak model to one score
data.brief: A verifier defect that inverts a benchmark's whole purpose: AutomationBench grades enterprise tool calls with hard-coded string matches — e.g. one of many valid phone-number formats, with the prompt never specifying which — so Haiku and Fable both score 20%, Haiku through mistakes and Fable through formatting variance on work that is 80% correct. A task that cannot differentiate those two models is not a useful task; and in a year when the room is watching for AI to remake industries, a hard-coded string match is not an instrument that can see it coming. Generalized as the two-way alignment rule: verifiers must cover everything the prompt asks and ask nothing it doesn't.

data.name: Impossible, self-contradictory and ungraded tasks bias model rankings
data.brief: Widely cited benchmarks contain tasks that are impossible, self-contradictory or ungraded, and the resulting noise is biased, not random. IFEval (on many model cards): prompts no user has ever asked, pairs of mutually exclusive instructions, a non-human sentence splitter, and unverified prompts where "write a story" is scored only on the count of the ASCII letter i — full marks for every response, including one that swaps in a Cyrillic homoglyph.
data.description: APEX: rubrics that contradict the files the agent was given (so following the ground truth scores negative) and visibly synthetic data full of placeholders and nonexistent places, which pushes models toward eval awareness and out of distribution. Closing generalization: when labs declare a benchmark "saturated" at ~80%, part of what they may be reporting is that the remaining 20% is broken — and you cannot tell which 20% until you've solved the rest, so a biased fraction of the reward surface distorts the relative model ranking you were trying to obtain.

data.name: An insider names the lab-side gaming playbook: vote brigading, watermarks, silent runs
data.brief: The gaming side, named concretely by an insider: (1) keep hill-climbing past the point where human eval flattens — or declines — if marketing, organizational politics or incentives demand it (the LMArena top-ranked "absolutely deranged" answer to "what time is it?"); (2) hire a crowdsourced army to vote for you in an arena that does no filtering of its voting workforce, and defeat anonymization by having your model emit a watermark that tells the crowd which response to pick ("I've heard stories of"); (3) run evals under conditions that aren't an apples-to-apples comparison and don't be fully transparent about them, so the community interprets a number without the context that would
data.description: invalidate it; (4) test many candidates silently — a published paper shows Meta tested 27 models on LMArena without disclosing it, distorting results and driving arena overfitting.

data.name: Benchmaxxing is a two-sided market failure, not simply labs cheating
data.brief: Benchmaxxing is not simply labs cheating — it is the equilibrium of a market where every side's incentives point the same way. Buyers cannot evaluate benchmark validity, so popularity substitutes for it; builders cannot afford correct construction ($15M+ per serious benchmark) so they take shortcuts that break tasks silently; labs face marketing and political pressure to keep hill-climbing past the point where the score stops tracking human value.
