data.description: That is why insider disclosure ("it can be easily gamed", "these aren't better models, they're better arena models") changes nothing about a benchmark's standing. The fix has to be applied on both sides at once — to the people making benchmarks and the people reporting on them.

data.name: A benchmark is an aspirational artifact expressing values, not a dry Q&A set
data.brief: A benchmark used to be a dry academic question-and-answer set; today it is an aspirational artifact — an expression of values about what you want AI to do and how you want it to behave. That reframing makes taste and product sense construction requirements, not garnish: a medical benchmark needs someone who knows the regulatory and legal environment, not only doctors who can answer medical questions, because that determines which tasks are worth testing at all. And because taste cannot be supplied from inside the frontier — not by AI assistance in authoring, not by LLM judges in grading — the expensive human expert is a structural requirement of the artifact, not a temporary inefficiency.

data.name: Build the benchmark around experts, then verify both directions
guidelines: Start with great human experts and let them determine everything downstream: which tasks the agent performs, how success is measured, what input files and tools it gets
Pair them with someone who has product/business sense for the deployment context (regulation, legal constraints) — domain answers alone don't tell you which tasks matter
Get high-fidelity input data from the real world with real people
synthetic is possible but very hard to do reliably, and obviously synthetic data breeds eval awareness
Make sure the tools work — buggy tools inject noise unless buggy tools are the subject
Align prompts and verifiers in both directions: verify everything the prompt asks, ask nothing the verifier can't see
Design rewards adversarially against a maximally lazy agent
QC everything, and keep a private hold-out set so you don't get contaminated

data.name: Read benchmarks as a consumer who assumes misalignment
guidelines: Treat popularity as zero evidence of validity — the loudest benchmarks are selected for incumbency and marketing, not for measuring value
Check whether the model card discloses contamination
assume it doesn't, because the industry has no such habit
Ask whether the verifier can actually separate a strong model from a weak one — if two very different models land on the same score, the task is noise
Watch for evals run under undisclosed conditions and for silent multi-candidate testing
Read "saturated at 80%" as possibly meaning "the last 20% is broken"
And remember what the benchmark is a proxy for: if the score is climbing while human eval is flat or falling, the score is the thing being optimized

data.name: When the target is taste, pay for human eval
guidelines: Don't mechanize domains that mechanical metrics can't reach: writing quality is too rich and nuanced for mechanical scoring, and LLM-as-judge fails because LLMs don't have good taste in writing — the same "can't extend the frontier from within it" limit that breaks AI-assisted task authoring

What works instead: recruit thousands of professional practitioners in the specific sub-domains (technical writers, poets, journalists, editors), run blind model comparisons rather than absolute scores, and aggregate into a leaderboard
Accept that this is expensive and budget for quality rather than for cost minimization

data.name: Benchmarks: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly (Ali Khial, G2i — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Ali Khial
G2i
data.brief: Engineering-talent company whose team spent the last two months defining a framework for authoring benchmark tasks; its "best engineers" are used as the human reference point for whether a benchmark prompt resembles real work, and its researchers did the task-level audits shown. `developer` is the closest enum fit — the schema has no "talent marketplace / services" type.

data.name: Benchmark anatomy (the five-stage reduction)
data.brief: Deliberately jargon-free decomposition arrived at after hitting "a wall of keywords" (graders, long horizon, verifiers, rubrics): a benchmark is a prompt/instruction fed to models and agents which produce solutions, verified and graded by verifiers and rubrics, all wrapped in a harness that isolates the run from external factors, emitting trajectories, scores and metadata used to rank models. Its analytic value is the implied conjunction: the equation only yields a meaningful ranking if every stage is sound, so a single weak stage (usually the prompt or the verifier) silently invalidates the score.

data.name: Leaky prompt
data.brief: Benchmark instruction that hands over the answer inside the task text — distinct from training-data contamination. Two observed shapes: the instruction points directly at the test file, so the model has everything it needs to implement against the tests rather than solve the problem; and the instruction specifies the complete interface of the intended implementation, locking the model out of any design freedom. Both convert a capability test into an instruction-following test.

data.name: Five principles for benchmark tasks (G2i)
data.brief: Vendor framework for authoring tasks: (1) human instructions — authored and reviewed by humans, expressing desired behaviors, objectives and hard constraints rather than implementation detail; (2) holistic graders — behavioral tests for broad surface plus precision where it matters (security, business logic get the full unit/integration/e2e stack; the rest doesn't need 100% coverage), mirroring how engineers actually test; (3) production grade — economically valuable tasks, judged by whether an engineer can say "if the LLM fixes this, I trust it to fix that"; (4) contamination-free by design — novel tasks only plus private hold-out sets, since today's benchmarks are drawn from public repos;
data.description: (5) informative leaderboards — the benchmark must tell a story and support a decision, surfacing the run data instead of only who won.

data.name: Leaderboard trust gap
data.brief: The demand-side consequence of benchmark quality problems: "I have not met an engineer in the last 6 months that would choose a model based on the leaderboards." Practitioners still read them for hype, then run their own tests and decide from those. Framed as quality gap to trust gap: the benchmarks kept their audience's attention but lost their decision authority.

data.name: Benchmark instructions don't resemble the work they claim to measure
data.brief: Benchmark instructions don't resemble the work they claim to measure. Measured: SWE-bench Pro averages 481 words per instruction — "that's a two-pager per task. That is not how people write prompts." Validated socially: three of G2i's best engineers were shown a benchmark prompt and all said they would never write one like it. Three failure shapes shown from real tasks: the leaky prompt that points straight at the test file; the leaky prompt that hands over the complete interface, "basically locking the LLM from any kind of creativity"; and the not-economically-valuable prompt — well-formed and properly abstracted, but asking the agent to build a C compiler in Rust (SWE-Marathon).
data.description: The task-authoring principle that follows: instructions should express desired behaviors, objectives and hard constraints, not implementation detail.

data.name: SWE-bench Pro accepts ~8.5% wrong and rejects ~24% correct implementations
data.brief: Quantified verifier unreliability, read off Datacurve's published DeepSWE-vs-SWE-bench-Pro comparison: SWE-bench Pro accepts wrong implementations on ~8.5% of tasks and rejects correct implementations on ~24%. Khial then pulled individual tasks to see why: one test asserts the existence of a variable that is (a) never specified in the instruction and (b) named in a way no LLM would independently choose — "cornering the LLM" into a false negative; another tests unexported functions, which he says would be rejected outright as a PR in G2i's own projects. That is what a weak verifier looks like at task level, not at aggregate level.

data.name: Reward-hacking rates rise with each model version while benchmarks fail to prevent it
data.brief: Models are getting measurably better at going around tasks — hunting for .git folders, searching the internet for traces of the solution — instead of patching the code, and the charts shown put the reward-hacking delta rising with each successive model version. Khial's framing is pointedly not a complaint about models: "that's what we want. We want LLMs to be smart. The benchmarks are lagging behind and they're not preventing it." The defect is assigned to benchmark construction, not to model alignment.

data.name: No engineer has picked a model from a leaderboard in six months
data.brief: Practitioner-market testimony from a company whose business is engineers: "I have not met an engineer in the last 6 months that would choose a model based on the leaderboards." They look, register the hype, then move on and test for themselves. Stated as the terminal consequence of everything before it — "there's a quality gap and it's causing a trust gap." The decision authority benchmarks were built to carry has already left them, while their attention share has not.

data.name: A second vendor publishes a five-principle benchmark-task construction framework
data.brief: A second vendor publishes a benchmark-task construction framework within weeks of the first: human-authored, human-reviewed, objective-level instructions; holistic graders (behavioral coverage plus precision where security and business logic demand it, explicitly modelled on the unit/integration/e2e testing pyramid rather than 100% coverage); production-grade tasks that are economically valuable; contamination-free by design via novel tasks and private hold-out sets; and informative leaderboards that "tell you why", exposing the run data instead of only the ranking.
data.description: Notable as convergence, not novelty: principles 1, 2 and 4 restate Datacurve's original-task-authoring and observable-behavior-verifier elements from an independent starting point (a talent company, two months of work, no ML background).

data.name: Task difficulty and task value are independent axes; the field optimized the wrong one
data.brief: Task difficulty and task value are independent axes, and the field has been optimizing the wrong one. "It is one thing to have a task that is failing the LLM, proving the LLM is not there yet. It is another thing for an engineer to look at a task and say: if the LLM is fixing this, I trust it to fix that." A benchmark's real output is transferred trust, so a task earns its place only if passing it licenses a real-world inference — which rules out both the artificially hard (build a C compiler in Rust) and the artificially easy-to-grade (string-matchable).
data.description: This is the same claim the trust gap measures from the other end: engineers stopped consulting leaderboards precisely because passing didn't license anything.

data.name: Benchmarks are ordinary software; the scarce input is engineering review, not ML expertise
data.brief: The jargon wall — graders, verifiers, long horizon, rubrics, harnesses — hides an ordinary five-stage software pipeline, and treating it as ordinary software is what surfaced the defects. A director with no ML background, working with his team for two months, reduced the field to five stages, opened individual tasks, and found leaked interfaces, tests asserting unstated variable names, and tests on unexported internals — the kinds of defects any senior engineer rejects in code review daily. The scarce input for fixing benchmarks is therefore engineering review, not ML expertise: "benchmarks are not hard. We need to look under the hood."

data.name: Author benchmark tasks like production engineering work
guidelines: Write and review instructions with humans, stating desired behavior, objectives and hard constraints — not implementation detail, and not so much detail that the task becomes self-contained
Grade holistically: behavioral tests for broad surface, full unit/integration/e2e precision only where it matters (security, business logic)
don't chase 100% coverage, and never assert on internals or names the instruction didn't specify
Make tasks production-grade and economically valuable — the acceptance test is an engineer saying "if the model fixes this, I trust it to fix that"
Make contamination structurally impossible: novel tasks only (everything mined from public repos is already compromised) plus private hold-out sets
Publish leaderboards that tell a story: expose the trajectory and run data behind the ranking, so a reader can act on it instead of digging for their own data points

data.name: Open the tasks and read them like a pull request
guidelines: Don't evaluate a benchmark from its leaderboard — pull individual tasks and read the prompt against the test
Does the instruction name the test file or hand over the interface? Then you're measuring instruction-following, not capability
Does the test assert names, variables or structures the instruction never stated? Then you're generating false negatives
Does it exercise unexported internals you'd reject in review? Same
Would you pay for this task to be done at all? Could the answer be recovered from .git or a web search instead of solved? Then measure how often models do exactly that
Finally, show the prompt to your own senior engineers and ask whether they'd ever write it — a benchmark whose prompts no working engineer would author is measuring a distribution that doesn't exist

data.name: Ending AI Slop (Thais Castello Branco, Taste Labs — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Thais Castello Branco
Taste Labs
data.brief: Came out of stealth "a few weeks" before the talk; mission stated as ending AI slop by decomposing subjective domains. Positions itself as the data and infrastructure layer for subjective domains across the stack, working in two directions: with frontier labs (evaluate and benchmark models, locate where they break, and decide which failures become RL environments vs post-training data problems) and with agent/application-layer companies (failures better solved by context and user-intent modelling than by the foundation model).
data.description: Operates a community of 1,000+ expert designers across mediums and styles. Explicit bet: billions of non-expert people are about to be creating, so understanding user intent matters as much as model improvement.

data.name: Subjective-domain decomposition
data.brief: Turning an unanswerable quality question into a verifiable one by decomposing it. "What is great design?" cannot be graded — it depends on audience, taste, situation, and it changes over time (what's good today differs from five years ago, unlike code or math). "Is this on brand?" can be graded, because a brand has already been decomposed by the designers who defined it: colors, typography, motion, animation, texture. Those components become codified ground truth. Key design property: the output is graded against the decomposition, not against the original artifact, so a genuinely new combination of the same components still passes.

data.name: Collapse to the mean (the mechanism of slop)
data.brief: Models predict the most likely next outcome and assume the most likely is the ideal. For math and code that holds — the average answer to "what is 2+2" is also the right and optimal one. For writing and design it fails: "a lot of greatness and creativity happens at the ends of the distribution... when you actively break from rules and from patterns." The pervasive feeling of slop is exactly this collapse plus repetition. Also afflicts the data side: preference data pooled from raters whose identities and reasons aren't modelled re-collapses to the mean, because genuine disagreement cancels instead of registering.

data.name: Verifiability routing
data.brief: The talk's stated single takeaway: treat a fuzzy capability as a routing problem. Decompose the domain into components arranged on an objective-to-subjective spectrum (vision alignment and typography near the objective end; style fit and creativity far from it), then route each component to the method that fits it — an RL environment where it can be made programmatically verifiable, post-training data where it can't, context and user-intent work at the application layer, and human judgment where it must stay human.
data.description: Codification is the lever that moves a component leftward: brand adherence starts as human-judgment territory and gets pulled "into the realm of verification" by identifying which pieces matter and making them observable.

data.name: Preference vector (multi-preference data)
data.brief: Attaching a modelled preference profile to the person a preference datum came from, so pluralism survives aggregation. Premise: "the world is multi-preference" — two people preferring different styles are not evidence that one is wrong, and the best answer is not the average of what they like. Without rater identity, context and reasons, preference collection produces datasets whose internal contradictions read as noise; with it, the same contradictions become a matching problem the model can learn.

data.name: Expert disagreement as diagnostic
data.brief: Human-QA rule for subjective data: run consensus checks, then interpret disagreement by attribute. Experts disagreeing on something objective — alignment, for instance — indicates a flaw in the data; experts disagreeing on style or aesthetics is good data, evidence of a real distinction in what people like. So consensus is used intentionally and per-attribute: screening for fundamentals on the objective components, preserving divergence on the subjective ones instead of averaging it away.

data.name: Grounded expert commentary
data.brief: Two measurable quality controls for subjective annotation. Specificity: the precision of an expert's language when asked to say why something is good or bad predicts how rich and high-signal the data point is, so specificity is scored rather than assumed. Code-linking: models struggle to connect a rendered visual to the source that produced it, so tying each critique to the exact code component it refers to (rather than accepting a free paragraph about a landing page) yields "data that is way less noisy and way more clear".

data.name: Capability follows measurability: code got solved because code decomposes
data.brief: Vendor thesis with a causal claim attached: AI got good at coding and math and stayed "super behind" on design, creative writing, personality and emotional intelligence — and the reason is not model architecture but the domains themselves. Capability follows measurability. Code decomposes, executes and verifies, so it was trainable; "we've made them great at coding, but realistically it's actually a fact about code." Subjective domains have three properties that break the loop: there is no single right answer, "great" is contextual (the same slide is excellent for a startup and inappropriate for a finance firm), and the standard changes over time in a way math and code do not.
data.description: Corollary the business is built on: solve the measurability problem and a large fraction of the domain follows.

data.name: Brand adherence converts a subjective capability into a gradeable RL environment
data.brief: Worked mechanism for converting a subjective capability into an RL environment. "Is this good?" is ungradeable; "is this on brand?" becomes gradeable because a brand is already a decomposed artifact — the colors, typography, motion, animation and textures that a company's designers defined deliberately, with reasons. Those components become the ground truth; an agent is tasked to build a net-new page adhering to the brand, and the output is graded against the decomposition rather than against the original, so novel-but-valid combinations pass instead of being penalized for not replicating.
data.description: Stated construction lesson: for subjective domains, task design is the hard part, not reward design — and LLM-as-judge applied directly to "is this on brand" is unreliable (reward hacking, characteristic hallucination patterns).

data.name: Slop is mode collapse: the most likely output treated as the ideal
data.brief: A definition of slop with a mechanism: models predict the most likely continuation and treat the most likely as ideal. That identity holds for arithmetic and code, where the average answer is also the correct one, and fails for writing and design, where "a lot of greatness and creativity happens at the ends of the distribution... when you actively break from rules and from patterns". The felt ubiquity of slop is that collapse plus repetition.
data.description: Consequence for method: the fix is not only higher-quality data but deliberately forcing the distribution back out — forcing true expert distributions across mediums and styles when decomposing a problem, and treating pattern-breaking as an intentional objective rather than an artifact.

data.name: Unmodelled rater identity makes preference data collapse to the mean a second time
data.brief: Data-side restatement of the same failure: preference data historically collected from a pool of raters "without necessarily understanding who they are, what they like, why they like it, when they like it" collapses to the mean a second time, because genuine disagreement cancels into noise. The fixes are all identity- and attribute-aware: attach a preference vector to each rater so the dataset expresses pluralism as a matching problem; force expert-distribution coverage deliberately (a 1,000+ designer community across mediums and styles); and interpret consensus per attribute — disagreement on alignment means the data is flawed, disagreement on style or aesthetics is good data showing a
data.description: real distinction in preference.

data.name: A data supplier gets no attribution from labs, so it optimizes what it can measure
data.brief: Data-economics testimony from a supplier to frontier labs, with an unusual admission: when working with labs "we oftentimes don't get that feedback loop of exactly what affected this" — attribution from data to model behavior does not come back — which is precisely why the firm optimizes the variables it can measure on its own side: problem decomposition, strictness of expert selection, specificity of the expert's language as a quality proxy, code-linked critique, and human QA. Stated recommendation for subjective domains: quality over quantity — expensive, deep, high-taste data "yields far better results than getting a bunch of noisy data".

data.name: Model competence is a property of domains, not of models
data.brief: The industry reads model competence as a property of models; it is better read as a property of domains. Code decomposes, executes and verifies — so code got solved. Everything that resists decomposition is still open, and will stay open until someone does the measurement engineering. That reframes the subjective frontier as a construction problem with a defined method: decompose the domain, find the components that are already codified somewhere (a brand book is a design domain that experts already decomposed and wrote down), make them observable, and route what remains.
data.description: It also predicts where progress will come from — not from a better base model, but from whoever can drag more of a fuzzy domain leftward into verifiability.

data.name: Ending slop means engineering pluralism back into every stage of the pipeline
data.brief: For subjective domains the optimization target itself is wrong, and the pipeline compounds the error at every stage: mean-seeking generation produces the most likely output, undifferentiated preference collection averages away the disagreement that carried the signal, and LLM judges reward fluency. Each stage is individually reasonable and collectively manufactures the exact thing everyone is trying to remove. So "ending slop" is not a quality-raising exercise — it is engineering pluralism back into the pipeline: model who the rater is, force distribution coverage, preserve aesthetic disagreement, and keep human judgment on the components that must stay human.

data.name: Decompose the fuzzy thing until it grades itself
guidelines: Don't ask "is this great?" — ask what "great" is composed of for a specific audience at a specific time

Look first for artifacts where the decomposition already exists and was done with care: a brand definition is a design domain that professionals already broke into colors, typography, motion, texture and reasons
Make that decomposition the ground truth
Then design the task so the output is graded against the components, not against the reference artifact, or you'll train replication instead of capability

Arrange the components on an objective-to-subjective spectrum and route: programmatic verification and RL environments for what you codified, post-training data for what you couldn't, context and user-intent work at the app layer, human judgment for the rest
Expect task design — not reward design — to be the hard part, and don't put a raw LLM judge on the subjective components (reward hacking and hallucination patterns are already known there)

data.name: Collect preference data that doesn't average itself away
guidelines: Know who your raters are, what they like and why — then attach that profile to every datum, so the dataset expresses a multi-preference world rather than a contradictory one
Force the distribution deliberately: select experts across mediums and styles so coverage is a controlled variable, not an accident of recruiting

QC on measurable properties rather than vibes — score the specificity of an expert's reasoning as a proxy for signal richness, and tie each critique to the exact code component it refers to, because models can't reliably connect a rendered visual back to its source

Run human QA in two passes: screen the objective fundamentals (spec adherence, alignment), then run expert consensus and read the disagreements by attribute — divergence on objective attributes means bad data, divergence on aesthetics means you found a real preference boundary and should keep it
And prefer depth to volume: high-taste expert data beats large noisy datasets in these domains

data.name: fighting slop with slop (Vaibhav Gupta, Boundary — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Vaibhav Gupta
Boundary
data.brief: Builds BAML, a programming language started ~3 years ago ("something that has absolutely no room for slop... you have to be correct"). Team of eight; ships with no code reviews, mandatory parallel work, and no standardization of AI tooling. Claim made on record: building a stable programming language would classically have taken "hundreds of thousands to tens of thousands of man-hours" and more than two years with more than eight people — and one engineer wrote a partial C compiler in BAML "just yesterday".

data.name: BAML (Boundary)
data.brief: Boundary's programming language, positioned as a from-first-principles substrate for a world where humans write no code. Demonstrated properties: inferred, exhaustively-checked error types; zero-cost per-file execution tracing; every function auto-exposed as a CLI command and bundleable into a standalone cross-platform/WASM binary; and callability from any host language (Python, TypeScript, Rust, Go, Ruby, Java, "anything new that comes up") with type-safe sync and async bindings and lambdas, closures and generics passed across the language boundary. No function coloring. Gloss from the talk: "basically a made-up language".

data.name: Slop as unread code
data.brief: Working definition: "slop is just any code you don't read" — a property of human attention, not of output quality — paired with the framing device repeated twice: "this is the least amount of slop your codebase will ever have. Cherish it." Consequence: the question is no longer whether generated code is reviewed but where to spend a fixed, shrinking review budget, and the tooling job is to make unread code safe rather than to make more of it read. Its demo form is opt-in comprehension: zoom into a visualized program, expand the parts you care about, and declare the rest "too much slop — let that be slop".

data.name: architecture.md (invariant-only agent guidance)
data.brief: A deliberately tiny, model-agnostic architecture.md instead of CLAUDE.md — "pick something every model can just understand" — containing only what will not change for months or years (in Boundary's case, the layers of the compiler), plus one procedural rule: work deeper in the compiler requires talking to at least one other person, which intentionally slows that work down. Adopted as the alternative to standardizing on tools: "the hard part about hiring great engineers is you sadly can't tell them what to do", so the invariant lives in the repo rather than in a policy.

data.name: Design-doc system (writing as the reviewed artifact)
data.brief: In-house replacement for Notion + GitHub for design docs — versioning, commenting — backed by plain markdown files and CLI scripts so agents can operate it like GitHub without being GitHub. Paired with a Slack integration that broadcasts every doc update, which became the company's most-read channel ("at 2 a.m. someone shipped a new design doc, three people started reading it right away"). Governing rule: "code can be slop, writing cannot." Failure and fix recorded honestly: the founder hit "a little bit of AI psychosis", shipped 10 design docs a day, and the team started fighting his slop — so a final rule was added, that shipping a doc requires recruiting people to actually read it, after
data.description: which doc quality rose sharply.

data.name: Architecture invariants in CI
data.brief: A visualized internal (plus some external) dependency graph with semantic boundaries and individual packages, and CLI tools that assert invariants over it inside CI. When an agent adds a leaky dependency or a package that violates a boundary, CI or a git-commit diff shows exactly where it broke — so architectural drift is caught mechanically rather than in code review. Reported outcome: architecture unchanged for three to four months while the codebase kept moving.

data.name: Agent-trace-driven language design
data.brief: Boundary's loop for designing the language itself: agents run continuously writing BAML programs from scratch; the full agent transcripts (tool calls, errors, retries) are then inspected — by humans and, more importantly, by other agents — for what worked and what didn't, including efficiency defects invisible to a test suite ("what took three tool calls when it should have only taken one"). Humans triage which findings are real, which are hallucinations and which "don't have taste"; agents then author the fixes.
data.description: The final step is the point: candidate language features and skills are A/B tested on tool calls consumed, errors produced and correct outcomes, so "you can start building data-driven systems without ever writing a single line of code".

data.name: Zero-cost execution tracing
data.brief: Language-level premise that in a world where nobody reads all the code, the execution trace is the comprehension surface — including where time was spent in which part of the program. Argued to be impossible to retrofit ("think about how slow your program would be if you had to trace everything in Python or TypeScript — it's untenable") and effectively free if designed in from first principles. Built for two consumers at once: humans, and agents — every file carries a tracing system Claude can navigate to find bugs, errors and inefficiencies and optimize the code itself.

data.name: Agent-first tooling
data.brief: Tooling designed for agent consumers rather than for humans, contrasted explicitly with decades of IDE tooling built for people. Three demonstrated shapes: describe-a-symbol replacing ripgrep — `describe calculate` returns docstrings, the actual source, and every place it's used, for local and external libraries, collapsing several tool calls (and a web search) into one; every function immediately runnable as a CLI command with its parameters attached, so an agent can execute rather than infer; and standalone bundled binaries for any target (Windows, Mac, Linux, WASM) so agents never handle deployment.
data.description: Rationale from the speaker's own training: "the code is always the source of truth. The docs may lie, the readme will definitely lie, but the code cannot lie".

data.name: Inferred, exhaustively-checked error types
data.brief: Errors as types inferred and propagated up the call graph without annotation: `divide` throws a division-by-zero error, so `calculate` (which calls it) knows it throws it, and so does everything above. The compiler can then prove whether an error is handled — an API declared never to throw fails to compile while an unhandled error remains, and catching it makes the guarantee provable. Contrast drawn with what agents actually do in existing languages: nest try/catch inside try/catch until they give up and console.log("some error happened").
data.description: Framing: "the type system never lies... the absolute center of truth that prevents invariants from entering your codebase", and "code is a matter of trust — the reason we don't use LLM code blindly is that the systems underneath don't have enough rigidity".

data.name: An eight-person team ships a production language with no code reviews
data.brief: An eight-person team has shipped a production programming language for three years with no code reviews, mandatory parallel work, and zero standardization of how engineers use AI. The substitutes are structural rather than procedural: a tiny invariant-only architecture.md any model can read (plus a rule that deeper compiler work requires talking to a human), CI-enforced architecture invariants over a semantic dependency graph, and a design-doc culture where prose — not diffs — is the reviewed artifact. Stated principle: you can't tell great engineers what tools to use, so put the invariant in the repo instead of in a policy.

data.name: Code can be slop, writing cannot: review capacity moves from diffs to design docs
data.brief: "Code can be slop, writing cannot." Boundary built a design-doc tool (versioning, comments, markdown + CLI underneath so agents can drive it) and then a Slack integration broadcasting every update — which became the company's most popular channel within days, with people reading new docs at 2 a.m. because "the most interesting stuff is design docs that are not going to change". The failure mode arrived immediately and from the founder: he shipped 10 design docs a day ("a little bit of AI psychosis") until the team was fighting his slop, which forced the final rule — shipping a design doc requires recruiting people to actually read it — after which doc quality rose sharply.
data.description: Review capacity is the scarce resource, and it was deliberately moved from code to prose.

data.name: Language features are A/B tested on agent tool calls, errors and outcomes
data.brief: Boundary designs its language from agent telemetry: agents continuously write BAML programs from scratch, other agents mine the full transcripts — tool calls, errors, what happened — for defects, including efficiency defects no test suite reports ("what took three tool calls when it should have only taken one"); humans triage which findings are real, hallucinated, or "don't have taste"; agents then write the fixes. The decisive step is the last one: candidate language features are A/B tested on tool calls consumed, errors produced and correct outcomes, so language design becomes measurable rather than a matter of opinion — "you can start building data-driven systems without ever writing a
data.description: single line of code".

data.name: The languages agents write in were designed for human productivity and bake in slop
data.brief: The talk's contrarian claim: the process fixes work, and we still lose the war, because the foundations are broken. TypeScript's design goal balances correctness against human productivity; JavaScript's coercion and its sort-by-string-conversion are "slop baked into the language"; and each successive layer (CoffeeScript, TypeScript, the next one) patches a substrate that was already wrong. "There are things you would never do in a programming language at the very core layer if you were designing for a world where humans never wrote a single line of code." Closing call: "I think we need a new Git, I think we need a new database, and yes, I think we need a new programming language."

data.name: With code unread by design, comprehension relocates to visualization and traces
data.brief: With code unread by design, comprehension is relocated to two surfaces. Visualization: a zoomable map of a program where clicking navigates to the exact lines, so a reader opts into which parts to understand and explicitly declares the rest "too much slop — let that be slop". Execution traces: per-file tracing at (claimed) zero performance cost, showing exactly how much time was spent in which part of the program, and navigable by Claude as well as by humans so the agent can locate bugs, errors and inefficiencies and optimize without being told. The generalization offered: the goal was never reading all the code, it was understanding the system, and tools can deliver that directly.

data.name: A new language ships as callable from every existing one, so nobody rewrites
data.brief: The migration answer to "nobody will rewrite their code in your new language", designed two years ago: BAML functions are callable from within any existing language — Python, TypeScript, Rust, Go, Ruby, Java, "anything new that comes up even after it" — fully type-safe, with a sync and an async variant of every function (no function coloring), and lambdas, closures and generics passing across the boundary so "engineers don't have to go fuss with it".
data.description: The stated payoff for agents: the type system never lies, so it becomes the center of truth preventing broken invariants from entering the codebase, regardless of which language the agent is writing in. Evidence of reach: one engineer built a partial C compiler in BAML the day before the talk.

data.name: You cannot out-review generated code, so the leverage moves into the substrate
data.brief: You cannot out-review generated code, and the amount of unread code in your codebase only goes up from here — so the leverage moves down a layer, into the substrate the code is written in. A compiler that infers and proves error handling, CI that fails on a violated architectural invariant, a trace on every file, and a symbol description that answers in one call are all the same move: making unread code safe rather than making more of it read.
data.description: Followed to its end, the argument indicts the whole foundation — languages, Git, databases were designed to maximize human productivity, and every system built on them inherits the compromises. The talk's ask is that the bravest of the audience go rebuild those layers for agent authors.

data.name: Abolishing code review relocated review rather than removing it
data.brief: Abolishing code review did not abolish review — it relocated it to where humans still add signal: design docs (broadcast, and mandatory to have readers), architectural invariants (asserted once, enforced by CI forever), and triage of agent-found issues into real / hallucinated / tasteless. The counterintuitive result is more process, not less, and the analogy offered is CI itself: teams that refused it because "it would slow us down" did slow down for three months and then moved much faster. "Our processes have to evolve if we're going to ship at agent speed" — the cost of the new process is paid up front, in the same shape as the old one.

data.name: Replace code review with invariants, writing and CI
guidelines: Don't standardize the AI tooling — you can't tell good engineers what to use, and the standard will be obsolete anyway

Standardize the invariant instead: one very small, model-agnostic architecture.md (not CLAUDE.md) containing only what won't change for months or years, plus an escalation rule for the parts of the system where mistakes are expensive ("go deeper into the compiler, talk to at least one other person")

Encode architecture mechanically — visualize the dependency graph with semantic boundaries, and write CLI checks in CI that fail when an agent adds a leaky dependency or breaks a boundary, so drift shows up in a commit rather than in review

Then move the review budget to prose: a versioned design-doc tool backed by markdown and CLI scripts so agents can drive it, a channel that broadcasts every update, and the rule that shipping a doc obliges you to recruit readers — without that rule, one enthusiastic person floods the team

data.name: Design your tools from agent transcripts, then A/B test the changes
guidelines: Keep agents continuously building things from scratch with your tool or language, and keep the whole transcript, not just the outcome — the tool calls are where the design defects are
Have agents read those transcripts for two classes of finding: correctness (what was wrong) and efficiency (what took three tool calls and should have taken one)
Put humans on triage only — which findings are real, which are hallucinations, which just lack taste — then let agents write the fixes
Most importantly, don't guess which feature or skill helped: A/B test candidates on tool calls consumed, errors produced and correct outcomes, and let the numbers decide

data.name: Build the tools for the agent, not the IDE user
guidelines: Replace grep-shaped search with one call that answers the question: `describe <symbol>` returning the docstrings, the actual source, and every use site — for external libraries too, so the agent never web-searches for API behavior

Make every function immediately executable as a CLI command with its parameters attached, and let any set of them bundle into a standalone binary for every target (including WASM), so agents never deal with deployment differences
Build tracing into the substrate at zero cost and make it navigable by the agent, so it can find its own bugs and slow paths rather than being told about them
And design error handling so the compiler proves it: infer error types up the call graph and check exhaustively, so "this API never throws" is a guarantee rather than a hope

data.name: Persona Engineering: A Field Guide to AI Synthetic Personas (Ishan Anand, InsightSci — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Ishan Anand
InsightSci (Insight Sciences)
data.brief: Constructs LLM synthetic personas for market-research and market-insights teams; positions synthetic personas as complementary to human research rather than a replacement, and the product endpoint as turning a client's human research data into "a living, queryable asset". Name form uncertain — captions say "Insight Sciences" and give the domain as "insightssciences.ai"; the talk metadata says InsightSci.

data.name: Simulmatics
data.brief: Historical control case (1960s), extensively documented by Jill Lepore: promised to simulate and predict the electorate from raw statistics and the computational power of the day, and did not deliver. Invoked as the reason to approach synthetic-persona claims "with some humility" — the difference claimed today is not just more compute but better modelling via LLMs. Defunct historical firm; `research` is the closest enum fit.

data.name: Synthetic persona
data.brief: An LLM steered to respond as a particular person or segment and then used as a survey respondent — companies test product concepts and messaging against panels of them. Grew directly out of ordinary role prompting ("you are a ___, now do this task") into a funded category with visible market momentum (headlines plus rising funding over recent years). The talk's governing frame: a synthetic persona is a forecast, not a person — like weather forecasting it was unlocked by compute plus data, it operates inside a regime beyond which it stops being accurate, and it is trustworthy only where validated against reality.

data.name: Latent-confounder invention
data.brief: The first and most fundamental persona failure mode: when context is missing, the model invents it, so parts of the experiment that should be held fixed silently become random variables. Documented case: asked about willingness to purchase at varying prices, humans slope downward as basic economic theory predicts, while LLMs produce an inverted-U — purchase probability rising with price over part of the range — because the model reads price as a proxy for unstated properties (expiry date, competitors' prices) that human respondents held fixed.
data.description: "If it's a poorly grounded persona, it's a little like the LLM is playing improv with you — gold watch on a table? We must be in a jewelry store." The fix inverts human-subject practice: paint the whole world in the prompt, including the study's own construction, which you would deliberately hide from a human participant.

data.name: Persona durability testing
data.brief: Stress-testing a persona for prompt sensitivity before trusting its answers, because sensitivity can exceed signal: in one study the same question with the same options but the order of the choices swapped produced such a strong order bias that averaging the two runs washed out to 50/50 noise. Humans have a first-order bias too, "but not to this extent". The discipline: test personas under reorderings, rewordings, and adversarial challenges to their stated opinions, and treat instability as a property of the instrument rather than of the respondent.

data.name: Attitude/behavior gap
data.brief: LLMs are trained on what people say, not what people do, so stated attitudes are easier to predict than actions. Evidence: across replicated social-science studies an LLM matched expert forecasters overall, but the two study families separate cleanly — surveys (natively language, measuring attitudes) are predicted well, field experiments (behaviors, which must be transcribed into text before they can enter training data) noticeably worse. Practical rule given to clients: build questions that triangulate to behavior from attitudes — to learn about gym attendance, ask about attitudes toward working out and test whether that proxies.

data.name: Semantic-anchor scoring
data.brief: Elicitation technique that recovers distributions instead of point estimates. Rather than forcing a persona onto a 1-5 purchase-intent scale (a format LLMs aren't used to producing), let it answer in free text — its native format — e.g. "I'm somewhat interested. If it works well and isn't too expensive, I might give it a try." Then have humans write anchor texts for each scale point ("Hell no, I'll never buy that" ...
data.description: "Absolutely, I'll buy 20"), measure semantic similarity between the model's text and the anchors, and read off a probability distribution over the scale. Result reported: the technique reconstructed not only accurate willingness-to-pay values but the shape of the distribution, which naive rating prompts flatten.

data.name: Subpop-style distribution fine-tuning
data.brief: Fine-tuning a model against known human response distributions: prompt template = demographic information + the survey question; compare the model's output distribution to the real human distribution; fine-tune until they align. The notable result is transfer — alignment improved on the populations supplied (expected) and nearly as much on unseen groups (not). Interpretation offered, with subsequent research cited as support: the model already holds a latent understanding of these groups and simply didn't know how to express it in survey format, so fine-tuning taught it the task, not the content.
data.description: "Your persona is in there; we just need to figure out how to summon it." Paper name from captions ("the Subpop paper").

data.name: Human noise floor
data.brief: Measurement discipline that sets the ceiling on any human-alignment score. In the field's best-known demonstration (~1,000 people interviewed for ~2.5 hours each, then put through personality tests and surveys; transcripts handed to agents that took the same battery), the headline 83% agent-human alignment is normalized against the humans' own consistency — the same people were brought back two weeks later and were only ~80% self-consistent.
data.description: Where re-testing humans isn't possible, approximate it: split the human ground-truth data in half, treat one half as "synthetic", measure the correlation, and repeat hundreds or thousands of times to estimate the floor. Corollary: because a persona is a forecast, re-running it does not buy certainty — a thousand rain gauges improve an estimate of today's rainfall, a thousand reruns of tomorrow's forecast improve only your estimate of what the model says.

data.name: Distribution-alignment metrics
data.brief: Evaluating personas as a comparison of distributions, not as right/wrong scoring: "unlike classic evals where there's clearly a right and wrong and you can score how many were right, now we need to measure the data as a comparison of distributions." Distributions fail in more than one way — wildly off, or (the common and dangerous case) average right and shape wrong, with the variation muddled into the middle — so use multiple metrics: a correlation-type metric plus a distribution-shape metric. Also: more synthetic samples do not confer statistical significance, so an underrepresented population can be extended but not made significant.

data.name: Generative agent-based modeling
data.brief: Named forward direction: rather than querying personas independently, simulate a population of them interacting — dynamics between personas rather than isolated responses — as the path to turning static human research data into "a living, queryable asset". Thin: named and framed in the closing minute, with "we didn't get time for this"; coined because it is the field's stated next step and connects the persona cluster to the corpus's simulation material.

data.name: Synthetic personas harden from role prompting into a funded market category
data.brief: Role prompting has hardened into a market category: companies now test product concepts and messaging against panels of synthetic respondents, with press coverage and rising funding over the last few years cited as evidence of momentum, and vendors (including the speaker's) selling persona construction to market-research and insights teams. The capability claim rests on a well-known demonstration — ~1,000 people interviewed for ~2.5 hours each plus a battery of personality tests and surveys, transcripts handed to agents that then took the same battery, yielding ~83% alignment with the corresponding humans (normalized).
data.description: Historical control offered by the speaker himself: Simulmatics made the same promise about simulating the electorate in the 1950s-60s on raw statistics and failed, "so you should approach claims like this with some humility" — what's different now is not only compute but a new modelling medium, since LLMs let you simulate in language rather than in equations, for phenomena (how we feel, how we act, what we choose) that never succumbed to formulas.

data.name: Anything left unspecified in a synthetic experiment becomes a random variable
data.brief: Measured failure mode with an economic tell: on a willingness-to-purchase test where price is the manipulated variable, a recruited human panel produced the downward-sloping curve basic economic theory predicts, while the LLM personas produced an inverted U — purchase probability increasing with price across part of the range. Follow-up experiments traced it to the model using price as a proxy for properties the humans held fixed (expiration date, competitors' prices).
data.description: The general principle: in a human experiment the environment is fixed and the participant is the random variable; in a synthetic experiment, anything you failed to specify also becomes a random variable, because the model has no universe outside the prompt. The corrective inverts standard research practice — you must describe the study's own construction to the participant, which you would never do with a human.

data.name: Option-order bias and behavior blindness bound what personas can be trusted for
data.brief: Two further failure modes that bound what personas can be trusted for. Prompt sensitivity: presenting the same question with the same two options in swapped order produced an order bias so strong that averaging the two runs collapsed the result to 50/50 noise — humans show a first-order bias, "but not to this extent" — so personas must be durability-tested under reorderings, rewordings and adversarial challenge. Behavior blindness: LLMs are trained on what people say, not what they do, so across a set of replicated social-science studies the model matched expert forecasters on surveys (natively text, measuring attitudes) and did measurably worse on field experiments (behaviors, which must be transcribed into text to enter the training data at all).
data.description: Working rule: triangulate toward behavior through attitudes rather than asking about behavior directly.

data.name: The persona is already in the model; the problem is elicitation and format
data.brief: Three techniques converge on one finding: the persona is already inside the model and the engineering problem is elicitation and format, not knowledge. (1) Prompting works and always has — the seminal early work used a text-completion model with "I am a strong liberal... in 2016 I voted for ___" and sampled the completions. (2) Fine-tuning against known human distributions (Subpop) improved alignment on the supplied populations and nearly as much on unseen groups, which subsequent research reads as the model having a latent representation of those groups and simply lacking the survey task format — "LLMs aren't used to doing surveys".
data.description: (3) The strongest result comes from asking in the model's native format: let the persona answer in free text, then map that text to a 1-5 scale by semantic similarity to human-written anchor texts, which reconstructs not just the right value but the distribution shape that naive rating prompts flatten. Counter-finding in the same set: more persona detail is not monotonically better — one team's four increasingly elaborate persona constructions for voting patterns amplified model bias and moved results progressively further from reality.

data.name: You cannot buy statistical significance by re-running a synthetic persona
data.brief: Measurement discipline that the vendor's own clients resist: you cannot use synthetic personas to buy statistical significance. You can extend an underrepresented population and get more values out of it, but reruns of a forecast with unchanged inputs improve your estimate of the model, not the accuracy of the forecast — a thousand rain gauges measure today's rainfall better; a thousand reruns of tomorrow's forecast do not.
data.description: What must be done instead: validate against what humans actually said, as a comparison of distributions rather than a right/wrong score (distributions fail by being wildly off, and more insidiously by getting the average right while muddling the variance into the middle), using at least one correlation metric plus one shape metric; and estimate the noise floor of the ground truth itself — the well-known 83% result is normalized against humans being only ~80% self-consistent when re-tested two weeks later, and where you can't re-test humans you can approximate the floor by repeatedly splitting the human data in half and correlating one half against the other.

data.name: Agent-mediated purchase decisions make human-only market research stale
data.brief: Market-structure claim used to argue personas and human research are complementary rather than rival: "we're entering an era where humans are no longer the sole economic actor." Every action a human customer takes — awareness, consideration, the purchase decision itself — is increasingly mediated by AI agents, so a human-only study is no longer the ground truth; what needs measuring is the human-plus-agent ecosystem.
data.description: Second argument in the same move: the realistic alternative to a synthetic persona is usually not human research but no research or somebody's opinion — the question you needed answered two months after the survey shipped gets answered by extrapolation from whoever is in the room, and expert-plus-persona beats that. Forward direction named: generative agent-based modeling, simulating populations of personas interacting, turning static human research into a living queryable asset.

data.name: Synthetic personas are forecasts, so validate like a forecaster not a pollster
data.brief: The whole field is better understood through weather forecasting than through polling. Both were unlocked by compute plus data; both are accurate only inside a regime and degrade predictably past it; both are trustworthy exactly to the degree they've been validated against what actually happened. Adopting that frame changes the methodology outright: you validate like a forecaster (compare distributions against what humans actually said, estimate the noise in your ground truth) rather than like a pollster (add samples until it's significant), and you accept that re-running the model improves your estimate of the model, never the accuracy of the forecast.
data.description: It also sets a ceiling nobody can engineer past — the humans being modelled are only ~80% consistent with themselves two weeks later, so "83% aligned" is a number about a noisy target, not about a solved problem.

data.name: Persona work is elicitation engineering, and more detail can amplify bias
data.brief: Across grounding, prompting, fine-tuning and scoring, the same result keeps appearing: the model already contains the persona, and every technique that works is a way of getting it out in a format the model wasn't trained to produce — or of preventing it from filling in a gap you left. Fine-tuning on some populations improves unseen ones because it teaches the survey task, not the groups; asking for free text and mapping it onto a scale beats asking for the scale directly; grounding works by removing the model's licence to invent.
data.description: And the corollary that stops this from being a "more context is better" story: richer persona construction amplified model bias in at least one study, moving reconstructions further from reality as detail increased — so the discipline is calibration against ground truth, not elaboration.

data.name: Paint the entire world in the prompt
guidelines: The model has no universe other than what's in the prompt, so anything you leave unspecified becomes a random variable in your experiment rather than a fixed part of the environment
Ground the persona richly in personality and context and — inverting human-subject practice — in the study's own construction, which you would deliberately hide from a human participant
Watch for the tell: a response curve that violates basic theory (purchase probability rising with price) usually means the model has recruited an unstated variable as a proxy
And don't assume more detail is safer — test whether added specification improves alignment or amplifies the model's own bias, because at least one careful team found the latter

data.name: Validate like a forecaster, not like a pollster
guidelines: Always validate against known human ground truth, and measure distributions rather than accuracy: report a correlation-type metric and a shape metric, because the common failure is getting the average right while the variance muddles into the middle

Estimate the noise floor of your ground truth before interpreting any score — ideally by bringing the same humans back and re-testing them (expect ~80% self-consistency), otherwise by splitting your human data in half, treating one half as synthetic, correlating, and repeating hundreds of times
Don't buy significance with sample count: re-running a forecast with unchanged inputs sharpens your estimate of the model, not of reality

Finally, durability-test the persona under reordered options, reworded questions and adversarial pushback on its stated opinions, and prefer questions that triangulate toward behavior from attitudes over questions that ask about behavior directly

data.name: Ask in text, score in distributions
guidelines: Don't force a persona onto a rating scale — surveys are a task format LLMs aren't practiced at, and the constraint flattens exactly the variance you were trying to measure
Ask for free text ("I'm somewhat interested

if it works well and isn't too expensive I might try it"), have humans write anchor texts for each scale point from "hell no" to "absolutely, I'll buy 20", then score by semantic similarity to the anchors — which yields a probability distribution over the scale rather than a point estimate
Where the gap is format rather than knowledge, fine-tune against known human response distributions and expect transfer to groups you didn't supply
the persona is generally already in the model, so budget your effort on elicitation and calibration rather than on teaching it who the group is

data.name: Data Quality Is the Compute Multiplier (Ari Morcos, DatologyAI — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Ari Morcos
DatologyAI
data.brief: Data-curation company — "the oil refinery for data": does not source new tokens, takes existing public / proprietary / licensed tokens and improves them. Name "literally means the science or study of data". About half the team are researchers, because curation methodology is barely published ("a very strong disincentive not to share how you do this").

data.name: Thomson Reuters
data.brief: Named customer: owns proprietary high-quality legal data and a sophisticated in-house post-training harness; partnered with DatologyAI to mid-train a legal-reasoning model. `media` chosen from the enum (information services / legal publishing has no fit).

data.name: Data quality as a compute multiplier
data.brief: The talk's thesis: better data makes the learning curve steeper, so the same compute budget buys the performance of a far larger one — and the x-axis is interchangeable (data = compute = time = dollars). Mechanism stated as maximizing marginal information gain per data point — "the maximum signal per token and per batch" — rather than adding tokens. Stronger form, from the founding paper "Beyond Neural Scaling Laws": correct data selection bends the scaling law itself, changing the exponent, because you stop spending compute on redundant or unnecessary data. Observed multipliers in this talk: 145x (VLM), ~8x (multilingual), ~35x fewer inference flops per correct answer.

data.name: The four C's (clean, curate, create, compose)
data.brief: DatologyAI's pipeline model. Clean: heuristic filters (Gopher-style, dropping 10-character or all-whitespace documents) plus rigorous benchmark decontamination at a low n-gram threshold against all downstream benchmarks — table stakes because "benchmaxing has become a real problem and makes it very difficult to interpret model results". Curate: quality classifiers, topic taxonomy and balancing, redundancy reduction (dropping points that are semantically near-identical even when not byte-identical), up/down-sampling by quality and relevance, and task-distribution matching to the intended outputs.
data.description: Create: synthetic generation to grow a now-high-quality but too-small set. Compose: mixing sources and sequencing them across training stages — "table stakes that any large model is trained for at least three phases of data" — up to continuous curricula.

data.name: BeyondWeb
data.brief: DatologyAI's synthetic-data platform, built on rephrasing and designed to be applied to anyone's proprietary documents in their own environment. Worked example: a document about a corporate takeover converted into one of hundreds of templates (e.g. a series of true/false questions). Two claimed properties: no model collapse, because all information originates in the source document; and the student can exceed the rephrasing model, because the rephraser only has to transform the document accurately, not understand and teach the concepts — a much easier task.
data.description: Critical caveat: what you rephrase matters — rephrasing randomly selected documents does not work; rephrasing the high-quality ones does.

data.name: Mid-training / continued pre-training
data.brief: The stage between pre-training and post-training: continued training of an existing base model on a domain-shifted mix, at a fraction of the pre-training budget (here 100B tokens, under 1% of the pre-training budget). Two properties demonstrated: (1) domain capability rises without catastrophic forgetting — general capabilities also went up — provided the majority of the mid-training mix stays representative of the pre-training distribution and only some is domain-specific; (2) it multiplies the subsequent post-training gain rather than merely adding to it, because the starting policy is more accurate.

data.name: Small-run scaling prediction (hero-run derisking)
data.brief: Using two small curated dense runs to predict a much larger one: two dense Llama-style models trained on 1T tokens of curated data define a line that passes through a 17T-token, 50x-larger hypersparse model's actual result. Requires that you "simulate token scarcity appropriately" at the small scale so the small runs sit on the same curve. Consequence: a hero run can be derisked with 50-100x less compute before you commit to it.

data.name: Compute scarcity has labs capping and forward-selling frontier token access
data.brief: Dated market claim opening the talk: compute availability has become extremely scarce over the last six months and is getting worse. H100 prices reversed a multi-year decline and are ~40% above their end-of-2025 lows — abnormal for hardware. Demand side: reasoning models consume ~8x the tokens of non-reasoning models, projected to 5x again within about a year. Two consequences already visible: Google capped Meta's Gemini usage because of inference constraints, and OpenAI has effectively started selling token futures (guaranteed capacity some period forward).
data.description: Morcos's read is that forward-selling is only necessary because the labs genuinely think access to frontier API tokens may be limited — not as a business decision but because there is not enough inference and first-party products will be prioritized.

data.name: Curation alone pushes VLMs past the public Pareto frontier at 145x less compute
data.brief: Quantified curation-only result on vision-language models, with everything but the data held constant. Curating Mammoth (~25B tokens, the set used to train the fusion adapter between the text and vision towers) produced a +14 absolute percentage-point improvement over the same pipeline on the uncurated input. Against a Pareto frontier defined by the best public VLMs (Qwen 3 series, Qwen 3.5, InternVL), the curated models sit well beyond it — with no post-training at all — and roughly match Qwen 3.5 4B within about a percentage point while using 145x less training compute.
data.description: Second-order result: curation also produced more concise answers (the three curated models are the shortest-response models in the comparison set), so on a flops-per-response axis they beat the frontier again at ~35x fewer flops per correct answer.

data.name: Curating English data alone improves non-English performance
data.brief: Multilingual result plus a scientific finding. Result: on multilingual MMLU the curated models beat a Pareto frontier of Qwen and Liquid models and Cohere's best multilingual model, coming in slightly better than Qwen 3 at roughly 8x less compute budget — while only 8% of the training data was multilingual, with at most ~6B tokens in any non-English language. Finding: curating the English data alone improves non-English performance, and the size of that transfer is strongly correlated with the language's similarity to English; the reverse also holds (curating non-English helps English) but weaker.
data.description: Framed as an access argument — "I don't want to live in a future where only developed countries can access this very effectively" — because the internet is "an extremely biased view of the world that does not represent the world uniformly at all".

data.name: Mid-training on 100B tokens nearly tripled the delta from unchanged post-training
data.brief: Customer result from Thomson Reuters: an open-source base model mid-trained on 100B tokens (a mix of TR's proprietary legal data and public data, under 1% of the pre-training budget) gained ~5 percentage points on LegalBench — and general capabilities went up too, i.e. no catastrophic forgetting, which Morcos attributes to keeping the majority of the mix representative of the pre-training distribution. The larger finding: TR then ran its existing, unchanged post-training harness on the mid-trained checkpoint versus on the default instruction-tuned model, and the delta from post-training almost tripled — because the starting policy is more accurate.
data.description: Stated corollary: pre-training, mid-training and post-training should be run synergistically, not as three independent stages handed between teams.

data.name: A fully open frontier-competitive model was built for under $20M total
data.brief: Cost-floor claim for a frontier-competitive open model. Arcee AI's Trinity Large: 17 trillion tokens curated from public datasets only — no proprietary data, no closed-model usage ("no asking Claude to do this for you") — producing a fully open, US-made model that is competitive with the open frontier, matching GLM 5 and Kimi on many tasks and outperforming Claude on a couple. The team had not trained a model before the middle of last year.
data.description: Total cost, "across salaries, across compute, across R&D, across everything... including all the repetitions" and several other models besides this one: under $20M. Explicit rebuttal: "if I want to customize a model it's going to cost hundreds of millions of dollars — that's just not true", with high-six-figures-to-low-millions cited for a narrow-domain model and $20M framed as the upper bound because Trinity is general-purpose.

data.name: When compute is rationed, curation is the only lever left and the least invested
data.brief: When compute is rationed, curation is the only lever left — and it is the least invested one. The performance-vs-X curve has interchangeable axes (data, compute, time, dollars), so improving the data does not shift you along the curve, it changes the curve, which is why the same budget buys 8-145x more capability and why the founding result was about bending the scaling exponent rather than the offset. The market context makes this urgent rather than academic: H100 prices are rising, reasoning models are multiplying token demand, and vendors are already capping and forward-selling access. "Data quality remains the single most underleveraged compute multiplier".

data.name: There is no golden dataset: a mix is only optimal for a target task distribution
data.brief: There is no golden dataset that is good for everything: a dataset is only optimal with respect to a particular set of output tasks — a great legal model wants legal data more than healthcare data, and vice versa — which is why curation has to start from the target task distribution rather than from a quality score. Three properties define a good mix and they are in tension: relevance to the intended outputs, diversity (most model brittleness comes from insufficiently diverse training data — the model answers correctly when the question is posed just so, and breaks when it is posed slightly differently), and correct mixing and sequencing across sources and stages.
data.description: The practical rule that falls out: past a threshold, repeating high-quality data beats showing low-quality data.

data.name: Pre-, mid- and post-training compound; the industry's relay org chart is wrong
data.brief: The industry's org chart is wrong about training. Pre-training, mid-training and post-training are run as a relay — "I hand it off to somebody else who mid-trains, who then hands off to somebody else who post-trains" — but the Thomson Reuters result shows they compound: the same post-training data and harness produced nearly three times the gain when applied to a mid-trained checkpoint, because post-training's leverage depends on where the policy starts. The implication is organizational as much as technical: whoever owns the data mix at one stage is silently setting the ceiling for the next.

data.name: Refine tokens through clean, curate, create, compose
guidelines: Clean: heuristic filters (Gopher-style
drop 10-character and all-whitespace documents) then decontaminate against every downstream benchmark at a low n-gram threshold — otherwise you cannot interpret your own results
Curate: run quality classifiers
build a topic taxonomy and balance across it
do redundancy reduction on semantic near-duplicates, not byte-identical ones
up- and down-sample by quality and relevance
match the data distribution to the tasks you actually want
Create: only once the set is high-quality-but-too-small, expand it synthetically — and rephrase your best documents, not random ones
Compose: decide the mix and the sequence across at least three training phases
continuous curricula are the frontier of this step

data.name: Mid-train for a domain without losing the general model
guidelines: Budget roughly 1% of the pre-training token count (100B tokens here)

Make the majority of the mix representative of the pre-training distribution and only a minority domain-specific — this is what prevents catastrophic forgetting, and done right the general capabilities rise alongside the domain ones

Then re-run your existing post-training harness on the mid-trained checkpoint rather than on the stock instruction-tuned model: expect roughly 2-3x the post-training delta from unchanged post-training data, because the initial policy is more accurate

data.name: Predict the hero run from two small curated runs
guidelines: Train two smaller dense models on curated data while simulating token scarcity so they sit on the same scaling curve as the large run
the line through them predicts a model trained with 50x more compute
Use it to discover that the hero run does not land where you want before you pay for it — the derisking costs 50-100x less than the run it protects

data.name: What's Next After RLHF? (Diogo Almeida, TypeSafe AI — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Diogo Almeida
TypeSafe AI
data.brief: Still largely stealth ("we are still kind of stealthy... these are some of the early [talks]"), releasing soon. Core question stated as "what if the AI stack was redesigned for reliability and automation?" — a third post-training branch optimizing for calibrated decision-making, with an API shape that differs from both RLHF's and RLVR's.

data.name: RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback)
data.brief: The algorithm behind ChatGPT and, by the speaker's estimate, roughly 100% of LLMs in use today. Reduced to two steps: collect human preferences, optimize for human preferences. The claim the talk builds on is that the objective is the product: the human is in the loop of every deployed LLM because the training loop literally put them there — "the goal of the loop is to optimize for human preference, not to run software autonomously".

data.name: RLVR (RL with verifiable rewards)
data.brief: The second post-training branch, distinguished by its North Star: it optimizes for log error rates of pure correctness rather than human preference. Used here as a contrast class — a purely-RLVR coding agent "would look very very different" from Claude Code — and as evidence that each post-training branch has its own optimization target and its own API shape.

data.name: The assistance / automation divide
data.brief: The talk's explanatory frame for why AI looks simultaneously superhuman and useless. Tasks where AI excels are not merely tasks that happen to have a human in the loop — their goal is to please the human in the loop (chat, coding agents, unsolved math). Tasks where AI fails are ones whose goal is to remove the human: ideally running in a server nobody looks at until it becomes boring legacy software. These "way way way easier" tasks — customer service decisions, back-office work — still require humans, and the divide, not the difficulty, is what predicts which is which.

data.name: Preference reward-model asymmetry
data.brief: The mechanism underneath the divide. An RLHF reward model has a GAN-like asymmetry: it is very easy to detect and punish a model that signals uncertainty, so the optimization pressure pushes models to drop modes and answer confidently. Consequences stated as design properties rather than bugs: overpromising is a feature, every RLHF model carries a structural gap between human preference and actual results even when the results are good, and hallucination is intrinsic to optimizing for human preference rather than a pre-training defect.
data.description: Illustrated with a ChatGPT response to an audio file of fart noises — "a very eerie vibe atmosphere piece". The end game of any RLHF model is engagement; automation needs the opposite — a model that "doesn't give a damn about the human and just does the task correctly in a calibrated way".

data.name: Calibrated decision-making as a post-training objective
data.brief: TypeSafe's proposed third branch. Each post-training family has one North Star — RLHF optimizes human preference, RLVR optimizes pure correctness — and this one optimizes calibrated decision-making, framed as "mainlining the intelligence of pre-trained models into being actually useful for software". Stated to be neither RLHF nor RLVR, with a different API shape from both, and reasoned about from scratch on the analogy that "no one thought about instruction following before we made instruction following happen": a genuinely new post-training branch "looks totally alien, and then in hindsight becomes super obvious".
data.description: Also carries his ordering of the stack — "data matters more than compute, and doing the right task matters way more than data" — offered as a correction to the bitter lesson, which he says holds in games but not in reality.

data.name: Smarter software (vs just-in-time software)
data.brief: The product-side consequence. SaaS has not changed since 2019 — the LLM era added a bolted-on chatbot and nothing else — which is exactly what you would predict if AI is assistance-native: what can you do to SaaS with an assistant except put it on the side? Garry Tan's "golden age of just-in-time software" is accepted as accurate and named a double-edged sword: we are automating the writing of software while its expressiveness stands still, so the building blocks are unchanged.
