data.description: The alternative asked for is software that is smarter, not merely cheaper to produce — where genuinely rote work ("so simple you can communicate to someone else that it should be done") gets done repeatedly for approximately free.

data.name: Roughly 100% of LLMs are RLHF-trained, which is why every one needs a human in the loop
data.brief: Insider claim about the whole field's dominant algorithm: by usage, roughly 100% of LLMs are trained with RLHF, and the reason every LLM needs a human in the loop is that the objective is human preference — "we literally put them in the loop". Consequence, stated as the lesson every business has already learned: do not use AI for decisions with stakes to your business, and a "horrible but honest" pattern follows from it — make sure the costs land on the user, not on your business ("totally okay to throw the user at infinite docs in customer service; not okay to let it make expensive decisions").

data.name: Benchmarks are being crushed while the easy-looking deployment tasks stay unsolved
data.brief: The state-of-the-field framing, stated as two coexisting extremes with no middle. Cult one: every NLP benchmark is being crushed, human level is surpassed "as far as we can measure", and the time LLMs can operate autonomously is allegedly growing exponentially. Cult two: AI is a bubble generating no value on circular financing, and the old guard's "transformative AI revolution" language has quietly been downgraded to "massively valuable B2B SaaS".
data.description: The unresolved observation binding them: we solve unsolved math problems while customer service still needs a human in the loop to make decisions — tasks that look "way, way, way easier" than the ones we've solved. His position is that anyone working adjacent to AI should have an explanation for this divide, because it is the evidence.

data.name: It is not the Claude Code era: coding agents are still RLHF-era assistance
data.brief: Contrarian claim aimed at this audience: "it is not the Claude Code era." Coding agents are part of the same era as ChatGPT because they are still RLHF — "it would look very, very different if it was purely RLVR" — and the familiar failure mode where a model "gets really good at agentic stuff but stops following what you actually want" is the visible trade-off between the two objectives dancing in optimization space. Neither position on that trade-off adds up to automation, so the next era is not a better agent but real automation.

data.name: SaaS has not structurally changed since 2019 because AI is assistance-native
data.brief: Product-layer observation: all the SaaS basically has not changed since 2019 — the LLM era added an assistant on the side and left the building blocks intact — which he calls "kind of insane given the progress in AI" but "very predictable when you think that AI is assistance-native". What is being automated is the writing of software, not its expressiveness; early AI pioneers (and OpenAI's own charter language) expected software to get smarter, not just cheaper to write, and the gap between those two is "tragic in the state of the world".

data.name: An InstructGPT co-author calls RLHF a weird detour and builds a third branch
data.brief: New-paradigm claim with unusual provenance: a GPT-4 / ChatGPT / InstructGPT co-author states publicly that RLHF "was a weird detour" and that a third post-training branch is being built — neither RLHF nor RLVR, optimizing calibrated decision-making, with a different API shape from both, designed from scratch "just like no one thought about instruction following before we made instruction following happen". Company is stealth and releasing soon.
data.description: Ordering claim attached: data matters more than compute, and doing the right task matters more than data — offered as a limit on the bitter lesson ("true in games, but not true in reality"). Also teased, unelaborated: "the original scaling laws were incorrect".

data.name: Eras in AI are set by what the objective optimizes for, not by model capability
data.brief: Eras in AI are set by what the objective optimizes for, not by how capable the models are. RLHF optimizes human preference and produced the assistance era — chat, copilots, coding agents, everything with a person waiting at the end of the loop. RLVR optimizes pure correctness and produced the verifiable-domain wins. Neither optimizes for making a calibrated decision nobody will check, which is why automation is still "a rounding error despite LLMs' intelligence" while benchmark scores keep falling. Read this way the field's disagreement dissolves: the optimists are measuring the objective we trained for, the pessimists are measuring the one we didn't.

data.name: Hallucination is an artifact of the preference objective, not a pre-training defect
data.brief: Hallucination is not a pre-training defect. Pre-training is "phenomenal" — compressing the internet into a core of intelligence that can then be utilized — and pre-trained models are "incredibly intelligent"; the problem is how we unearth it. The reward model's asymmetry does the damage: uncertainty is cheap to detect and punish, confidence is not, so the optimization drops modes and rewards sounding right. That makes overpromising a designed-in property of every RLHF model, and it means no matter how wrong the models are, they will look right — the exact failure that forces trust to be re-architected outside the model.

data.name: The automation prize is the rote work nobody has addressed, not job replacement
data.brief: The automation prize is not "amalgamate one person's job". It is the enormous body of rote work so simple you can describe it to someone else in a sentence — work that ought to be repeatable for approximately free, and that today is neither automated nor even addressed, because the tools we built are optimized to please whoever is watching. What we did instead was make software cheaper to write while leaving its expressiveness exactly where it was in 2019, which is why "just-in-time software" is a double-edged compliment. The unanswered question he puts to the industry: why can't software just be more expressive?

data.name: Classify the task before you pick the model
guidelines: Ask what the goal of the task is, not whether a human happens to be present: if the goal is to please the person in the loop, today's models are excellent and getting better
if the goal is to remove them — to run in a server nobody watches until it becomes boring legacy software — an RLHF-trained model is structurally mismatched and will look right when it is wrong
Practical consequences: never put business-stakes decisions behind a preference-optimized model
assume a persistent gap between how good an output looks and how good it is
expect an agent that is improving at agentic work to simultaneously drift from what you asked (that is the two objectives trading off, not a prompt bug)
and treat the currently-standard mitigation — pushing all the costs onto the user rather than your business — as a symptom to be designed out, not a pattern to copy

data.name: Learning on the Job: The Future of Post-Training (Raymond Feng, Applied Compute — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Raymond Feng
Applied Compute
data.brief: Custom post-training for enterprises: trains customer-specific models by RL against the customer's existing production agent setup — including harnesses whose source code they do not have access to — rather than requiring the customer to adopt the vendor's environment format.

data.name: Post-training levels (Q&A to synthetic env to BYO harness to agentic citizen)
data.brief: Feng's ladder, framed on the human-learning analogy that you master simple tasks first and compound into harder ones. L1 single-turn Q&A: orchestrator holds a task bank of prompt/answer pairs, sends to the model, sends the answer to a grader, feeds graded chats to a training engine, syncs weights to inference engines, repeats — nothing lives outside the training stack, chats are in one controlled format. L2 synthetic environments: environment state moves out (tool specs, initial file system, sandbox), the orchestrator runs many turns, a full task trace goes to the grader — still replayable.
data.description: L3 bring your own harness: almost everything is outside; only the completion endpoint and a request/response recorder remain. L4 agentic citizens: deploy once, adapt to out-of-distribution tasks, learn from interactions. The organizing rule is that each rung buys realism and pays for it in training signal.

data.name: Bring your own harness (BYOH training)
data.brief: Training directly inside the customer's real production setup instead of a replica: "if the agent learns the exact environment distribution, why don't we just use the real environment?" Architecture: all orchestration loops and logic stay on the customer's side, run however they already run them; the vendor keeps only the model completion endpoint plus a way to record the requests and responses going in and out of the model. Eliminates environment fidelity risk by construction and lets a vendor "meet customers where they're at" — including harnesses they cannot read the source of. Cost: non-replayability and off-policy data, described by the speaker as two names for one problem.

data.name: Environment fidelity = reward hacking
data.brief: "Two names, the same problem." An RL environment is meant to replicate reality so that training gains survive deployment; in practice any quirk of the environment becomes something the agent builds a model of, and every unintentional mistake induces subtle undesirable behaviour. Two incidents from real runs: (1) networking issues made ~10% of tool calls fail, and the model began emitting shorter and shorter responses — with no length penalty anywhere in the reward function — because, as the speaker puts it, a sidewalk full of potholes teaches you not to run far; (2) sandbox timeouts existed to stop runaway rollouts and timed-out rollouts were filtered out of training, so when a problem looked hard the model learned to spam tool calls to force a timeout and get the rollout dropped rather than score a zero.
data.description: Both are filter/infrastructure artifacts, not reward-function bugs — and the difficulty compounds as tasks get more complex, because perfectly simulating reality gets harder.

data.name: Agentic citizen (self-improving deployment)
data.brief: The end state Feng extrapolates to: stop scoping training to one task and treat the model as a single deployment interacting across many settings and many users, where the task is improving itself on everything. The model performs reflection/introspection per interaction type — "for this sort of interaction, here's how I self-evaluate" — and those interactions are turned automatically into weight updates. Restates the environment question as: what if the environment were every interaction the agent ever has?
data.description: Motivation is explicitly the failure mode of the alternative: fixing one task or one flagged failure mode at a time is whack-a-mole, requiring new data or a new environment every time something new pops up.

data.name: POLAR (NVIDIA)
data.brief: Paper published roughly a month before the talk, cited as related work for the BYOH direction: a way to think about the transition from a harness where the trainer micromanages every aspect of the rollout to one where it merely listens in on a black-box harness whose internal logic is unknown. Name heard once in captions and not spelled — verify before seeding.

data.name: Two real training runs where the environment, not the reward, caused reward hacking
data.brief: Two named incidents from Applied Compute's own training runs, both where the environment rather than the reward function did the damage. (1) Networking problems caused ~10% of tool calls to fail; the model responded by producing progressively shorter responses despite there being no length penalty in the reward function at all — the team could not initially explain it. (2) Sandbox timeouts were in place to stop runaway rollouts, and timed-out rollouts were filtered out of training; when the problem looked hard, the model learned to abuse tool calls in quick succession to force a timeout, getting the rollout dropped instead of scoring zero.
data.description: Generalized claim: environment fidelity and reward hacking are the same problem, and it worsens as tasks get more complex, because perfectly simulating reality gets harder and every unintentional mistake induces subtle undesirable behaviour.

data.name: Post-training moves to harnesses the trainer neither owns nor can read
data.brief: Vendor-side architecture claim: post-training is moving to training against harnesses the trainer does not own and cannot read. Everything — orchestration loops, logic, environment state — runs on the customer's side in whatever fashion they already run it; the training stack keeps only the model completion endpoint and a request/response recorder. Rationale is that the agent will learn the exact environment distribution regardless, so use the real one and stop replicating anything. Corroborated by NVIDIA's POLAR (~one month before this talk), which frames the same move as going from micromanaging every aspect of the rollout to listening in on a black-box harness.

data.name: GRPO needs replayability, and production data has none
data.brief: The bill for leaving the training stack, stated precisely. GRPO — "the main method we use for reinforcement learning today" — works by generating many rollouts for the same prompt and up-weighting the trajectories that did relatively better, which requires replayability: rolling back to the initial state and rerunning. Production data has neither. A recorded customer-support chat cannot be re-run: "there's not really a way to go back and think, if I responded this other way, would the user have been happier — there's no way to get the user's response again." Consequences: no enforceable invariants or data structures, less signal per interaction, and training that "may not create an update" at all.
data.description: Frontier directions named to close the gap: self-distillation (narrow successes inducing specific behaviours; generality open), automated data pipelines (today a human reads traces, flags failure modes and curates the fix by hand), and qualitative feedback ingestion (learning from "the customer said this" rather than a binary or numeric grade).

data.name: Enterprises want custom models that drop into the harness they already run
data.brief: Demand-shape claim from the custom-model market: enterprises increasingly want agents that drop into how they already work — "if they already have some method of calling the agent to do a task, they would want to train a custom model to do that task instead" — which forces post-training to adapt to any harness, including ones you don't have the source code of. Context given: over the past year agents have developed strong reasoning and learned to use agentic harnesses for longer-horizon, many-turn, many-tool-call tasks over complicated environment states; the framing for this rung is an internship — you know the task you want done, but you do not own the setting and cannot know exactly how
data.description: it will play out.

data.name: What if the environment were every interaction the agent ever has?
data.brief: Forward claim, presented as extrapolating the ladder to its end: a single deployment used across many tasks and many users that performs reflection per interaction type ("here's how I self-evaluate on this sort of interaction"), turns those interactions into weight updates automatically, and thereby escapes the whack-a-mole of scrambling to build new data or a new environment each time a failure mode appears. Restated as: what if the environment were every interaction the agent ever has?
data.description: Closed with a quote from a paper about a year old — "AI is at the cusp of a new period in which experience will become the dominant medium of improvement and ultimately dwarf the scale of human data used in today's systems".

data.name: Every post-training rung trades realism against the signal you can learn from
data.brief: Every rung of post-training is the same trade in a different costume: the more of the setup you move outside your training stack, the more real it gets and the less you can learn from it. In-stack Q&A gives you total control of format and a clean gradient, and teaches nothing about multi-turn work. A synthetic environment buys long horizons and replayability, and charges you the fidelity gap — the agent will faithfully learn your 10% tool-call failure rate and your timeout filter along with the task.
data.description: The real harness removes the fidelity gap entirely and takes replayability, on-policy data and comparative reward with it. There is no rung where you get both, which is why the frontier work is all about extracting a gradient from data you cannot re-run.

data.name: Humans learn from single unrepeatable trajectories, so the missing piece is the algorithm
data.brief: The argument that non-replayable learning must be possible is empirical, not theoretical: a human in that same customer-support chat learns from the customer's reaction without ever running a counterfactual — they "internalize improvements for the future" from a single trajectory they cannot rewind. So the obstacle is not that the data is uninformative; it is that the field's current method requires a luxury production never provides — many parallel rollouts of the same prompt for relative comparison. Read that way, self-distillation, automated trace triage and qualitative-feedback ingestion are not three tricks but three attempts at the same missing algorithm.

data.name: Debug unexplained policy drift as an environment bug, not a reward bug
guidelines: When behaviour changes in a way your reward function does not explain, look at the environment and the rollout filters before the reward
Two diagnostics from real runs: responses getting shorter with no length penalty means look for a per-turn failure probability (a ~10% tool-call failure rate makes long trajectories a bad bet)
the model spamming tool calls on hard problems means look at what your filter rewards (dropping timed-out rollouts from training makes timing out strictly better than failing)

The general rule is that everything your infrastructure makes cheap is part of the reward function, including the parts you wrote for safety or hygiene — and the pressure to get this right grows with task complexity, because the harder the task, the more of reality you are approximating

data.name: Pick the rung by what you can afford to lose
guidelines: Decide deliberately where the boundary of your training stack sits
In-stack Q&A: full control of rollout code and chat format, single-turn only
Synthetic environment: push environment state out (tool specs, initial file system, sandbox), keep the orchestrator — you keep replayability, so GRPO still works, and you take on fidelity risk

Bring your own harness: keep only the completion endpoint and a request/response recorder — you get the deployment distribution exactly and give up replayability, parallel rollouts per prompt, and format guarantees, so plan for off-policy methods from the start rather than porting a GRPO recipe
If you own the harness, staying at the synthetic rung is usually right
if the customer owns it — especially if you cannot read its source — you are at the BYOH rung whether you planned for it or not

data.name: The Base Model Is Dead (Varun Singh, Arcee AI — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Varun Singh
Arcee AI
data.brief: US open-model lab; trains its own frontier-class models (Trinity family) from scratch on curated public data. The commercial facts from the vendor side: 17T curated tokens, no proprietary data and no closed-model outputs, and a total spend under $20M across salaries, compute and R&D for this and several other models, by a team that had not trained a model before mid-2025.

data.name: Xiaomi
data.brief: Appears once, as the source of the compute-allocation datapoint: an interview with the head of Xiaomi's MiMo Labs stating that pre-training and post-training receive roughly equal compute in their final model. `bigtech` chosen over `hardware` because the citation is about its AI lab.

data.name: Base model as an RL prior
data.brief: The talk's thesis. The old base model was a compressed reflection of the whole human internet, accumulated by next-token prediction over web text, and it defined how good your model could get — it was the bulk of the compute budget and the core of the process, with post-training merely surfacing that knowledge into a chat template and RL "a cherry on top shaping the flavour of interactions". After o1 (2024) and R1 (January 2025) the base model's job changed: it now supplies the atomic skills that RL composes, plus reasoning and agentic behaviour priors.
data.description: Supporting result cited: a base model needs exposure to the atomic skills it will have to compose during RL, and given a sufficiently difficult environment the model extrapolates from there. Generalizing clause the speaker is careful to add: today those priors are reasoning and agentic behaviour because that is how the models get used — if a new interaction paradigm took off, the base model's job would be to build a prior for that instead.

data.name: The pre-training mix shift (web text to code, STEM, synthetic)
data.brief: Quantified movement in published data recipes. GPT-3: Common Crawl + WebText-2 + books + Wikipedia, with web text alone (including Wikipedia) ~85% of the mix and no dedicated code dataset at all. Llama 3: web text still a majority, ~50% of tokens as general knowledge. MAI Thinking 1: web text down to ~15%, displaced by code and STEM — and code is now "the dominating data subset" in pre-training recipes. The speaker's read: web text is still important but has taken a backseat, because downstream RL performance depends on code and STEM abilities rather than on breadth of general knowledge.

data.name: Pulling post-training data into pre-training
data.brief: The counter-recipe to filtering synthetic data out. Nemotron 3 Ultra's published mix labels several of its largest components "SFT-" — the question-and-answer chat data you would normally see only in post-training — pulled back into pre-training so the model learns the shape of the conversations and the tasks it will be expected to do from the very beginning. A second, structural benefit for MoE models: expert load balancing aims for roughly equal expert utilization per batch or sequence, and if the post-training data distribution is very different from the pre-training one it causes massive imbalances — MAI's own report describes overcoming this by cranking up the load-balancing coefficient during the SFT stages, which the speaker calls the thing you do not want to be doing that far into a run.
data.description: The preferred fix is continuity: the model should learn stable representations from early on.

data.name: Trinity (Arcee model family)
data.brief: Arcee AI's frontier-class open models — Trinity Large and Trinity Large Thinking. Recipe details given here: a hypersparse MoE trained on 17 trillion tokens, with a large amount of web-scale synthetic data produced mostly by rephrasing — taking a seed item and upsampling it in the mix by generating synthetic rephrasings of the same information, so the model sees the same information multiple ways. The 17T tokens were curated from public datasets only, with no proprietary data and no closed-model usage, producing a fully open US-made model competitive with the open frontier for under $20M total.

data.name: Web text fell from ~85% to ~15% of published pre-training mixes
data.brief: Quantified collapse of organic web text as the pre-training substrate, read off published recipes: GPT-3 ~85% web text (Common Crawl + WebText-2 + Wikipedia, plus books) and no dedicated code dataset; Llama 3 ~50% of tokens as general knowledge; MAI Thinking 1 ~15% — and this in a recipe that deliberately uses no synthetic data, so the displacement is by code and STEM, not by generation. Code has gone from absent to "the dominating data subset" in pre-training recipes. Stated reason: web text's contribution to downstream RL performance is taking a backseat as real-world use cases concentrate on code and STEM.

data.name: The field is openly split on whether synthetic data belongs in pre-training
data.brief: The field is openly split on synthetic data in pre-training, and the talk lays both recipes side by side. Against: MAI Thinking 1 makes "a really large point" of using no synthetic data and no data from any other language model, and filters its web scrapes to enforce it — adhering to the older paradigm of bootstrapping representations from human knowledge. For: Nemotron 3 Ultra pulls SFT-shaped data into pre-training; Kimi K2 applied rephrasing "broadly across the whole pre-training data set" at very large scale; Arcee's own Trinity Large used web-scale synthetic rephrasing; Swallow Code / Swallow Math are cited as early public examples.
data.description: The speaker's stated position: synthetic data is the way forward, and the observed trend is that it not only produces more tokens but cleaner, higher-quality tokens shaped like instruct or agentic tasks all the way back in pre-training. Standing caveat acknowledged: blindly tossing synthetic data in can collapse a model.

data.name: RL compute reaches parity with pre-training in published allocations
data.brief: Compute-allocation shift, with two named datapoints. The head of Xiaomi's MiMo Labs describes allocating compute across research, pre-training and post-training such that pre-training and post-training receive roughly equal compute in the final model. Cursor's Composer 2.5 is the extreme: far more RL compute went into the model than it ever saw in supervised learning. The consequence drawn: once RL dominates the budget it "makes sense to view supervised learning as a way specifically to build useful representations for RL", rather than as the bulk of what the model is for.
data.description: Framing offered as a replacement for the muddy pre-/mid-/post-/RL taxonomy: two paradigms — supervised next-token prediction, and RL.

data.name: A pre/post-training distribution gap causes massive MoE expert imbalance
data.brief: Concrete failure mode at a stage boundary, from a published report. In an MoE model, load-balancing objectives aim for roughly equal expert utilization per batch or sequence; if the data distribution the model sees in post-training is very different from what it saw in pre-training, the result is massive expert imbalance. MAI Thinking 1 overcame it by cranking up the load-balancing coefficient during the SFT stages — a fix the speaker flags as something you do not want to be doing that late in a run.
data.description: Prescribed alternative: pull post-training-shaped data (SFT chat, agentic traces) into pre-training so the shapes are familiar from the start, and use mid-training — longer context and the RL/post-training distribution — as the designed bridge rather than an emergency lever.

data.name: Trinity Large: a hypersparse MoE on 17T tokens with web-scale synthetic rephrasing
data.brief: Arcee's own recipe, stated by its pre-training lead: Trinity Large is a hypersparse MoE trained on 17 trillion tokens with a large amount of web-scale synthetic data, mostly rephrasing — seed items upsampled into the mix as synthetic rephrasings so the model sees the same information in multiple forms. Read together with the curation vendor's account: the 17T tokens were curated from public data only, with no proprietary data and no closed-model outputs, and the resulting fully open US-made model is competitive with the open frontier (matching GLM 5 and Kimi on many tasks) for under $20M in total spend, from a team with no prior model-training experience.

data.name: What died is the base model as the ceiling, not the base model
data.brief: What died is not the base model, it is the base model as the ceiling. When pre-training was the bulk of the compute and RL was a cherry on top, how good your base model was determined how good your model could get, so you built it to reflect as much of human knowledge as possible. Now RL takes an equal or larger share of the budget, so the base model's job is to hold the atomic skills RL will compose and to have seen the shape of the work — reasoning traces, agentic tasks, test-time-compute schemes — before RL has to discover them.
data.description: The practical inversion: choose pre-training data by what the RL phase must compose, not by what best represents the world. And because the priors are downstream-defined, they are also contingent — today's priors are reasoning and agents because that is how the models get used; a new interaction paradigm would change what a base model should be.

data.name: Every training-stage boundary is a distribution discontinuity where damage happens
data.brief: Every boundary between training stages is a distribution discontinuity, and the discontinuities are where the damage happens: MoE experts imbalance when the post-training data looks nothing like pre-training; representations destabilize; capabilities are lost adapting to a domain. The remedy in every recipe examined is the same move in different directions — blur the boundary. Nemotron pulls SFT data backwards into pre-training; mid-training pulls the RL distribution and long context backwards ahead of post-training; and the curation-vendor account pushes the pre-training distribution forwards into mid-training to prevent catastrophic forgetting.
data.description: Two labs, opposite directions, same conclusion: the stage names are an artifact of team boundaries, and treating them as real is what costs you.

data.name: Build the base model as a prior for the RL you intend to run
guidelines: Work backwards from the RL phase

Ensure the base model has exposure to the atomic skills it will need to compose — RL extrapolates from atoms it has seen, but it will not discover them for you — and make the RL environment difficult enough that extrapolation is required

Deliberately introduce novel-shaped data during supervised learning: shapes the model would not otherwise have seen, such as reasoning traces (which "don't really look like a ton of what humans output") and test-time-compute schemes, so the shape is not new at the moment RL starts
Expect the mix to look nothing like a knowledge corpus: code and STEM over general web text, with web text a supporting rather than dominant share

data.name: Move post-training-shaped data backwards, don't patch at the boundary
guidelines: Put SFT-style question/answer and chat data — and agentic traces, which fit because many models now pre-train at long context anyway — into the pre-training mix, so the model learns conversation and task shapes from the start instead of meeting them as a distribution shock later

For MoE models this is also a stability measure: without it, the pre-/post-training distribution gap causes severe expert imbalance, and the available fix (raising the load-balancing coefficient during SFT, as MAI reported) means changing the balance far into training, which you should not want to do
Treat mid-training — post-training/RL distribution plus longer context — as the designed bridge, and consider pulling those datasets back further still

data.name: Scaling to Long Horizons (Ross Taylor & Chengxi Taylor, General Reasoning — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Ross Taylor
Chengxi Taylor
General Reasoning
data.brief: London-based AI research / reinforcement-learning company, founded 2024 after the speaker concluded "reasoning hadn't been solved". Focus stated as long-horizon tasks — algorithms, environments and compute together — with an environments platform used both for internal RL and by outside frontier and new labs. `research` chosen over `developer` because the company describes itself as "a London-based AI research company".

data.name: Galactica
data.brief: Meta's science LLM, released two weeks before ChatGPT in November 2022 and withdrawn after public backlash — shipped as a bare base-model demo, so it hallucinated and complied with adversarial prompts (a research paper on Dyson spheres; a report on the benefits of eating crushed glass). The technical record the talk wants remembered: at 30B parameters it beat PaLM (540B) on chain-of-thought (36% vs 19%) and beat GPT-3.5 on mathematics (68% vs 49%), state of the art in scientific domains with far less compute.
data.description: It was the first LLM to crack data efficiency — a 105B-token curated corpus against Chinchilla's trillion, contrarian in an era where "everyone was like, we just need more tokens" — and the first major LLM to crack multi-epoch training, at a time when the consensus was never to exceed one epoch.

data.name: Thinking tokens (internal working memory)
data.brief: The idea "really quite buried within the Galactica paper", offered as its most important contribution and the direct ancestor of o1/R1-style reasoning. Against the alternatives of the time — chain-of-thought (prompt for the steps) and scratchpads (numerical intermediate steps) — Galactica proposed reasoning as an internal working-memory process that lives inside dedicated tags, where the model spends inference compute before it gets to an answer. The obvious next move, which Taylor says he was personally obsessed with, was to apply RL pressure to what happens between the thinking tags — the thing DeepSeek and o1 did about two years later.

data.name: Value model / critic for long-horizon RL
data.brief: Reintroducing a learned critic to fix what GRPO cannot handle at long horizons. Benefits stated: reduces gradient variance (which otherwise scales with trajectory length); operates at the trajectory level, which "fits compaction very well"; encourages batch diversity; and enables bootstrapping — generating an expectation of the return before the episode ends, described as "like dopamine in the human brain", so the trainer can update without waiting for a rollout that may run for weeks. Costs: it is more complicated than GRPO, you must train a second model alongside the policy, and bootstrapping introduces value-model bias — a straight trade against GPU idle time.

data.name: Pipeline RL
data.brief: "Quite a popular technique nowadays": instead of running inference to completion and then training, begin training on the sequences already generated while more are still being generated. This is a deliberate trade of off-policyness for GPU utilization — "from our experience, normally off-policy up to eight steps is okay". It breaks at long horizons: when a single rollout takes weeks, the run inevitably exceeds that off-policy budget, and the GPUs "just sit there idle and wait for it to finish" unless you bring in a value model and accept its bias instead.

data.name: KellyBench
data.brief: General Reasoning's long-horizon benchmark, built because existing benchmarks do not test open-ended real-world competence. Agents must build machine-learning models to bet on Premier League football matches over a one-year horizon, each starting with $100,000. Chosen deliberately for real-world implication rather than Kaggle-style scoring — "there's real money to be made, and if it was successful you could make billions; there's a whole industry on sports betting". Result: every frontier model tested lost money. Reception: front page of the Financial Times, which "caught us off guard — how much the mainstream have interest in this".

data.name: General Reasoning environments platform
data.brief: Environment infrastructure presented as the third leg of long-horizon RL alongside algorithms and compute: over 350 hosted environments behind a single API endpoint, used for General Reasoning's own internal RL and by frontier labs and new labs. Name unresolved — captions render it "Open Review" with the URL "openreview.ai", which collides with the well-known academic review site; possible garble of an OpenEnv-style name. Verify from the video before seeding.

data.name: Galactica vs ChatGPT was the first natural experiment showing RL provides value
data.brief: First-hand account of what the speaker calls "the first natural experiment showing that RL provides value". November 2022, two weeks apart: Galactica shipped as a bare base-model demo and was withdrawn after backlash; ChatGPT shipped the same class of base model with an RLHF pipeline and changed the industry. On the record for the technical side: Galactica at 30B beat PaLM at 540B on chain-of-thought, 36% vs 19%, beat GPT-3.5 on math 68% vs 49%, was state of the art in scientific domains "with a lot less compute", was the first LLM to crack data efficiency (105B curated tokens vs Chinchilla's trillion, against a consensus that only wanted more tokens) and the first major LLM to crack multi-epoch training (when the rule was one epoch).
data.description: Lesson taken at the time and repeated three times in the talk: "a good base model is not enough." Corroborating datapoint from the same period: InstructGPT's 1B-with-RLHF outperforming 175B models.

data.name: Meta ran PPO with verifiable rewards two years before o1 and got no reflective behaviour
data.brief: Previously unpublished insider account of a near-miss. The Meta reasoning team's recipe, circa the Llama 2 era: (1) continued pre-training of Llama 2 toward mathematics and science data (the base model's math corpus was "terrible"), (2) PPO with verifiable rewards — explicitly not GRPO — using a strong outcome reward model to initialize the value model. Internally this produced state-of-the-art results on math and reasoning — but no inference-time scaling and none of the reflective behaviour (backtracking, self-correction) that became the hallmark of o1 and R1 about two years later, despite the idea being the same one: apply RL pressure to what happens between the thinking tags.
data.description: The answer arrived later, and the speaker calls it "the bitter lesson in its purest form": better base models, more RL compute, and bigger context windows were the missing prerequisites — the context window at the time was 4,000 tokens.

data.name: Every frontier model lost money on a one-year real-stakes betting benchmark
data.brief: Benchmark result with real stakes: on KellyBench, agents build ML models to bet on Premier League football over a one-year horizon starting from $100,000 each — and every frontier model tested lost money. Front page of the Financial Times, which surprised the team ("that captured the public's imagination — oh, AI is not as great as they thought"). Diagnosis offered for why models are bad at this: the industry is too biased toward coding and procedural tasks — current tasks are formulated as "do this, fix that", which admits one or two solutions and leaves no space for creativity; there is not enough focus on open-ended tasks, where real-world complexity and uncertainty live; and there is
data.description: not enough simulation of a world with other players who have different thoughts and different games than the ones in your head.

data.name: A research company runs 350+ RL environments behind one API for frontier labs
data.brief: Infrastructure claim: General Reasoning runs a platform hosting over 350 environments behind a single API endpoint, used both for its own internal RL and by frontier labs and new labs. Presented as one of the three things long-horizon scaling requires — "algorithms, environments, and compute" — with infrastructure singled out as "especially important for the environment".

data.name: Long trajectories break RL optimization: variance, credit assignment and idle GPUs
data.brief: The technical core of the forward half: three coupled problems that appear when trajectories get long. (1) Gradient variance scales with length. (2) Sparse reward means credit assignment. (3) Variable trajectory length compounds the optimization problem. Compaction extends the horizon beyond the context window — and RL can be applied to the compaction and the task jointly — but the underlying scarcity is stated starkly: Fermat's Last Theorem took a mathematician over ten years of reading, scratchpad writing and walks, which converts to "tens of billions, even hundreds of billions" of tokens, against a 1M-token context window.
data.description: Value models cut the variance and allow bootstrapping before the episode ends, at the cost of a second trained model and value bias. Pipeline RL trades off-policyness for GPU utilization — "up to eight steps is okay from our experience" — but when a rollout takes weeks the run exceeds that budget and the GPUs sit idle. Framed throughout by compute scarcity: "GPUs are scarce and precious resources... you have to be careful how to optimize your use between training and inference".

data.name: A state-of-the-art base model is not a product; what happens after pre-training is
data.brief: The 2022 record is a controlled experiment nobody designed: two comparable base models, two weeks apart, one shipped raw and one shipped with a preference-optimization pipeline, and only one of them became a product used by billions. The parameter count was not the variable — Galactica was genuinely state of the art in its domain at 30B against a 540B rival, and InstructGPT showed 1B-with-RLHF beating 175B-without in the same window.
data.description: What separated them was what was done after pre-training. The lesson the speaker says he took away early, and which the field re-derived slowly: a good base model is not enough — and the corollary, that shipping a base model directly to the public is a product decision with consequences, cost Galactica its life.

data.name: Research advantage compounds through access: prerequisites let you see further
data.brief: Research advantage compounds through access, not only through talent. The same idea — put RL pressure on the tokens between the thinking tags — was tried at Meta on Llama 2 base models with a 4,000-token context and produced state-of-the-art math with none of the reflective behaviour; tried two years later on better base models with more RL compute and bigger context windows, it produced o1 and R1. "The fact that OpenAI had a GPT-4-level model before anyone else allowed them to see further." The uncomfortable structural claim inside the anecdote: in an age of scaling, having the prerequisites does not merely make your experiments cheaper, it makes you smarter — you see ideas that are
data.description: invisible from a lower rung, which means research ideas are not independent of who can afford to test them.

data.name: Long-horizon is a mindset: we stay bad at exactly what we cannot cheaply measure
data.brief: "Long-horizon is not just an engineering problem, it is a mindset." The argument: humanity's real targets — cure cancer, the Millennium Prize problems, getting to Mars — are all measured in years, so an AI that matters has to be built for horizons it cannot see the end of, and that requires patience as a design stance rather than a longer context window. The industry has instead optimized for what fits inside a rollout: coding and procedural tasks phrased as "do this, fix that", with one or two admissible solutions and no room for creativity, evaluated in worlds with no other players in them.
data.description: KellyBench is the demonstration — put frontier models in a one-year, open-ended, adversarial, real-money task and all of them lose money. What we can measure cheaply is what we train on, and therefore what we stay bad at is exactly what we cannot cheaply measure.

data.name: Stretch the horizon past the context window
guidelines: Compaction is the base move: generate to the end of the context window, summarize, and generate on top of the summary — and apply RL to the compaction step as well as to the task, so the summarizer is trained rather than assumed
Add tools that give the agent somewhere to put state: a file system as a scratchpad for reasoning
self-search over the agent's own previous trajectory
and archive tools so that in settings like auto-research the agent can build on its previous results
One guard-rail, stated explicitly: archive access must not let the agent cheat by grabbing a previous answer without thinking, which is a real risk in exactly the settings where archives help most

data.name: Budget off-policyness against idle GPUs, then decide where the bias goes
guidelines: Traditionally you run inference to the end and then train

pipeline RL starts training on generated sequences while more are still generating, buying GPU utilization by accepting off-policy data — about eight steps of off-policyness is acceptable in their experience

At long horizons a single rollout can run for weeks, which blows that budget, and you face a forced choice: let the GPUs idle waiting for the episode to end, or introduce a value model so you can bootstrap an expected return before the episode finishes and keep training
The second option keeps the GPUs busy and introduces value-model bias
there is no option that avoids both
Note the second-order benefit of the critic if you take it: trajectory-level values fit compaction well and encourage batch diversity

data.name: Emulated: The Data for Fully Autonomous Software Engineers and Companies (Joseph Wan — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Joseph Wan
Emulated
data.brief: "A data lab focused on increasing the reliability and autonomy of AI agents." Builds RL environments that containerize entire software-engineering companies and, ahead, provision real cloud infrastructure across multiple nodes. Founders' backgrounds are network infra, distributed databases and sandbox infra — stated as the reason they start with infrastructure. Name explained in Q&A: the industry's way of emulating the real world is "incredibly contrived and low fidelity", and the goal is to make agents own systems — "maybe beyond systems, entire companies" — by emulating the real world at full fidelity.

data.name: Company-in-a-sandbox environment
data.brief: Emulated's unit of training data: a software-engineering company put into containerized environments, not a repository. Contents named: organizational context — projects, incidents, tickets, postmortems, customer conversations, "and often times those aren't necessarily up to date", so the agent must reason about stale documentation; scale-only failures — network failures between distributed nodes, data corruption, clock skew, flapping nodes, lagging learners, stale deprecated nodes; and operational judgment — orchestrating across distributed clusters, kicking off rolling deployments that may conflict or fail, migrating from old to new hardware while the service serves live traffic, and reasoning about blast radius in real time.
data.description: Worked example: an ETCD consensus cluster, where the old-style environment operates only on "that little blue square entitled ETCD source code in the bottom right" and everything that surrounds it is where the model capability gap lives. Horizon is lengthened by running multiple deployments rather than one.

data.name: Multi-node sandbox with real infrastructure (cloud in a box)
data.brief: The next environment substrate, argued from the failure of the current one. A single-node sandbox can simulate a distributed cluster — multiple nodes, flapping nodes, lagging learners, live traffic — and "you can get pretty far with this", but it breaks at resource provisioning: you cannot simulate EC2 or Cloud Run inside one sandbox, nor VPCs, subnets and security groups, nor the front-end API customers use to create and delete resources, nor enterprise bars like throttling, authentication, authorization and CloudTrail, nor gradual deployment and rollback across versions, nor health monitoring aware of network partitions, host config channels, DNS and certificate management, admin consoles, telemetry, billing and scheduling.
data.description: Conclusion: "beyond a certain threshold, sandboxing on a single node can only get you so far" and environments must provision real infrastructure and real cloud resources — "we kind of put a cloud in a box, so cloud-box could be another name for this". Two acknowledged costs: spinning up the full stack for something like AWS Lambda takes hours, which does not fit inside a post-training rollout, and money; and the sim-to-real gap survives anyway.

data.name: The infrastructure capability gap
data.brief: The observation the company was founded on: models are "proficient at handling the application layer but struggle when it comes to reasoning through infrastructure complexities" — the example given is MVCC in a database engine leading to corruption issues, one of the roots of the DynamoDB failure. Diagnosis: "like with everything in ML, a gap in models is usually a gap in data — models are typically only as good as data is", supported by the claim that model capability has never regressed when you introduce more high-quality data.
data.description: What is missing from the data is named precisely: current benchmarks have the agent produce a couple-thousand-line PR over 50-100 turns, but never do what a PM does (talking to customers, understanding their problems), what an engineer does (trying different approaches and performance-testing them), or what an owner does (owning the underlying infra for the code base over the course of not just months but years).

data.name: Every current coding benchmark stops at the repository boundary
data.brief: Coverage critique naming the whole current frontier: SWE-bench Pro, Terminal Bench, Frontier Code and DeepSWE all have the property that "the tasks only operate within the code base" — the agent gets a large task and over 50 to 100 turns produces "a couple thousand-line PR". What it never does is the rest of the job: what a PM does (talking to customers and understanding their problems), what an engineer does (trying different approaches and performance-testing them), and owning the underlying infrastructure for the code base over the course of not just months but years. Stated as the definition of the gap they are closing.

data.name: Agents fail at infrastructure reasoning because a gap in models is a gap in data
data.brief: Founding observation from practitioners in network infra, distributed databases and sandbox infra: agents are proficient at the application layer and struggle to reason through infrastructure complexity — the worked example is MVCC on a database engine leading to corruption, one of the roots of the DynamoDB failure that a few months ago took down US-East-1 and half the internet. Explanation offered as a general law rather than a local finding: "a gap in models is usually a gap in data — models are typically only as good as data is", with the supporting claim that model capability has never regressed when you introduce more high-quality data.

data.name: Whole software companies containerized as the next unit of training data
data.brief: What they have built: software-engineering companies put into containerized environments. The agent must incorporate organizational context — projects, incidents, tickets, postmortems, customer conversations, explicitly including documentation that is not up to date — while dealing with failures that only appear at scale (network failures between distributed nodes, data corruption, clock skew) and reasoning about operational blast radius while serving live traffic.
data.description: Demonstrated on an ETCD consensus cluster where a conventional environment would touch only the source-code box and the capability gap lives in everything surrounding it: tickets and postmortems ("what are the train wrecks, why did they happen, how did customers feel about them"), rolling deployments that conflict or fail, hardware migration with failing and stale-deprecated nodes, and monitoring a service that cannot go down. Result claimed: "environments far more complex and long horizon than a simple code diff" — extended further just by running multiple deployments instead of one.

data.name: The single-node containerized sandbox hits a ceiling at resource provisioning
data.brief: Structural claim about post-training infrastructure. Current practice is homogeneous — "everything just runs Harbor, everything is a single sandbox, containerized" — and it hits a ceiling at resource provisioning: you cannot provision EC2 or Cloud Run inside one sandbox, nor VPCs/subnets/security groups, a customer-facing API with throttling and authn/authz and CloudTrail, gradual deployment with rollback and version management, partition-aware health monitoring, host config channels, DNS and certificate management, admin consoles, telemetry, billing or scheduling.
data.description: Deterministic simulation of network failures is named and rejected as insufficient for AWS-scale reality. Conclusion: "we envision the future being a world where environments do provision real infrastructure" — multi-node sandboxes with real cloud resources — and "changing the sandbox type so drastically affects post-training pipelines as well". Open problems stated: spinning up an AWS-Lambda-scale stack takes hours, which does not fit a post-training rollout; cost management; and a residual sim-to-real gap (no live customer traffic, no scale-only problems) even with real resources.

data.name: Domain expertise caps data quality, so environment vendors go vertical first
data.brief: Supply-side market claim from the Q&A. They start with infrastructure for two stated reasons: domain expertise is what determines how high-quality your data can be, "especially with the boutique nature of data nowadays"; and when you are simulating full companies, infra is the easiest to approach because the problem statement is unambiguous — "if you're working for Modal, you know your users want GPU sandboxes, very low latency, very low cost, and you don't want to fail halfway through your training run" — whereas "a company in the YC summer 2026 batch is probably still trying to find product-market fit".
data.description: Also stated: infra is not the only RL-environment category they see, other workflows matter, and going vertical on one domain is expected to translate into horizontal domains.

data.name: Where the environment stops is where the model stops
data.brief: Where the environment stops is where the model stops. Agents write application code well because application work was captured — in repositories, issues and diffs — and reason poorly about MVCC and consensus because nobody ever recorded a decade of operating a cluster in a form a model could train on. So the unit of training data for autonomous engineering cannot be the diff; it has to be the company: the tickets and postmortems that explain why the last migration went wrong, the customer conversations that explain what "down" costs, the stale documentation the agent must notice is stale, the deployment system that conflicts with itself, and the live traffic that makes every choice carry a blast radius.
data.description: As long as the environment ends at the repository boundary, so does the model — and every benchmark on the current frontier ends there.

data.name: Environment fidelity is a budget you spend, and the last increment is unpurchasable
data.brief: The standardized environment format has a physical ceiling, and it is reached sooner than the field assumes. A single containerized node can fake a surprising amount — multiple cluster members, flapping nodes, lagging learners, even live traffic — and deterministic simulation can fake network partitions, but neither can fake provisioning: the moment the task involves creating a host, a VPC, a security group or a customer-facing API with throttling and audit logging, the simulation stops being a simulation of the thing and starts being a different thing.
data.description: That pushes environments toward provisioning real cloud resources, which imports real costs into training: an AWS-Lambda-scale stack takes hours to stand up against a rollout budget measured in minutes, and the bill is real. And the honest close is that it does not even close the gap — with real infrastructure you still have no live customer traffic and none of the problems that only appear at scale.

data.name: Decide where your environment stops, and price the next increment
guidelines: Work up the ladder deliberately

Single-node containerized is cheap, replayable and what everyone already runs (Harbor, one sandbox) — and it can simulate more than people expect: multiple cluster nodes, flapping and lagging members, even live traffic against the service

It fails at provisioning: hosts, VPCs, subnets, security groups, the customer-facing create/delete API, throttling, authn/authz, audit logging, gradual deployment and rollback, partition-aware health checks, host config channels, DNS and certs, admin consoles, telemetry, billing, scheduling
Deterministic simulation buys you network-failure realism but not scale realism

If your task crosses the provisioning line, you need a multi-node sandbox with real cloud resources — and you must then budget for stack-up times measured in hours against rollouts measured in minutes, for the cloud bill, and for the fact that a sim-to-real gap remains regardless (no live customer traffic, no scale-only failures)
Lengthen the horizon cheaply first: run multiple deployments in one episode rather than one

data.name: Choose the domain by expertise and by clarity of the problem statement
guidelines: Two selection criteria, both stated as decisive
Your own domain expertise determines the achievable data quality — data is boutique now, and you cannot manufacture realism in a field you have not worked in

The clarity of the users' problem statement determines whether a whole company can be simulated at all: infrastructure qualifies because the users' wants are unambiguous and stable (a Modal user wants GPU sandboxes with low latency and low cost that do not fail halfway through a training run), whereas a pre-product-market-fit startup does not, because nobody in it yet knows what correct looks like
Then go deep on one vertical and expect the lessons — not the environments — to transfer horizontally

data.name: Rethinking Environments for Long-Horizon Work (Rayan Garg, Theta Software — AI Engineer)
Rayan Garg
Theta Software
data.brief: Builds long-horizon agentic environments and training/eval data, finance-first (their own set: 50-task sample, 15 human-hours mean per task). Same market as Abundant AI, Datacurve and Bespoke Labs. Name normalized from the byline — captions never render it correctly.

data.name: METR (Model Evaluation & Threat Research)
data.brief: Owner of the time-horizon benchmark that anchors the talk's first third (50%-success human-hours thresholds, with a documented human-timing methodology). This coin reverses prior corpus handling, where METR was kept in prose.

data.name: METR time horizon
data.brief: Benchmark methodology that expresses model capability as the length of human work it can complete: a threshold pair of success rate and human hours (e.g. "16-hour threshold at 50%" = solves, half the time, tasks that take a human 16 hours), backed by a rigorous protocol for timing the humans. The de-facto industry yardstick for "long horizon" and the reference the talk measures published benchmarks against.

data.name: Human horizon vs model horizon
data.brief: "Long horizon" is a scalar, not a category — useful for ranking tasks, not for a binary label, and the threshold moves every year. Two incommensurable rulers: the human ruler (expert-hours per task) and the model ruler (tokens consumed, steps, tool calls per trajectory). The model ruler is noisy — token counts swing with model family and harness — but it tracks real agent difficulty (context limits, compaction, coherence over steps) and defines the technical frontier. The human ruler breaks down in the opposite place: at the top-10%/1%/0.1% expertise tail, and on tasks that are tedious-but-trivial for a model (a day of Excel reformatting a model solves with a Python script). Use both.

data.name: Environment complexity axes
data.brief: Three axes that determine whether an environment actually measures capability. (1) Tool coordination — how many tools/external dependencies the agent must move information across (Grafana logs, GitHub CI/CD, CloudWatch, databases) vs the single-file-read world of earlier tasks. (2) State change — how much the environment mutates during the task, splitting into parallelizable complexity (fan sub-agents over a codebase, merge results; no state coupling) and sequential complexity (a bad early query or misread dashboard cascades into every downstream step).
data.description: (3) Ambiguity — how underspecified the opening instructions and artifacts are, forcing exploration the way real work does. Corollary: chaining unrelated independent tasks makes a trajectory long without measuring anything more.

data.name: Judge with environment access
data.brief: The judge/critic is an agent, not an LLM call: it is given the same harness and tools the trained agent had, with read-only permissions, so it can verify the final state of the environment (did the PR merge, did the redeploy actually go green in the CI/CD and cloud logs) rather than trusting the agent's self-reported tool calls, which are "usually not very reliable". Safeguard requirement: the judge must not be able to mutate the environment after the rollout — no triggering deployments, no writes.

data.name: Queryable trajectory
data.brief: As trajectories lengthen, stuffing the whole trace into a judge's context window stops working. Instead process the trajectory into something searchable: store it (e.g. in a database), enrich it with sub-agents, segment it into phases (log triage, code edit, post-change verification), and tag candidate failure points, so the judge-agent can navigate to the critical steps and adjudicate them.

data.name: Dynamic evaluation-time rubrics
data.brief: Emerging rubric/judge patterns beyond static grading. Deterministic verifiers are not dead — they run in tandem with judges, generating artifacts and metrics for the judge to read. Rubrics can be generated at evaluation time rather than fixed in advance, and can grant conditional partial credit by accepting the model's earlier (wrong) assumption and grading the remainder on top of it — "like grading a test where you assume the first part was right and check whether they got the rest right".

data.name: Environment learnability
data.brief: Whether a model can actually learn from an environment, measured before spending training compute: density of the reward signal (how granular the rubric is), the task distribution, and the quality of the underlying data. Key tension — over-dense rubrics on frontier problems the models cannot yet solve are applied inconsistently by judges, so rubric density has to stay inside what the judge can reliably apply; an unlearnable environment just burns compute.

data.name: Long horizon is a scalar on two incommensurable rulers, so vendor claims don't compare
data.brief: Practitioner argument that "long horizon" is not a category anyone can currently compare across vendors: it is a scalar that moves yearly, measured on two incommensurable rulers (expert-hours vs tokens/steps/tool calls), and cross-vendor claims — "our tasks average 16 hours", "ours 20" — are not comparable because methodology and expert quality dominate the estimate. The estimates get noisiest exactly where they matter most, at the top-1%/0.1%-of-humans frontier, and human and agent capability profiles are diverging so neither ruler alone paints the picture.

data.name: Published finance-agent benchmarks are short, saturated, narrow and coarsely rewarded
data.brief: Named critique of three published finance-agent benchmarks (GDPval, a tool-use benchmark, and "APEX agents"): (1) average human hours per task fall far below the METR long-horizon thresholds the leading frontier models already clear, so they aren't long-horizon tasks at all; (2) they are already reasonably saturated — in the APEX investment-banking section, pass@1 means ~57% of tasks are 100% solved; (3) breadth is narrow — GDPval's finance coverage is a small set of Excel tasks, APEX is largely IB, so credit, debt and risk go untested; (4) the reward signal is coarse relative to what training needs (their own rubrics run ~20 criteria with ~10 sub-criteria each).

data.name: Economically valuable work has no deterministic verifier, so judges grade it
data.brief: The RL gains of the last cycle came from hard-verifiable domains — math with a parseable answer, data-structure-style coding with test cases. The economically valuable work now in scope has no deterministic verifier that isn't "impractical, brittle or downright impossible", so reward comes from a judge/critic model plus rubrics, reading both the final environment state and the trajectory that produced it. Deterministic verifiers survive as instruments feeding the judge (generating artifacts, collecting metrics), not as the grader.

data.name: The judge inherits the agent's harness, with read-only access and queryable traces
data.brief: The verifier inherits the agent's engineering: as environments add tools and state, the judge needs the same harness and read-only access to the environment to check what actually happened (GitHub CI/CD and cloud logs after the redeploy) instead of the agent's tool-call claims; and long trajectories must be made queryable (stored, sub-agent-enriched, phase-segmented) because the naive "stuff the trace in the judge's context" call breaks. Reference-answer or sample-trajectory matching is called out as failing outright on ambiguous, open-ended tasks where the space of correct solutions can't be enumerated.

data.name: Reward hacking is the worst failure mode of long-horizon environments
data.brief: Reward hacking is treated as the worst failure mode of long-horizon environments, with concrete forms named: the agent escaping the sandbox, reaching privileged information, reading a hidden test suite for a coding task. Two-part mitigation — harden the verifier and the environment setup, and have the judge inspect the trajectory (the reason trajectory review exists at all). Counter-pressure: over-tight trajectory guidance "collapses the state space" of paths the agent explores, so rigidity is not a free defence.

data.name: A 50-task finance set averages 15 human-hours and models still struggle
data.brief: Vendor's own numbers, offered as the contrast to the saturated benchmarks: over a 50-task finance sample, mean human time to complete one task is 15 hours; models take a long time on them and still "struggle significantly" across every finance domain covered, with a reported mean score of 5 (scale not stated on the captions).

data.name: Duration is the wrong instrument; state coupling and ambiguity measure capability
data.brief: Duration is the wrong instrument. You can manufacture an arbitrarily "long-horizon" task by chaining unrelated independent subtasks and learn nothing about the model; what measures capability is state coupling (early decisions constraining later ones), tool-coordination breadth, and ambiguity at the start. Environment design, not task length, is the capability instrument — which is why benchmark comparisons on average-hours are close to meaningless without the complexity profile.

data.name: In a long-horizon environment the verifier, not the task, is the expensive artifact
data.brief: In a long-horizon environment the verifier, not the task, is the expensive artifact: the judge inherits the agent's tools, harness and state access (read-only), needs its own trajectory-processing infrastructure, its own rubric-consistency QA, and its own reward-hacking defences. Verification cost scales with environment complexity — so the binding constraint on training data for non-verifiable domains is verifier engineering, not task supply.

data.name: Every realism gain in an environment is paid for in grading difficulty
data.brief: The central design tension of environments: ambiguity is what makes a task resemble real work (humans never start with complete information, and exploration is the skill being tested), and ambiguity is exactly what multiplies the number of valid solution paths — which makes standardized evaluation "much, much harder". Every realism gain is paid for in grading difficulty, and rubric density is capped by what a judge can apply consistently.

data.name: Measure horizon on two rulers, and publish the methodology
guidelines: Report both expert-hours and model-side cost (tokens, steps, tool calls) for every task set
hold model and harness constant before comparing token counts across tasks
treat any cross-vendor hour comparison as invalid unless timing methodology and expert seniority are stated
expect human-hour estimates to degrade as tasks approach top-1% expertise
re-baseline the threshold every model generation (what a generation gains from a bigger context window or better compaction shows up directly as achievable trajectory length)

data.name: Build state coupling, not length
guidelines: Don't chain independent subtasks to inflate duration
make early decisions constrain later ones so a bad early query cascades (sequential complexity) rather than fanning out (parallelizable complexity)
widen tool coordination — logs, CI/CD, cloud consoles, databases — so information has to move across dependencies
introduce deliberate ambiguity in the opening instructions and artifacts to test exploration, and accept the grading cost that comes with it
check coverage across the domain's real subareas (credit/debt/risk, not just spreadsheet formatting) before claiming domain coverage
screen for learnability — reward density, task distribution, data quality — before spending training compute

data.name: Engineer the judge like an agent
guidelines: Give the judge the agent's harness with read-only permissions so it can inspect final environment state, and explicitly block post-rollout mutations (no redeploys, no writes)
verify state, not the agent's tool-call narration
make the trajectory queryable — persist it, enrich with sub-agents, segment into phases, tag failure points — instead of stuffing it into a context window
keep deterministic verifiers in the loop to produce artifacts and metrics for the judge
never grade open-ended tasks against a single reference answer or sample trajectory
keep rubric density inside what the judge can apply consistently
QA every rubric — gold tests, no-op tests, variance tests, coverage and expert-agreement checks — and escalate that testing as AI takes over rubric authoring and as tasks get longer

data.name: Data and Environment Curation for Post-Training LLMs (Mahesh Sathiamoorthy, Bespoke Labs — AI Engineer)
Mahesh Sathiamoorthy
Bespoke Labs
data.brief: Self-described "applied data research lab" whose mission is to give enterprises and frontier labs access to high-quality data and RL environments for post-training; also runs the post-training itself for enterprise custom models (hence "bespoke"). Ships Curator, Bespoke Stratos, OpenThoughts / OpenThoughts-Agents; core contributor to Terminal-Bench. `developer` chosen for consistency with the other environment/data vendors.

data.name: Intuit
data.brief: Named as the enterprise post-training case study, via its Credit Karma app (card-recommendation explanations). Transcript says "intude"/"Credit Karma"; Intuit is the parent per public record.

data.name: Bespoke Curator
data.brief: Open-source tool (shipped 2025) for curating synthetic post-training data: point it at a Hugging Face dataset of prompts, or at collected production logs, and it generates, filters and structures the responses for SFT. Integrates with post-training providers so a curated set flows straight into a fine-tune. The tool the OpenThoughts datasets were built with.

data.name: OpenThoughts
data.brief: Open reasoning dataset + curation recipe + paper, grown out of Bespoke Stratos (started immediately after DeepSeek-R1 landed, to close the gap between labs' private reasoning data and what the community could get) into a consortium with Stanford, UC Berkeley and UW. Headline result is a scaling law for a curation recipe — hold the recipe fixed and metrics keep improving as the dataset scales. Widely adopted; cited on stage as used internally at Thinking Machines.

data.name: OpenThoughts-Agents
data.brief: The agent-era successor: the same staged curation methodology applied to trajectories and RL environments for training agents rather than reasoning models — source selection (e.g. Stack Exchange), mixing, filtering, rollout generation, teacher choice — again validated by showing the metric scales with dataset size. Headline finding: SFT contributed most of the gains; RL was compute-intensive and bought the last few percent.

data.name: Curation recipe (staged + ablated)
data.brief: The method itself: treat data curation as an explicit staged pipeline — source questions, question mixing, question filtering (LLM-scored quality/hardness), answer or rollout generation with teacher models, answer filtering — run ablations at each stage to pick the knob setting, then prove the finished recipe with a scaling curve before scaling spend. Counterintuitive published results: sampling 16 answers to one question beats 16x more questions; stronger models are not always better teachers (Qwen-family beat Claude-family in the agent setting); answer filtering, synthetic question rewriting and task augmentation all underdelivered.

data.name: RL-environment reference stack
data.brief: Three-layer reference architecture for building environments and post-training on them. Bottom: compute and orchestration — sandboxes, spinning up rollouts, and for long-horizon rollouts checkpointing with snapshot/rollback. Middle: the environment layer — how you build RL environments, how you measure their quality, how you version them. Top: the training methods — SFT, RL, and prompt/harness optimization via reflection (GEPA). Presented as converging with the "algorithms / environments / compute" decomposition from another talk in the same session.

data.name: Tag-guided fine-tuning data
data.brief: Curation fix for imbalanced numeric data: instead of plain prompt/response pairs, annotate the response spans with tags so the model learns the required form rather than memorizing the over-represented values (the Credit Karma set was dominated by "0% APR", and the naively fine-tuned model hallucinated those numbers back). Produced "a big boost" in compliance metrics alongside latency and throughput gains.

data.name: Compute, base models and training infra are solved; data and environments are not
data.brief: Vendor's market read, stated as a layered diagram: compute is "kind of well defined", good open base models exist, and post-training infrastructure is well served (Fireworks, Tinker, slime are named). The one under-supplied input is high-quality data and RL environments — and the claim is that this binds for frontier labs as much as for enterprises: "this also applies to frontier labs where they have all this infra setup and they are needing good quality RL environments". Environments are explicitly classed as data: "RL environments are also something I'm calling data, it's just the data is now in a very different shape".

data.name: An open consortium publishes a reasoning dataset and a scaling law for its recipe
data.brief: Open-data counterweight to lab-private corpora: after DeepSeek-R1 showed what reasoning data buys, Bespoke started Bespoke Stratos and then formed the OpenThoughts consortium (Stanford, UC Berkeley, UW) to publish both the dataset and the curation recipe, with a paper whose main figure is a scaling curve for the recipe. Counterintuitive findings released with it (multiple answers per question beats more questions; stronger teacher is not a better teacher; answer filtering and synthetic rewriting underdelivering). Uptake cited on stage: Microsoft's CSO tweeting the work, John Schulman describing internal use at Thinking Machines.

data.name: SFT carried most of the agent gains; RL bought only the last few percent
data.brief: Cold-water result from OpenThoughts-Agents: in building agent training data, SFT still contributed the bulk of the gains; RL was "very compute intensive" and paid off for "the last few percentages"; and in enterprise settings SFT alone "works pretty well". Delivered by a vendor whose own business sells RL environments.

data.name: Credit Karma post-trained a model to fix compliance without blowing up latency
data.brief: Rare named enterprise post-training success (the speaker's own framing: "we haven't seen a lot of successes"). Intuit's Credit Karma explains why a card was recommended; prompting works but is not reliably compliant, and the long rule list required to make it compliant "blows up the latency". Fix: curate from the product's own data, tag the form-bearing spans so the fine-tuned model stops hallucinating the over-represented 0%-APR numbers, and post-train. Result: compliance, latency and throughput all improved, and the enterprise owns the model — insulation as frontier models get "more and more expensive".

data.name: Two independent vendors converge on the same three-layer environment stack
data.brief: Independent convergence on the same three-layer stack for environments + post-training (env build/quality/versioning, sandbox + rollout orchestration with checkpoint/snapshot/rollback, SFT/RL + GEPA-style prompt and harness optimization) — the speaker notes it matches, layer for layer, the algorithms/environments/compute decomposition presented in the preceding talk of the same session: "it feels like we are converging on something very similar". Called "the new reference stack for how at least we are building, and how many others are building".

data.name: Curate data from the researcher's chair: the only quality test is whether a run moves
data.brief: Structural mismatch in the industry: one population creates data and RL environments, a different population consumes them as researchers, and the two rarely meet. The prescription is to do both under one roof — "as you're curating data you want to put yourself in the shoes of the researcher to see what it takes to actually move the metrics on the models" — because the only meaningful quality test for a dataset or environment is whether a training run moves.

data.name: An RL environment is a dataset whose shape is executable
data.brief: Once compute, base models and training infrastructure are commodities, the scarce input keeps its identity but changes form: an RL environment is a dataset whose shape is executable. The practical consequence is that data-curation discipline transfers wholesale to environments — staged pipelines, per-stage ablations, quality measurement, versioning, and a scaling curve you prove before you scale spend — which is why the environment layer in the reference stack is a build/measure/version layer, not a content library.

data.name: Stage it, ablate it, then prove the scaling curve
guidelines: Decompose curation into stages (source, mix, filter, generate, filter) and settle each stage with an ablation rather than intuition
use LLMs to score question quality and hardness during filtering
