data.brief: The architecture the speaker claims is common to every production agent — personal (OpenClaw, Hermes) and coding (Codex, Cursor, opencode, Claude Code) alike: events arrive from many surfaces (chat, webhook, timer/heartbeat, other systems) → a control plane maps each event to a session key → the session key defines the state boundary and its session lane gives that mutable state exactly one active writer → the runtime calls models and tools → tools act through approvals and policy → the audit trail becomes the run receipt. The runtime itself is stateless: the harness rebuilds the working set (transcript, session state, memory, policy version, tool definitions) every turn, and the model sees only what the harness supplies.

data.name: State ownership (system of record)
data.brief: Every fact an agent might use later must have one named owner whose persistent state is the truth, and one replay path: a calendar event belongs to the calendar system, a support status to the ticketing system, a code change to the repo/workspace, a conversation turn to the session transcript, a user preference to the memory store. "Storage tells you where the bytes live; ownership tells you who can reconstruct reality." Operational test: for every such fact, who owns it and how would you replay it — if no owner can replay it, the system did not reliably remember it.

data.name: One ordered commit path
data.brief: One ordered commit lane per mutable state boundary — queue, mutex, transaction or lock (locks/mutexes across sessions, queues/transactions within one) — deliberately not a ban on concurrency: fan-out sub-agents, parallel reads, independent retrieval and many concurrent sessions all stay allowed. Serialization is scoped to commit time, never system-wide. Rejects "last writer wins" as a consistency model: two locally-correct writers doing load-modify-save silently erase each other.

data.name: Run receipt
data.brief: Evidence that survives the turn, recording the whole chain — what the model proposed, what policy allowed or denied, what execution attempted (tool/API, arguments, attempt number, idempotency key, external result), and what the user-visible edge confirmed or failed to confirm — plus the terminal outcome of every external boundary (success / failure / timeout / cancel / max attempts). Explicitly distinguished from a transcript (what the agent said) and from a tool result (what one component claimed): "a transcript is not the proof".

data.name: Approval as scoped execution state
data.brief: Human approval modelled as an object bound to the action it authorized rather than a vague memory that someone clicked yes: who approved, in which session and run, for which tool, for which arguments, for how long, with what outcome, and a pointer to the receipt. Expiry must terminate, not loop. If those fields fall off during a retry, replay or channel callback, the harness can no longer prove the executed action is the approved action. Governing rule: "capability is not execution — the model can request, the system decides".

data.name: Five harness failure shapes
data.brief: Diagnostic taxonomy derived from real OpenClaw issues: (1) state hole — delivery succeeds, the durable turn is never written; (2) overlapping writers — load-modify-save race, second save silently erases the first; (3) dangling tool call — a tool call with no matching result, so the run waits on an event that can never arrive and new messages queue behind the silence; (4) approval drift — an expired approved callback treated as retryable, surviving restarts and blocking later channel work; (5) missing edge proof — the message tool reports success but nothing renders for the user. Each is read with the same three questions: what did the user see, which boundary broke, what would the receipt have caught.

data.name: OpenAI Agents SDK
data.brief: Named at the close as the reference implementation where the harness primitives in this talk (session/state boundaries, ordered commits, approvals, audit) "are already built in", offered as the build-your-own-agent starting point.

data.name: Model proposes, harness commits, receipt proves it — agent failures are harness failures
data.brief: An OpenAI core-data/AI-infrastructure engineer states as the talk's whole program that most production agent failures are not model failures but harness failures, and formalizes it as a production contract: the model proposes, the harness commits, the receipt proves it. The model may suggest a message, a tool, an edit or a command, but "the model is not the production boundary" — the harness owns the state transition, the authority check, the ordered commit and the evidence. Car analogy for the split: the model is the engine, the harness is steering, brakes, road rules, dashboard and black box; "a powerful engine with no brakes is not autonomy, it is a liability with good acceleration".

data.name: Silent success: the durable turn is never written and the next turn inherits a lie
data.brief: The failure shape the talk opens and closes on: an agent is asked to remember a refund for a customer, replies that it recorded the fact, the interface looks normal — no error, no red screen — but the turn is never written to the durable record, so the next turn cannot reconstruct it. "The user experienced success; the system inherited incomplete reality." A crash at least gives you a boundary and a last-known-good point; silent success gives you a lie, and the next turn still sounds confident because the model is coherent over a broken history. Diagnosis: "coherence does not prove the working set was complete" — the missing boundary was state ownership, not intelligence.

data.name: OpenClaw's public issue tracker yields five reproducible harness failure shapes
data.brief: Method and finding: OpenClaw's public issue tracker is used as an open case study of harness failure, yielding five reproducible shapes — state hole, overlapping writers (load-modify-save race where two locally-correct writers produce one wrong outcome), dangling tool call (tool call with no matching result; the agent "simply looks stuck"), approval drift, missing edge proof. Claim attached: these are all classic distributed-systems failures — timeouts, retries, idempotency, locks, ordering, state ownership — not novel AI failures.

data.name: The button click existed, the valid authority did not: capability is not execution
data.brief: Authority boundary, from the approval-drift issue: an expired approved callback was treated as retryable, the callback state survived restarts and went on to block later channel work — "the button click existed, the valid authority did not". Generalized: capability is not execution; least privilege narrows the tool surface, scoped credentials ensure the right identity acts, and approval plus audit decide what happens before and after execution. "The model can reason about the boundary but it should not be the boundary".

data.name: A transcript is not proof — only a receipt ends at the user-visible edge
data.brief: Proof is a chain, not a claim: model proposed → policy allowed or denied → execution attempted → user-visible edge confirmed. The inverse of the opening incident is the missing-edge-proof issue, where the message tool reported success for a web-chat/TUI run but the message never rendered — internal success is not external proof, and the agent may later say "I already sent it" while the user truthfully says "I never saw it". A transcript records what the agent said; a tool result records what one component claimed; only the receipt records what can be verified at the boundary the user cares about.

data.name: Classic distributed-systems failures return, easier to trigger and harder to explain
data.brief: None of these failure modes are new — timeouts, retries, idempotency, locks, ordering and state ownership are decades-old distributed-systems problems. What changed is the setting: they now sit around a probabilistic planner with dynamic plans that rebuilds its context every turn, with more event sources feeding it and more action surfaces to act through. Agents do not invent new failures; they make the familiar ones far easier to trigger and much harder to explain, because the system stays fluent while it is broken.

data.name: Ordering is a product feature: users read concurrency bugs as personality
data.brief: Users never see queues, locks or commit paths — they see behaviour, and they read ordering bugs as personality: a lost correction feels forgetful, a stuck lane feels dead, completion-before-delivery feels confused. Concurrency control in an agent is therefore not an internal implementation detail but a user-facing product property.

data.name: Run the five-question receipt audit on one production trace
guidelines: Pick one agent system and one real production path, not all of them, and ask for the receipt
(1) What woke it up? — user message, webhook, timer, tool result, sub-agent or replay
name the trigger and its identity, or you cannot reason about deduplication, order or authorization
(2) What state did it inherit? — transcript, session state, memory snapshot, policy version, tool surface
the model only reasons over the working set the harness assembled
(3) Which authority did it use? — actor, session, tool, run, arguments, scope, lifetime
a model request is not permission, and authority should bind to one pending action
(4) What executed? — tool or API call, arguments, attempt number, idempotency key, external result: the side-effect boundary, not a summary of intent
(5) What evidence survived? — did the ticket update, did the message render, did the file change, does the calendar event exist
the receipt should end at the boundary the user cares about
these questions turn a fluent conversation into an inspectable production run

data.name: Give every mutable state boundary exactly one ordered commit path
guidelines: Name an owner (system of record) for every fact the agent may use later and make sure it can be replayed
then give that boundary one ordered commit lane — queue or transaction within a session, lock or mutex across sessions
keep parallel reads, independent retrieval, fanned-out sub-agents and concurrent sessions
be conservative at commit time only, never across the whole system
treat "last writer wins" as a bug, not a policy

data.name: Bound the work before the work bounds you
guidelines: Silence is not a terminal state: give runs deadlines and cancellation, add a watchdog so stuck work is visible, give tools timeouts and error results (so a missing result is impossible rather than invisible), and give channels recovery commands that do not queue behind the stuck work they are meant to fix
every external boundary needs an ending — success, failure, timeout, cancel or max attempts — and the receipt must record which one happened so the next step does not have to guess

data.name: Skills are new features: Building Skill-Centric Harness (Yogendra Miraje, FactSet — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Yogendra Miraje
FactSet
data.brief: Financial data and research company. Appears as an AI builder — agent-first product surface, an in-house harness with skill support, and an enterprise skill library under formal governance. Also named in the Kepler talk as a vendor of a structurally read-only terminal bought to displace culpability.

data.name: Skills as features
data.brief: The talk's thesis. When the agent becomes the product's main interface — the user talks to it, or it decides behind the scenes how the user navigates — the question "where do features live?" gets a new answer. Framing offered: prompts define who the agent is, tools define what it can connect to, skills define how a task gets done — and how is where the business logic that shapes agent behaviour belongs. Worked case: equity research and wealth management, two core finance workflows that used to be screens, buttons and dropdowns, are now merely skills. Two consequences he draws: a skill can be shipped by anyone in the company who understands the product, not only engineers; and the engineer's role shifts from shipping features to shipping harnesses — "smooth vehicles for your skills to run".

data.name: Skill registry
data.brief: The minimum viable implementation of skill support in a custom harness — three things: a skill registry (a collection of skills as name, description and path), a system prompt, and a basic file-read tool (plus bash or a code sandbox only if skills ship executable scripts). Discovery works by concatenating each skill's name, description and path into the system prompt — never the body — so the agent reads only the bodies it selects, which is progressive disclosure in its literal form. Around it sits a plain agentic loop: keep a messages array, call the model with messages and tools, append every tool call, terminate when a turn produces none.

data.name: Descriptions as routing signals
data.brief: The most operational lesson: skill descriptions are routing infrastructure, not documentation. Demonstrated with two near-identical skills (report-HTML and report-PDF) where only the description — "use this skill only when the user asks for a PDF report" — decides which fires; PDF is the trigger word. Rules: write descriptions about the user's request, not about the skill itself; keep them distinct enough that the agent doesn't get confused; don't let them go stale — those three are the reasons skills fail to trigger. In agentic products (unlike coding harnesses) skills are almost entirely model-driven, because non-technical users cannot be asked to carry the cognitive load of remembering which skill to invoke.

data.name: Skill library governance
data.brief: Five aspects, each answering one question, all borrowed from decades-old code practice. Admission — should this skill exist at all or fold into an existing one? (an automated gate on the registry with a human in the loop, analogous to PR review). Ownership — who maintains it? (named skill owners, like CODEOWNERS; skills maintained by the same application teams that maintain the features). Boundaries — allow-listed, access-controlled tools per skill. Lifecycle — semantic versioning, deprecation warnings, changelogs. Coherence — periodic audits and skill-validation checks so a large library still makes sense.

data.name: Blueprints
data.brief: FactSet's pre-skills in-house format, presented at the same conference a year earlier: a simple set of steps or recipe handed to an agent so it doesn't have to rediscover its path each time. Retrospectively described by its author as "simply a skill in a very naive form". Retired once Anthropic open-sourced Agent Skills — "since Anthropic had already open-sourced skills, there was no point trying to maintain our own standards" — making this one of the corpus's clearest first-person accounts of an enterprise abandoning a private format for a vendor-published open one.

data.name: FactSet's product features became skills; engineers now ship harnesses
data.brief: An incumbent financial-data vendor reports that product features have become skills: equity research and wealth management — two core finance workflows that were screens, buttons, dropdowns and dashboards — are now skills in an agent-first surface where the user talks to the agent or the agent decides how they navigate. Two structural consequences stated: skills can be shipped by anyone in the company who understands the product, not just engineers ("one of the most underrated things about skills"), and the engineer's role shifts from shipping features to shipping harnesses. Placement rule offered: prompts = who the agent is, tools = what it connects to, skills = how a task gets done, and that's where your business logic lives.

data.name: FactSet dropped its in-house "blueprints" format for Anthropic's open Agent Skills
data.brief: Dated standard-consolidation account, first-person and unusually clean: the speaker presented "blueprints" — his own recipe format for agents — at the same conference the previous year; Anthropic shipped Agent Skills in October 2025; FactSet dropped blueprints and adopted skills fully, because "since Anthropic had already open-sourced the skills, there was no point in trying to maintain our own standards". In hindsight blueprints were "simply a skill in a very naive form". A vendor-published open format displacing an enterprise's private one inside a year.

data.name: Skill routing changes mechanism as the library scales, it does not just get tuned
data.brief: Scaling account with thresholds: with a handful of skills, concatenating them into the system prompt just works; past roughly 10 skills that falls apart and you need to shortlist before injection — embeddings plus similarity search, or a smaller model that picks candidates; at hundreds of skills you need a hierarchy of skills, metadata filters and governance to keep the library searchable and coherent. His summary takeaway is the shape of the change rather than the numbers: "the routing mechanism doesn't get tuned as you scale — it changes the mechanism itself".

data.name: A model upgrade broke skill obedience with no line of any skill changed
data.brief: Production failure with a precise root cause: FactSet upgraded its stack to a new model and agents began failing to obey the skills — not a single line of any skill had changed. Cause found under the hood: the new model weighted the beginning of the skill file and the team's critical instruction sat at the end. Conclusions drawn, both quotable: "skills without evals are really just wishful thinking", and "skills are not documentation — they are contracts versioned to a model", so every model upgrade requires rerunning the skill eval suite.

data.name: Enterprise skill libraries need admission, ownership, boundaries, lifecycle and audits
data.brief: An enterprise formalizing skill governance, with the practices lifted directly from code: admission (an automated gate on the registry with a human in the loop, "very analogous to how we do the PR review process"), ownership (named skill owners like code owners; skills maintained by the application teams that own the corresponding features), boundaries (allow-listed, access-controlled tools per skill), lifecycle (semantic versioning, deprecation warnings, changelogs), coherence (periodic audits and skill-validation checks). Verdict: at enterprise scale, skill-library governance is "non-negotiable" — and "the good news is we can borrow a lot of good practices from code that have worked for decades".

data.name: Cut the skill library by user intent, not by your data model
data.brief: Hard-won library-design lesson, offered with the refactors admitted: he started from the data model — a skill for estimates analysis, a skill for fundamentals, a skill for news and analyst ratings — and real usage did not match, because users don't arrive with data-model-shaped requests. The correct cut is by user intent: an earnings preparation skill instead of an estimates-analysis skill; a pre-market briefing skill instead of news-and-ratings. And the expectation is set explicitly — start narrow, discover real use cases, refactor the library repeatedly, "and that is okay". This is the same lesson the descriptions teach one level down (write them about the request, not the skill).

data.name: Skills are contracts versioned to a model, not documentation
data.brief: Reclassification of what a skill is: not documentation for a model to consult, but a contract whose counterparty is a specific model version. Two consequences follow immediately and neither is obvious from the coding-agent discourse. A model upgrade is a breaking change — same skill text, different attention profile over the file, different behaviour — so the eval suite is the only instrument that detects it, and rerunning it is part of the upgrade. And the description is routing infrastructure, so a stale or overlapping description is a routing bug rather than a documentation debt. Skills inherit the obligations of code, which is why the governance model borrows from code.

data.name: Three components are the whole minimum
guidelines: To support skills in a harness you wrote yourself you need exactly three things: a skill registry (each skill as name, description and path), a system prompt, and a basic file-read tool — plus bash or a code-execution sandbox only if your skills ship executable scripts
build discovery by concatenating each skill's name, description and path — never the body — into the system prompt
the agent picks what to open and reads the body itself, which is progressive disclosure working as intended
keep the loop plain: a messages array, model called with messages and tools, every tool call appended, terminate the turn when the model returns no tool call
structure each skill as a SKILL.md whose front-matter name and description drive discovery and whose body carries the business logic and instructions, with references out to files and scripts

data.name: Write descriptions as routing signals, then govern the library like code
guidelines: Descriptions first: phrase them in terms of the user's request rather than the skill's contents, include the trigger vocabulary ("only when the user asks for a PDF report"), keep them mutually distinct, and refresh them — vague, overlapping or stale descriptions are why skills don't fire
cut the library by user intent, not by your data model, and expect to refactor as real use cases arrive
scale the routing in stages: system-prompt concatenation up to ~10 skills, embedding similarity or a small shortlisting model beyond that, hierarchy plus metadata filters at hundreds

then govern: an admission gate on the registry with a human in the loop (PR-review-shaped), named skill owners on the application teams that own the features, allow-listed access-controlled tools as each skill's boundary, semantic versioning with deprecation warnings and changelogs, and periodic audits and validation checks for coherence
rerun your skill evals on every model upgrade — the skill is a contract against that model

data.name: Let's integrate AI Agents in Event-Sourced Systems (Divakar Kumar, FlyersSoft — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Divakar Kumar
FlyersSoft
data.brief: Software engineering services firm; appears here through the payments/fraud platform its speaker architects — an AI-integrating enterprise system builder rather than an AI vendor.

data.name: Event sourcing
data.brief: Storage methodology where a user command appends an immutable business fact to an append-only event store instead of mutating state; domain events (transaction created) and integration events from other bounded contexts (payment approved, transaction rejected) accumulate as the system of record. Because the store is write-optimized, reads are served by separately projected read models (timelines, customer view, risk/fraud-indicator view) kept in sync by CDC — in NoSQL terms a change feed — rather than by querying the log.

data.name: Event-sourced agent context
data.brief: Using the event backbone as the agent's context supply: domain/integration events from every bounded context (transaction, accounts, device, payment) are propagated by CDC or by message-broker publication into a worker process, massaged in a projection layer, and landed in a materialized view the speaker calls a semantic layer — denormalized counts and averages, device trust scores and location/IP history, KYC status and account age, recent payments and chargebacks. Agent tools read the projection, never the source contexts, so agents need no privileged cross-context access and inherit the domain's own asynchronous boundaries.

data.name: Gray-zone triage
data.brief: Deployment discipline for non-deterministic components: keep the existing deterministic tier 1 (static rule engine + trained ML risk score) for the confident tails — below threshold approve, above threshold block — and route only the residual gray zone, where neither system can conclude, to an agentic tier 2. The stated rationale is explicitly not-replacement: "our thought process is not to exclude the systems we already had"; the agent earns its non-determinism by being applied precisely where the deterministic system is already uncertain, and by having real-time cross-domain context that the rule and ML engines never received.

data.name: Fan-out agent consensus with a verdict agent
data.brief: Tier-2 topology: one inbound event is fanned out to specialist agents in parallel — a risk-analyzer (fraud-history tool, device-trust tool, migrated business rules) and a behaviour-analyzer (transaction-pattern plugins) — after which a third agent reads both agents' responses and issues the verdict, which is published back to the message broker as an event. Coined because the alternative was tried and failed: collapsing the verdict into a metric or an if condition "goes back to the same criteria as the rule engine" and reproduced its false positives.

data.name: Agentic saga orchestration
data.brief: The existing saga orchestrator — the layer that already sequenced distributed transactions across bounded contexts — is where the agentic tier is installed, as sub-orchestrators (tier 1 deterministic, tier 2 agentic) rather than as a new service. The agent's verdict re-enters the saga as an ordinary event, the payment context approves, and the flow returns to the transaction context; no consumer of the saga needs to know an agent participated.

data.name: Azure Cosmos DB
data.brief: NoSQL database used as the production event store; its change feed is the CDC mechanism that drives projections into read models and into the agent-facing semantic layer. Ran in serverless mode in the demo — where the cold start visibly delayed the live POC.

data.name: Agents scoped only to the gray zone the rule engine and ML score cannot decide
data.brief: Production payments practitioner: the incumbent tier — a five-year-old static rule engine (unmaintainable against adapting fraudsters) plus a third-party-trained ML risk score — resolves the confident tails, and a new agentic tier 2 is scoped only to the gray-zone band neither can decide. The counter-intuitive defence is stated head-on ("why introduce a non-deterministic thing into an already uncertain case?"): the old engines failed for lack of real-time cross-domain context, not for lack of determinism. Opening anecdote is the failure mode being fixed — a $3,500 laptop purchase blocked three times, with the bank's own support staff unable to say why.

data.name: The event store, not a vector database, is the agent's context layer
data.brief: The agent's context problem is solved with infrastructure the business already owns: events are appended to a Cosmos DB event store as immutable business facts, a CDC change feed (or a message broker, for teams that don't do event sourcing) propagates them to a worker and projection layer, and the result is a materialized view — the speaker's "semantic layer" — from which agent tools read denormalized transaction, device, account and payment context. No vector store, no agent memory system, no new persistence layer is introduced anywhere in the architecture.

data.name: A decade of DDD and saga orchestration becomes the agent's substrate
data.brief: The decade of DDD investment turns out to be the agent's scaffolding, not an obstacle: bounded contexts stay isolated (transaction knows nothing of customer or device), the saga orchestrator gains an agentic sub-orchestrator rather than being replaced, agent verdicts publish back to the message broker as ordinary events, and downstream contexts subscribe as before. The talk's framing claim: agents are not just chatbots and coding assistants — the value shows up when they are applied to existing business workflows.

data.name: A dedicated verdict agent beats collapsing agent output into a threshold
data.brief: Collapsing the agentic tier's output into a single metric or if condition regressed straight back to the rule engine's behaviour — "many false positive cases". The fix was structural: fan out to a risk analyzer and a behaviour analyzer with distinct toolsets, then add a third agent whose only job is to read both responses and decide, publishing the verdict as an event. Business rules from the old engine are being migrated into agent tools rather than deleted.

data.name: A sub-500ms SLA rules out long-term agent memory and frontier-model latency
data.brief: A sub-500 ms transaction SLA is the binding constraint on every agent design choice: short-term in-memory memory only — long-term memory is explicitly ruled out; the language model "need not be an LLM, it could be an SLM or an open-source model"; and the decompose-act-check loop needs an explicit break metric, because "you should be really careful about avoiding this infinite loop" and the stopping rule differs per use case.

data.name: An event-sourced system is already agent-ready context
data.brief: An event-sourced system arrives pre-fitted for agents: it already holds immutable, time-ordered business facts, already has a propagation mechanism (CDC / change feed / broker), and already builds purpose-shaped read models. Adopting agents therefore reduces to adding one more projection — an agent-facing semantic layer — rather than to adopting a memory product. The corollary is the portability claim the speaker makes explicitly: any event source and either a relational or NoSQL store will do, and teams that don't practise event sourcing can reach the same place via the message broker.

data.name: Put the non-deterministic component where determinism already fails
data.brief: The right place for a non-deterministic component is precisely the band where the deterministic system is already uncertain — not everywhere, and not nowhere. Static rules degrade because adversaries adapt faster than the rules can be edited; ML scores collapse a rich situation into one number and threshold it; the agent's advantage is that it can be handed real-time, cross-domain context and asked for a reasoned verdict. Keeping tier 1 intact bounds the blast radius, bounds cost, and keeps the latency budget spendable on the few cases that need it.

data.name: Project your event stream into an agent-facing semantic layer
guidelines: Keep bounded contexts isolated and asynchronous — don't let agents read across them
append commands as immutable events rather than mutating state
drive propagation with CDC/change feed where the store supports it and with the message broker where other teams don't practise event sourcing
put a worker process between the stream and the view to massage and denormalize (counts, averages, recent activity, trust scores, KYC status, account age)
land the result in one materialized "semantic" view and expose it to agents only through tools
keep separate read models for separate purposes (timeline, customer, risk) instead of one general store
never serve agent reads from the event store itself

data.name: Tier an agentic layer into a transactional system
guidelines: Leave the rule/ML tier in place and route only the uncertain band to agents
install the agentic tier as a sub-orchestrator inside your existing saga rather than as a parallel system, and publish its verdict back as an ordinary event so downstream contexts are unchanged
fan out to specialist agents with distinct tools and add a dedicated verdict agent — a bare metric or if reintroduces the false positives you were escaping
migrate existing business rules into agent tools rather than discarding them
set an explicit loop-break metric per use case
and size memory to the SLA — under half a second, that means in-memory short-term context and possibly an SLM instead of a frontier model

data.name: Wearing the Agent: From Group Chats to Glasses (Sai Krishna Rallabandi — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Sai Krishna Rallabandi
Judith (multi-user always-on agent)
data.brief: Personally built agent deployed for 8 months in a real group setting — friends, family, and a conference attendee group — across group chat and glasses. Behaviours shown from production: answering a venue question by DM instead of in the group because the answer was privacy-sensitive; syncing multiple calendars to find a shared slot; noticing sleep-deprivation and adjusting; speaking to the wearer through the glasses rather than the car's speakers while driving so passengers wouldn't hear; curating a months-long evolving group conversation down to what stays relevant; and tutoring the speaker's three-year-old while reporting progress to the parents.

data.name: Jatayu (action-surface guard)
data.brief: The agent's security layer. Premise: an agentic system cannot be secured the way an LLM is — an LLM's output can be inspected, but an agentic system acts, so its exposed surface is vastly larger (every web page crawled, every group message and pasted screenshot, every GitHub issue, every promotional email) and larger still in a group. Design consequence: do not gate the input — let the agent read everything and place a deterministic guard at the action boundary (reading bash or secret/config variables, exporting data), fast enough to add no latency, classifying actions into three buckets: allow, require approval, block.

data.name: Skill-collision attack
data.brief: Attack class where two agent skills that are individually benign — and whose static scans are "pristine" — become malignant in composition at runtime: an OCR skill extracts attacker-planted content from a page, and a reporting skill then exfiltrates the user's PII along with the report to a third party. The skills themselves are uncompromised; the attacker owns only the content the agent reads. Reported at ~90% of observed attacks, with the accompanying finding that static-scan-surviving code can break at runtime. Punchline: "we can't read our way — or model-check our way — to safety".

data.name: Data/instruction channel separation
data.brief: Learned second layer above the deterministic gate: a LoRA-fine-tuned SLM, supervised on the guard's own traffic, that separates the data channel from the instruction channel and forwards only demonstrably benign content — so that when the instruction is "summarize this page" and the crawled page carries an injection, the injected text is obscured and the task still completes. Motivated by a concrete evasion the deterministic layer cannot catch: text interspersed with dots defeats regex and static approaches while a learned model catches it. Benchmarked against an agent-security eval where the naive baseline sits at ~50%, "a coin flip".

data.name: Atomic-fact memory
data.brief: Group-chat memory strategy: instead of storing the whole transcript and compacting it once it becomes overhead, extract atomic, high-value facts as the conversation accumulates (a plan, a date, an added constraint) and store those. Requires purpose-built auto-raters, on five axes: did we extract high-value atomic facts; are they the relevant ones for this conversation; are they hierarchically related; is their temporal weighting right; and is retrieval returning the right set — ideally intelligent, graph-organized retrieval rather than crawling everything.

data.name: Continual relevance scorer
data.brief: Forgetting mechanism for bloated memory: train a small ML model or SLM that scores stored context for importance continually rather than once, because in a group setting the context keeps evolving and different things matter at different times. The payoff is knowledge-based compaction — real token savings from dropping what has stopped mattering, instead of summarizing everything uniformly.

data.name: Per-user LoRA permissions
data.brief: Privacy architecture for a shared agent: one common shared memory layer with a separately trained LoRA adapter per user on top, so each person's permissions are baked into the weights that serve them — "baking the permissions not by using code but by using machine learning itself" — rather than enforced by an access-control layer over a single store. Explicitly analogized to how the human brain holds shared and private context.

data.name: Recipient routing
data.brief: The third harness concern for multi-user agents, and explicitly not model routing to save tokens: routing the finished information to the right person, channel and moment — DM rather than the group when the answer is sensitive, glasses rather than the car audio when passengers are present, silence when nobody asked. Includes the observed failure mode (group-deployed agents are "over-articulative when they are not asked questions") and the proposed fix: a small learned classifier for role and speaking permission.

data.name: Agents move from a customer of size one to groups, wearables and always-on
data.brief: Framing claim from 8 months of production experience: "almost every agent we build today has a customer of size one" — including enterprise coding assistants — and the next one won't. The next agent serves a group, is wearable, and is on all day, and group deployment is qualitatively different, not a scaling factor: it adds three harness concerns the single-user case never had (a guard, group memory, and routing of the answer to the right person). The observation that the field has "won" at building single-user agents — "we can build an agent in an afternoon and it does useful things by evening" — is what makes the question shift.

data.name: Individually clean skills become malignant in composition at runtime
data.brief: Two cited papers: a runtime skill audit finding that static-scan-surviving skill code can break at runtime, and a "when safe skills collide" finding that two individually benign skills become malignant when run together — OCR extracts attacker-planted content, the reporting skill then ships the user's PII to a third party alongside the report. Reported at ~90% of observed attacks, i.e. the composition case is the normal case, not the tail. Consequence stated directly: you cannot review or model-check your way to safety, and you cannot remove everything at the door.

data.name: Stop gating the input; guard the action surface deterministically, then learn on top
data.brief: Security design inversion for agentic systems: because the read surface is unbounded (every page, message, screenshot, GitHub issue, promotional email — all day, and multiplied in a group), stop trying to gate the input and gate the action. First layer: a deterministic regex/classical-NLP check at the action boundary (bash variables, secret/config reads, exports) sorting into allow / needs-approval / block — deterministic so it costs no latency. Second layer, because the deterministic one is beatable (dotted text walks straight through regex): a LoRA-fine-tuned SLM separating data channel from instruction channel, measured against an agent-security benchmark where the naive baseline is a 50% coin flip, giving something to hill-climb.

data.name: The model is just the engine; the memory is what the agent becomes
data.brief: "The model is just the engine … the memory is what the agent becomes, and it's becoming in real time." In a group deployment naive memory (embeddings, files, store-everything-then-compact) fails, and the working design is: extract atomic high-value facts; build auto-raters for extraction quality, relevance, hierarchical relation, temporal weighting and retrieval; organize for intelligent graph-style retrieval instead of crawling; run a continually adapting relevance scorer ("learning what not to forget") so compaction is knowledge-based; and make the memory-injection engine KV-cache-aware, because "KV caches break when we try to do something cute with the model" — under both cloud and local serving. Less stored is also fewer tokens and lower latency.

data.name: A shared agent is a new social contract: sensitivity belongs to the room, not the datum
data.brief: A shared assistant "is not just a large model shared between people — it's almost a new social contract": the same fact is public or private depending on the room, not on the data (a grocery list is benign for everyone; salary or health is not — "the data has not changed, the room in which it is deployed has changed"). Two mechanisms proposed: a common shared memory layer with a per-user LoRA adapter, so permissions are learned rather than coded; and a learned role/floor classifier for when to speak and when not to, since group-deployed agents are consistently over-proactive when unasked.

data.name: Guard the effect, not the input
data.brief: An agentic system's read surface is unbounded and adversarial by default, so input filtering is the wrong control point — it either lets attacks through or gates everything and destroys the agent's usefulness. The tractable control point is the action: a small, fast, deterministic decision at the moment of effect, with a learned model layered on top for the evasions determinism cannot see. The corollary that makes this urgent is compositional: the units being audited (skills) are individually clean, so audit-per-unit is structurally blind and only runtime, effect-level checks can see the attack.

data.name: Multi-user agents need a social layer: guard, memory and recipient routing
data.brief: Moving an agent from one user to a group changes the engineering problem, not its size. Three properties that are trivial or absent for a personal agent become the whole design: what gets in (a guard, against a surface that now includes everyone's messages and pastes), what is kept (memory that is curated, temporally weighted and continually re-scored, because a group's context evolves under you), and who hears the answer (channel, recipient and moment — DM vs group, glasses vs car speaker, and often silence). The privacy rule underneath is contextual, not classificatory: sensitivity is a property of the room, so permissions have to travel with the audience rather than with the datum.

data.name: Build the guard at the action surface, not the input
guidelines: Let the agent read everything — gating the input gates the product
put the check where the agent takes an effect (bash/secret/config reads, exports, sends) and keep that first layer deterministic (regex/classical NLP) so it adds no latency
sort actions into three classes — allow, require approval, block — rather than binary pass/fail

expect the deterministic layer to be evaded (dotted or interspersed text defeats static approaches) and train a second, learned layer on the guard's own traffic — a LoRA-fine-tuned SLM that separates the data channel from the instruction channel and passes only benign content
benchmark it (a naive baseline is a coin flip, so there is real headroom to hill-climb)
assume skills are individually clean and audit compositions at runtime, not units at scan time

data.name: Curate group memory and route the answer
guidelines: Don't store the transcript and compact it later — extract atomic, high-value facts as the conversation goes
build auto-raters for the five axes (extraction quality, relevance, hierarchical relation, temporal weighting, retrieval quality) or you cannot tell whether the memory is working
organize memory for intelligent retrieval (graph-style) instead of crawling everything
train a continually adapting relevance scorer so forgetting is knowledge-based and tokens actually drop
keep the memory-injection engine KV-cache-aware — clever per-request memory surgery invalidates the cache
give each user a LoRA adapter over a shared memory layer so permissions are learned rather than policed

and route the output deliberately — DM instead of the group when it's sensitive, the personal device instead of the shared speaker, and train a role/floor classifier so the agent stops talking when nobody asked

data.name: Your Finance Agent's Bottleneck Is You (Ramana Siddanth Emani, Auditoria AI — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Ramana Siddanth Emani
Auditoria AI
data.brief: Builds production AI agents for finance/accounting teams. Appears as a vendor whose internal engineering loop is the talk's subject; the finance-specific content is the SOX/accountability constraint on that loop.

data.name: Dev loop velocity
data.brief: The talk's thesis: the binding constraint on production agent quality is the speed of the internal developer loop, not the model, the chips or the framework. Each of those refreshes on a known cadence and is swappable — a new model roughly every 3.5 months, new GPUs roughly annually, new frameworks constantly — so none of them is where a team's differential lives. Production bugs, by contrast, arrive by the hour once demos become pilots and the agent meets customer data it has never seen. Four primitives named for compounding the loop: sub-agents, skills, MCP connectivity, and minimal UX.

data.name: Parallel worktree sub-agents
data.brief: The parallelism mechanic: git worktrees as isolated folders, one per task, so sub-agents write code without fighting over the same files. Claimed density: ~50 active worktrees / sub-agents on a 48 GB MacBook, with the human acting as orchestrator. Task supply comes from the existing backlog — each QA-reported Jira ticket becomes its own worktree, handled by an agent that may spawn further sub-agents. Explicit rule: do not queue the tasks yourself, the agent does it better.

data.name: Single-pane agent console
data.brief: The "minimal UX" primitive, built as a macOS widget: the production agent software, project dashboards, Kubernetes services and pods, system logs, Jira tickets, GitHub PRs and a Claude Code session on one surface, replacing multiple windows across two or three monitors. Its stated metric is unusual and memorable — the number of neck rotations required to ship one change. Rationale: with many parallel sub-agents the orchestration surface, not the work, becomes the human's cost.

data.name: Human as verifier, not throughput ceiling
data.brief: The talk's closing design rule and its answer to its own title. In a nine-step pipeline (parse requirements → root-cause analysis → implement fix → local end-to-end test → PR → review → merge → build/deploy to dev → deploy to stage), the human is needed at step 1 and step 9 only — to see what the agent is doing and to validate before it reaches QA. "Always have the human as a verifier, but not the throughput ceiling, because human attention is very limited." The finance corollary makes it non-optional: an auditor reviews and a controller signs for SOX compliance, and agent reviewing agent leaves accountability nowhere.

data.name: Dev-loop velocity, not the model, chips or framework, is the binding constraint
data.brief: Vendor-side diagnosis of the demo-to-production gap: demos are trivial to ship ("writing code is very easy"), but once promoted to pilots with new customers the agent meets data it has never seen and production bugs arrive by the hour. The four candidate culprits are dismissed in turn as swappable on a schedule — a new model roughly every 3.5 months, new chips roughly yearly, a new framework any day, and the agent loop itself — leaving dev-loop velocity as the thing a team actually controls. Model capability rises exponentially; the developer's daily job is automating their own loop to keep up.

data.name: Fifty parallel worktree sub-agents on one laptop, human at steps 1 and 9 only
data.brief: Concrete parallelism claim from a production finance-agent vendor: ~50 active git worktrees, each an independent sub-agent, on a 48 GB MacBook, with the engineer as orchestrator. Backlog becomes the task queue — each QA-reported Jira ticket gets its own worktree and its own agent, which spawns further sub-agents — and the human is told not to sequence the work because the agent does it better. The nine-step pipeline (requirements → RCA from traces and logs → TDD → fix → local end-to-end → PR → review/merge → dev image → stage) runs with human involvement at steps 1 and 9 only.

data.name: Ask the agent to enumerate and remove the loop's bottlenecks, daily
data.brief: The compounding mechanic, described as a repeatable month-long procedure rather than an aspiration: production failures become the loop's input; run the loop for a day or two, close five or six bug tickets, then ask the agent to enumerate every bottleneck in the process, list them, and remove them one at a time, daily. Claimed end state after ~a month: one sentence ("fix this bug") drives the agent to connect to the databases, pull logs, traces and tickets, ship the fix and move it through the Jira-to-QA pipeline. Framed as recursive self-improvement applied to the internal developer harness, not to the model.

data.name: SOX requires a human signer, so agent-reviewing-agent has nowhere to put the blame
data.brief: The regulated-sector constraint, and the batch's clearest statement of why finance loops differ: with AI removed from the picture, a human auditor reviews the code and a controller signs off under SOX. Agent-reviewing-agent has nowhere to put that accountability — "if something goes wrong in production you can't say Claude is doing this" — and "moving fast and breaking things in the finance sector is a lot different". This is what pins the human to the loop boundary even as everything between the boundaries is automated; the bottleneck that remains is therefore human attention, not model capability.

data.name: Goals, loops and background "dreaming" as everyday autonomy mechanics
data.brief: Three autonomy mechanics named as current practice, notable for how casually they are stated: goals ("you can set a goal and forget about it"), goals combined with loops (set a goal on a data discrepancy between source data and agent output, close the laptop, steer from a phone), and "dreaming" — letting the agent run in the background over accumulated customer sessions, where many users hit the same patterns and problems, compacting them into data points the system uses to upgrade itself. Model context given for why this is now plausible: the arrival cadence of Fable 5, Mythos 5 and GPT 5.6.

data.name: Human attention becomes the ceiling once sub-agent parallelism is cheap
data.brief: The title's argument, generalized: once sub-agent parallelism is cheap, the constraint migrates from model capability to the orchestrator's attention. Fifty parallel agents do not make a team fifty times faster if a person must watch them; the cost surface becomes windows, monitors and context switches (hence a metric as blunt as neck rotations per shipped change). Two responses follow, and they are different in kind: collapse the orchestration surface into one pane, and remove the human from the middle of the loop while keeping them at its boundary — because the boundary role is verification, which is not a throughput function.

data.name: What compounds is automating the loop, not any individual task
data.brief: What compounds is not any individual automated step but the daily removal of bottlenecks from the loop itself — and that meta-work is itself delegable: the agent is asked to audit the process it just executed and name what slowed it. The artifact that improves over a month is the harness, not the model and not any one automation. Corollary he draws for the job: "sitting behind a desk from 9 to 5 just writing code is not valid anymore", because a developer's variety of work is exactly what the loop absorbs.

guidelines: Treat git worktrees as the isolation primitive — one folder per task so parallel sub-agents never contend over the same files — and drive them from the backlog you already have: every QA-reported bug ticket becomes a worktree with its own agent, which spawns its own sub-agents

keep the human at intake and final validation and out of everything between

collapse the whole surface — services and pods, system logs, tickets, PRs, agent session — into one pane so orchestration costs no window switching, and measure yourself on how many times you turn your head to ship one change

guidelines: Feed the loop the four primitives first: skills as your organization's (and your customers') secret recipes so agents follow the correct workflow rather than improvising one

data.name: Build for the Memo, Not the Demo (Shawn Chan, China Resources Holdings — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Shawn Chan
China Resources Holdings
data.brief: Hong Kong-headquartered state-owned conglomerate; appears here purely through its investment/deal-committee function, which is the vantage point of the whole talk.

data.name: Memo versus demo
data.brief: The talk's organizing distinction between two machines the industry keeps conflating. A demo: one clean document in, one fluent answer out, whose entire job is to make a room say "oh" for five minutes. A memo: the real committee document written before real money moves — hundreds of pages, filings, transcripts, broker notes, someone's rushed notes from a call last Tuesday, half the sources disagreeing with each other — whose job is not to impress but to survive an argument. The claim: almost every AI finance product is built for the first and none for the second. And the closing twist — "there is no safe demo anymore": the moment real money is watching, every sentence becomes a memo sentence.

data.name: The 30-second click-through
data.brief: The single acceptance test he applies: someone points at a sentence and says "show me where this comes from", and you either click once and land on the exact source paragraph, or you open seven browser tabs and start scrolling. Requirement stated for the product: every claim links straight to its source paragraph with the source's trust level attached — not a citation tab at the end of the document. "If you remember one sentence from this whole talk: the click-through is the product. Everything else is well-written packaging".

data.name: Fact/guess separation
data.brief: Facts and estimates must live in visibly separate boxes, because fluent generation melts them into one smooth sentence — "the company will likely receive approval next quarter" reads like a fact and is a guess wearing fact-shaped clothing. A committee's entire job is to argue with the guesses while trusting the facts, which it cannot do if it can't find the seam; the only remaining options are to approve or reject the whole document. Observed failure: "approval expected" drifting to "approval received" across three drafts, nobody lying, until nobody remembered it began as a guess — and the approval didn't arrive. Fix is cheap: a label, a tag, a colour — anything that survives being copy-pasted into someone else's slides three weeks later.

data.name: Contradiction surfacing
data.brief: "A contradiction is not a bug, a contradiction is a gift." When the CEO's number on the earnings call and the number in the official filing disagree, that gap is the most interesting fact in the story and is exactly what real diligence hunts for. Trained to be smooth and helpful, AI does the opposite: it quietly picks whichever version reads better and moves on, and the reader never learns there was a disagreement. Design rule: the builder's job is not to resolve the argument, it is to make the argument happen in front of a human rather than silently inside the box.

data.name: Accountable human signature
data.brief: At the bottom of every real decision a human signs, and accountability cannot be delegated to software. Evidence offered is an airline whose website chatbot invented a bereavement-refund policy and which then argued at tribunal that the chatbot was a separate legal entity responsible for its own actions — "the corporate version of my dog ate my homework"; the tribunal disagreed and the airline paid. Product requirement: a real human approval gate that is logged — who reviewed what, what changed, when they signed — and that log is the audit trail. "If your architecture doesn't have an accountable human at the end of it, you have not built a product, you have built an excuse generator."

data.name: Almost every AI finance product is built for the demo, almost none for the memo
data.brief: Buyer-side verdict from ~200 investment-committee meetings across 15 years of cross-border deals: "almost every AI finance product is built to impress people for five minutes, and almost none are built to survive a room whose entire job is to not be impressed." The committee's currency is not intelligence — "money doesn't follow intelligence, money follows trust" — and trust is fragile when the thing that wrote the page has never once said "I'm not sure". Increasingly the confident person handing him the paper is a chatbot, and it is better written than the humans: better grammar, nicer formatting, never defensive under follow-up.

data.name: One unchecked demo sentence cost roughly $100B of market value in February 2023
data.brief: The dated demonstration that demo-grade and memo-grade are not separate worlds: February 2023, a major tech company launches its AI assistant with a promotional demo; the assistant answers a simple question about a space telescope wrongly; the market notices and the stock falls ~8% in a day — roughly $100 billion of value on one unchecked sentence. His reading: nobody in that company asked the question every junior analyst on his team is trained to ask before anything leaves the building — "wait, where does this claim come from, did anyone check it?" Even the demo failed the memo test.

data.name: Six ways AI output loses a finance room, from source trust to no accountable signer
data.brief: A practitioner's taxonomy of how AI output loses a finance room, each with a case attached: (1) undifferentiated source trust — an expensive AI tool quoted a rough guess texted in a group chat six months earlier while the audited number sat three rows away in the filing, because "the model loved the confident phrasing"; an audited filing is an accountant under oath, an analyst note a confident friend at a party, an internal email something overheard in an elevator, and most retrieval systems cannot tell them apart. (2) figures that don't reconcile — 18% on page 1 versus 17.4% in a table on page 11 killed a memo, not for the 0.6 but for what it implied about the hard checks. (3) smoothed-over contradictions. (4) guesses in fact-shaped clothing. (5) unfindable provenance. (6) no accountable signer.

data.name: An unsupervised pricing model produced a ~$500M write-off and a unit shutdown
data.brief: The industrial-strength version of the reconciliation failure: a large US real-estate company let an algorithm buy houses at scale; the algorithm was "extremely confident about house prices, the houses disagreed"; the company wrote off ~$500M, shut the unit and let go ~25% of staff. Diagnosis, and the reason this sits in a harness argument rather than a model argument: "the model wasn't stupid, the model was unsupervised — nobody built the boring machinery that forces the numbers to keep agreeing with reality".

data.name: You cannot outsource accountability to a chatbot — courts and tribunals agree
data.brief: Two liability cases used to establish that a human must sign. A New York lawyer filed a chatbot-assisted brief citing six court cases that did not exist, with correct-looking citation formatting, real-sounding names and page numbers — and, before filing, asked the chatbot whether the cases were real and was told yes ("like asking the guy who sold you the watch whether the watch is real"); the judge fined him. An airline's website chatbot invented a bereavement-refund policy, and the airline's tribunal defence was that the chatbot was a separate legal entity responsible for its own actions; the tribunal rejected it, the airline paid, "and every one of us in our boardroom quietly took a note that day".

data.name: In a memo domain the shipped artifact is the ability to defend the answer
data.brief: The five things he demands of a vendor before letting a system near a live deal are, he notes, conspicuously not intelligence problems: receipts on every claim, visible fact/guess separation, automatic figure reconciliation, surfaced contradictions, and a logged human approval. "Notice what's not on the list… all five are plumbing and honesty problems." So the category won't be won on benchmark points — it will be won because "a tired, skeptical finance person can trust the output at 11 at night without opening seven tabs". In a memo domain the shipped artifact is not the answer, it is the ability to defend the answer.

data.name: Your pitch deck becomes someone's internal memo
data.brief: The promised second half, and the reason he frames the talk as one muscle rather than two: "your deck becomes a memo — literally, someone like me sits down and writes an internal memo about you", and every number said out loud in the pitch gets checked against the data room. The discipline that makes a product survive an investment committee is the same discipline that gets the product funded, because the buyer and the investor are the same reader running the same test. Confidence is not the qualifying signal — "some of the most confident people I've met in finance were also the most wrong; AI just learned that trick faster than the rest of us".

data.name: The five things a buyer demands before a system goes near a live deal
guidelines: (1) Every claim comes with a receipt — each sentence linked straight to its source paragraph with the source's trust level attached, not a citation tab at the end
(2) facts and guesses stay visibly separate — at a glance on the page, what is proven versus what is someone's best estimate, labelled in a way that survives copy-paste into someone else's slides
(3) numbers agree with each other automatically — the system refuses to ship a document whose figures don't match, with no human checking at 2 a.m.
(4) contradictions get surfaced, never smoothed over — when sources disagree the system raises its hand instead of picking the more fluent answer
(5) a real human approval gate, logged — who reviewed what, what changed, when they signed
that log is the audit trail
then test it with the 30-second challenge: point at any sentence and demand its source — one click, or seven tabs

data.name: Rank evidentiary authority before retrieval ranks proximity
guidelines: Not every source deserves the same trust, but most AI systems treat them as if they do — they grab whichever text is nearest the question and hand it over as gospel

tier them explicitly and carry the tier with the claim: an audited filing is an accountant speaking under oath, an analyst note is a confident friend at a party, an internal email or group chat is something overheard in an elevator
expect the model's failure direction to be predictable — it prefers the more enthusiastic phrasing, which is systematically the least authoritative source
assume the audited number is present and three rows away, and that the system will not reach it on similarity alone
if your system can't tell an accountant under oath from a rumour in a group chat, it is not ready for real money

data.name: How Kepler Built Verifiable AI for Financial Services (Vinoo Ganesh — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Citadel
data.brief: Hedge fund. The talk's recurring worked example, not just a resume line: analysts scouring sources as the historical origin of edge; the portfolio manager as the model for how an AI system should be scoped; and the two-TMT-desks example that grounds the "verification is not ground truth" claim.

data.name: Atomic provenance
data.brief: Kepler tenet 1. The model is never allowed to write or manipulate a number — it writes a reference to the number and hands off to a system built for numbers (a database). Every produced figure runs through a deterministic check against the provenance ledger; anything that can't be independently verified is stripped out and never reaches the user, and the cycle repeats at least twice. Explicitly not a multi-model cross-check ("these are not probabilistic systems evaluating each other's work") — the atomicity is database atomicity: extract, persist, confirm the process occurred. The ledger resolves a number to one of three origins: extraction from a filing, a derivative calculation, or the firm's internal documents.

data.name: Scope determinism
data.brief: Kepler tenet 2. The model decides what to compute; it never does the computation. Reasoning and planning stay with the model ("intelligence is commoditized"); parsing a PDF or XBRL and running the arithmetic is code, and the deterministic layer persists the result outside anything the model can see. Rationale is both correctness and cost: "why would I run 1 + 1 through a multi-billion-parameter model instead of one CPU cycle?" Described as a contrarian position with VCs a year earlier that has since become mainstream.

data.name: Derivation chains
data.brief: Kepler tenet 3. Reconciliation for figures that exist in no filing — gross margin, enterprise value, EBITDA adjustments, recurring-vs-non-recurring classification — where every firm calculates differently. The firm's conventions are codified into the processes that run, and a chain of events records what went into each individual number and each outcome, replayable and rewindable. Framed as the machine version of the chain of reasoning an analyst performs on a desk before a risk/reward decision.

data.name: Verification over citation
data.brief: The talk's core distinction. A citation shows where information came from and is "effectively an after-the-fact audit"; it got the industry "50% of the way there" and is undermined by uncurated sources (a random Substack, Seeking Alpha, Reddit are data points, not vetted sources). A verification is a deterministic, repeatable, numerically checkable mechanism proving a specific number is the correct one from a specific source. Corollary stated hard: "evals are not verifiable — you cannot take a non-deterministic LLM and eval your way to something deterministic", and fine-tuning to 94% extraction accuracy is not a fix because "a wrong number is still wrong if you're in that unfortunate 6%".

data.name: Culpability displacement
data.brief: Why incumbent financial-data terminals are actually bought: not for information (much of it is free in SEC filings) but to transfer blame — a central vetted instance means "at least if it's wrong, everyone on Wall Street has the same incorrect information". The structural consequence is that every such tool is read-only: the analyst consumes and then produces the work product by hand, which is named as the biggest wall to meaningful AI adoption on Wall Street. Verifiable work product is the thing that dissolves the arrangement — a system that can prove its own numbers absorbs both the data-vetting contractors and the culpability.

data.name: Kepler's three tenets: atomic provenance, scope determinism, derivation chains
data.brief: Kepler's shipped architecture for numerical accuracy, presented as the distillation of an Anthropic customer case study: atomic provenance (model writes a reference, never the number; deterministic check strips anything unverifiable; provenance ledger; cycle repeats), scope determinism (model decides what to compute, code computes it, result persisted outside the model), derivation chains (replayable, rewindable record of what produced each derived figure under the firm's own conventions). Output claim: consolidate financial statements in seconds with every number tied back to its individual source, and build a DCF in the requested format without the model hallucinating a row that shouldn't exist. Explicitly displaces the contractor-vetting model of the incumbent data vendors.

data.name: You cannot eval your way from a non-deterministic LLM to determinism
data.brief: Direct attack on the industry's trust vocabulary from a finance builder: "trust and verifiability have been largely abused — evals are not verifiable; you cannot take a non-deterministic LLM and eval your way to something deterministic." Supporting datum: Kepler trained an extraction model that outperformed foundation models at ~94% accuracy and he dismisses it on stage — "who here would trade off something that's 94% accurate? … a wrong number is still wrong if you're in that unfortunate 6%" — calling fine-tuning your way to probabilistic accuracy something "TechCrunch will be really excited about" and nobody else. Citations are an after-the-fact audit worth ~50% of the problem.

data.name: AI has made a writing problem a reading problem
data.brief: The value-migration claim: "AI has made a writing problem a reading problem." Producing content — code, marketing, a DCF — is now nearly free ("heavily subsidized, thank you VCs"); the hard part is trusting what was produced. Historically edge came from consumption capacity (Citadel hiring hundreds of analysts to scour sources); once a model reads everything, that edge decays. Concrete cost of the unsolved reading problem: analysts still working till 4 a.m., "folks in investment banks actually dying because of the hours", and regulators (SEC, OCC) requiring that any trading decision be justifiable from named sources.

data.name: Bloomberg and FactSet terminals are bought to displace culpability, not to inform
data.brief: Market-structure claim, delivered as the talk's "more aggressive" statement: people buy Bloomberg and FactSet to displace culpability, not to obtain information that is free in SEC filings — the value is that a vetted central instance means everyone on Wall Street is wrong together. Every such tool is read-only, so the analyst still produces the work product by hand; that is named as the biggest wall to AI adoption across Wall Street. Once AI can produce verifiable work product, the contractor-vetting layer behind the incumbent data providers is what gets absorbed.

data.name: Token-maxing rewards will give way to an ROI and cost-optimization wave
data.brief: Called turn in the market's spending posture, from someone who watched the previous one: token consumption is currently rewarded — a conference club with gold cards for people who consumed a billion-plus tokens, companies "giving bonuses on people token maxing" — which he calls historically absurd ("in what time in history has an employee been rewarded for your company to pay another vendor?"). He predicts the same ROI/cost-optimization wave he watched hit Snowflake and Databricks four years earlier, arriving as "the right tool for the right job — sometimes you don't need a multi-billion-parameter model when one CPU cycle will just work". Adjacent datum: GLM 5.2, downloadable from Hugging Face, is put on par with a frontier Opus release as evidence that intelligence is commoditized.

data.name: Verifiable work product is AI's pre-SSL moment
data.brief: The industry is "pre-SSL in the e-commerce ecosystem": the TAM is trillions, and the number of people willing to put a credit card on the internet before security existed was zero. Verifiable work product is the missing security layer, and the mechanism generalizes past finance — a pre-processing step that deterministically extracts and stores case citations for legal AI so briefs can't hallucinate them, or drug-discovery formulations out of NIH papers so no compound is missed. Corollary he draws: the RAG platforms that codified workflows are why the foundation labs can attack every one of these categories — even "Claude for science" is still a RAG system, not a deterministic one, so the deterministic-substrate layer is the part nobody has built.

data.name: Verification is firm-relative, not ground truth
data.brief: Verification is not ground truth — it is proof that an output respects the nouns, verbs and rules of your organization. Finance is one of the rare industries where two people with identical information can take opposite sides, and two TMT desks at the same fund can run the same verification mechanisms to opposite conclusions. So the last mile is not accuracy but personalization: verifiable ontologies that proxy a specific firm's investment process, the finance analogue of mining a company's PRs, commits and reviews to reconstruct its ontology. This is the same lock-in claim as his batch-14 talk, now stated as a correctness requirement rather than a moat.

data.name: Let the model choose the computation, never perform it
guidelines: Model the AI on a portfolio manager: it plans and decides inside a grounded scope with a risk threshold, and reaches for deterministic tools to act
never let the model write or manipulate a number — have it emit a reference and hand off to a system built for numbers
parse the PDF or the XBRL in code and persist the result outside the model's reach
run every produced figure through an independent deterministic check and strip anything that fails, rather than surfacing it with a caveat
do not build a probabilistic cross-check (one lab's model checking another's) — that is still probability checking probability
repeat the extract → persist → confirm cycle at least twice
side benefit: it is materially cheaper, because the model stops doing work it should never have been doing

data.name: Codify the firm's conventions, then record the chain
guidelines: Every derived figure that appears in no filing — gross margin, enterprise value, the EBITDA adjustment set, what counts as recurring — is calculated differently by every firm, so the firm's conventions must be codified into the processes that run, not inferred per query
record a chain of events for each number and each outcome so both can be replayed and rewound, the way an analyst's reasoning on a desk can be walked back

declare up front which data points the system is allowed to produce (structured filings, numerical data) and which it is never allowed to produce — if it would have to extract from prose or a raw table, it doesn't
then every consolidated statement can be shipped with each number tied to its individual source, and the work product itself becomes the proof

data.name: Why Off-the-Shelf AI Doesn't Understand Money (Udi Menkes, Intuit — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Udi Menkes
The fluent bluff
data.brief: The speaker's name for the failure mode: a generic, fluent, confident answer about money, learned from what people wrote about money on the internet — blogs, books, advice columns — rather than from what actually happened when businesses acted. His claim is that almost every money-related answer from a frontier model is one. Measured shape from the Intuit study: across ~100,000 business situations, 40% of frontier-model advice reduced in essence to "acquire a new customer" and a further 14% to "increase revenue from your product" — over half of all advice collapsing into two generic moves, regardless of the business's actual constraints.

data.name: Business trajectories (state-action-outcome)
data.brief: Intuit's training substrate. From the general ledger, P&L, cash-flow statements and invoices across QuickBooks, TurboTax, Credit Karma and Mailchimp, build business states (detailed point-in-time summaries of a business), derive actions from the ledger itself (a marketing campaign was funded, payroll was paid, hiring costs rose), and attach outcomes over multiple horizons (profit, revenue, cash flow, or combinations). The result is millions of state-action-outcome vectors — the raw material for learning which actions lead to which outcomes for businesses in comparable situations.

data.name: Outcome-grounded model
data.brief: The model trained on those trajectories, in a three-step stack: (1) frontier models generate hypothesis candidates for actions a business could take; (2) a reinforcement-learning model trained on the trajectories decides which candidates are actually right versus which would drive the business down; (3) an LLM trained to generate the advice — "opinions go in, evidence comes out". Tested head-to-head against all leading models; a mid-size, cheaper model outperformed the frontier models because of the grounding. The stated lesson for product people: it is not about model size or model access, it is about the data.

data.name: CATE / conditional average treatment effect
data.brief: The measurement discipline that makes outcomes usable: you cannot run the same business twice, so take two groups of similar businesses with the same propensity to take an action, where one group took it and one didn't, and compare. Worked example: businesses that raised prices gained $4,200/day in profit, those that didn't gained $2,800/day — the naive read is a $1,400 impact, but the price-raisers were already more successful (which is why they could raise prices), so the corrected impact is nearer $1,150.

data.name: Intuit AI business advisor
data.brief: The productization, in research-preview beta with customers at the time of the talk. Uses the outcome-grounded LLM to proactively raise opportunities for a business at any given point in time — what to do, why, grounded in "who is like you, who's similar to you, what they did" — with drill-down into the reasoning and the ability to turn a recommendation into an action plan. Design requirement he attaches: grounded science alone is insufficient; the experience must also understand the user's preferences and make them feel part of the decision.

data.name: Frontier models give generic and sometimes harmful business advice to SMBs
data.brief: Intuit study (unreleased at talk time) across thousands of businesses and ~100,000 situations and time frames, with worked cases: a first-time landlord in negative cash flow with an open loan was told by a frontier model — holding all of the business's data — to acquire a second rental property, while the outcome-grounded model recommended raising the existing tenant's rent 5-10% before renewal. An egg supplier with 70% of revenue from one customer and nearly all cost from one vendor was told to raise prices 15-20% (risking almost all revenue) where the grounded model went to the cost side and recommended negotiating the vendor down 5-10%. Aggregate: 40% of frontier advice was "acquire a new customer", +14% "increase product revenue" — over half of all advice, generic and sometimes actively harmful.

data.name: Princeton study: most leading models bankrupt a simulated 500-day business
data.brief: Third-party corroboration, published weeks before the talk: Princeton researchers asked whether leading models can drive long-horizon business decisions, giving each model a harness with tools and data, $1M of starting capital and a 500-day simulated business. Most models drove the company bankrupt, and in less than the full 500 days. A simple rules-based system outperformed almost all of the models; the rare profitable model runs did not replicate on re-run and also ended in bankruptcy.

data.name: Context is not experience: one company's full record is still one observation
data.brief: The scoped counter-claim, stated pre-emptively against the room: "some of you are thinking it's just a matter of context — just give it more context." His answer: even the complete financial record of a company (general ledger, P&L, cash flows, invoices) handed to a frontier model is still just one group of data points on one company — it contains no information about what comparable businesses did and how it turned out. Worked case: an apparel company where 80% of cost came from one vendor who was also enabling 97% of revenue — the textbook "cut your biggest cost" answer yields "great margins on zero dollars". Analogy offered: given a very smart, freshly-read adviser and an experienced one, everyone picks experience.

data.name: A mid-size outcome-grounded model beat every frontier model on business advice
