data.brief: Measured head-to-head from a large incumbent: a mid-size, cheaper model trained by Intuit researchers on millions of small- and medium-business trajectories outperformed all of the leading frontier models on business advice. Architecture: frontier models generate candidate actions, an RL model trained on state-action-outcome vectors selects which are right, an LLM generates the advice. Stated conclusion, framed as a surprise to a product person: "the moat is not model access, it's the data itself that you have" — model size did not determine quality.

data.name: The era of outcome-driven AI: the best systems of record become the moat
data.brief: Generalization claim: "we are entering the era of outcome-driven AI" — the question stops being which model is better and becomes how to steer AI toward the outcomes a domain actually wants. The winners will be whoever holds the best systems of record, turns them into unique datasets of situations-actions-verified-outcomes, and trains models against them — anti-fraud, healthcare, logistics, developer tools alike. Verified-outcome training is called far advanced in coding and essentially unexplored in finance and most other domains. Closing instruction to the audience: go look in your own data for situations across entities where outcomes can be verified.

data.name: Models have read about your domain but never watched the outcomes
data.brief: The talk's compressed thesis: "every model has read about your domain, but none has watched the plays and the moves and their outcomes — and that gap is the whole game." A frontier model has read about money; a grounded model has watched what happened. The gap does not close with a bigger model or with more context, because both scale the same input class (descriptions of what people say works); it closes only by adding a different input class — verified outcomes at scale. The uncomfortable corollary for domains without instrumented outcomes is that they cannot buy their way out of the fluent bluff.

data.name: Advice is a trust artifact before it is an information artifact
data.brief: Opening audience test, unusually clean as evidence: nearly every hand went up for "have you asked an LLM for financial advice", and most went down for "did you trust the answer and follow it". His own worked case — a full-context, all-models investment decision that flipped A → B → A on two small assumption tweaks — is offered as why. So a correct answer is not a sufficient product: a great advisory experience needs grounded science plus an understanding of the person (their preferences, what they like and don't), and must make the user feel they were part of the decision.

data.name: Find where your data shows many entities, many actions and verifiable outcomes
guidelines: Look in your own data for a place where you can see a lot of different situations across entities, what those entities did, and how it turned out — that is the one thing off-the-shelf frontier models do not have

then build it into training data: construct states (a detailed point-in-time summary per entity), derive actions from the record itself rather than asking anyone (a campaign was funded, payroll was paid, hiring costs moved), and attach outcomes across multiple horizons (profit, revenue, cash flow, combinations)
assemble state-action-outcome vectors at scale
keep frontier models in the loop for what they are good at — generating candidate actions — and train the grounded model to decide which candidates are right
do not assume the biggest model wins
a mid-size model with the grounding beat the frontier

data.name: You can't run the business twice — match on propensity, then subtract the selection effect
guidelines: Outcome data is not causal by default

to learn what an action is actually worth, take two groups of similar entities with the same propensity to take the action — one that took it, one that didn't — and compare outcomes after a suitable interval

then correct for the fact that entities who take an action are often the ones already able to: in the worked example, price-raisers gained $4,200/day and non-raisers $2,800/day, but the honest impact of raising prices is nearer $1,150 than the naive $1,400 difference
use CATE (conditional average treatment effect) as the measure that connects action to outcome
without this step, an outcome-grounded model learns which businesses were already winning, not which actions work

data.name: Morgan Stanley's AlphaLab: Open Source Multi-Agent Quant Research (Brendan Rappazzo — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Brendan Rappazzo
Morgan Stanley
data.brief: Investment bank. Appears as an enterprise builder — a ~30-PhD internal AI research group that ships open-source research infrastructure and pushes models into production through a risk process.

data.name: AlphaLab
data.brief: Morgan Stanley's open-source agentic harness for automated quant research. Input is a path to a dataset (or an API spec) plus a natural-language description of what to predict; output is a suite of trained, containerized ML models. Three phases: research (~3-4 hours: builds and works a to-do list, sets up its Python environment, loads data, runs statistical tests, reads arXiv and technical blogs via web search, taking markdown notes per item that later agents query), eval building, and mass experimentation. Deliberately not built on any off-the-shelf agent framework — all custom code, itself largely written by Claude, for maximum freedom to tweak; functional tool calling keeps it provider-agnostic across OpenAI, Anthropic and open-source models. Three main tools: full shell access, web search, and a Slurm abstraction where the agent declares hardware and submits a job. 1.0 released ~April 2026 with a ~40-page tech report and all code on GitHub.

data.name: Strategist/worker experiment board
data.brief: AlphaLab's experimentation core, and its human-steering surface, formulated deliberately as a Jira/Kanban board. A strategist agent queries all context from earlier phases and keeps proposing experiments as cards in a "to implement" column; worker agents pull cards, write the implementation, write the Slurm config, submit to the cluster, wait for the job, inspect the training curves (underfit/overfit) and eval results, then write a postmortem back to the strategist — which is how the strategist self-evolves. The board shape is what makes human steering natural: cancel cards, add your own, or chat with the strategist to push it toward a method. An ever-growing leaderboard ranks models against both the agent-visible eval and a held-out private validation set, with full lineage from idea to code.

data.name: Builder/critic eval construction
data.brief: AlphaLab's answer to "if you optimize against a bad eval the whole thing falls apart". One agent builds the evaluation — writing all the code — and hands it to two critic agents with different mandates: one high-level, hunting conceptual errors and forward leakage of information; one programmatic, writing unit and integration tests against it. Findings return to the builder and the loop does not terminate until every critic is satisfied. Rationale stated: "LLMs aren't malicious, but they make very silly mistakes".

data.name: Environments as the enterprise moat
data.brief: The talk's thesis and its 2.0 architecture. "Evals and environments are the same thing — you just train in environments." Fix a strict Kaggle-shaped boundary (data + description in, containerized model submissions out, public leaderboard score to the agent, private held-out score to the user), build on the order of 10-20 very careful environments, and that becomes a reinforcement-learning signal rather than only a measurement. The proprietary data is one half of the moat; the other is qualitative rubrics derived from watching traces and asking "what makes a good researcher" — grading each rollout on adherence to the firm's research process, which is how human expertise gets encoded. Consequence he accepts explicitly: general auto-research becomes a commodity, whatever sits in the middle is disposable, and the plan is to keep open-sourcing the harness because the environments hold all the value.

data.name: Morgan Stanley open-sources AlphaLab, its multi-agent quant research harness
data.brief: A ~30-person PhD AI research group inside an investment bank built an automated quant-research harness and open-sourced all of it — full code on GitHub plus a ~40-page tech report, released ~April 2026 — on the explicit reasoning that the harness is not where the value is. Custom code rather than any off-the-shelf agent framework; provider-agnostic functional tool calling; three tools (shell, web search, Slurm job submission); three phases (research → eval building → mass experimentation) ending in trained containerized models. Motivation stated in production terms: a lot of shipped algorithms where more search cycles would find improvements, transferable models across desks (credit bonds → muni bonds), and new desks with little ML where "even a reasonably trained model" moves the needle.

data.name: Long-horizon automated research first felt possible in December 2025
data.brief: A dated capability threshold from a practitioner who had been waiting for it: long-horizon automated research "really felt possible for the first time" in December 2025, attributed jointly to Opus 4.5 and to harnesses like Claude Code and Codex — "the models were at a point where they could do these long-horizon tasks, and also the idea of putting them in these harnesses that allow them to do so". He notes this is now a common sentiment. The team's serious effort started immediately after.

data.name: AlphaLab results reported with failures attached: top 12% at Kaggle, wins into production
data.brief: Mixed, specific results — reported with the failures attached. Wins: beat a Karpathy-style single-agent-in-a-loop baseline by finding a better training config in an LLM speedrunning task; top 12% of submissions in an NVIDIA-hosted Kaggle competition fine-tuning a NeMotron model into a reasoning model, on only ~10 iterations because the team joined late; internally, "a handful" of already-decent models handed to AlphaLab to churn on produced meaningful improvements now working through risk into production. Failures: real, repeated, and concentrated on the hardest problems — enough to raise "how real is any of this?" as the driving question of the 2.0 redesign. He also concedes AlphaLab is hard to benchmark.

data.name: A bank's moat is 10-20 careful environments, not the harness
data.brief: The strategic claim, from a bank: general auto-research will become a commodity (GLM 5.2 already showing it), so "all of your value as an enterprise or human expert comes from building environments". Concretely: on the order of 10-20 very careful environments built as RL signal, with proprietary data as one half of the moat and qualitative process rubrics — derived from watching traces and asking what a good researcher does — as the other; each rollout graded on adherence to the firm's research process. Building good environments is called "really, really hard work", and the harness is being open-sourced because the environments hold the value.

data.name: AlphaLab 2.0 hands harness design to the model as a verifiable loop
data.brief: AlphaLab 2.0 hands the design decisions to the model. Having asked "isn't the strategist/worker split arbitrary — how do you motivate these design choices?", the answer taken is "we shouldn't be making these decisions at all; this itself is a verifiable loop, and an LLM should be doing this meta-optimization". The LLM reads traces and results and rewrites the harness itself; humans retain manual hill-climbing only as the interim. In parallel: collecting good traces from open models and touching weights via GRPO / on-policy distillation, with the expectation that the best system is an orchestration of open and closed models optimized together.

data.name: Start from the eval, not from trusting the agent like a human researcher
data.brief: The team's most-repeated lesson, learned "over and over, like monthly": you must start with a good eval, and the failure mode was being overeager and treating the agent like a human researcher — trusting it to define its own measurement while it optimized against it. The correction is to make the eval boundary opinionated and Kaggle-shaped (data and description in, containerized submissions out, public score to the agent, private held-out score to the human) rather than to make the agent smarter. Two structural consequences: bad evals are silent — "LLMs aren't malicious, but they make very silly mistakes" — and once the boundary is strict, every harness change becomes measurable, which is the precondition for handing harness design to the model at all.

data.name: Institutional expertise encodes as environments and rubrics, not prompts
data.brief: The mechanism by which a domain-expert organization injects proprietary knowledge into a self-improving system is neither prompt engineering nor context stuffing — it is environment construction. The verifiable metric is "maybe the easy part"; the expertise lives in the qualitative rubric that grades a rollout on process (what a good quant researcher actually does), because that is the signal the model then learns from. This inverts the usual enterprise-AI posture: the institution stops guarding its harness and starts guarding its measurement surface.

data.name: Own the harness code; abstract the cluster, not the agent
guidelines: Write your own harness rather than adopting an agent framework — in the Claude Code era you get max freedom to tweak anything, and the model writes most of it
use functional tool calling so the whole thing stays provider-agnostic across frontier and open-source models

give the agent three things: full shell (so it writes code, manages its own Python environment, runs things), web search (so it can read arXiv and technical blogs and reach the public state of the art), and a cluster abstraction where it declares hardware needs and submits a job instead of orchestrating hardware

in the research phase, force a to-do list scaffold — prompt it to enumerate everything it must finish before experimenting, so you can re-prompt when it tries to exit early — and make it take per-item markdown notes that later agents query to manage their own context
formulate experimentation as a board so humans can cancel cards, add cards and chat with the strategist
keep an ever-growing leaderboard with a private held-out set and full idea-to-code lineage
design so you rise with the tide of the models rather than having your work consumed by the next one

data.name: Separate the eval builder from its critics, then freeze the boundary
guidelines: If the agent builds its own evaluation, do not let the builder also be the judge
split the roles: one builder writes the eval code, one conceptual critic hunts design errors and forward leakage of information, one programmatic critic writes unit and integration tests against it
issues route back to the builder and the loop only terminates when every critic is satisfied
then freeze the interface: data and a natural-language description in, containerized model submissions out, an agent-visible public score and a user-only private validation score

once that boundary is strict, environments and evals are the same object — the same construction can be reused as RL signal — and every subsequent change to the harness becomes measurable rather than a matter of taste

data.name: MCP Tasks (async): Why Aren't Any Agents Supporting Them? (Cornelia Davis, Temporal — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Cornelia Davis
Temporal
data.brief: Durable-execution platform (workflows, signals, retries) — the candidate ledger's canonical durable-execution vendor, appearing in the corpus in person for the first time. In-talk role: supplies the durable server side of the demo *and* the speaker's MCP-client implementation ("task tracker workflow")

data.name: MCP Tasks (async MCP extension)
data.brief: MCP extension for asynchronous, long-running tools: tools/call returns a handle instead of a response, with a spec-defined lifecycle (working → input_required → working → completed / cancelled / failed) and a hard durability requirement — per the spec, once launched a task must survive client crashes, server crashes, dropped connections and humans-gone-on-vacation. V1 (November 2025, marked experimental) was a stateful protocol: task/list for server-side enumeration (no filter — a million-task scan at scale) and input_required tunneled through a held-open connection with server-driven elicitation. V2 (announced May, spec "coming out in July") rebuilds it as an extension on a stateless core: task/list removed, a client-initiated update endpoint replaces the elicitation session (effectively a *signal* into the running task), clients are told to persist task IDs ("should", though an unpersisted ID is unrecoverable), and the lifecycle model is unchanged. A notifications protocol (one "did anything change?" endpoint replacing per-task polling) is the sketched path to million-task scale

data.name: FastMCP
data.brief: Widely used MCP framework; already carries server-side MCP Tasks support (and some client pieces) and is what both demo processes run on. Davis's stated plan: land a full client-side tasks implementation in FastMCP within a month or two, "so you can use the same framework you're using probably for your MCP servers today"

data.name: Temporal (durable-execution platform)
data.brief: Workflow engine used on both sides of the demo: the invoice-processing MCP server is a workflow (ERP validation, human-in-the-loop approval via signals, programmed retries, survives being down at submission time), and — the talk's novelty — the MCP client itself is implemented as a "task tracker" workflow so the client-side protocol handling (long-lived connections, reconnect/resume, multiplexing concurrent input_required) is durable too

data.name: Mcp tasks zero client adoption
data.brief: The durable-execution vendor's own talk title concedes the adoption gap: no agent clients support MCP Tasks, and Davis's explanation is that the holdouts are being *smart* — the November spec was marked experimental, the protocol is "super involved," and V1's core mechanics (a stateful, unfilterable task/list; input_required tunneled through a held-open elicitation session) were bad enough that "radical changes" landed within ~8 months. The V1 reference implementation's client couldn't even multiplex: with several tasks in input_required, responses were FIFO — you could only answer the first. She had to build her own client implementation to demo the spec at all

data.name: Mcp spec mandates task durability
data.brief: Durability is being standardized at the protocol layer: the MCP Tasks spec's own verbage says a launched task can't disappear — it must survive network blips, client and server crashes, disconnections, and approvers who leave on vacation — and V2 shifts part of that burden to the client ("should persist task IDs"; Davis: unclear why not an all-caps MUST, since an unpersisted ID is unrecoverable). Her demo makes the requirement concrete: a purchase order submitted while both servers were down was captured and completed once they returned, and the client side survives because the protocol handler itself runs as a Temporal workflow — her argument for why the client half stayed unbuilt is precisely that this recovery/resume machinery "has all sorts of complexity in it"

data.name: Mcp v2 stateless core extensions
data.brief: MCP is being restructured ~8 months after the tasks spec shipped: per the May announcement from the Agentic AI Foundation (where MCP now lives), the protocol gets a stateless core with extensions — tasks become an extension, task/list is deleted ("just because you can doesn't mean you should"), and server-driven elicitation over a long session is replaced by a client-initiated update endpoint that Davis maps directly onto Temporal's *signal* primitive. Her distsys reading: "stateful protocols are the absolute worst thing in large-scale distributed systems," and even V2 doesn't yet scale — a million tasks means a million polling clients until the spec's notifications protocol matures. The agent ecosystem's core protocol is churning through 30-year-old distributed-systems lessons in public, with breaking rewrites inside a year

data.name: Async agent protocols are distsys again
data.brief: Nothing in this 20-minute frontier-conference talk is a model problem. The hard parts of long-horizon agent work — handles, lifecycles, durable state, signaling into running work, reconnect/resume, notification fan-in versus polling — are the classical distributed-systems curriculum, being relearned at the MCP layer by an engineer who lived it once already at Cloud Foundry/Kubernetes scale. The engineering frontier of "async agents" sits entirely in the periphery around the model, and the periphery is where the industry's protocol effort is going

data.name: Non adoption as competence
data.brief: In a fast-churning extension ecosystem, refusing to adopt is information, not lag: the agent clients that skipped experimental MCP Tasks V1 dodged a stateful protocol that is being discarded within a year, while any early implementer would now be rewriting. When the spec surface itself is unstable, adoption timing is a risk decision — and the vendor most invested in the capability is the one telling you the holdouts were right

data.name: Implement MCP Tasks without getting burned
guidelines: Target the V2 extension model, not V1 — the stateful protocol is going away
persist task IDs on the client and treat the spec's "should" as MUST (an unpersisted ID is unrecoverable)
don't build on task/list (unfilterable, deleted in V2)
on the server, map the spec's task lifecycle (working / input_required / completed / cancelled / failed) onto your own domain state machine rather than replacing it
expect multiple concurrent input_required tasks and multiplex them (the V1 reference client was FIFO-blocked)
make the client protocol handler itself durable — Davis runs hers as a workflow so reconnect/resume survives process death
at scale, replace per-task polling with the spec's notifications endpoint ("did anything change?" then fetch)
and build on FastMCP, which already has server-side task support and is where the client implementation is headed

data.name: MCP Apps: Extending the Frontier (Ido Salomon & Liad Yosef — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Ido Salomon
Liad Yosef
Aura
data.brief: "A research lab for the agentic web," recently co-founded by Liad Yosef — stated in the talk, which is why it is coined despite thinness. ⚠ Name is caption-only ("Aura"); the promised "more about it later" never arrives in the transcript. Verify spelling/existence before public-facing use

data.name: View tools (host→app channel)
data.brief: The reverse direction of MCP Apps interactivity, in the spec now and "released very soon": until this, the flow was app→host (user clicks, app raises an event, host decides); view tools ("app tools" — both names used in-talk) let the chat drive the app — "fill out this form for me" and the host operates the embedded UI on the user's behalf. Explicitly framed as MCP Apps standardizing what WebMCP (Google's standard for agent↔web-view interaction) addresses

data.name: WebMCP
data.brief: Google's standard for how agents interact with web views; named in the talk only as the thing MCP Apps absorbs into view/app tools — the two standardization efforts converging on one host-mediated channel

data.name: Generative-UI spectrum
data.brief: The speakers' map of UI-production strategies for agent hosts: predefined UI (MCP Apps' sandboxed iframe — the app ships finished UI) ↔ declarative UI (JSON-render, A2UI — the app returns build instructions, the chat builds the UI) ↔ fully generative UI (the model writes the UI; Claude's ask-for-a-UI feature "is actually based on MCP Apps" underneath). MCP Apps positions itself as agnostic to where UI comes from, plus the interop layer: a just-released guide shows one server shipping A2UI to Gemini and the same payload wrapped as an MCP App to ChatGPT, and one codebase running in LibreChat and ChatGPT unchanged

data.name: UI atomization (the agentic web)
data.brief: The thesis under the spec: websites stop being destinations and decompose into branded, interactive UI atoms that a personal assistant composes with the user's own context — the calendar chunk, the storefront chunk, the map chunk — so the user never leaves the assistant. The three-way payoff as the speakers state it: the user keeps a brand they recognize and trust, the brand keeps its identity instead of being reduced to text, and the host gains capabilities it didn't build. The structural consequence: no application controls the user journey anymore — every interaction routes through the chat, which is also what makes the journey auditable

data.name: Mcp apps cross vendor consolidation
data.brief: An interactive-UI-over-MCP protocol went from one person's project (MCP-UI, May 2025) to the official MCP extension co-created with Anthropic and OpenAI in months: launched with Claude and VS Code; ChatGPT Apps "are actually based on MCP Apps" and OpenAI *recommends* it as the protocol for building them; clients now include Cursor, GitHub Copilot, LibreChat, and Goose — which was the first MCP-UI client a year ago and now underlies Block's just-shipped agentic-commerce product. Governance matured with it: an open working group in the MCP committee convening every three weeks with Anthropic, OpenAI and partners, plus a community of plugins, integrations and courses

data.name: Brand loss blocked mcp servers
data.brief: The spec authors' origin story names the adoption blocker for the whole MCP server ecosystem: companies refused to build servers because chat "reduces them to a textual database" — losing brand identity and the UX they invested in. MCP Apps exists to reverse that: services ship their own branded, interactive UI chunks into the chat (the demo: a PostHog funnel widget rendering inside Claude, "the PostHog experience within ChatGPT or Claude"), so a service can live inside the assistant without dissolving into text

data.name: Host owns the user journey
data.brief: The architecture transfers journey control from apps to hosts, by construction: the app's UI renders in a sandbox, and when the user clicks, the app cannot call its own backend — it raises an event to the host ("I recommend calling this tool") and *the host decides*. The spec defines three levels of app control — notify the chat, ask the chat to run a prompt, or release the flow entirely — and the speakers draw the consequence explicitly: "no application will control the user journey anymore… Amazon won't be able to see my flow; everything goes through the chat for auditability"

data.name: Generative ui approaches converge
data.brief: The competing UI-for-agents strands are converging on one interop surface: MCP Apps declares itself agnostic across the predefined ↔ declarative ↔ fully-generative spectrum; a days-old guide shows the same server shipping A2UI to Gemini and the wrapped MCP App to ChatGPT; Claude's generate-me-a-UI feature is MCP Apps underneath; WebMCP-style host-drives-the-view interaction is being standardized in as view/app tools; and "write once, run everywhere" is demonstrated with one codebase running in open-source LibreChat and ChatGPT

data.name: Chat hosts reach app store scale
data.brief: The distribution claim: ChatGPT alone was cited months ago at 800M weekly users — ~10% of world population — a number the web took ~13 years to reach, making the assistant surface ~"170 times the total addressable market of the Apple App Store when it launched." The speakers' conclusion is categorical: MCP Apps "isn't just a technology… this is an entirely new way to distribute applications," with 2026 called as the year it becomes "a global standard for UI"

data.name: Chat host is the new app platform
data.brief: The assistant host is accreting every property that historically defined a platform: distribution (app-store-scale reach inside ChatGPT/Claude), the interaction contract (three spec-defined levels of journey control), trust and auditability (everything routes through the chat), and the customer relationship itself (the app no longer sees the user's flow). SaaS frontends don't get destroyed in this shift — they get demoted to branded atoms whose composition, context and journey belong to the host. The spec authors present this as the win-win that unblocks adoption; it is also a one-way transfer of power to whoever owns the chat surface

data.name: Standardize the channel not the ui
data.brief: MCP Apps won cross-vendor convergence by standardizing the *channel* — how UI is transmitted, sandboxed, and how it communicates with the host — while staying agnostic about how the UI is produced (shipped iframe, declarative A2UI/JSON instructions, or model-generated). That neutrality is what let Anthropic, OpenAI and Google-adjacent standards converge on it rather than fight it, and it means the predefined-vs-generative UI question can be settled later, per use case, without re-litigating the protocol

data.name: Ship interactive branded UI through MCP Apps
guidelines: Link the tool to a prefixed UI resource returning HTML — "pretty simple code"
on the host side use the MCP-UI SDK (a React/web component taking the resource plus a callback) and render in the sandbox
never let the app call its own backend — raise events to the host recommending tool calls and let the host keep flow control
choose the journey-control level deliberately (notify / run-a-prompt / release to chat)
expect resources to be preloaded rather than fetched at click time
for heavy views (3D renders), plan for reusable-view identifiers rather than re-rendering per turn
for multi-host reach, author declarative payloads (A2UI) and wrap them as MCP Apps where needed — one codebase can serve Gemini, ChatGPT and LibreChat
and build against the official ext-apps repo SDK, where spec changes land immediately

data.name: Gadgets: Personal app vibe coding that is actually safe (Kenton Varda, Cloudflare — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Kenton Varda
Cloudflare
data.brief: Edge/cloud developer-infrastructure company (Workers, Durable Objects, workerd). ⚠ Nearest-fit enum coercion flagged: at Cloudflare's scale bigtech is arguable; typed developer because it appears here purely as a developer-platform vendor (same tilt as co-vercel)

data.name: Gadgets (Cloudflare personal-app platform)
data.brief: Vibe-coding platform with an office-suite model: like Google Docs, but the unit is a *gadget* — an app with its own code — and a user accumulates hundreds of them, instantiating one per shareable thing (one slide deck = one instance of the slides gadget). Shown from Varda's own use: a one-shot collaborative whiteboard, a Spanish-email filter, a GitHub PR-sorter, a slide builder. Sharing is a platform feature (a Docs-style share dialog), not app code — "the platform can implement the sharing model and the access control such that the gadget itself can't possibly get that wrong." Every gadget automatically integrates with agents, which can both use it and rewrite it. Entire stack (minus the LLM) runs on Cloudflare Workers: no containers (dynamic workers), no database (Durable Objects)

data.name: Blueprints (code-without-data sharing)
data.brief: Gadgets' distribution mechanism: export a useful gadget's code without its data as a blueprint; others instantiate fresh gadgets from it (document editor, kanban board, slide builder). Distribution becomes template-instantiation of per-user code rather than deployment of one multi-tenant service — and the blueprint author's "roadmap" ends at v1, because each user's agent forks features locally

data.name: Double-ended vibe-code confinement
data.brief: The safety architecture that gives the talk its title: assume the AI-written code is buggy and make the bugs non-events. Client UI runs in a null-origin iframe sandbox with CSP — no network, no cookies, nothing but postMessage to the parent; over that channel a Cap'n Web RPC session forwards to the gadget's server code, a Durable Object running in a dynamic-worker sandbox equally cut off from the world. A vibe-coded client and vibe-coded server can talk only to each other, so "there is no security bug you can have in this code that matters" — demonstrated with an agent-added paste-SVG feature where potential XSS simply has nowhere to go. External-service access exists but only through a platform-mediated system

data.name: Cloudflare Workers
data.brief: Serverless application-hosting platform (2017–), millions of developers, trillions of requests/day; Gadgets is built entirely on it — the talk's aside is that "you can actually build complex apps on Workers," containerless and databaseless, with dynamic workers as the sandbox substrate

data.name: Durable Objects
data.brief: Cloudflare's stateful serverless primitive; in Gadgets each gadget's server code is a Durable Object, serving as both compute and the only persistence layer ("there's no database involved") — one addressable, stateful object per gadget instance, which is what makes the per-instance app model cheap

data.name: workerd
data.brief: The open-source, self-hostable Cloudflare Workers runtime. The entire demo ran locally on Varda's laptop on workerd (which is why the venue's dead internet didn't matter), and his stated intent is basement self-hosting for home automation via Home Assistant and Spotify connectors

data.name: Cap'n Web RPC
data.brief: JavaScript RPC system (Cap'n Proto lineage, ⚠ captioned "captain web") used as the single communication channel of the confinement architecture: a session over postMessage from the sandboxed iframe, forwarded to the gadget's Durable Object server code

data.name: Personal codegen breaks cloud infra
data.brief: The declared one-point takeaway from the creator of a major serverless platform: personal AI codegen breaks traditional cloud infrastructure. 25 years of cloud architecture "ran in the wrong direction" — one blessed version of an app on the developer's server for every user, which is convenient for developers and structurally forbids per-user customization — while mobile's alternative spent 15 years gatekept ("there's like five companies that can build mobile apps now"; easier to buy a gun than install unsigned software). His verdict on the current wave: vibe-coding platforms are targeting exactly this wrong substrate. The personal-software future needs per-user code instances — apps as numerous and disposable as documents

data.name: Confinement neutralizes vibe code bugs
data.brief: The safety claim is architectural, not procedural: nobody reviews the AI's code — instead, client and server are both sandboxed (null-origin iframe + CSP; dynamic-worker Durable Object), can talk only to each other over one Cap'n Web/postMessage channel, and sharing/ACL are implemented by the platform so the app "can't possibly get that wrong." Consequence, stated flatly: "there is basically no security bug you can have in this code that matters" — an agent-added paste-arbitrary-SVG feature (a textbook XSS surface) is shrugged off live because leaked script has no origin, no cookies and no egress. This is the strongest corpus statement yet of securing generation by making verification unnecessary

data.name: User agents fork features in place
data.brief: The feature-request pipeline (user → PM → Jira → roadmap → plugin-system rewrite that never ships) is replaced by the user's own agent editing the app: every gadget is agent-integrated, and when Varda's slide spec needed strikethrough, centered text and freehand diagrams, Claude read the app's code and added the features — including a paste-SVG box "not very useful for any human, but perfectly useful for Claude, who then generated the SVG." Features useful to one user, or even only to the agent itself, become rational to build; the developer's core stays clean; a Cloudflare PM one-shot the slides app in an afternoon ("these days all product managers are also prolific engineers")

data.name: Gadgets self hosted and productizing
data.brief: Two trajectory facts: (1) the whole platform runs on the open-source, self-hostable workerd runtime — the demo ran offline on a laptop, and Varda's stated goal is basement self-hosting with Home Assistant/Spotify connectors; (2) the promised talk-closing "yeet onto GitHub" was cancelled by Cloudflare's CTO days before — "a lot of excitement inside Cloudflare and this has become a more serious project," release "in a few weeks" under deliberate discipline. A personal-software experiment crossing from side project to company-strategic product in real time

data.name: Confine dont verify personal codegen
data.brief: When authorship industrializes to every user (and to agents adding features only agents will use), per-artifact verification cannot scale — no one will review a million personal apps, and the XSS question stops being answerable app by app. Gadgets' move is to relocate trust from the code to the environment: confine both halves of every app so bugs are non-events, and pull the properties that must actually hold — sharing, access control, external-service mediation — up into the platform where they are implemented once, correctly. It is the verification-gap thesis executed in infrastructure: generation gets free rein precisely because trust was re-architected outside it

data.name: Personal software inverts distribution
data.brief: The unit of software inverts: from one blessed multi-tenant deployment serving all users to per-user instantiated code — gadget as document, blueprint as code-minus-data template, one Durable Object per instance. That single inversion dissolves both incumbent distribution regimes at once: the app-store gatekeeping model (nothing to review or sign when every instance is confined by construction) and the SaaS roadmap model (no feature backlog when each user's agent forks the app locally). The infrastructure precondition is the part incumbents lack: isolation cheap enough to give every user, per app, their own sandboxed client and server

data.name: Host AI-written personal apps so their bugs can't matter
guidelines: Run the app's UI in a null-origin sandboxed iframe with CSP — no cookies, no network, no DOM escape
give it exactly one channel: postMessage to the parent, carrying an RPC session (Cap'n Web) to the app's server half
run that server half per-instance in its own sandbox (a Durable Object / dynamic worker) with no egress either — client and server may talk only to each other
never let app code implement sharing or access control — make instances small enough (one gadget per shareable thing) that the platform owns the share model outright
mediate any external-service access through a platform-level system rather than granting the app network
make every app agent-readable and agent-writable so features are added in place instead of through a roadmap
and prefer a self-hostable runtime (workerd) so the personal-software stack can itself be personal

data.name: The New Primitives: Building AI Native Software (Kwindla Kramer, Daily — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Kwindla Hultman Kramer
Tavus
data.brief: AI video/avatar company (⚠ captioned "Tavis"); appears for one load-bearing dated fact — weeks before this talk it released a reimagined Knowledge Navigator video "entirely built on real and available technology," a 4-minute single take. ⚠ Thin — single-mention company, drop-option documented in review note 6

data.name: Agents plus
data.brief: Kramer's name for the current frontier just past bare agents, anchored on the played Nadella clip: multi-model harnesses ("you want the harness to define the models, the data and the tools, so you have a loop across those three") with tool access, progressive disclosure of tools for token efficiency, and rich context feeding; software copilots embedded in every piece of software; organization-level harnesses. The through-line from last year's loops/tool-calls/context-engineering to this year's emerging ideas

data.name: AI-native software
data.brief: The proposed post-agents category: software built from the ground up with LLM inference at the core of every interaction at every moment — not a model bolted onto conventional software. Positioned by analogy: AI-native software is to today's agents what the modern internet (web apps, native mobile) is to the hand-written web pages of 1995 — and, per the talk's method, it will be *discovered by building*: "we now actually have the ability to build the memex, and Jarvis from Iron Man, and Knowledge Navigator, for real, completely working — and by building those things we'll figure out what we want to build next"

data.name: Knowledge Navigator (1987 concept video)
data.brief: Apple's 1987 concept film — foldable tablet, touchscreen, a conversational voice assistant with strong personality, global + personal information access, real-time vision and video generation, seamless calls, delegation of complex tasks for autonomous execution, and what "we might call today continual learning." Kramer's yardstick artifact: it "divides our timeline neatly in half," the web was "a conscious attempt to make that video real," and Tavus's weeks-old remake — one 4-minute take on real, available technology — is the talk's evidence that the target is now buildable

data.name: Gradient Bang
data.brief: Massively-multiplayer game Kramer is building with friends "as a canvas to really think about what AI native software can be": LLMs at the core of every interaction, hundreds of inference calls in play, real-time agent orchestration — "we couldn't have built anything like this even a year ago." Demonstrated patterns, per its own narration: asynchronous non-blocking context compression; long-running sub-agents that share context; progressive skills loading; dynamic user-interface generation; conversational voice ("Eagle is on five trade loops, Hawk and Raptor are on five exploration loops each — your fleet is busy")

data.name: Nadella org level harnesses
data.brief: Microsoft's CEO, in a clip Kramer plays as the state of the art (No Priors / Latent Space crossover, ~2 weeks prior): "you kind of want the harness to define the models, the data and the tools, so that you have a loop across those three" — and every Microsoft product, "whether it's GitHub Copilot or the security copilot… or the discovery for science," is being built as a multi-model harness with tool access, progressive disclosure of tools for token efficiency, and rich context. Kramer's gloss: the frontier is "agents plus" — copilots embedded in every piece of software and organization-level harnesses

data.name: Pipecat neutral voice layer
data.brief: The voice-agent orchestration layer is consolidating on vendor-neutral open source: Pipecat is stated as "the most widely used framework for building voice agents today," open source, used by AWS, Nvidia and Anthropic "and thousands of startups and scaleups and enterprises" — frontier labs and hyperscalers building their voice products on a neutral third-party harness rather than in-house pipelines

data.name: Knowledge navigator now buildable
data.brief: The 40-year vision claims are now build claims: "we actually have the ability to build the memex, and Jarvis from Iron Man, and Knowledge Navigator from that 1987 video for real, completely working" — evidenced by Tavus's weeks-old Knowledge Navigator remake, a 4-minute single take "entirely built on real and available technology" that Kramer says feels "both familiar and brand new." Paired with the category framing: agents today are the web pages of 1995 — still important, but the transitional artifact of an era whose mature software category (AI-native software) hasn't been invented yet

data.name: Gradient bang llm at every interaction
data.brief: An existence proof for the category, built by the voice-infrastructure vendor as research: a multiplayer game with LLMs as the core of every interaction at every moment — hundreds of inference calls — showcasing asynchronous non-blocking context compression, long-running context-sharing sub-agents, progressive skills loading, dynamic UI generation and conversational voice, with the explicit timing claim "we couldn't have built anything like this even a year ago"

data.name: Agents are the web pages of 1995
data.brief: The historically-informed read on the present: every platform era began with a primitive that felt like the whole story (HTML pages in 1995) and matured into a category nobody had named yet (web apps, native mobile). Agents are this era's web pages — and since the models are already sufficient to rebuild Knowledge Navigator "for real," the remaining work is category invention: the primitives (org-level harnesses, realtime voice, context machinery, dynamic UI) are this cycle's compilers and databases, and the mature form gets discovered by building against the old visions

data.name: Visicalc against ai unemployment
data.brief: Offered explicitly as "a counterargument to the fear that AI leads to mass unemployment": VisiCalc took work that "required a room full of people" and specialized knowledge and made it generally accessible — and it did not put accountants out of business; it made "much much much more accounting-like work possible" plus categories of work previously inconceivable. The precedent's claim applied to AI: industrializing execution expands the addressable work and moves humans up the stack rather than out of it

data.name: Build software with inference at the core, not bolted on
guidelines: Treat the LLM as the substrate of every interaction rather than a feature behind a button (expect hundreds of inference calls in a session and design for it)
compress context asynchronously and non-blockingly so the hot path never waits on housekeeping
run long-lived sub-agents that share context instead of monolithic per-request calls
load skills progressively rather than front-loading capability
generate UI dynamically as part of the interaction loop (show/hide the map on request) instead of pre-building every screen
make conversational voice a first-class modality, not an accessibility layer
and orchestrate all of it in real time — the patterns Gradient Bang exists to exercise

data.name: Local Models: Trust, Control, Optimization (panel — Carter Abdallah, NVIDIA, moderating Prime Intellect / Arcee AI / NVIDIA Nemotron — AI Engineer)
Carter Abdallah
Lucas Atkins
Chris Alexiuk
Open MDW (Model-Data-Weights) license
data.brief: License recently adopted by both Nemotron and Trinity, built because "AI is very different than traditional software": it makes crystal clear that using a model's outputs to train another model is permitted — the exact thing closed-provider ToS language is written to dissuade. Framed on stage as the license layer maturing to fit the use case ("even the lawyers are on board"), and as the legal half of trace ownership: with an open model you can save every trace from your harness and legally fine-tune on it

data.name: NeMo Gym / NeMo RL (NVIDIA post-training environment stack)
data.brief: NVIDIA's tooling named alongside Prime Intellect's Verifiers as the way builders turn saved production traces into RL environments and "hill climb" their own models ("use Verifiers or Nemo RL or Nemo Gym to create these environments"). Ships alongside Nemotron's open datasets and environments. ⚠ both names from captions; treated as one node for the environment-tooling role — split at seeding if both products get independent corpus weight

data.name: Frontier access shock meets open convergence
data.brief: The trust section's pivot event: for years "you can't trust Chinese models" was code for "you can't trust open models" — then "Anthropic had to put Fable away" and people realized access to frontier systems might not be universal, so "a tremendous number of enterprises and developers started going to these new Chinese models because they could trust that they would always have access to them". The "Fable and GPT-5.6 embargo" left open questions about at what capability level intelligence gets politicized and held back, with those decisions "happening behind closed doors" — while, simultaneously, open capability converged: GLM 5.2 a month earlier read as the open-model Opus-inflection, and the panel predicts better-than-Fable capabilities in open models within 12 months. Trust redefined as: do I know what I'm running, and can I be sure I'll keep getting it

data.name: Open weights are inspectable trust
data.brief: The steel-man the moderator explicitly asked to arm the audience with: trust ≠ safety (a "weaponized" conflation), and on trust the asymmetry runs *against* closed models — "you don't know what went into them; the same is true for closed models, even more so." Open models are files of matrices you can inspect, served by code you can read (Prime RL, vLLM, SGLang); it is "rather straightforward to validate what data went into a model" from the weights alone; NVIDIA additionally publishes the data-mixture spreadsheet ("a couple trillion tokens of this data set…"), the datasets, and the environments. The only way to be sure the output is what you expect is a model you run or can fully validate

data.name: Post train open on your harness
data.brief: The panel's call to action, argued from the labs' own behavior: OpenAI/Anthropic/Google release custom versions of their models for each product (Deep Research was RL on O3, not a for-loop over search; Atlas got its own variant) — "if their off-the-shelf GPT-5 isn't good enough for their browser, why should it be good enough for our apps?" The "mismanaged genius" framing: enormous capability is left on the table because we don't fit models into harnesses. Open models close the gap: post-train the best open model on *your* harness ("Nous Research can create a post-train of whatever model for their harness"), the way a customer specialized a finance agent in a week or two to beat Opus at a fraction of the cost of Haiku. "If you want to build the next Claude Code, the next Cursor or Perplexity… take the best open model and post-train on your harness"

data.name: Rl environment specialization flywheel
data.brief: Prime Intellect's product thesis stated end-to-end: the concrete way to make a specific use case work today is build an RL environment for it, post-train an open model on it, deploy it into production, then continuously learn from production traces — a million accountants using a tax agent, a bank shipping a finance agent to millions of customers, computer-use agents improved from "millions of traces from production data". Post-training is "the most economically viable way" to customize; environments+evals are the unit of specialization; the ecosystem (NVIDIA releasing environments with models, Verifiers, NeMo RL/Gym) is productizing the loop; and the "white pill" for AI application builders is that this data flywheel is the moat

data.name: Open outputs ownable data
data.brief: The control argument extended from weights to outputs: closed providers monetize your usage the way cloud-era platforms monetized your data — usage data improves their models directly or as an acquisition signal — while their ToS "do a lot to try to obfuscate" that you shouldn't train on Claude/Fable/GPT-5 outputs. With open models you save every trace from your own harness, fine-tune smaller models on them, or mine them for signals to build environments — "owning your stack, owning your intelligence… it's also owning your outputs." The Open MDW license (adopted by Nemotron and Trinity) exists precisely to make output-training explicitly permitted rather than merely tolerated

data.name: Frontier overkill cost control
data.brief: The economics half of "control": most people "do not need frontier-level intelligence for like 90% of their tasks" — the hyper-generalized capability horizon (also good at chemistry) is wasted on users doing one or two things — and specialization at the expense of everything else is "exactly what we should be doing". Meanwhile total spend rises even as per-token cost collapses (GPT-4 → GPT-5.5): tokens per session grow exponentially, companies "burned through their Opus [budget] in a couple months", and CFO trust now means knowing exactly what a workload costs — cost predictability, deprecation-proofing, and margin the closed APIs keep ("they might drive down the optimization but not pass through those savings"). Reframed as outcome-maxing: more than a dollar of value out per dollar in

data.name: Open models are the linux layer
data.brief: Open/self-hosted LLMs are re-running the Linux playbook, and the coexistence is structural, not transitional. Closed frontier ≈ the Mac/ChatGPT tier — accessible, individually optimal, $20/month; open models ≈ the Linux layer that ends up running enterprises, clouds, hyperscalers and neoclouds (Fireworks, Together, Baseten), because hyper-optimization "is not possible behind closed doors — you're shutting too many people out of the room" and resource-constrained contributors are who optimize a stack hardest. Both grow; the headline-friendly either/or never arrives

data.name: Specialized pareto beats the frontier
data.brief: The frontier is no longer the ceiling for a specific use case: an open model post-trained on the right RL environment and deployed into production sits past the frontier on its domain — better than Opus, cheaper than Haiku, faster — and improves from its own production traces. Capability inflections in open models (the GLM 5.2 moment, like the Opus moment before Cursor) are the trigger events that spawn "hundreds of these inflections for startups"

data.name: Distribution is this years frontier question
data.brief: Both non-moderator panelists independently call the coming year "the most consequential year" for how AI gets distributed — not how capable it gets. The pieces: capability-level gating negotiated behind closed doors (the Fable/GPT-5.6 embargo), ~0.000001% of the 1–2B AI users ever having run an open model (target: 10–15%), on-device compute converging with open capability (day-to-day-capable model on a MacBook within the year; a 4B phone model already more useful than launch-day GPT-4), agent operating systems preloaded on hardware, and a September iPhone/Siri moment about to introduce local AI to the mass public the way DeepSeek did

data.name: Specialize past the frontier with an environment, not a prompt
guidelines: Pick the one or two things your product actually does and accept being worse at everything else. Build an RL environment for the use case (post-training is the most economically viable customization path)
post-train the best available open model *on your harness*, not in isolation

deploy to production users early — deployment is where the last-mile capability comes from (the Tesla-autonomy analogy: a chatbot isn't good at self-driving because it was never trained or deployed there)
save every trace (open licenses like Open MDW make this legal) and feed traces back as fine-tuning data or environment-mining signal via Verifiers / NeMo RL / NeMo Gym
let the open ecosystem (vLLM etc.) keep driving your serving cost down

data.name: Argue trust without conflating it with safety
guidelines: Separate the words: safety is its own discussion
trust means knowing what you run and that you'll keep being able to run it. Point out the asymmetry — closed models are *less* knowable, not more

inspect the weights, read the open serving code, and check the released data mixture (HF datasets pages, NVIDIA's per-dataset token spreadsheet). Treat every model's output — closed included — as the output of an inherently random system needing safeguards and judgment. Price in access risk: deprecations, quota cuts, and capability embargoes are trust failures no closed ToS protects you from

data.name: Compression at the Edge (panel: NVIDIA / Unsloth / Hugging Face / Ollama — AI Engineer)
Identified by first name + company
Ollama
data.brief: Maker of the eponymous local-model runtime — "one of the easiest ways to run local models"; rose to popularity by letting people run larger models on small machines through quantization; curates default quantization per model as a UX decision (leaves small models at higher precision when quants degrade them); works with model labs pre-release, sometimes implementing five variations of an unreleased model

data.name: NVFP4 (micro-block-scaled FP4 format)
data.brief: NVIDIA's 4-bit floating-point format: groups of 16 elements share one FP8 scaling factor (micro-block scaling, design lineage credited on stage to "bits-and-bytes Tim" = Tim Dettmers). Does weight compression *and* math acceleration (4-bit GEMM). Target: <1% aggregate accuracy degradation across benchmarks; ships with every Nemotron release; described as close to par-optimality for pure weight quantization (1–3 more bits of headroom at most)

data.name: Quantization-aware training / distillation (QAT/QAD)
data.brief: Training-side compression: below ~20B parameters PTQ stops sufficing and accuracy must be recovered by quantization-aware distillation. Pain point stated: QAD needs the *original* training data, and modern models are multi-stage RL-trained with multiple teacher distillation (per-domain expert teachers), so assembling correct QAD data is hard — "if we do QAD with wrong data it most commonly breaks the model." Labs increasingly ship QAT variants themselves (Gemma QAT, Q8/MXFP4-style release formats)

data.name: KL-divergence quant evaluation
data.brief: Verification instrument for compressed models: compute KL divergence between the BF16 model's and the quantized model's output logits over calibration data — goal: distance → 0 while size shrinks. Positioned as better than accuracy benchmarks for quant QA (benchmarks need sampling, many trials, averaging); reference: the paper "Accuracy is not all you need"

data.name: Big-quantized beats small-full-precision
data.brief: Paper-backed claim: at equal disk footprint, a ~4× larger model quantized to 4-bit (120B@4bit) beats the smaller full-precision one (35B@BF16) on intelligence — so the resource-optimal recipe is "train a ginormous model, then quantize it down." Mechanistic basis: current models are undertrained relative to parameter count (~30T tokens vs a hypothetical ~300T saturation), so ~86% of weights "do not need to be there"; the panel notes compression may stop working if training ever saturates the weights. Caveat: throughput — a big compressed model may decode at 5–10 tok/s where a small native one does 200

data.name: llama.cpp
data.brief: The de-facto open local-inference engine, now acquired by Hugging Face (team hired/absorbed — ⚠ caption phrasing, see Review note 4); previously cited in-corpus as "the most bug-free path" for self-hosting (batch 3, prose). Active development aimed at running "everywhere," explicitly including phones; the runtime layer under much of the quant ecosystem

data.name: Ollama (local model runtime)
data.brief: Local runtime whose UX popularized quantized models: ships a curated default quantization per model, chosen by quantizing, then testing in real harnesses ("is it actually usable after"); deliberately leaves very small models at higher precision when quantization degrades experience. Also the panel's demo substrate for agentic local use: Qwen 3.6 quants running OpenClaw on long-horizon tasks, "fixing its own harness"

data.name: Quantization is the distribution layer
data.brief: Compression as what makes "own your intelligence" physically real: GLM 5.2 shrinks 1.5TB → 250GB (86%) while keeping 76% of accuracy via dynamic quantization; DeepSeek R1's 1.58-bit quant was the community's proof moment ("it randomly worked… we were quite surprised"); Qwen 3.6 quants now run OpenClaw on long-horizon agentic tasks and "fix their own harness" — a bar that "wouldn't be possible before"; and the next push is edge/phones, explicitly driven by privacy demand for sensitive and personal data (llama.cpp "so that it runs everywhere"; "I see intelligence going to phones thanks to the quants"). Closing vision: frontier models runnable on your own hardware = "you can control your own destiny; you do not need to be controlled by some model labs"

data.name: Labs absorb compression into releases
data.brief: Compression moved from community afterthought to model-launch requirement: labs now ship QAT variants themselves (Gemma QAT; gpt-oss released in MXFP4; Q8-at-release), NVIDIA ships NVFP4 checkpoints with every Nemotron release, and Hugging Face acquired llama.cpp. The clearest community datapoint: for the Qwen 3.6 release the Qwen team asked which single checkpoint to ship — and everybody chose the midsize one, planning to quantize down rather than asking for small natives ("this goes to show how quantization is adopted")

data.name: Train big then compress
data.brief: The direction-of-travel claim: models will keep getting bigger, and at equal disk size a big-quantized model beats a small full-precision one (120B@4bit > 35B@BF16, paper-backed), so the optimal pipeline is train ginormous → quantize down. The mechanism is undertraining — at ~30T training tokens the weights aren't saturated, so ~86% "do not need to be there" (with an honest expiry condition: at ~300T-token saturation "maybe you can't do compression anymore"). Consequences: at 15TB-scale models "not even enterprises can serve" without compression, and yesterday's big-model capability keeps arriving in today's smaller quants

data.name: Quant quality is unverified
data.brief: The verification gap inside compression, from the people who ship it: after a couple of hours of PTQ "our pain starts there — we have to evaluate these models to match the model card; that is where we spend a lot of our time." Benchmarks only cover verifiable tasks, not the vibe — Ollama tests candidate quants inside real harnesses because "putting it in [a coding agent] and running the model — it's like, no, it doesn't feel right" in ways no benchmark captures; quantized linear-attention layers "look like they're doing good" on standard evals, then produce gibberish in long-context production; a quant-arena is dismissed because a Cohere paper showed arenas "are very much hacked"; and the audience's closing question — where do I find benchmarks for the Frankenstein quants of a model? — gets "if you find something like that, let me know… right now it is not being done comprehensively." Best available instrument: KL divergence against the BF16 logits, not accuracy suites

data.name: Architecture cambrian taxes compression
data.brief: The transformer++ monoculture is over and every compression assumption breaks per-family: hybrid/linear/sliding-window attention, MLA-descended sparse and indexed attention ("DeepSeek started it — I blame them"), sparse MoE, per-lab layer-norm epsilon tweaks; old heuristics ("quantize the middle layers to 1-bit") fail on new families (linear-attention layers can't be quantized at all); labs bring Ollama five variations of an unreleased model to implement; QAD data assembly breaks on multi-stage RL models with per-domain teacher distillation. And yet the panel *welcomes* it: "we need more different architectures… it's very good to have a variety of different opinions" — architectural diversity as a feature of the open-model era, priced in engineering

data.name: Most jobs below frontier
data.brief: The demand-side sufficiency claim, from the HF seat: "most of the jobs still do not require a Fable-level thing — we are kind of in a bubble as software developers"; businesses distill midsize models down to very small ones for tasks like reranking "that don't require LLM outputs, cutting millions of costs"; quantization buys concurrency and in-house deployment most companies don't know exist ("people aren't aware of it… it's kind of shocking to me"). Compression's business value is mostly *not* frontier chasing — it is right-sizing work that never needed the frontier

data.name: Compression is a release primitive
data.brief: Compression stopped being post-processing and became a structural layer of the open-model release cycle: labs ship QAT/NVFP4 variants at launch, release strategies assume community quantization (one midsize checkpoint, the ecosystem fans out the quants), runtimes make default-quant selection a product decision, and the quant pipeline (Unsloth, Model Optimizer, Ollama, llama.cpp) is effectively the distribution channel of open AI. Without it, open weights at 1.5TB are open in name only

data.name: Compression outruns its instruments
data.brief: The ecosystem can make a model 86% smaller far more reliably than it can say what was lost: model-card matching consumes more time than the quantization itself, benchmarks miss production behavior (long-context gibberish, harness feel), arenas are gamed, and no comprehensive quant-benchmark resource exists. The field's most honest instrument — KL divergence against the uncompressed logits — measures *distance from the original*, not capability, which is an admission that capability itself can't currently be measured well enough to verify a quant

data.name: Leverage the architecture; never quantize uniformly
guidelines: Uniform/random compression at 86% doesn't make a model 86% dumber, it makes it 100% dumber — exploit structure instead. First and last layers are critical, middle layers compressible
keep linear-attention projections and QKV layers high-precision (quantizing linear attention passes benchmarks then breaks long context)
vision/audio layers stay 8/16-bit
sparse MoE layers take aggressive quantization
choose layers via calibration data + gradient-based sensitivity analysis (LP/knapsack solvers automate it)
treat selection as combinatorial (layer pairs/triples, per-tensor decisions), and hunt super-weights — one wrongly quantized number can cost 20% of capability. PTQ works out of the box ≥~20–30B dense
below that use QAD — with the *right* data, since wrong-data QAD usually breaks the model

data.name: Verify the quant like a release, not a checkbox
guidelines: Budget more time for evaluation than for quantization (that's where the shipping teams spend theirs)
target and publish a degradation bound (<1% aggregate for FP4 checkpoints)
prefer KL divergence between quantized and BF16 output logits over accuracy benchmarks (fewer sampling artifacts)
always test inside a real harness — run your coding agent on it, feel for wrongness benchmarks can't see
add long-context tests specifically for new attention variants
release benchmarks with your quants, because nobody else comprehensively benchmarks compressed variants

data.name: Big-quantized vs small-native is a throughput decision
guidelines: At equal disk size, prefer the big model quantized (intelligence-per-byte wins)
but check decode speed against your GPU — a big quant at 5–10 tok/s may lose to a small native model at 200 tok/s for interactive use
split the difference with routing (big model plans, small model executes)
respect runtime defaults that keep tiny models at higher precision (very small models quantize badly)
and remember lab-released small natives (Nemotron Nano, Gemma small tiers) exist precisely for the cases where the quantized giant is impractical

data.name: The State of Model Routing (panel: NVIDIA / Cognition / OpenRouter — AI Engineer)
OpenRouter
data.brief: Marketplace for language models ("we exist at" the aggregation layer — can't see into providers' KV caches, passes cache-hit savings through to customers). Ran an auto-router for ~2 years with near-zero adoption before the January-2026 OpenClaw explosion; now ships multiple routers (Pareto code, Fusion) and publishes public usage rankings (top model by dollar spent per task category). Self-describes as ecosystem-driven, building orchestration primitives (sub-agent, advisor tool) for partners

data.name: Devin Fusion (Cognition model router)
data.brief: Cognition's just-released router: Fable-level intelligence at ~40% lower cost by letting the frontier model do planning and hard decisions while delegating implementation to a cheaper (often open) model — which, being cheaper, can attack the task with *more* depth (e.g. three sub-explorations of a codebase can beat one frontier pass). Design philosophy: never route the user to a dumber model and strand them — a frontier agent always "keeps tabs" even when not doing the work, detecting when the delegate is out of its depth. Explicitly framed as v1 of a young field: "I hope a year from now people look back on these as really legacy ideas"

data.name: Sidekick delegation (persistent single delegate)
data.brief: Cognition's alternative to main-agent + sub-agent fan-out: one sub-agent ("sidekick") with a continuously running context, so the main agent never re-provides history — it all stays in KV cache at ~10× cheaper token pricing; smart/cheap roles can swap between the two ends without cache loss. Context flows are asymmetric by design: most context goes to one model only; the delegate is tuned to *present* condensed context back (files referenced by path, not dumped). ⚠ naming: distinct from el-monday-sidekick [registry] — unrelated products; captions also garble it as "psychic"/"sidecar"

data.name: Jagged model capabilities
data.brief: The routing-side premise: coding (or any domain) is not one capability — within data-science work, scikit-learn vs matplotlib vs model-building strengths differ per model, driven by each lab's training corpora and post-training teacher/sub-task mixes. A model that wins a coding benchmark is not "plain better at every task"; overlapping strengths create an arbitrage an orchestrator can harvest — "up to 10% higher accuracy" on router benchmarks (⚠ "LM router bench" garble), depending on model pool and task. Routing = "intimately understanding the behavior, strengths and weaknesses of different models, and applying them thusly"

data.name: Flex Run (NVIDIA elastic model footprints)
data.brief: NVIDIA technology (⚠ name from captions): a main model is distilled into smaller footprints inside one model artifact, and the system switches which footprint does the decoding per task — activating "a class of model or a section of weights depending on the complexity at hand." Paired claims: with access to the training recipe you can literally determine whether a question is in-distribution, and distillation-gap studies across teachers tell you where the small footprints are weak — both "work very well for open models"

data.name: Hallucination/lostness probes
data.brief: Routing trigger built from model internals: linear/magnitude probes (and other classifier heads) over internal state — the prefill "is just a vector at the end of the day" — rating how strongly a model is tending toward hallucination, as a proxy for "how lost a model is in its thinking." Proposed as the principled alternative to token-count heuristics for deciding when a small model needs rescue

data.name: KV-cache economics
data.brief: The cost physics under multi-model systems: cached tokens are ~10× cheaper, so architecture follows the cache — switching models or compacting takes a cache miss; cache lifetimes (~5 min) are operational choices (GPU memory eviction), not physics, and self-hosters can extend them; a scheduled cache refresh can carry a "free" frontier-model check; providers amortize everyone's workload shape into one price, so self-hosting a known shape (e.g. 32K cache / 1K in / 1K out) "you'll likely pay much less"; futures floated: S3-backed cache offload, dynamic cache durations, switching-tolerance knobs. ⚠ merge-check vs el-prompt-caching / el-prefix-caching — those nodes name the mechanism; this one is the economics-as-design-constraint claim. Fold at seeding if preferred

data.name: OpenRouter platform (auto-router, Pareto code, Fusion, rankings)
data.brief: Product node for the marketplace + its routers: auto-router (2 years old, adoption ≈ 0 until OpenClaw made it explode — previously "a discovery play"); Pareto code (Pareto-optimal coding model under a tunable threshold); Fusion (orchestrates multiple models into a fused result; published deep-research results a couple weeks prior — smart model as the outer/wrapper model won); public usage rankings by dollar spent per category; cache-savings passthrough. Goal stated: "good primitives developers can use to get really advanced with model orchestration… and an easy slug that works with all harnesses"

data.name: Routing becomes a product layer
data.brief: Model routing is crystallizing from research into a product category in real time: Cognition ships Devin Fusion (Fable-level intelligence at ~40% lower cost — frontier model plans, cheaper implementation model executes with *more* depth: three sub-explorations of a codebase can out-comprehend one frontier pass); OpenRouter ships Pareto code and Fusion on top of its marketplace; NVIDIA runs router research and evals; and the moderator's framing — "there isn't a very clear solution here… a lot of space for startups" — is stated as the opportunity. The mechanism-level premise is jagged capability: per-model subtask strengths from divergent training corpora create an arbitrage worth "up to 10% higher accuracy," and cheaper per-token delegates can spend many more tokens within the same budget

data.name: Small models thrash out of distribution
data.brief: The panel's counterweight, from both router vendors: cheap models are only cheap in distribution. "If you run Terminal-Bench on Opus and Haiku, Opus will do about three times better at 1/10 the cost of Haiku" — out-of-distribution small models inflate cost through crazed tool-calling loops; on OpenRouter's public rankings the top model by dollar spent on classification tasks is Opus; naive task-type routing is "extremely fragile" for agentic work because task complexity mutates mid-session (explore → implement → live-debug) and "you don't want to be left with some subpar model for the task you're now on"; larger models are also more token-efficient readers (subset reads, single-command verification). Cognition's mitigation: the guarantee of frontier intelligence always present — a watcher agent detecting when the delegate is out of its depth

data.name: Openclaw heartbeat segmented the market
data.brief: A dated adoption discontinuity: OpenRouter's auto-router ran ~2 years with "no real usage" (people wanted specific models; it was a discovery play) — then exploded around January 2026 with OpenClaw, whose ~10-minute heartbeats to your default model made Opus-as-default economically absurd. One very popular app with two completely different intelligence needs, plus open models good enough for the low tier, segmented the market overnight; "a lot more segmentation blossomed afterwards" into today's router products. The fusion rationale generalizes it: "you want to benefit from all the data being trained on across all the labs, and not just the data from one lab"

data.name: Collaboration moves into the weights
data.brief: Routing's endgame per the panel is not harness logic but trained behavior: Cognition RLs its models in both orchestration roles (model-as-orchestrator deciding delegation; model-as-executor following another model's instructions) and expects co-designing models with the orchestration system to be "a big lift in the next step"; new frontier models (Fable family, GPT-5.5/5.6) are "themselves naturally collaborative and better at delegation" — "smarter models get better and better at delegating"; NVIDIA post-trains Nemotron for harnesses including routing, and Flex Run moves the routing switch *inside* the model artifact (per-task footprint activation). Closing consensus: "models are going to get good at routing to other models"

data.name: Routing needs open interiors
data.brief: The routing instruments the NVIDIA seat describes all require seeing inside the model: determining whether a question is in-distribution "works very well for open models — or any model you have access to its data for," because you can check the training recipe directly; distillation-gap studies across teachers locate where small footprints are weak; hallucination probes read internal state (linear/magnitude probes over prefill vectors) to score how lost a model is. The marketplace seat states the complementary limit: OpenRouter "can't see into the KV caches of models unless we're running them ourselves" — aggregators without interior access are structurally confined to price/cache optimization. Routing quality is thus a function of model transparency

data.name: Local cloud hybrid routing
data.brief: The routing axis "most relevant to this crowd": when to run locally vs reach for frontier. Named cases — privacy routing (detect sensitive information in a prompt, keep that inference on-device, anonymize before sending derived work to the cloud) and utilization routing (an under-used DGX Spark costs "only the electrons coming in from my power bill, but I'm paying full price for the tokens in the cloud" — so schedule heartbeats and background work onto idle local compute, and spawn collaborative agents to raise edge utilization when memory, not compute, is the bound). NVIDIA states in-flight work here; "the hybrid of local and cloud starts to really emerge as its own sector"

data.name: Routing centralizes into a controller
data.brief: Routing is evolving from per-prompt model picking into a persistent session-level controller — and the panel argues the controller is structural: applications built on non-deterministic components "operate in a very low-trust environment," no participant has a perfectly visible world, so "there will have to be some form of arbitration… at the orchestration level," with the web's history as precedent (traffic-based routing controls centralized over time). The open question the panel splits on is *where* it lives — product, plumbing, or the models themselves — with the closing synthesis that "there's not going to be a really great harness in absence of a really great model and vice versa"

data.name: Cache is the physics of multi model systems
data.brief: KV-cache economics quietly dictate multi-model architecture: the sidekick pattern exists to avoid re-paying for context; compaction and model switching are priced by the cache miss, not the tokens; cache lifetimes are operational fictions self-hosters can escape; and the move that made agents economically possible at all — Cognition buying direct compute in 2024, "before cache tokens was a thing API providers paid for" — was a cache-economics arbitrage. Any router design that ignores the cache optimizes the wrong bill

data.name: Route sessions, not prompts — and keep a frontier watcher
guidelines: Don't route on task type: agentic complexity mutates mid-session, so think in subtasks/phases and re-decide as the session evolves. Keep frontier intelligence present even when it isn't working — a watcher that detects the delegate going down a rabbit hole
piggyback those checks on cache refreshes you were paying for anyway ("a free frontier call"). Prefer one persistent sidekick over sub-agent fan-out (running context stays in cache
roles can swap). Send most context to one model only
tune the delegate to report back by reference (file paths, high-level thinking), not by dump. For detection beyond heuristics, use internal-state probes (hallucination/lostness scoring)
