token-burst heuristics are unproven ("we have to be very empirical to actually know"). Mine production signals — user model upgrades/downgrades, detected mis-routes — as a label stream and iterate the router against real usage. For prompts, prefer heavyweight smart-model repair (ask the model why it chose wrong, patch the prompt, rerun as regression) over gradient-style prompt tuning (GEPA-class)

data.name: Design against the cache bill, not the token bill
guidelines: Compact for intelligence, not cost — past ~200K tokens (under 100K if you can) intelligence falls off a cliff regardless of advertised windows

and remember compaction itself takes a cache miss, so schedule it when you were switching models anyway. Treat the ~5-minute cache lifetime as an ops parameter, not physics: self-hosting lets you pin caches as long as business logic wants. If your workload shape is known (e.g. 32K cache / 1K in / 1K out), self-hosting or direct compute beats providers who amortize everyone's shape into one price — the move that made 2024-era agents affordable. Pass cache savings through your own stack the way marketplaces do, and expose switching-tolerance (how much remaining cache you'll sacrifice for a better model) as a tunable

data.name: Building Turbopuffer (Gergely Orosz, The Pragmatic Engineer, interviewing Simon Eskildsen, CEO — AI Engineer)
Simon Eskildsen
Gergely Orosz
Turbopuffer
data.brief: S3-native search/vector database ("so many AI companies are using you as an infrastructure layer"): object storage as the source of truth, cache hierarchy above it. Launched October 2023 from a single 8-core GCP instance; first customer Cursor (bill cut 95% vs prior vendor); customers include AI labs/startups (Reflection named). Bootstrapped-profitable culture: raised only for R&D (~$700K seed with an offer to return it) and employee liquidity; full-remote with "campfires"; runs on CPUs + NVMe + S3 by design ("AVX-512 is so sick" — to Jensen Huang's face)

data.name: Turbopuffer (S3-native search engine)
data.brief: Search/vector database where all writes commit directly to object storage (invariant from day one: shut down every VM, no data lost) and hot data hotloads into NVMe/RAM caches. V1 was deliberately primitive: clustering over vectors, files named cluster-1…n plus a centroids file, search = download centroids + n closest clusters; an NGINX reverse-proxy as the entire cache layer. Launch price point: ~$1 per million vectors when the cheapest working alternative was ~$100 — the two-orders-of-magnitude claim that made Cursor's use case viable. "Why can't you work on a database like it's SaaS? If anyone uses it, we'll do it properly"

data.name: Object-storage-native data architecture
data.brief: The architectural thesis under Turbopuffer (and Cursor's independent wish for it): durability and source-of-truth live on S3-class storage (P99 ~200ms for a 256–512KB object; design to P99/P999 and minimize round trips), while "the actual code bases actively being used" sit in memory, everything else hotloading in and out of cache. Extends beyond vectors — Aman's early tweets about S3 for KV caching are cited as ahead-of-their-time ("barely anyone is still doing [it] even though the economics… it will happen"). The napkin numbers that justify it: DRAM ~$2/GB, S3 ~2¢/GB

data.name: Napkin math (first-principles performance accounting)
data.brief: Eskildsen's public project and method: a GitHub table of ~50 system invariants (DRAM bandwidth, S3 round-trip cost/latency, NVMe/EBS throughput, per-GB prices on demand/spot/committed) regenerated by script, drilled via flashcards. Use: when a benchmark disagrees with the first-principles estimate — "you tell me the benchmark takes 10 [seconds]; one of us is wrong" — either the mental model has a gap or the benchmark measured the wrong thing (e.g. an accidental distributed query dragging P99). Origin: repeatedly watching teams make infrastructure decisions on poor benchmarks

data.name: Toxiproxy (fault-injection proxy)
data.brief: Shopify-era open-source layer-4/7 proxy sitting between an app and its databases: API calls make a dependency go down, slow, or misbehave, so driver/application failure handling is tested through the real protocol rather than mocks — implementing a service×dependency failure matrix in CI. Uncovered "tens of issues" in the MySQL driver and Rails that nobody in the ecosystem had tested; per Eskildsen still running in Shopify CI today. Lineage: began as a GDB hack closing the database file descriptor mid-test

data.name: Rl and agents drive cpu scarcity
data.brief: An infra vendor's ground truth against the GPU-only scarcity narrative: CPUs are no longer easy to get. "As RL is becoming a very large amount of the workloads" the labs are "sucking up a lot of CPUs" — teaching models to search, use git, "boot up bash… run real things and learn from that takes a lot of CPU" — and all the agents themselves run on CPUs; the feedback loop is explicit: applied gaps ("models are not that good at CAD or shipbuilding") → "spin up even more RL environments" → more CPU. NVMe SSDs and DRAM are tightening too; "it gets a lot worse before it gets a lot better"; even the big companies fight each other for allocations — Turbopuffer sells to companies it also competes against for CPUs; a customer (Reflection) is maxed out on the longest contracts available; region planning now follows power ("where is the power… is generally where they're going to ship the new CPUs")

data.name: Object storage collapsed retrieval economics
data.brief: The unit-economics story of AI retrieval infra, with numbers at both ends: in 2022–23 vectors-in-DRAM made obvious features unshippable (Readwise's working recommendation engine: $30K/month against $5K total other infra — killed; Cursor's founders: "the unit economics of all the vectors in DRAM are not working"). Moving source-of-truth to S3 with cache hierarchy repriced the category — ~$1/million vectors vs ~$100 for the cheapest prior working option — and Cursor, ~8 people, migrated everything in about two weeks for a 95% bill reduction (promised on napkin math before the software deserved it). Context that forced retrieval in the first place: 2022 context windows of 4–8KB meant "you had to reach for search very quickly." The generalization is still early: S3-for-KV-caching "barely anyone is doing… I think it will happen"

data.name: Profitable infra counterculture
data.brief: A counter-instance to AI-infra capital norms, stated as method: Turbopuffer launched as one person's summer project on a single 8-core instance, promised Cursor a 4K/month bill and then built toward it ("this number should just be lower than the other number… I don't think I'd spent enough time in San Francisco, because the money over here works a little bit differently"), raised ~$700K with an explicit offer to shut down and return every dime absent PMF — "terrifying" to West-Coast ears — became profitable later that year, and formalized a six-reasons taxonomy for raising (R&D, growth, founder ego, employee liquidity, strategic partnership, M&A), having used only #1 and #4. Meanwhile its customers raise billions; the vendor underneath them runs on gross margin discipline

data.name: The agentic era runs on general purpose compute
data.brief: The AI buildout's scarcity has quietly spread from accelerators to the unglamorous half of the datacenter: RL rollouts and production agents do "very general purpose things" — bash, git, browsers, file systems — so CPUs, NVMe and DRAM are now allocation-contested the way GPUs are, and power location decides where capacity lands. The GPU-shortage frame under-describes the constraint surface an agentic industry actually sits on; vendors that can run on "many different machine types" hold a structural advantage

data.name: Object storage is the ai storage endgame
data.brief: S3-as-source-of-truth with hot caches is doing to AI-era data what commodity cloud did to compute: a ~100× price collapse turned retrieval from a killed feature into a default layer, an 8-person Cursor bet its business on it, and the same shape is queued up for KV caches and beyond. The durable insight is architectural, not product-specific: design storage to object-store durability + P99 round-trip math, and the workloads that "couldn't line up" economically start lining up

data.name: Replace benchmark trust with first-principles accounting
guidelines: Maintain (or adopt) a table of system invariants — DRAM/NVMe/EBS bandwidth, S3 round-trip latency and cost, per-GB prices across purchase modes — and drill them until they're reflexive (flashcards). Before accepting any benchmark: compute what the operation *should* take (terms × documents × list sizes ÷ DRAM bandwidth

pages visited × ~1ms random SSD read). When benchmark and estimate disagree, treat it as a contradiction to resolve — "one of us is wrong" — and hunt the gap: wrong query plan, accidental distributed fan-out inflating P99, buggy discs, or a hole in your model. Design object-storage systems to P99/P999 (you fire many requests per logical operation, so you *will* hit the tail) and minimize round trips structurally. Batch effects break naive arithmetic (10K MySQL writes/sec on 1ms fsyncs — because fsyncs batch): verify mechanisms, don't stop at the first clean number

data.name: Test failure handling through the protocol, not through mocks
guidelines: Put a controllable proxy between the application and every stateful dependency
drive it by API to take dependencies down, slow them, or corrupt responses
encode the full "when component X is down, service Y behaves like Z" matrix as CI tests. Mocks hide the layer where failures actually land — the drivers

proxy-level injection found tens of upstream driver/framework bugs nobody had ever exercised. Default failure mode to design away: session store down ⇒ entire storefront down. Start crude if needed (close the DB file descriptor via debugger) but graduate to the proxy so it runs in CI forever

data.name: Name which of the six reasons you're raising for
guidelines: The six: (1) fund R&D, (2) fund growth, (3) founder ego, (4) reward/liquidity for employees, (5) strategic partnership, (6) M&A. Be honest about which one applies — ego raises are "very dangerous… you're diluting all of your employees" and pricing future hires' upside for a status game. Bootstrapping discipline as default (revenue > bills before salaries)
offer investors the shutdown-and-return option if conviction is unproven
raise #4 deliberately so employees don't wait a decade for an IPO to see upside

data.name: Open Source Is Dead. Long Live Open Source. (Saoud Rizwan, Cline — AI Engineer)
Saoud Rizwan
Cline
data.brief: Open-source coding agent (captioned "Klein"/"client"): claims first-ever coding agent status and first to ship custom rules and plan mode, both community-derived; open source as the trust mechanism that let users "inspect our code… connect to any API… know they weren't getting screwed over" while spending heavily. Runs on CLI / VS Code / JetBrains, bring-your-own-key, any provider; launched an open-weights subscription plan this week (volume discounts via inference-host partnerships, quota rising as open models get cheaper — cline.bot)

data.name: Cline (open-source coding agent)
data.brief: The product node (company ≠ artifact): open-source coding agent, any-API/bring-your-own-key, CLI + VS Code + JetBrains; origin of custom rules and plan mode (claimed firsts); positioned in-talk as the neutral harness for feeling out how far open-weights models have come, and now as the vehicle for an open-weights subscription

data.name: OSS contribution lockdown
data.brief: The emerging control set open source is adopting against AI-era contributions: Zig's code of conduct bans all AI use in PRs, issues, even comments (rationale: the team values *contributors* over contributions — review exists to grow trusted people, and AI assistance breaks that); curl is "effectively DDoSed by AI-generated bug reports" and considering shutting its bug-bounty program for the first time in decades; tldraw auto-closes all pull requests, AI or not; GitHub shipped disable-third-party-PRs, with big projects expected to opt in. The community layer priced out: "not worth cultivating anymore, especially because building software is so cheap"

data.name: LiteLLM (and the 2026 compromise)
data.brief: Python LLM-gateway package, ~3.5M downloads/day, widely embedded in enterprise internal gateways. Compromised for three hours: attackers used a GitHub app to steal PyPI publishing tokens and shipped a version installing a credential harvester (API keys, SSH keys, crypto keys) plus a remote-command-execution backdoor. Detection was luck — the malware had a bug that crashed Cursor when the LiteLLM MCP server ran, and a security researcher noticed. "A single compromise and a massive chain of contributors to get pwned"

data.name: Open Compute Project (precedent)
data.brief: The talk's load-bearing analogy: Facebook, beaten to cloud infrastructure by Amazon/Google in 2011, open-sourced its datacenter/server/networking/cooling designs — and the supply chain reorganized around the shared standard: proprietary small-run manufacturing became massive standardized runs, components commoditized, no vendor could charge a premium, and costs fell for the whole industry including Facebook. The lesson as stated: "the industry will adopt and standardize on something they can build on top of even if it isn't the best thing" — offered as the exact template for open-weights models

data.name: Oss community collapse under slop
data.brief: A founder who owes his company to open source declares its community half dead: GitHub has become "an archive of slop PRs and issues and security reports," the old sense of community replaced by "deep skepticism and distrust of each other's responsible use of these tools." The lockdown responses are structural, not rhetorical — Zig bans AI outright because AI assistance breaks the grow-trusted-contributors loop that PR review actually exists for; curl is DDoSed by AI bug reports into considering ending decades of bug bounty; tldraw auto-closes all PRs; GitHub productized disabling third-party PRs. Root cause named: when generation is nearly free, unverified contributions are net-negative, and the community "is just not worth cultivating anymore, especially because building software is so cheap"

data.name: Litellm compromise anatomy
data.brief: The supply-chain case study: LiteLLM (~3.5M downloads/day, embedded in enterprise internal gateways) compromised for three hours via a GitHub-app token theft → poisoned PyPI release → credential harvester (API/SSH/crypto keys) + RCE backdoor. Caught only by luck: the malware crashed Cursor when the LiteLLM MCP server ran and a researcher investigated. "It's become more dangerous than ever to depend on third-party software, where it takes a single compromise and a massive chain of contributors to get pwned" — had it run longer, "catastrophic damage" concentrated exactly in the AI-adopting enterprises

data.name: Enterprise ai spend shock
data.brief: Quantified enterprise dependence, in one slide sequence: an anonymous CFO "accidentally spent $500 million on Claude in a single month" for lack of dashboard usage limits across thousands of employees; Uber's CTO reports 95% of engineers using Claude, ~70% of committed code coming from it, monthly spend up to $2,000/user, and the entire 2026 budget consumed in four months; and the room's show of hands confirms work now *stops* during Claude/GPT outages. AI coding spend has become a first-order budget line and a single-vendor operational dependency inside ordinary engineering orgs

data.name: Subsidize lockin then gouge
data.brief: The lab strategy as read by a harness vendor: SemiAnalysis experiments show a $200 Claude plan yields ~$8,000 of API-equivalent usage and a $200 Codex plan ~$14,000 — labs are losing money per subscriber on purpose, subsidizing "until they have as many engineers dependent on their tooling as possible" (agents in CI, background agents, looping agents — "every new feature and marketing push seems to be a new workflow to standardize on, to use even more tokens and be locked in even more"), with price gouging to follow "once your developers can't work without the tools." It explains the API-business → application-layer migration: building the moat "for the day these models inevitably become a commodity." Rizwan's counter-thesis: it won't work — buyers jump to value

data.name: Open weights value inflection
data.brief: "We're at an inflection point where raw intelligence lead doesn't matter as much anymore": open-weights models (largely Chinese) are powerful enough that "you don't always need the best one," and cost now dominates. Cline's real-repo test — skeptical of benchmarks, they ran GLM vs Opus on an actual Cline bug: both fixed it; GLM used 2× the tokens at half the cost, cleaned up dead code, and verified the build compiled before finishing; Opus was faster with half the tool calls but left type errors and broke the production build ("GLM was trained to spend more tokens verifying its output — fine, the tokens are cheaper"). Adoption following: Coinbase's CEO reports defaulting to GLM and Kimi in the internal gateway, cutting AI spend nearly in half while token usage grows; more businesses expected to build internal routing for dollar-efficiency, even at the cost of the newest closed-tool features

data.name: Open compute precedent for open weights
data.brief: The macro argument: open weights will do to models what Open Compute did to servers — the industry standardizes on what it can build on, "even if it isn't the best thing," and the supply chain reorganizes to commoditize it. Fuel for the curve: ~$3T and 100+ GW of new datacenter capacity by 2030 (roughly doubling global capacity); inference hosts (Baseten, Fireworks) whose "whole purpose is to beat each other" with dedicated hardware, caching, batching and inference silicon; estimate that 1T-parameter inference costs ~90% less by 2030; and the 2014–15 cloud-price-war precedent, after which commoditized layers stopped being the competition and value moved up-stack. The plea: American labs should release open *weights* (not research — "that's what gives us the lead"; weights let others extract traces and train copycats "but not in a way that can leapfrog"), because if foreign models become the standard "there won't be a reason to switch back to GPT or Claude no matter what the marginal improvements are — and then we lose control over the development of this technology," including who funds safety research and whose values ship inside it

data.name: Open source bifurcates
data.brief: AI split the meaning of "open source" in two, and the halves are moving in opposite directions. The community half — contribution, review, trust-building between strangers — is dying, because free generation destroyed the economics of verifying strangers' work (slop PRs, bug-report DDoS, contribution lockdowns). The artifact half — things freely usable and buildable-upon in public — is becoming more economically important than it has ever been, because open weights are the substrate the industry can standardize and commoditize on (the Open Compute mechanism). "Open source is dead; long live open source" is a precise claim: the social institution failed while the licensing institution ascends

data.name: Verification infra flattens model quality
data.brief: "The intelligence is better placed in the system and guardrails around the model": with project skills and rules, systems of verification and quality gates, "even a mediocre model can produce similar results as a more intelligent model — it just might take more tokens" — and the GLM/Opus bug test is the demonstration (the cheaper model's *verify-before-finish* behavior beat the smarter model's speed). This decouples product quality from frontier access, which is precisely what makes the open-weights economics viable

data.name: Distrust the leaderboard; run the candidate on your own bug
guidelines: When a benchmark claims model A beats model B, test on a real issue from your own repo with your production harness. Score what matters commercially: total cost (not token count — cheap tokens change the math), wall-clock, tool-call count, whether the model *verified its own output* (build compiled, tests run) before declaring done, and side effects in both directions (dead-code cleanup vs type errors / broken production build). Expect verification-heavy models to look worse on speed and better on outcome
judge the end result, not the trajectory aesthetics

data.name: Choose a contribution policy before the slop chooses one for you
guidelines: Decide explicitly what your review process is *for* — if it exists to grow trusted contributors (the Zig position), AI-assisted contributions break it and a ban is coherent

if it exists to absorb code, expect DDoS-scale AI bug reports and slop PRs and budget triage accordingly (curl's bug-bounty crisis). Blunt instruments are now legitimate: auto-close all PRs (tldraw), platform-level third-party-PR disabling (GitHub). Assume the community layer no longer verifies itself
treat every inbound contribution as unverified generation, and weigh whether cultivating contributors still pays when software itself is cheap

data.name: Guide, Verify, Solve (Anirban Chatterjee, Sonar — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Anirban Chatterjee
Gitar
data.brief: AI code-review company based in San Mateo, acquired by Sonar a few weeks before the talk (~July 2026). Product: LLM-driven code review plus building/automating the full CI workflow — find issues, block merges on quality, write fixes, and (trust permitting) approve and merge PRs fully automatically. ⚠ captioned "Gitarr" and "Guitar" — normalized to Gitar

data.name: Verification debt
data.brief: The gap between the quality AI tools produce by default and the quality the application actually needs — a gap that scales with criticality. For experiments, solo projects and short-lived internal tools the gap is small enough to live with; for large codebases with many users (some adversarial), many concurrent changes and regulatory exposure, the needed quality is far above the default, and humans are pulled in to close the gap before shipping. Causes named: models are error-prone by construction; they are missing context (the wider codebase, the business, "the meeting you had 2 weeks ago"); and they don't know your objectives. ⚠ merge-check vs el-reviewdebt and el-cognitive-debt — see Review note 5

data.name: SonarQube
data.brief: Sonar's zero-trust, multi-layered verification platform: syntax issues, data-flow issues, architectural issues, control-flow issues, across essentially any language; assigns grades across quality, security and maintainability and blocks PRs that don't pass the quality gate; provides "deep hooks" giving agents first-party access to verification. Scale stats stated: >7M developers, ~750B lines of code analyzed per day. ⚠ deliberately NOT coined in batch 2 (carried in the co-sonar brief) — promoted here because this talk makes the product itself load-bearing; see Review note 4

data.name: Gitar (AI code review + CI automation)
data.brief: The acquired product: LLM-driven "superhuman review" living in the PR flow alongside SonarQube's computational review; can block merges when issues breach quality criteria, write fixes, and approve/merge PRs completely automatically — but defaults to find-and-show-and-discuss, with automation features turned on progressively as trust is earned

data.name: Sonar remediation agent
data.brief: GA'd the week of the talk: point it at backlog issues, tech debt and legacy code and it improves the codebase "almost in the background" at a scale human developers don't have bandwidth for, while humans stay on front-end innovation work

data.name: Sonar LLM Leaderboard
data.brief: Sonar's public model benchmark: every major new model gets ~4,000 coding tasks and is scored with SonarQube's own metrics — correctness, complexity, task-solve rate, maintainability, reliability, security — and graphed across those axes. The worked example: Sonnet 4.6 is strong on correctness/solve-rate; Opus 4.6 wins on maintainability, security and lower complexity — so users toggling models "to control token burn rates" are also toggling quality profiles. ⚠ vendor-owned benchmark — see Review note 1; batch 2 carried the same instrument as a signal only (sig-sonar-model-quality-bench)

data.name: Cmu ai productivity spike reverts
data.brief: The CMU GitHub study, in more detail than the batch-2 keynote: projects sorted by metadata into traditional-tooling vs AI-tool (Cursor) cohorts show a temporary productivity spike lasting ~3 months, then reverting — while a persistent increase in static-analysis warnings and code complexity (measured with SonarQube) continues well past the 3-month mark. The debt is what reverts the spike: the accumulated issues "end up actually slowing developers down even more". ⚠ near-duplicate of sig-cmu-velocity-fade — same study, same vendor, second speaker; merge option in Review note 2

data.name: Humans rubber stamp ai code review
data.brief: Human review as the verification backstop is measurably compromised: in a Wharton study where the AI assistant was covertly instructed to confidently lie some of the time, participants followed correct AI advice 92.7% of the time — and wrong AI advice nearly 80% of the time. Extrapolated to code review under AI throughput (more code, multiple agents writing simultaneously, all merging into one application): "the load is just too great… there's a lot of rubber stamping that I'm sure is happening in all of your organizations. It's happening everywhere." Conclusion drawn: human review must be backstopped by automated verification, not the other way round

data.name: Model quality profiles diverge
data.brief: No two models are the same and their quality issues are diverse along independent axes: on Sonar's ~4,000-task leaderboard, Sonnet 4.6 is strong on correctness and task-solving while Opus 4.6 delivers better maintainability, security and lower complexity — so the common practice of toggling models to control token burn is silently a quality-profile decision, and model choice should be per-task-type. The standing consequence: "none of these models are ever going to be perfect. You're always going to have some kind of need for verification in the loop"

data.name: Verification moves into both loops
data.brief: Verification is being re-architected from post-hoc human review into both loops of AI development: in the *inner agentic loop*, the agent gets guardrails and scoped context up front (guide), calls verification in real time as it writes, and fixes findings immediately so they don't propagate into later loops (solve) — demoed live with Cursor calling Sonar Vortex and refusing to proceed until it passes; in the *outer CI/CD loop*, an LLM-driven "superhuman review" (Gitar) runs alongside computational review (SonarQube), grades the PR across quality/security/maintainability, and blocks it from production without a passing grade, with a fix agent for what's found. Autonomy is a ratchet: Gitar defaults to find-show-discuss and earns its way to auto-fix/auto-merge

data.name: Enterprises demand one verification rulebook
data.brief: What customers say drives verification adoption, per Sonar's customer conversations: (1) consistency — one standard rulebook across every project, team and AI tool, not per-team verification silos; (2) tool effectiveness — token efficiency and right-model-for-right-project discipline; (3) shift-left security — with CVEs now "announced and then immediately exploited… almost often the same day", issues must be caught at write time; (4) compliance — regulated industries need an audit trail proving verification ran constantly and consistently. Closing prescription: standardize on a *single independent* multi-layered verification platform to eliminate the blind spots created by tool silos

data.name: Verification is the scaling unlock
data.brief: The talk's core argument, and the cloud-computing analogy that frames it: AI coding is at the turning point "from experimentation to engineering", and what cloud needed to expand access — repeatability, scalability, consistency — AI coding gets from safety and trust, i.e. a governance and verification regime. The verification-debt gradient explains why: the default-vs-needed quality gap is negligible for experiments and decisive for critical systems, so verification is precisely the capability that determines how far up the criticality ladder AI-written software can climb. "A key enabler and a key unblocker", not overhead

data.name: Code is provable software is not
data.brief: The comfort of code — write the function right and it runs the same way every time — does not survive scale: requirements and externalities shape behavior, accumulating code interacts unpredictably, and users (including adversaries) do things you didn't expect. "Software is not provable in the same way that code is provable — software can break in interesting and novel ways." So generation quality can never retire verification: as AI writes more software against bigger problems, you hit the unprovability limit more often, and automated verification is the risk control you buy back for the control you released over how the code gets written

data.name: Run agentic coding as guide → verify → solve, in both loops
guidelines: Before any loop: write down and encode your specs (desired architecture and architectural constraints, coding standards and acceptable patterns, dependency allow/deny lists, syntax standards, logging/observability/tracing practices) and your quality criteria (acceptable security/quality/maintainability levels — ship-with defaults exist, adjust per org). *Guide*: give the agent scoped context and guardrails for the task at hand — never the whole codebase, which produces thrashing, exploring and token burn. *Verify*: in the inner loop, have the agent call verification in real time and fix findings immediately so they don't propagate into later loops

in the outer loop, run LLM-driven and computational review together, grade the PR across quality/security/maintainability, and hard-gate merges on a passing grade. *Solve*: give the agent the tools and the agency to remediate its own findings, then repeat the loop. Keep verification multi-layered and reasoning-based, spanning quality, security and compliance

data.name: Bounded autonomy: free generation, centralized verification
guidelines: Establish bounded-autonomy guidelines: agents get freedom to generate, inside a centralized scheme of verification and constraints. Never let the generating model validate its own output — use a different methodology (and diversity of tools) to review than to write. Make verification zero-trust (source-agnostic — human or any AI), auditable, explainable, algorithmic and repeatable, so you can prove it ran the same way every time (compliance). Standardize on a single independent multi-layered verification platform across all projects, teams, developers and AI coding tools — silos of per-tool verification create blind spots. Ratchet automation trust: start at find-and-show-and-discuss, enable auto-fix and auto-merge only as confidence accumulates. Equip developers as orchestrators — they design the context frameworks and processes the agents run inside

data.name: Always-on agents run production without the on-call tax (Justin Smith, Resolve AI — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Justin Smith
Resolve AI
data.brief: Production-operations AI: on-call agent (per-alert triage + full root-cause investigation), incident agents (cross-team sync/impact coordination), and always-on background agents for the operational long tail — running on an agent architecture of models + context + reasoning + actions over a continuously-updated learning/knowledge system. Founding hypothesis stated on stage: AI-driven coding velocity would create an influx of production issues, so AI would be needed to *operate* the systems, not just build them. Customers described as "world-class engineering teams… at crazy scale"; surface-of-record is Slack/MS Teams; capabilities exposed over MCP for grafting into customers' own harnesses

data.name: Background agents (ops long tail)
data.brief: Always-on agents for the production work that has no owner and no page: watching deploys out to health, morning incident digests, chasing the returned P99 drift nobody alerts on, capacity reports against quarterly goals, recurring health checks "not waiting for a customer to complain first". Trigger model: schedules, weekly ceremonies (Thursday on-call handover), event streams (CI/CD deployments, Slack messages), or direct message ("go do some work"). Runtime model: always running, in the cloud ("if you close your laptop, it's okay"), inside a sandbox with a filesystem underneath so the agent self-organizes its work; a task system plus imported skills plus integrations tell it what to do; a shared learning loop reflects on each task and carries lessons across tasks

data.name: Production context vs execution
data.brief: The talk's task decomposition: a task = execution (knowing what to do, tool access, loading the dashboard) + production context (the judgment that "that metric smells off… this feels wrong and I don't know if I can even explain why"). Execution is necessary but commodity; production context is what makes a background agent's work worth anything — it decides what is important, not just what is checkable

data.name: Production learning system
data.brief: The stated hard part and moat: not model smarts ("models have gotten incredibly capable… especially over the last 6 months") but *truly understanding your environment* — how services interact, where the hotspots are, the current causal chains — captured in an underlying learning/memory system that must grow as the system evolves, because the system now evolves faster than ever. Reflection after each task feeds it; knowledge learned in one task applies to others; "we spend so much time on our knowledge system" is the company's differentiation claim. ⚠ pattern-relevant to the uncoined pat-agent-memory-layer — no pattern edge, Review note 2

data.name: Change-aware deployment verification
data.brief: Deployment monitoring beyond fixed CI/CD checks: on each release event (a GitHub tag in Slack), the agent reads the actual changes, works out which telemetry would evaluate those changes, and builds a customized check plan for that specific release — e.g. checkout replaces the currency service → watch checkout latency and error rates *and* the Kafka pipeline as the causal chain. Nothing hard-coded: the agent chooses its own re-check cadence and watch window ("maybe I'll come back in 3 days"), and the same mechanism covers change systems that bypass CI/CD entirely — feature flags, infra changes — which today get no monitoring beyond "trusting that an alert might fire"

data.name: Resolve AI platform
data.brief: The productized stack: on-call agent (alert triage + root-cause investigation), incident coordination agents, and background agents over the shared learning system; visibility UI (task inspection, previous runs, per-task work traces) but the first-party surface is Slack/MS Teams, "where you live"; conversational setup (the agent explores your environment, asks clarifying questions, drafts the recurring task, you test then share); behavior tuned by replying in-thread ("this is too verbose — make it shorter" persists into the task definition); exposed via MCP servers so internal harnesses can graft in Resolve's execution and learned production context; bring-your-own skills supported ("don't go duplicate a bunch of stuff")

data.name: 70pct engineering time is ops
data.brief: The ops-economics quantification: per a survey study, 70% of an engineer's time is not spent writing code — it goes to running what shipped: maintaining platforms, scaling infra, debugging incidents, on-call, hot fixes, alerts, runbooks, restoring services, escalations, cross-team questions. "Really, coding was never the big bottleneck." AI wave 1 accelerated exactly the 30%, and the talk's conclusion is the model-periphery claim verbatim: "we need full stack AI — it's not just about the models anymore, it's about the context around the models and what the models can do inside of a specific domain"

data.name: Ai velocity outruns prod structures
data.brief: The wave-1 aftermath from the ops side: bigger PRs, code shipped much faster, and now "maybe even from non-developers that don't actually know the code or what it's doing or the operating principles behind it"; "AI is creating a lot more issues in production as AI code goes through," and "it's not clear we have the right structures in place to deal with the amount of changes coming through." A cost-pressure rider: "unlimited tokens is coming to an end… they're starting to clamp down, prices are going up, companies are getting a lot more stringent" (see Review note 3)

data.name: Background agents absorb ops long tail
data.brief: The dedicated-layer vendor positioning, complete: the operational work with no owner ("doesn't show up in your job description") becomes agent workload via four proven workloads — deployment monitoring, scheduled health/anomaly checks, operational reports/handoffs, first-responder to engineering questions — delivered as always-on cloud agents in a sandbox with a filesystem, a task system, and a shared learning loop, composable across schedules, event streams and Slack triggers. Includes the emergent trust mechanic: the first-responder agent watches critical channels passively, answers only above a confidence bar, and will DM a human first — "I think I know the answer to this, but I'm not sure. Can you confirm before I respond?"

data.name: Ops agent value is learned context
data.brief: The moat claim, stated as an engineering necessity: models are "incredibly capable… especially over the last 6 months," but for an ops agent to succeed it "has to have an underlying learning system" that captures how *your* system operates — service interactions, hotspots, current causal chains — and keeps that understanding current as the system evolves faster and faster. Every company is unique, so the knowledge system is where Resolve says it spends its time; the same learned context is offered over MCP to augment customers' own agents. Execution loads the dashboard; the learned context says the metric smells off

data.name: Agents write their own deploy checks
data.brief: Verification of production change is becoming synthesized per change rather than pre-authored: on each release the agent reads the diff, derives the telemetry that would validate it, builds a bespoke check plan (including causal-chain checks like the Kafka pipeline behind a currency-service swap), and sets its own watch window — an hour, or back in 3 days for slow-burn failure modes. This also extends verification to the changes CI/CD never sees (feature flags, infra changes), where today the only safety net is "trusting that an alert might fire and an on-caller will wake up and say 'who changed what?'". Explicitly positioned as patching, not replacing, the CI/CD pipeline — the alternative, "a single engineer just focused on watching all the things on every release", is "really expensive" cognitive load

data.name: Execution is commodity context is the product
data.brief: The talk's task decomposition is a market claim: with capable models, the execution half of any ops task (load the dashboard, run the check, call the tool) is commodity — what's scarce is production context, the learned, environment-specific judgment that a metric "feels wrong" before anyone can articulate why. That is why an ops-agent vendor's differentiation lives in the learning/knowledge system rather than the model, why the models slide is one bullet and the learning slide gets the "we spend so much time here", and why the sellable interface (MCP) exports *learned context*, not model access. The ops-agent market is a context market

data.name: Every change gets a bespoke verifier
data.brief: Production verification is escaping the pipeline: instead of a fixed battery of checks authored in advance, each change event gets a verification plan generated *for it* — derived from the change's content, scoped to its causal chain, scheduled on its risk profile — and change paths that never had verification (feature flags, infra edits) get it for free. Combined with confidence-gated human confirmation (the agent DMs before it answers publicly), this inverts on-call: the always-on agent watches continuously and the human becomes the escalation path, rather than the pager being the system's first responder

data.name: Start background agents on the four proven workloads
guidelines: Begin with the workloads proven in production: (1) deployment monitoring — watch every change event, including the ones CI/CD doesn't pipe (feature flags, infra changes)
(2) scheduled health/anomaly checks — routine morning sweeps, plus time-boxed worry-watches ("watch this third-party service for the next week, then stop")
(3) operational reports and handoffs — incident digests, capacity-vs-goal reports, weekly on-call handover prep summarizing the week's trends for the next rotation

(4) first-responder to engineering questions — passive channel watching with a confidence gate and human DM-confirmation before public answers. Pick the trigger per workload: schedule, weekly ceremony, event stream, or direct message. Set up conversationally — let the agent explore the environment and ask its clarifying questions

test before sharing with the team. Tune by replying in-thread ("too verbose — make it shorter" should persist into the task). Keep the surface where people already work (Slack/MS Teams), with a UI for inspecting tasks, runs and work traces. Graft into existing harnesses over MCP and bring existing skills rather than duplicating. Then get creative — the primitives compose well beyond the four

data.name: Benchmarking Coding Agents on New vs Legacy Codebases (Denys Linkov, Wisedocs — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Denys Linkov
Wisedocs
data.brief: Processes complex medical claims — PDFs "more than 10,000 pages in size… some files bigger than video files" — through an ML-model pipeline; scaling pains in 2025 (too slow for customer demand, pipeline too complicated to update, 10+ legacy repos nobody wanted to touch) drove the 6-month monorepo refactor the talk audits. Typed developer per the vertical-AI precedent (co-risa-labs, co-filed, co-sondermind — enum has no healthcare)

data.name: Longitudinal same-task re-run
data.brief: Private capability measurement by re-running an identical, real, already-completed task on each model generation and diffing the outcome. The talk's worked run (a Temporal activities/workflow refactor replicating the legacy pipeline): O3 (2025) — 3 hours of back-and-forth in Cursor, 10 major mistakes, constant manual intervention (guide the model, hand-edit, delete code); Sonnet 4.6 — solved with one additional iteration; Opus 4.8 — "basically able to one-shot" it. Also captures what leaderboards can't: the *interaction shape* changed — O3 made few substantial tool calls; modern harnesses spawn sub-agents, plan calls, shell commands and verification passes, costing more per model-step but far less human attention. Net: same task ≈ 1/5 the time to rebuild today

data.name: High-accuracy horizon reading
data.brief: Read time-horizon capability curves at the 80% (better: 90–99%) success threshold, not the 50% headline: the exponential trend survives at 80%, but the "models can do 18+-hour human tasks" claims do not — and the planning mental model that matters (write a spec, hand off, walk away confident) lives at 90–99%. A 50%-success hour-long kickoff is a coin-flip that wastes the compute *and* your attention span. On METR's frontier-model preview data, success declines sharply at the ~4-hour mark, and some tasks fail even below the 15-minute mark. ⚠ same argument as batch-2's ins-accuracy-collapses-capability (Shaukat/Sonar) — independent second statement, see Review note 2

data.name: Refactor-now-vs-wait calculus
data.brief: The decision the talk audits: treat tech debt like financial debt (it compounds "in mysterious and sometimes unexpected ways" and can outrun the ROI it bought), against the fact that refactoring later gets exponentially easier as models, tools and infrastructure (sandboxes, monitoring frameworks) improve. The counterweight: AI-native development at velocity *recreates legacy conditions* — lots of code, low performance/quality, "people don't actually understand what's happening there" — so waiting without guardrails compounds the debt you'd be deferring. Decide on business value (throughput, cost, feature latency), and partial isolation of codebase layers is a legitimate alternative to a full refactor

data.name: Monorepo as agent infrastructure
data.brief: The 10-repos→monorepo consolidation, justified in agent terms: models now navigate multi-repo file trees fine, but end-to-end testing, verification and deployment across repos is still much harder, and multi-repo sandbox setup (cloning everything, wiring it up) taxes any "full AI factory" environment. Human effects compound it: within 6 months the rebuild hit feature parity and the commit curve steepened; nearly every developer in the company now commits to the monorepo outside their expertise area (schemas, API calls, cross-stack changes), and its patterns spread to other repos

data.name: AI psychosis (unverified-artifact trust)
data.brief: The failure mode of AI-accelerated research: "you look at a deep research report that's 20 pages long and you say 'wow, this looks good' — and then those features don't actually exist in the product, and you've set yourself back." Named in the talk as the reason acceleration (evaluation work "90% faster now") must keep the old quality bar: hidden assumptions surface late (an open-source library's feature that was actually in beta). ⚠ merge-check vs el-automation-bias (same psychology, artifact-trust flavor) and name-collision check vs el-benchmark-psychosis (different claim — that one is misreading benchmark numbers; this is trusting fluent research output)

data.name: Private task reruns over leaderboards
data.brief: A practitioner measures coding-agent capability by re-running his own completed production tasks across model generations instead of consulting any public benchmark: the identical Temporal-refactor task goes from 3 hours + 10 major mistakes + constant manual intervention (O3, 2025) to one extra iteration (Sonnet 4.6) to a one-shot (Opus 4.8), with the harness interaction reshaping along the way (sub-agents, plan calls, shell commands, verification passes) — "if I was rebuilding the same task… it would take around 1/5 of the time." No leaderboard appears anywhere in the decision loop; the talk's only public instrument is METR, used for *mental-model calibration* rather than model selection

data.name: Metr 50pct headline inflates capability
data.brief: The 50%-accuracy convention on time-horizon charts overstates deployable capability: re-read at 80% the exponential survives but the 18+-hour-task claims vanish, and the thresholds that match how engineers actually plan (spec → handoff → walk away) are 90–99% — at 50%, an hour-long kickoff wastes the hour half the time. METR's own frontier-preview data shows success declining significantly at the ~4-hour mark and some tasks failing "in all its glory" below even 15 minutes. "We're still not there where you can just kick off an agent and have something be completed reliably"

data.name: Shipping faster products not better
data.brief: The audience-poll wedge: everyone agrees tech products improved over 20 years; hands drop at 5 years; almost none at 1 year. Meanwhile shipping velocity has never been higher — and uptime at two leading companies (names deliberately blurred) sits below three nines, even four nines. "Even though we're shipping faster and faster, the code quality and the product quality has not necessarily gone up" — customer focus, maintainability and reliability degraded while the technology life cycle accelerated

data.name: Agent era favors monorepos
data.brief: Codebase topology is now agent infrastructure: Wisedocs consolidated 10+ repos into a monorepo and reports that while models navigate multi-repo directory trees fine, end-to-end testing, verification and deployment remain much harder across repos, and multi-repo sandbox environments (for a "full AI factory") pay a setup tax on every clone. Post-consolidation: parity in 6 months, a visibly steeper shipping curve after parity, near-company-wide contribution to the monorepo beyond expertise areas, and the repo's patterns propagating to other codebases

data.name: Zero shot refactor scaffolds without validating
data.brief: The frontier zero-shot probe: GPT 5.5 extra high, told to refactor the legacy codebase (repo names, models, components supplied), "completed its goal" in 10 minutes 22 seconds — writing only ~2,000 lines, "which was a little bit fishy." Inspection: scaffolding only, ML models unimplemented, and the agent's own output admitting "I did not add a Ray Serve deployment or bootstrap command yet." Verdict: "we're still not there where models can self-validate and just one-shot these kinds of problems, but we're getting close" — with a stated forecast of ~6 months to consistently completing substantial refactors (citing the Stripe case)

data.name: Ai psychosis in ai accelerated research
data.brief: The 2-month, 3-person, 17-criteria orchestrator bake-off (5 open-source candidates, Confluence docs, manual POCs) would be "90% faster now" — deep research + sub-agents per criterion + POC generation — *but the quality bar cannot move*: polished 20-page research reports describe features that don't exist in the product (AI psychosis), and hidden assumptions bite late (a library feature that was actually in beta). Ground truth from the manual era: they got 15 of 17 requirements right — the number any accelerated replacement has to beat, not just match faster

data.name: Refactor timing is the judgment call
data.brief: Execution industrialized out from under the decision: the same refactor now costs 1/5 the effort and will soon zero-shot, so "should we refactor?" has become almost entirely a *judgment* question — weigh compounding tech debt and business ROI against exponentially cheapening future execution, knowing that deferring without guardrails lets AI-velocity recreate the legacy conditions you're deferring escape from. Wisedocs' answer (pause, consolidate, forge ahead) is vindicated in business terms: pipeline time down, costs down, larger files supported, multi-month features shipping in under a week — and the codebase developers *ask* to work in. The talk's closing instruction is literally a call to judgment: "think about the business value of delivering a big refactor and the tradeoffs of doing it now versus in the future"

data.name: Codebase shape is agent throughput
data.brief: What bounded Wisedocs' agent productivity was never model choice — it was the environment: repo topology (E2E verification and sandbox setup dictate monorepo), spec quality (a well-constructed spec is what unlocks high-capability execution), lifecycle guardrails adopted as they appeared (plan mode, local review skills, human PR review used deliberately as *context-building* for a new repo), and "a number of different frameworks and primitives… in order to have good agentic development" — without which teams "waste time just running in loops with models." The refactor's payoff came from reshaping the code for agents and humans at once

data.name: Benchmark coding agents on your own completed work
guidelines: Keep a set of real, finished tasks and re-run them on each model generation
log wall-clock time, iteration count, major-mistake count, and how much manual intervention (guiding, hand-editing, deleting) was needed

watch the *interaction shape* too — tool-call volume, sub-agents, plan calls, shell use, self-verification — because harness behavior shifts as much as accuracy. Add a zero-shot probe on a hard end-to-end goal and inspect for silent scaffolding-only completion (suspiciously few lines

the agent's own "not added yet" admissions). Read public horizon curves at 80–99% accuracy, never the 50% headline, and match the threshold to your handoff model (spec-and-walk-away needs 90%+). Verify AI research output against the actual product — features may not exist or may be beta — and keep a manual-era baseline (theirs: 15/17 requirements right) as the bar. Expect conclusions to age in months
re-run, don't cache

data.name: Decide refactors on business value under exponential agent progress
guidelines: Cost tech debt like financial debt against the ROI it bought (features, customers) — complexity can outrun the ROI. Weigh that refactoring later gets exponentially easier (better models, tool calling, sandboxes, monitoring), but that AI-native velocity without guardrails recreates legacy conditions (much code, low quality, no one understands it) — so guardrails are mandatory whether you refactor fully, partially, or not at all

isolating codebase layers is a legitimate middle path. If you commit: consolidate to a monorepo first (agent E2E testing/verification/deployment and sandbox economics favor it), reach parity, then build features
use human PR review early as deliberate context-building for the new repo

adopt lifecycle primitives (plan mode, review skills) as they mature. Measure the outcome in business terms — pipeline time, cost, max file size, feature latency, parity time, post-parity commit velocity, contributor spread — and in whether developers *want* to work in the codebase

data.name: Multiplayer agentic engineering (Arjun Singh, Superconductor — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Arjun Singh
Superconductor
data.brief: Multiplayer agentic-engineering platform (shared agent sessions across Slack/app/GitHub, meeting-bot signal ingestion, cloud sandboxes, per-codebase agent benchmarking), built by the ex-GradeScope team. ⚠ The talk's sign-off says "sign up at superagent.com / arjun@superagent.com" and once "Superagent is the best way" — byline and title say Superconductor; treat the domain as a caption garble and verify before public-facing use

data.name: Superconductor (multiplayer agent platform)
data.brief: Platform implementing the talk's six lessons: one agent session reachable from Slack, desktop app, mobile app and GitHub; participant/visibility trails on every session; artifacts (screenshots, video) visible from every surface; meeting-bot ingestion of external signals; isolated cloud environments with a configurable network sandbox and an environment-setup assistant; per-codebase agent benchmarking feeding a planned per-task auto-router

data.name: Shared agent sessions across surfaces
data.brief: The same agent session — same context, same memory — addressable from every relevant interface rather than trapped on one laptop or "trapped in Slack": start a session in Slack, continue in the desktop/mobile app, finish in GitHub. Sessions carry a visible participant trail (who created, interacted, got notified, has seen it — "has this been vetted by an engineer or not?"), and a reviewer can interrogate the session directly ("why did you do it this way?") instead of waiting for the human author, because "the answer is almost certainly in this thread" and you can ask the agent rather than read the thread

data.name: Ambient signal-to-code ingestion (meeting bot)
data.brief: Turning every external signal — Slack threads, customer/onboarding/sales calls, internal meetings, Sentry, bug reports, emails, feature requests — into prioritized, evaluable work automatically. Flagship: a meeting bot invited to Meet/Zoom/Teams that listens all day, links to existing work instead of duplicating it, files tickets, and starts implementing: at the expo booth a spoken idea (agents should get explicit acceptance criteria before declaring done) became a ticket, a working form change and a screenshot with "none of us doing anything manually." The gap it closes is stated precisely: MCP hookups already let agents *read* email/Notion — "but how does it know what to work on?"

data.name: Configurable network-egress sandbox
data.brief: Isolated cloud environment per project with an explicit allowlist of reachable destinations; any out-of-list access attempt pauses and prompts ("tried to access something — do you want to give it access?"), grantable per ticket or per project. Coupled with least-privilege credentials (agents get only what they need — not whatever tokens live on a developer's laptop) and anti-exfiltration (code/secrets/content can't be pushed somewhere they shouldn't be). Also what lets non-technical teammates trigger real work: no local dev environment required

data.name: Per-codebase agent benchmarking
data.brief: Benchmark harnesses/models on *your own repo*: select pull requests that represent great engineering work (agent-, human- or hybrid-authored), run the candidate agents, and read quality-vs-cost and quality-vs-time curves for your codebase — because public benches don't transfer ("SWE-bench is all in Python, we're Ruby on Rails"). Their curves: Anthropic agents consistently better but not faster and far more expensive; Codex fast, good and cheaper; open models improving but slow. Feeds the roadmap claim: per-task auto-routing grounded in your own data, since no third party can know what routes best for your codebase. ⚠ merge-check vs el-private-benchmark — see review note 4

data.name: Frontier withdrawal forces agnosticism
data.brief: Lesson zero is stated as insurance against the labs: be model- and harness-agnostic because "the best one can change weekly — a new one comes out, or the best one got taken away." Lived instance: Fable (⚠ "Fiable" garble) became their default "for like the few days we had it, and then it went away" — they switched back to Codex with zero disruption *because* they were agnostic. Open-weight models are the hedge ("actually pretty good now — we've been really happy with GLM 5.2… much cheaper"; "more and more is happening through GLM 5.2, going to invest in that"), and the incentive argument is explicit: "the incentives of the people selling you tokens aren't really aligned with yours… they want to sell you more tokens"

data.name: Agent sessions as team surface
data.brief: The multiplayer mechanic: the identical agent session is reachable from Slack, the desktop/mobile app and GitHub — the agent "didn't forget what you did in one place" — with participant/seen trails answering "has this been vetted by an engineer?", reviewers interrogating the session instead of the author, and artifacts visible from everywhere. The payoff claim is organizational: support and growth people now meaningfully change the product — they hit a bug, say "fix this" in Slack, screenshots come back, an engineer merges — where before "they'd put it in Linear and a PM would triage it." HELD PATTERN-LESS — pat-ai-native-org ledger (uncoined): non-technical staff shipping through shared agent sessions

data.name: Meetings compile to prs
data.brief: The meeting bot ran all day on a 4-hour expo-booth Google Meet: it linked existing work, filed tickets from overheard ideas, and implemented one live — an attendee's acceptance-criteria suggestion became a modified ticket form plus an on-request screenshot, no human in the loop. "Every onboarding or customer call or team meeting, we almost always have dozens of new ideas prototyped, but more importantly at least a few shippable PRs with very minimal intervention. We talk, stuff comes out, we look at it, we ship it." The bottleneck it removes is not generation but routing: signals already lived in email/Sentry/Notion and MCPs already exposed them — what was missing was knowing what to work on

data.name: Laptop agents are a credential hazard
data.brief: The case for moving agents off laptops is a threat model, not convenience: laptops hold credentials agents shouldn't see, and teams are "either approving a bunch of stuff or hoping the auto-approval flow / YOLO mode (⚠ "yellow mode") and sandbox are configured properly." Resourceful, eager-to-please agents plus stray tokens produce the failure he names: told to "wipe this agent database," an agent finds a laptop token, believes it's on staging, and deletes production — "not constantly, but it still happens." The remedy: isolated cloud environments, least-privilege access, a configurable egress allowlist with per-ticket grants, and anti-exfiltration — which also eliminates "lid anxiety" (laptops open at the airport, tethered in cars driving home)

data.name: Benchmark on your own codebase
data.brief: Public leaderboards are dismissed on transfer grounds — "SWE-bench is all in Python, we're Ruby on Rails… the results can be very, very different" — replaced by benchmarking agents against the team's own great PRs for quality/cost/time. The hard numbers: ~1.5B tokens in a month for a small team; 3,300 Claude Code runs/day at ~$10K/day token-equivalent (covered by plans); Codex ran 4× the sessions for less total cost — so the default flipped to Codex ("matched our vibe check, we wanted hard data too"), with GLM 5.2 rising. It also kills new-model FOMO: instead of "two wasted hours" trying Kimi/MiniMax/GLM on hearsay, the bench answers overnight. Roadmap: per-task auto-routing from this data. HELD PATTERN-LESS — pat-benchmark-trust-crisis ledger (uncoined): behavioral/irrelevance leg + the owned-measurement countermeasure (joins Almeida/Khial b15, Boundary's private-loop scope note b15)

data.name: All agent prs still human reviewed
data.brief: The output stat and its governor, in one breath: "essentially 100% — like 99.9% — of our pull requests are heavily agent-generated. We know quality and reliability and security are really important, so we still have humans look at everything. We have agents help with it all, but everything's human reviewed"

data.name: Multiplayer is the unbuilt layer
data.brief: The industry is centering agents; the unsolved layer is the people around them. Individual agent leverage is real but strands work on laptops and in single-player chats — the compounding gains come from team infrastructure: one session addressable from every surface, visibility trails that answer "who vetted this," ambient ingestion that turns organizational exhaust (meetings, bug reports, support chatter) into evaluable code, and sandboxes safe enough that non-engineers trigger real work. The model was never the blocker for any of this; the coordination fabric was

data.name: Owned benchmarks buy agility
data.brief: A private benchmark on your own codebase converts model churn from a loyalty problem into an empirical one: when the frontier shifts — or a frontier model is withdrawn days after arriving — switching is a data-backed default change, not a workflow migration. Agnosticism plus owned measurement is what keeps a team "at the right part of the frontier of cost, speed, quality" without being captured by any token seller, and it is the only credible substrate for per-task routing, since no third party knows what works on your repo

data.name: Make agent work multiplayer, not single-player
guidelines: Get the codebase running in an isolated cloud sandbox first — it unlocks everything else
use an agent to do the migration ("get Claude Code or Codex to do this for you")
expose the *same* agent session in every relevant human interface (Slack, desktop/mobile, GitHub) instead of new bots per surface
give sessions visible participant/seen trails so anyone can tell whether an engineer has vetted the work
let reviewers ask the session, not the author
surface artifacts (screenshots, video) on every surface
ingest external signals automatically (meetings, Sentry, email, support) and link to existing work rather than duplicating
scope credentials to what the agent needs and run all egress through an allowlist with per-ticket exception grants
then let non-technical teammates trigger real work directly

data.name: Benchmark agents on your own codebase
guidelines: Select PRs that represent great engineering work — agent-, human- or hybrid-authored
benchmark candidate models/harnesses against them for quality vs cost vs time on your repo
don't assume public benchmarks transfer across stacks (Python-heavy benches say little about a Rails codebase)
re-run when new models land so trying the new thing costs a run, not two hours of vibes
switch defaults on data but keep multiple models for their different strengths
keep humans reviewing everything regardless of who authored it
aim the accumulated results at per-task routing

data.name: Realtime multiplayer, automation, and you! (Idan Gazit, GitHub — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Idan Gazit
GitHub Agentic Workflows
data.brief: Background-agent automation where markdown is the source code: "if GitHub Actions and Copilot had a baby and it ran on markdown." A workflow is a three-line-ish natural-language playbook ("the message I'd send to a junior developer") plus YAML front matter of deterministic guardrails; Copilot expands it into a full playbook, and the compiled Actions YAML is "a compiled artifact — you never look at it"; to change behavior "just edit the English." Demoed as a super-Dependabot: nightly dependency watcher that read release notes across two major Astro versions, applied the code changes, verified the build, flagged manual steps, and opened one PR with a preview deploy. Ships with a library — issue triager (basis of GitHub's internal spike), repo-assist (a swarm of workflows maintaining a project), CI doctor, N+1-query hunts in GitHub's monolith, daily status homework "for product managers too." In public preview

data.name: Declarative agent guardrails (safe outputs)
data.brief: The control model for *unsupervised* agents: guardrails live in deterministic front matter, never in the prompt — "if you're prompting the guardrails at the agent, you're effectively letting the fox loose in the henhouse," because anyone can prompt-inject past instructions. Declares read/write permissions, allowed tools, a network allowlist (default sites + the npm ecosystem + explicitly named docs — "it's not allowed to just go to bitcoin.com"), and safe outputs: the complete list of writes the agent may perform (e.g. create-pull-request, single — 500 injected PRs is a denial of service) including the explicitly-permitted *do nothing*, "because the last thing I want is the agents denial-of-servicing me" with noise. Secrets stay outside the agent's jail: to use one, the agent asks the warden ("mother, may I talk to that service?"). Four burn-into-your-brain principles: defense in depth; never trust agents with secrets (an agent-visible secret is already compromised); stage and vet all writes; log everything

data.name: Ace (GitHub Next realtime multiplayer dev)
data.brief: Realtime multiplayer software development in one Slack-shaped surface: every session is a branch of the repo checked out in a cloud microVM ("none of this is running on my machine"), holding team chat, a terminal, and a browser preview together. The agent reads the entire team backscroll, so after a human discussion you say "yo, Ace, do it" and it acts on the conversation — including fishing the *final* state out of meandering engineering threads ("let's try it this way… no wait, edge case… back to the first idea") so "I don't need to work for the robots." Plans arrive as markdown docs the *team* edits together, then "we've updated the plan — do it"; plus ambient awareness panes of what teammates' sessions are doing. Chat is where the facts-not-in-code live (political considerations, "that VP will vibe with this direction," the sweetheart Azure deal); everything in code, agents read from code. Technical preview "hopefully later this month"

data.name: Background automation is the ballgame
data.brief: GitHub's category bet, stated flatly: "we actually believe this is going to be a bigger category than interactive AI, because automations that run in the background while you sleep — that's the ballgame." The framing is industrial: the giant software industry has been "pre-industrial" because its only automations were heuristics ("make sure there's a semicolon at the end of every line"); AI automates work requiring basic judgment — Home Assistant's first workflow walks Python stack traces to close third-party-code issues, "not possible before AI, not possible with heuristics." And scale comes from widening authorship: workflows are plain markdown, so product managers write them too — "we can start to get everybody involved in automation; that's how you actually get industrial scale." Public preview now. HELD PATTERN-LESS — dual ledger: the b16 "AI-native software category" candidate (background automation as a category claim) and pat-ai-native-org (non-engineers authoring org automation)

data.name: Guardrails must be deterministic
data.brief: Unsupervised agents get their limits from *config, not prompts*: "it's not enough to prompt the agent 'listen, bro, I don't want you to buy Bitcoin for me ever' — somebody else can prompt-inject it… prompting the guardrails is letting the fox loose in the henhouse." The deterministic front matter declares permissions, tools, a network allowlist, and safe outputs (max one PR — 500 would be a DoS; do-nothing explicitly allowed to stop agents DoSing humans with noise). Secrets never enter the jail — "if an agent can know a secret, treat it as already compromised" — the warden brokers calls; all writes staged and vetted; everything logged; defense in depth, "one layer is never enough"

data.name: Typing was five percent
data.brief: The quantified reframe: a longitudinal study (~100 developers, thousands of hours) found hands-on-keyboard typing is ~5% of the job — and "for the past few years, AI has helped me to type." The next target is the other 95%: where is the system I want to touch, how does it work today, what do others think about how we should mutate it. The team corollary: "my personal understanding was never sufficient for shipping code inside a team" — us-level understanding can't wait for the end of a process that now runs at agent speed, where "a small misalignment can snowball into a ton of wasted work, and that work costs tokens, and tokens cost real money now" (explicitly building on Litt's understanding-is-the-bottleneck talk — ia-aie-litt-understanding-bottleneck, b6)

data.name: Multiplayer surface for realtime dev
data.brief: What replaces the solo-illuminated-by-monitor era: "planning isn't before, and review isn't after — we iterate on the direction together, AI takes a step, we iterate more." Ace's answer: sessions as branches in cloud microVMs, chat + terminal + preview in one place; the agent acts on the whole team backscroll; plans are markdown docs edited *together*, then made real — "to change something about my application, I'm going to edit a document and tell AI: make the document true." Slack is dismissed as the wrong substrate ("designed to be better than email for the average office worker — never for making software"), but chat matters as the home of facts-not-in-code. The conviction line: "I don't email Word documents around anymore; I create and collaborate in the same surface. This is coming for code, a trillion percent." HELD PATTERN-LESS — pat-ai-native-org ledger (uncoined): realtime-multiplayer + ambient awareness as the team's operating surface, from the platform incumbent, same-batch-independent of Ref's decision-doc version

data.name: Agents invoke humans now
data.brief: The "weird inversion of our relationship with the agents": the better we articulate goals, the less they need us; improving models "spot underspecified behaviors and ask us to clarify," and "whenever they need a pair of hands, they can ask us to be the pair of hands" — interfaces now let agents listen to everything and invoke the human on demand. He names the convergence himself: "we're coming at it from this side and OpenClaw's coming at it from that side, but we're landing in a similar spot"

data.name: Guardrails outside the prompt
data.brief: For agents that run while you sleep, safety properties must be properties of the *system*, not requests to the model: any rule expressed as a prompt is one injection away from gone, so the real guardrails are declarative and deterministic — enumerated writes (including "nothing"), allowlisted egress, secrets held by a warden outside the jail, staged writes, total logging. This is what makes unsupervised background automation shippable at platform scale: trust re-architected into scaffolding the model cannot talk its way past. The industrial-revolution corollary: automation only compounds into bought-back time for craft when nobody has to babysit it

data.name: Collaboration is the 95 percent
data.brief: AI industrialized the 5% of engineering that was typing; the remaining 95% is shared understanding — and at agent speed, misalignment stops being a soft cost and acquires a token-denominated price. So the next tool generation targets alignment rather than codegen: one surface where the team and its agents share the same backscroll, the same editable plan, and the same preview, with documents as the interface ("make the document true"). The bottleneck moved from generating code to agreeing on what should be true

data.name: Guardrail agent automations you won't supervise
guidelines: Never encode a guardrail as a prompt — assume prompt injection and make limits deterministic config
practice defense in depth (one layer is never enough)
treat any secret an agent can see as already compromised — keep secrets outside the agent's jail and broker their use through a mediating warden
enumerate allowed writes explicitly (safe outputs), cap them (one PR, not 500), and *allow doing nothing* so automations don't DoS humans with noise
allowlist network egress to named destinations
stage and vet all writes before they land
log everything for auditability

author the automation as a short natural-language playbook plus a skill document and let the agent expand it — then iterate by editing the English, treating compiled YAML as an artifact you never touch

data.name: Velocity Sickness: What Happens When Your Whole Team Gets 10x Faster (Matt Dailey, Ref — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Matt Dailey
Ref
data.brief: Startup building a decision-layer tool for engineering teams ("individual engineers are going really fast with AI, but the team as a whole is not — we're working to close that gap"); works alongside existing implementation tools

data.name: Velocity sickness
data.brief: Named team pathology: "the stress caused by sudden output increases thanks to AI… the result is output without impact." Four presenting symptoms, each individual-level and magnified at team scale: (1) too many PRs to merge (merge queue breaks down); (2) moving in many directions at once (engineers sprinting apart, colliding); (3) declaring agent bankruptcy — 12 terminals cranking all day, next morning "a room of strangers," so you discard the agents and redo the work, "spending tokens twice"; (4) the most important: critical decisions being made by agents — "you are ceding control of your code… if engineers across your team give up ownership of the code, you no longer own the product"

data.name: The decision layer
data.brief: The stratum of engineering work the IDE was never built for: work has re-shaped into planning (exploratory, creative, collaborative — understanding a complex system's contours, pulling out what's relevant, expressing engineering taste) and polish (holding what the agent made and asking "is this what I wanted?"), with implementation in between belonging to agents ("arguably should not even be on this slide — it's not our human work anymore"). The skill becomes knowing which gear you're in and whether your tool serves it; the decision layer is where key decisions are surfaced, made and recorded — framed as a "portal to the software system": Tony-Stark-style *show me what matters*, with AI laying the relevant pieces on the table

data.name: Doc as state, agent as action
data.brief: The conceptual flip under docs-not-chat: chat is "the relic of building for implementation" — isolated, ephemeral, brain-off, with decisions disappearing into a session and into unexplained code. Instead separate the agent (action) from the doc (state): do the context engineering in a durable, shared doc so every agent is stateless and starts from the same place, spawn parallel agents from one doc, and let the team read the doc to see exactly which decisions are being made. Yields a durable decision log by construction — decisions agreed up front and saved, "rather than some LLM summarizing it and maybe picking the wrong things later." Positioned deliberately between plan mode (a rich but still ephemeral chat message) and full spec-driven development (too far from engineering reality)

data.name: Idea velocity
data.brief: Shifting the unit of velocity from code shipped to ideas explored: when teams adopt decision-layer work, "people start to plan and then *not* implement their plan — and this is actually a really good sign," because ideas get fleshed out, compared and triaged before any build. The cure for shipping too much code that goes nowhere: escape "prototype gravity" (building the first navigable path and falling in love with it) and explore the whole idea maze to "find the gold around the corner." ⚠ terminology convergence with the b6 Snap talk (see review note 3)

data.name: Ref (decision-layer tool)
data.brief: "A tool built for the decision layer" — doc-centric planning surface that works with existing implementation tools; the productization of the talk's docs-not-chat / stateless-agents model

data.name: Velocity sickness pathologies
data.brief: A vendor names the team-scale failure mode of AI adoption and gives it a symptom taxonomy: unmergeable PR floods; engineers sprinting in incompatible directions; agent bankruptcy ("you come back and it's like walking into a room of strangers… you're doing the same work and spending tokens twice"); and agents making critical decisions, which at company scale means "you no longer own the product." The emblem story: a newsletter author with an impressive, decidedly non-slop agent pipeline who is "basically writing a book every week" — asked whether his audience reads a book a week: "no, they're probably not." Output without impact, at 10×. HELD PATTERN-LESS — pat-ai-native-org ledger (uncoined): this is the candidate's pathology/dark-side texture, the team-velocity quantification the ledger has been missing between the adoption stats (Yaron, Uber) and the restructure narratives (Block)

data.name: Work shape flipped ide obsolete
data.brief: The tool-category claim: pre-AI engineering was plan → heads-down build → polish, and "all our history of coding tools" — the IDE, "our workhorse" — was built for the middle. Now implementation belongs to the agent and the human work is the two ends, so the load-bearing tool slot moves to the decision layer: "a tool built for docs and not chat." A structural claim that the incumbent tool category is mis-fit to the new shape of work, and that a new layer is being productized above it

data.name: Humans must own decisions
