data.brief: Ranked "the most important" of the four problems: an engineer letting an agent make a critical decision "is ceding control of your code — you are no longer the owner; the agent is," and at scale the company no longer owns its product. The prescription re-defines the job: "our work now is figure out what decisions matter, then make those decisions, and then get out of the way while the agents fill in the rest" — humans owning decisions is "how we retain ownership of our software and make it a true expression of what we're trying to create"

data.name: Docs replace chats as work atom
data.brief: The mechanism: make the doc, not the chat, the atom of work. Chats are isolated, ephemeral and "brain off" (the agent proposes, you hit the recommended option without thinking); decisions made there vanish into code. Docs bring key decisions forward for the team, and the deeper flip is architectural — pull the state out of the session: doc as state, agent as stateless action, parallel agents spawned from one shared context, agent bankruptcy dissolved ("the result of their work is in the doc — to rebuild your human context, you just read the doc"), and a durable decision log with no LLM-summarization lottery. HELD PATTERN-LESS — bears on the uncoined pat-agent-memory-layer and pat-durable-execution candidates, on the *convention* side: the state layer here is a shared document, not a memory product (see review note 4)

data.name: Code velocity to idea velocity
data.brief: What actually happens when teams adopt the model: "people start to plan and then not implement their plan — and this is a really good sign," because exploration and triage replace reflexive building; velocity shifts "from code velocity to idea velocity." And the review economics invert: aligning on key decisions up front moves the review point earlier — "the hardest part of any code review is *what actually matters here*; if you move that earlier, the code review becomes much simpler" — which is his answer to the unmergeable-PR flood. Closing claim: "the future of engineering is multiplayer… multiplayer by default sooner than we think"

data.name: Review moves to the decision point
data.brief: When generation industrializes, the scarce reviewing resource stops being code-reading capacity and becomes decision-alignment capacity. Post-hoc review of an agent-authored PR flood cannot answer "what matters here?" fast enough; moving review to the decision point — shared plans aligned before anyone (human or agent) spends a day building — converts unreviewable output back into simple reviews, and catches direction-divergence before it costs a prototype. Verification is re-architected *earlier in the pipeline* rather than scaled at the end

data.name: Stateless agents durable docs
data.brief: Extracting state from agent sessions into a shared doc inverts who is durable: the agents become disposable actuators (spawn as many as you like from the same context, discard without loss) while the doc accumulates the team's actual asset — its decisions. That single move dissolves agent bankruptcy, makes parallelism cheap, gives humans a re-grounding surface, and produces the decision log everyone is otherwise trying to reconstruct with LLM summarizers. The layer around the model — shared, durable, human-legible state — is where team leverage lives

data.name: Work in decision docs, not chat sessions
guidelines: Think of your work as two gears — planning and polish — and notice when you drift between them inside one session and whether your tool still fits the gear you're in
treat the plan as a portal to the software system: ask AI to pull out and arrange exactly what's relevant to the decision at hand ("show me what matters")
do context engineering in the doc so every agent is stateless and starts from the same shared state
bring key decisions forward in the doc and agree on them *before* implementation, so code review reduces to checking against decisions already aligned
expect and welcome plans that never get implemented — that is idea triage working
and share the plan with a teammate before giving it to an agent — "very unnatural for a lot of people… but your smart teammates have great context in their heads
they will give you good feedback"

data.name: Anthropic's CCA Exam as a Field-Guide for Agentic Engineering (Frank Coyle, UC Berkeley — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Claude Certified Architect (CCA) exam
data.brief: Anthropic's certification for agentic engineering, released March (⚠ 2026 presumed; verify official name/date — captions say "Claude Certified Architect"/"Claude Certified Exam"). Scenario-based, timed, proctored; offered to companies in the Anthropic ecosystem, and individuals can pay $99 to sit it once every 6 months. Multiple-choice, but grounded in realistic constraints. Five weighted domains: agentic architecture 27%; Claude Code configuration & workflow 20%; prompt engineering / structured output (JSON everywhere); tool design & MCP integration; context management & reliability. Six production scenarios — customer-support resolution agent, code generation with Claude, multi-agent research system, developer productivity, Claude Code for CI, structured data extraction — of which each sitting randomly draws four and centers all questions on them

data.name: Stop-reason loop control
data.brief: The exam's canonical agentic loop: while true, call the model with the message history, then branch on stop_reason rather than consuming whatever came back. tool_use means the LLM — "a probabilistic next-word predictor; it can't execute tools, it can't do anything except talk back to you" — has emitted parameters for *your code* to execute; run the tool, append the result, continue; loop exit is followed by a confidence check with human escalation. The trap the exam tests: an out-of-tokens stop reason, where a truncated response still looks like an answer — "it's going to give you a response, but you need to take action." Anti-pattern: fire the agent, take the response, use it. ⚠ merge-adjacent to el-loop-flow-control — see review note 4

data.name: Context forking with summary-only return
data.brief: Subtask isolation as the exam teaches it: fork the agent's work into a separate context ("a separate thread — whatever the agent does and thinks and adds tokens to does not come back and pollute the main context"), then merge back only the summation. Explicitly analogized to multi-threaded programming: shared memory forces synchronization and locks, so keep threads — and agents — independent. Paired with budget hygiene: check the token count, and past a threshold (~150K in his example) run compaction. Anti-patterns: every subtask dumping full output into the primary thread; letting context grow unbounded — "a million-token context window? No, don't put everything in there… the more context, the more confused the LLM"

data.name: Agent anti-patterns (design-patterns redux)
data.brief: The talk's method claim: the 1990s design-patterns movement has re-run for agents — "we now have patterns for agents, but there's also anti-patterns," and the anti-patterns are the pedagogy, often the key to the exam questions. The walked set: consume responses without checking stop_reason; the overloaded generalist agent ("you hire a carpenter and the guy shows up with plumbing tools, carpenter tools, electrical tools — 'I can do anything'; maybe you want a professional carpenter" — specialize to one job, one or two tools); subtask context spilling into the main thread; unbounded context growth; sharing the generator's reasoning with critic agents (groupthink); interactive modes inside CI pipelines. ⚠ merge-check vs el-pattern-anti-pattern-catalog — see review note 5

data.name: Anthropic certifies agentic engineering
data.brief: A frontier lab now runs a proctored professional certification for agentic engineering: the Claude Certified Architect exam (released March) — scenario-based, timed, $99 per individual sitting every 6 months, offered through the Anthropic ecosystem, with five weighted domains (architecture 27%, Claude Code 20%, prompting/structured output, tool+MCP design, context management & reliability) drawn over six production scenarios. The messenger matters: a 30-year CS educator assigns it because "computer science is no longer the magic pathway to a job" and the exam is his best proxy for what employable agentic judgment looks like — "Anthropic knows how people are using their system and what the issues are going to be"

data.name: Exam canon is harness discipline
data.brief: What the certification actually tests is scaffolding discipline, not model capability: branch every loop iteration on stop_reason (including the out-of-tokens trap); configure hierarchical CLAUDE.md rule files; specialize agents to one job with one or two tools; fork subtask contexts and merge back summaries only; watch token counts and compact; strip interactive prompts from CI; batch non-urgent work. The model itself is dismissed as the object of study — "the LLM can't do anything; it is just a probabilistic next-word predictor; it can't execute tools" — everything examinable lives in the harness around it

data.name: Agent groupthink breaks critics
data.brief: A multi-agent failure mode with an exam-blessed fix: collaborating agents "seem to devolve into one idea" the way party guests cave on pizza — so a critic/validator agent must not see the generator's thought process. Pass it only the claim and the evidence ("every agent gets its own slice"), keeping the judgment independent of the reasoning that produced the artifact — the generator/validator separation applied inside multi-agent topologies, with hub-and-spoke orchestration and how-much-should-each-agent-know as explicit exam material

data.name: Loop is the turing step
data.brief: Why "loops are the new thing" is deeper than fashion: Böhm–Jacopini (1966) proved sequence + conditional + iteration suffice for Turing completeness. Prompt-era LLM systems had sequences and some branching; the agentic loop supplies the third primitive — which is exactly why the field's figureheads describe their job as writing loops (Cherny; Steinberger: "I don't code anymore, I just design loops that prompt agents"). The excitement is the arrival of general computability in the LLM stack — and it is a property of the *harness structure*, not of the model inside it

data.name: Vendor exams reveal production truth
data.brief: A lab's certification exam is a leaked map of its production reality: the scenarios are the deployments it actually sees, the domain weights are where its users actually spend effort, and the anti-patterns are the failures its support and safety teams actually field. Reading the CCA is therefore field intelligence even for engineers who never sit it — the syllabus tells you, from the vendor with the best vantage point, what agentic systems break on ("whether you take the exam or not, this is going to help you get ready for whatever the agentic world throws at you")

data.name: Run agentic loops on stop reasons
guidelines: Structure the loop as while true → call the model with the accumulated messages → branch on stop_reason
remember the LLM only *emits tool parameters* — your code executes the tool and appends the result
continue until the model stops requesting tools
then gate the final answer on a confidence check and escalate to a human below threshold
always handle the out-of-tokens stop reason — a truncated response looks like an answer and must not be used as one
never consume a response without reading why generation stopped

data.name: Manage agent context the way the exam expects
guidelines: Layer rule files hierarchically (project root, project folder, per-directory CLAUDE.md) so control is inherited, not repeated
specialize each agent to one job with one or two tools — no carpenter arriving with plumbing gear
fork subtask contexts and merge back only summaries, never raw output
give critic agents the claim and evidence but not the generator's reasoning, to break groupthink
monitor token count and compact past your threshold (~150K in the walkthrough
compaction logic is customizable — e.g. extending Mastra's base class)
disable interactive permission prompts in CI pipelines so runs go straight through
and push non-urgent work through the batch API — 50% fewer token costs with results promised within 24 hours

data.name: Codex, Behind the Harness (Dominik Kundel, OpenAI — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Dominik Kundel
Cerebras
data.brief: Inference hardware provider; runs GPT-5.3 Codex Spark at ~1,000 tokens/second — the deployment that exposed the network, not inference, as the agent-loop bottleneck

data.name: LM Studio
data.brief: Named as a partner in the open Responses-schema governance body (local-model desktop runtime)

data.name: Responses API
data.brief: OpenAI's agentic replacement for chat completions, "released last year as a rethinking of the chat completions API in a more agentic world" — restructured message shape plus built-in agent capabilities (web search, image gen, tool search, server-side compaction, WebSocket transport). Deliberately not proprietary: OpenAI worked with Ollama, LM Studio, NVIDIA and others to codify an open Responses schema with a governance body, so any Responses-compatible provider can be plugged into the Codex harness. The talk's central claim rests on it — the standout Codex features "are actually features that are exposed in the Responses API… you can use those directly regardless of what harness you're using"

data.name: Codex app server protocol
data.brief: The UI↔harness protocol (the Responses API being harness↔inference). Powers the first-party Codex app, so third parties building on it inherit full Codex functionality; community clients include Theo's T3 code and Remote X, and the speaker used it to embed Codex inside Claude Code as a plugin and inside Doom. Framed explicitly as open-ecosystem surface area: "if you're building your own UI… you can actually build on top of the Codex harness"

data.name: Deferred tools and tool search
data.brief: Context-budget mechanism: tools can be marked deferred loading (since GPT-5.4, in the Responses API) so they are absent from the context window and reachable only through a tool-search call — either the built-in tool-search tool or your own implementation "if you feel like you can better do that discovery yourself." Paired with a hard cap on the available-skills list at 2% of the maximum context window, above which per-skill descriptions are progressively shortened. Motivated by three simultaneous constraints: size (token budget *and* contradiction-induced confusion), flexibility (arbitrary skills/plugins/MCPs), and cacheability

data.name: Apply patch tool
data.brief: Diff-based file-editing tool that all models from GPT-5 onward were trained on — used both to edit and to create files, with a general shell tool for everything else. The training-shaped-the-harness consequence is explicit: the model "naturally" reaches for Ripgrep because that is what it saw in training, so the Codex harness ships Ripgrep for users who lack it; on Windows the model was trained to emit PowerShell natively

data.name: Codex sandbox layer
data.brief: All file-system and network interaction routes through a per-platform sandbox: Seatbelt on macOS, Bubblewrap on Linux, and a custom open-source Windows sandbox OpenAI had to build itself (shipped in the same repository; a companion article covers the rejected Windows alternatives). The layer that makes auto-approval decidable rather than advisory

data.name: Auto review (auto-approval subagent)
data.brief: Answer to approval fatigue and to the "IT and security really hates that you turn on full access" problem. When a sandboxed action escalates, the harness spins up a read-only auto-review subagent that cannot itself spawn subagents, and hands it the user authorization, a risk taxonomy, judging criteria, and the transcript plus the pending tool calls. It returns a judgment on authorization strength, blast radius, and disposition — auto-approving the unpredictable-but-benign while holding the line on data exfiltration. Applies symmetrically to file-system and network actions ("curling Google to see if the internet works is fine, but maybe not uploading a file"). Context-sensitivity is the point: deleting a .git folder is fine if asked for and catastrophic if not

data.name: WebSocket mode (stateful Responses transport)
data.brief: Replaces server-sent events over HTTP with a persistent WebSocket carrying stateful context, so each turn sends only what changed — a tool call returns just its result rather than replaying every item (demoed as 1 item versus 9). Built because at ~1,000 tok/s "inference was no longer the bottleneck, it was actually the network"; the win compounds across the many tool calls an agent makes

data.name: Goal continuation prompt
data.brief: The mechanism under /goal: the harness re-injects a continuation prompt carrying the user's stated objective after every turn, and keeps doing so until the model calls an update-goal tool declaring the objective met. The operational consequence is a prompting rule — "you don't want to write full essays into your goal, but instead have very concrete and verifiable prompts, so it's easy to detect when things are done"

data.name: Harness features move into the api
data.brief: A frontier lab argues its coding agent's differentiators are not in the agent: tool search, apply patch, WebSocket transport and server-side compaction are all Responses API features, usable "regardless of what harness you're using," and the harness itself is open source in Rust. Paired with an open Responses schema under a governance body with Ollama, LM Studio and NVIDIA, so third-party providers are pluggable into Codex and Codex is pluggable into third-party UIs. The differentiation moves down into the inference protocol and sideways into an ecosystem standard, rather than being defended at the agent layer

data.name: Context budget becomes explicit mechanism
data.brief: Context construction is presented as the harness's first and "arguably one of the most important" jobs, with the unpredictable parts — installed MCPs inflating the tool registry, an unbounded skills list — handled by explicit mechanism rather than prompt discipline: deferred tools kept out of the window and reached via tool search, and a hard 2% cap on the skills list that degrades descriptions as it fills. The stated motivation includes a quality argument, not just a cost one: "the more context you have, the higher it is that you have contradicting information and it causes confusion for the model"

data.name: Read only judge gates agent escalation
data.brief: Approval fatigue answered with a constrained second agent: sandbox escalations spin up a read-only auto-review subagent that cannot spawn subagents, receives the risk taxonomy and the live transcript, and rules on authorization and blast radius before the action proceeds. The threat model is stated in behavioural terms rather than adversarial ones — a high-agency model told to email a file, unable to attach it, uploading it to a file share instead; or bad escaping deleting too much — and the explicit design goal is to keep data exfiltration outside the auto-approved set. Verification of the agent's actions is delegated to a smaller, permission-boxed agent rather than to the user

data.name: Network is the new agent bottleneck
data.brief: At ~1,000 tokens/second on Cerebras (GPT-5.3 Codex Spark), the constraint on an agent loop stopped being inference and became the network: per-tool-call HTTP/SSE overhead and the re-sending of unchanged state. The fix is transport-level — a persistent WebSocket with stateful context that returns only the changed item — and the framing generalizes past this vendor: as inference approaches free, the remaining latency in agentic systems is the plumbing around the model

data.name: Models trained into their harness
data.brief: The harness is shaped by the model's training, not the reverse: every model from GPT-5 on is trained on the apply-patch tool, trained to reach for Ripgrep (so the harness bundles Ripgrep as a dependency of the model's habits), trained to emit PowerShell on Windows, and trained on the server-side compaction format "in a way the model got trained with, so that the performance stays the same." Swapping the model out of this harness — the thing an open Responses schema is supposed to enable — means giving up the behaviours the harness was built around. Counter-evidence: the model here is the least swappable component, not the smallest one

data.name: Agents script their own computer use
data.brief: Computer use is re-architected from an enumerated action API — "it only allowed you to do one action at a time and you had to declare that you wanted it to do computer use" — into code execution: the agent writes JavaScript or Python that scripts the interaction itself. Browser use runs this way, against a persistent Node REPL held across turns driving a Chromium instance with Playwright, which changes the economics of repetitive work: read one page, infer the structure, then write a script that handles the rest. Async work generalizes the same way, with spawn-agent/send-input tools for subagents and long-lived background terminals fed over stdin

data.name: Harness differentiation migrates to protocol
data.brief: When a lab open-sources its harness *and* pushes that harness's best features into an openly-governed inference protocol, it is conceding that the harness is not the moat — and simultaneously making the protocol the place where lock-in can still accrue. The interesting competitive surface stops being "whose agent is better" and becomes whose API shape the ecosystem standardizes on: tool search, patch semantics, compaction format and transport are all decisions that, once adopted by third-party runtimes, are far stickier than any agent UI

data.name: Verification delegated to a boxed agent
data.brief: The auto-review design answers the verification problem with the same substance that created it — another model — but makes the answer trustworthy through structural constraint rather than capability: read-only permissions, no recursive spawning, a fixed risk taxonomy, and full transcript context so authorization can be judged rather than guessed. It is a working template for using agents as verifiers without recreating the failure mode: the verifier is boxed so tightly that its judgment can be wrong without being dangerous

data.name: Budget agent context with mechanism, not discipline
guidelines: Treat context construction as a first-class harness stage with three simultaneous targets — size, flexibility and cacheability — and keep the predictable parts (model instructions) structurally stable so the cache prefix survives
assume the unpredictable parts are user-installed (MCP servers inflating the tool registry, an unbounded skills list) and bound them in code rather than by asking users to install less
mark rarely-used tools deferred so they cost nothing until a tool-search call retrieves them, and supply your own discovery implementation if you can beat the built-in one
cap any growing list as a fraction of the context window rather than a fixed count, and degrade gracefully by shortening descriptions
and remember the reason is quality as much as cost — surplus context raises the odds of self-contradiction, which reads as model confusion

data.name: Write goals an agent can prove it finished
guidelines: Understand that a long-running goal loop works by re-injecting a continuation prompt containing your objective after every turn, and only stops when the model itself calls the update-goal tool — so the objective's job is to make completion detectable, not to be comprehensive
write concrete, verifiable objectives rather than essays, because a goal that cannot be checked cannot terminate the loop

and pair long autonomous runs with an auto-approval layer that judges escalations in context (the same action is fine or catastrophic depending on whether the user asked for it), so that "full access" is not the price of not being interrupted

data.name: Taking Reinforcement Learning Cross Datacenter (Nan Jiang, Modal — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Nan Jiang
Modal
data.brief: Serverless GPU compute platform; the talk's institutional vantage point is capacity brokerage — elastic GPU supply across providers and regions — which is what makes the cross-datacenter RL framing natural to them. Author of Stitch. ⚠ captioned "Moto" and "model" throughout

data.name: Cathedral vs bazaar compute
data.brief: The framing device for the capacity mismatch. The cathedral — one region, fast interconnect, many GPUs wired together — is the right shape for a trainer and the hardest thing to get. The bazaar — different providers, regions, prices and availability — is where most usable compute actually lives. RL's default loop demands the cathedral for the whole system, so it inherits the scarcest resource's constraints: "RL wants all four of these at the same time — enough GPU, same region, fast fabric, and available now. Any of these is manageable, but all four is pretty hard." Underneath sits the asymmetry that training capacity is not elastic the way inference capacity is: "you cannot assume you can grow the trainer cluster halfway through a run just because rollout wants more nodes"

data.name: Rollout serving island
data.brief: The unit that turns out to be movable. Training is one tightly coupled job — every step has collectives, all-reduce and model-parallel communication, which genuinely want RDMA — but rollout is a fleet of serving jobs with no global all-reduce between them. So the thing that leaves the cluster is not backpropagation; it is the rollout island: a coherent endpoint or local group of endpoints serving one policy version, free to keep local parallelism and prefill/decode disaggregation inside itself. Across islands the dependency collapses to two directions: policy version in, trajectories and metadata out

data.name: Adam absorption
data.brief: Why the weight-sync link can shrink by three orders of magnitude. Two ingredients. The floor: the optimizer keeps high-precision master weights, but the rollout engine serves a low-precision *view*, and a BF16 value only changes if the update crosses the nearest rounding boundary — roughly half a ULP, about θ/256, ≈0.0039 for weights near 1. The push: an Adam step is the learning rate times a normalized direction (the raw gradient is divided by running gradient statistics), so the per-weight push is bounded on the order of the learning rate — at RL post-training rates, ~3e-6. The push is more than a thousand times smaller than the floor, so the served value does not move. Crucially this is *not* a claim that the master weights are frozen: "it is saying the value that the rollout engine would serve does not change." Small weights move; large weights absorb their updates

data.name: Sparse rollout-weight delta
data.brief: The object shipped instead of a checkpoint. Cast weights to the dtype the rollout engine serves, diff version *t−1* against version *t*, and encode changed positions plus replacement bits and metadata — via selective override, XOR, or any lossless scheme. Because the patch is bit-level equivalent rather than a floating-point addition, there is no additive delta drift: a rollout engine applying it reconstructs the synced served version bitwise. Shrinks the cross-region link from ~500 GB to ~500 MB, i.e. from minutes-to-hours down to seconds. Measured across model families at ~99% of parameters bit-identical per step, and the property survives staleness — a lagging rollout still has a small changed set. Lower serving precision makes it stronger: the visibility floor scales as θ/2^(mantissa+1), so FP8 and NVFP4 change even less than BF16

data.name: Immutable rollout weight version
data.brief: The synchronization contract that replaces "the current checkpoint." After each optimizer step the trainer publishes an immutable, named version to a shared bulletin board; requests become version-aware, stating which version to serve and which versions are acceptable, and responses carry the version back alongside tokens, logprobs, router-replay information and metadata — "exact same information as if they are in the same cluster as the trainer." Artifacts are materialized in Hugging Face safetensors layout so any standard engine can load and shard them itself, which is what keeps the scheme engine-agnostic across SGLang, vLLM, attention backends, parallelism strategies, serving dtypes and GPU generations

data.name: Version-aware rollout sidecar
data.brief: The small piece of machinery that makes an ordinary, unmodified rollout engine participate. Three cases: if the engine is already at an acceptable committed version, the sidecar proxies the request; if it is behind but can catch up, it applies the missing transitions; if it cannot, it returns not ready. That last case is what makes the fleet genuinely elastic — any idle GPU anywhere can be enrolled, and a straggler degrades to unavailable rather than to silently-wrong

data.name: Stitch
data.brief: Modal's concrete implementation of the whole protocol: the trainer side publishes what defines a rollout weight version and records it on the bulletin board; the rollout side pulls the latest weights and self-syncs across regions and providers. Deliberately framework-agnostic about trainer, engine and transport, and described as async-first and agentic-first. The payoff claim: rollout engines autoscale globally, each self-syncing and returning rollout metadata, so "scattered inference capacity became one elastic rollout fleet… inference capacity can now become RL capacity"

data.name: Rl compute shape mismatch
data.brief: A capacity provider reframes RL post-training as a physical-plant problem rather than an algorithms one: "a lot of RL discussion right now is about algorithms, environments, sandboxes, GRPO, low-precision training, deterministic kernels — but when you run those experiments at scale the problem becomes more physical." The default loop demands the cathedral shape (enough GPUs, one region, fast fabric, available now) for the *entire* system, while the compute that actually exists is bazaar-shaped, so the whole run inherits the scarcity of its hardest-to-source component — and unlike inference, trainer capacity cannot be grown mid-run. HELD PATTERN-LESS — opens the pat-compute-liquidity ledger (see review note 3)

data.name: Rollout fleet decouples from trainer
data.brief: The architectural decomposition: backpropagation is one tightly coupled job whose collectives genuinely need RDMA and must stay put, but the rollout fleet is a set of serving jobs with no global all-reduce between them, so it can leave the cluster entirely. Once the movable unit is defined as the serving island rather than the process, the cross-island contract reduces to policy-version-in / trajectories-and-metadata-out, and the only remaining coupling is the weight-update link. The bottleneck in a frontier training loop is located in the plumbing between components, not in the learning algorithm

data.name: Rollout weights 99pct bit identical
data.brief: The empirical core, and a result that inverts an intuition: ~99% of rollout-visible weights are bit-identical between consecutive versions, measured across model families by casting to BF16 and comparing bitwise — with the explicit warning that this is *not* gradient sparsity and *not* optimizer-state sparsity. "A common misconception is that it works because gradients are sparse. They are not — about 99% of parameters get non-zero gradients, and the FP32 master update is also dense. It's just small." The mechanism is Adam's bounded step failing to clear the serving dtype's rounding floor by a factor of >1,000. Modal's own run serving GLM 4.7 Air in FP8 shows ~0.15% of weights changing on the first high-learning-rate step, settling to ~0.05% per step; the property also survives rollout staleness

data.name: Checkpoint is wrong sync unit
data.brief: The engineering consequence, stated as a unit-of-synchronization error rather than a bandwidth problem: "the problem is not whether rollout can leave the cluster — the problem is that the full checkpoint is the wrong unit of synchronization." A Kimi-scale NVFP4 checkpoint runs ~500 GB and takes minutes to hours to move, while even fully async RL wants weight-update latency in seconds; shipping a lossless bitwise patch instead collapses that to ~500 MB and seconds, with the rollout engine reconstructing the identical served version rather than an approximation. Version-aware requests and a sidecar that answers *not ready* rather than serving stale weights keep correctness explicit while the fleet is elastic

data.name: Inference capacity becomes rl capacity
data.brief: The payoff claim and the reason this matters beyond one vendor: with a cheap bitwise delta and a version-aware sidecar, "scattered inference capacity became one elastic rollout fleet… instead of being limited by the trainer cluster, rollout can be the global pool — inference capacity can now become RL capacity." Shipped as Stitch, deliberately agnostic about trainer framework, serving engine and transport, and interoperable by leaning on Hugging Face safetensors plus standard engines. If it holds, the supply of compute eligible for frontier post-training stops being the supply of contiguous RDMA-connected clusters. HELD PATTERN-LESS — the thesis statement of the pat-compute-liquidity ledger

data.name: Precision view is the sync boundary
data.brief: The load-bearing move is choosing *which representation* to synchronize. Nothing about the optimizer changed — the master weights and the FP32 update stay dense — but by defining the synchronized object as the low-precision view the rollout engine actually serves, an intractable 500 GB transfer becomes a 500 MB patch, and the argument gets *stronger* as serving precision drops toward FP8 and NVFP4. It is a reminder that in systems built from stacked numeric representations, the cheapest available abstraction boundary is often the one the hardware already rounds to, and that "bitwise equivalent" is what makes a delta safe to apply repeatedly where "approximately equal" would drift

data.name: Couple only what needs coupling
data.brief: The generalizable design lesson is a scarcity-inheritance one: a distributed system built as a single deployment unit inherits the availability constraints of its most demanding component, so every subsystem pays for the trainer's fabric requirement even when it has no collectives of its own. Auditing a pipeline for which parts genuinely need tight coupling — and then defining the loosest possible contract across the seam, here two directions and an immutable version number — converts a scarce shape into an abundant one. The sidecar's *not ready* response is the small piece that makes this safe: elasticity without it would mean silently serving the wrong policy version

data.name: Disaggregate RL rollouts from the trainer
guidelines: Separate the parts of a training loop that need one fast fabric from the parts that only look like they do — keep backpropagation and its collectives in a single RDMA-connected cluster, and treat the rollout fleet as serving jobs that can live anywhere because nothing all-reduces between them

define the movable unit as a serving island (one coherent endpoint or local group serving one policy version) rather than a process, so local parallelism and prefill/decode disaggregation stay an implementation detail inside it
make the cross-seam contract as thin as possible — policy version in, trajectories and metadata out

stop synchronizing full checkpoints and ship a lossless bitwise patch over the served low-precision view instead, so the engine reconstructs the exact version rather than an approximation and no additive drift accumulates
publish immutable, named weight versions to a shared board and make requests state both the target version and the acceptable set, returning the served version in the response
put a sidecar in front of unmodified engines to proxy, catch up, or answer *not ready*, so an out-of-date node degrades to unavailable rather than to silently wrong
and materialize artifacts in a standard layout (Hugging Face safetensors) so any engine, parallelism strategy, serving dtype or GPU generation can join the pool

data.name: Intelligence + Continual Learning = Expertise (Yu Su, NeoCognition — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Yu Su
NeoCognition
data.brief: Startup building agents and continual learning; the talk's thesis (scaling expertise, per-microworld specialization) is its positioning

data.name: The Ohio State University
data.brief: Speaker's academic affiliation; coined to carry the dual-affiliation edge per the b8 co-university-of-maryland precedent

data.name: The Continual Learning Turn
data.brief: The frontier of model improvement is shifting from pre-training scale to post-deployment learning, making the accumulation loop — not the base model — the locus of compounding advantage. Six legs in the evidence: a claimed new axis of scale (expertise as orthogonal to intelligence; compute-on-context as a fourth axis once data and model size are fixed); algorithms that learn from production rather than curated environments (on-policy self-distillation, offline/online hint taxonomies); measurement built to detect accumulation rather than point capability (the gain metric; benchmark instances being designed independent and therefore unchainable); supply economics (public data exhausted, and the commercial data layer structurally cannot cross into private corpora); systems already shipping the loop outside the weights; and enterprise reality — most organizations sitting on production traces asking to be made better. Contested from birth: an observability vendor with cross-customer visibility reports seeing little real continual learning in production, an independent benchmark finds plain in-context learning beating engineered context management on both cost-adjusted frontiers, and the field's own practitioners describe the current state as "pseudo continual learning" — batch updates offline, then re-upload

data.name: Intelligence vs expertise
data.brief: The talk's load-bearing distinction. Intelligence = "the capacity to reason through unfamiliar problems from available context" — what frontier models are increasingly good at, where every episode is independent. Expertise = "accumulated and situated competence… the ability to act reliably, efficiently, and with judgment" in a particular domain. They differ on which way context flows (intelligence *consumes* supplied context; expertise *knows what context to bring*) and on search behaviour (intelligence expands the search, brute-forcing 100 parallel attempts; expertise compresses it, having learned the shortcuts). Drawn from cognitive science: experts don't know more facts, they *see differently* — pattern recognition, deep structure, conditional rules with known exceptions, and taste including "when it's good enough"

data.name: Millions of microworlds
data.brief: Why generalist agents underperform outside code: "modern society is really not just one unified world, it's millions of these micro worlds." Every domain, profession and company is idiosyncratic — even the same software is configured differently per company — each with "its unique local physics: different structures, constraints, affordances and dynamics." Too heterogeneous and dynamic "for any monolithic model to compress into one static representation," so agents must learn on the job per microworld. ⚠ terminology collision with el-microworlds — see review note 3

data.name: The modern Moravec's paradox
data.brief: The framing for why coding worked first: classical Moravec says hard things are easy for AI and easy things hard; the modern version is that models excel at symbolic reasoning — coding, maths, "the crown jewel of intelligence" — while still failing at everyday digital work, because those require a different set of cognitive competencies. Code was the privileged first market precisely because it is "already a language-native world": symbolically represented, structurally recorded, with rewards and tests already in place

data.name: Continual learning as adaptive compression
data.brief: A working definition offered to disambiguate an overloaded term: "adaptive compression of experience into reusable structures for future behavior," with four independently-instantiable axes — *what experience* (episodes, semantic facts, procedures, human or environment feedback), *how compressed* (embeddings, symbolic indexes, distillation into parameters, RL), *into what structure* (adapters, vectors, graphs, skills, world models), and *used how* (recall, state prediction, planning, actuation, value function). The claim that the field is confusing because these four axes are conflated is the definition's main work

data.name: Escape intelligence (unbounded expertise from bounded intelligence)
data.brief: The talk's most speculative claim, presented as its most interesting future: plot raw intelligence on x and expertise on y and they are largely orthogonal. Without continual learning, scaling intelligence produces "the world's smartest novice" — brilliant at any single problem, accumulating nothing, brute-forcing every time. With it, the continual-learning algorithm sets the *slope*. The conjecture: past some intelligence threshold, a strong enough algorithm yields unbounded expertise without stronger models — "do we need to continually train these larger and larger models, or are they already good enough and what we're missing is better continual learning algorithms?"

data.name: Coding was the privileged market
data.brief: An explanation, from an academic-turned-operator, for why agent success is so unevenly distributed: code is "already a language-native world" — symbolic representation, structured records, tests and rewards already in place — so it was the one domain where language agents could be dropped in whole. Evidence offered is Anthropic's revenue curve (≈400× in under two years, largely coding-driven). Outside that privileged world, deployment goes badly enough that Andrew Ng's "decade of agents, not year of agents" is quoted as still standing. The corollary is uncomfortable for generalist-agent roadmaps: the first market was not a beachhead but an outlier

data.name: Expertise not intelligence is scarce
data.brief: The reframing: "intelligence is already becoming abundant — the frontier models are probably smarter than average humans — but expertise is still scarce." Expertise is defined as accumulated situated competence, distinguished from intelligence on two operational axes: expertise *supplies* the right context rather than consuming it, and *compresses* the search rather than expanding it. That second axis is offered as the direct cause of the token-inefficiency now driving company-wide token-maxxing crackdowns — a smart novice brute-forces because it has no learned shortcuts

data.name: Scaling expertise as new axis
data.brief: The call to action and the track's organizing thesis in one line: "let's start scaling expertise" as a new axis of scale, orthogonal to raw intelligence, with the continual-learning algorithm setting the slope. Pushed to its strongest form as *escape intelligence*: past a threshold, a good enough algorithm might yield unbounded expertise from bounded intelligence, which would make further pre-training scale optional. The anchor statement of pat-continual-learning-turn, coined in this file

data.name: Private microworlds next data frontier
data.brief: The economic argument under the thesis: public training data is exhausted, and "the next internet-scale data opportunity is actually in all of these different private worlds." If specialized agents can learn in situ inside each company's idiosyncratic configuration, that learning can be channelled back to the general model. Paired with a sovereignty framing borrowed from Satya Nadella — every company building its own learning loop into institutional memory, "to still be in charge of their means of production." A data-supply claim and an enterprise-moat claim in the same breath

data.name: Reliability plasticity tension
data.brief: The open problem named as the field's central conflict: agents must be simultaneously reliable and plastic, and these are inherently opposed — "reliable systems resist change; plastic systems like change." Offered with an existence proof rather than a solution ("we are incredibly plastic but manage to be dependable most of the time") and a technical bet that both parametric and non-parametric learning are needed, with the synergy between them unsolved. The stability/plasticity leg of the pattern; the same tension Asawa's benchmark operationalizes independently in this batch

data.name: Agent success tracks symbolic legibility
data.brief: The distribution of agent success across domains is better predicted by how symbolically legible a domain already is than by how hard it is. Code came with its own representation, its own version history, and its own oracle — so the agent inherited a world it could read and a verifier it could trust. Every domain that has resisted agents so far lacks one of those three, and no amount of model scale supplies them. The implication for anyone picking an agent market is to audit for pre-existing representation and reward before capability

data.name: Orthogonality changes the scaling question
data.brief: If intelligence and expertise are genuinely orthogonal axes rather than points on one curve, then the industry's central question stops being "how much smarter can the model get" and becomes "how steep can the accumulation slope be." That reframing is what makes the whole continual-learning track commercially coherent: it locates a source of compounding advantage that is not buying more pre-training compute, and it explains why the same frontier model can be transformative in one company and useless in another — the model is the intercept, the learning loop is the slope

data.name: Pick agent domains by symbolic legibility, then build the learning loop
guidelines: Before committing an agent to a domain, check what code got for free — is the world already represented symbolically, is the work already recorded structurally, and does a cheap oracle already exist? Where any of the three is missing, expect the brittleness that shows up outside coding, and plan to supply it rather than to out-scale it
treat each customer, team or configuration as its own microworld with local physics that must be learned rather than assumed, instead of expecting one static model to compress them all

when specifying a continual-learning system, force the four axes to be answered separately — *what* experience you capture, *how* you compress it, into *what* structure, and *how* it is used at inference — since most disagreement in this space is people instantiating different axes and using the same word
expect to need both parametric and non-parametric learning rather than picking a side
and hold reliability and plasticity as an explicit trade-off to be tuned, not a bug to be fixed

data.name: Scaling Compute on Context (Jack Morris, Engram — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Jack Morris
Engram
data.brief: Continual-learning startup, launched the week before the talk; building methods to train private corpora into models. ⚠ captioned "N gram"/"Ngram" throughout — normalized from the closing URL ngr.am

data.name: Scaling compute on context
data.brief: The talk's name for the problem and its proposed fourth scaling axis. The three classical axes — more data, more compute, bigger models — have driven the entire deep-learning revolution but operate only on public data. For a private corpus the data axis is unavailable (you cannot create more of it) and training from scratch is off the table (you want the world knowledge), which leaves compute as the only axis: *how do you spend arbitrarily more compute on a fixed D and keep getting a better model?* Explicitly catalogued as one concept under many names — sleep-time compute, continual learning, neural memory, write-time compute, note taking, dreaming, studying, machine studying, and classically amortized inference — with the naming chaos read as evidence the paradigm is pre-paradigmatic

data.name: Breadth versus depth
data.brief: The framing of what current models lack. Models have superhuman breadth across public knowledge but not the "almost subconscious intuition" that comes from prolonged practice in one area. Three concrete failure classes: no knowledge of anything after the training cutoff; poor long-tail skill acquisition where public examples are thin (AMD kernels given as the example — "there are not that many good kernels written on AMD GPUs that are public"); and no knowledge of *you* — your emails, your writing style, your company's partnerships — "unless you happen to be famous enough to appear in the pre-training data"

data.name: The θ→θ\* problem
data.brief: The problem stated formally enough to compare methods: given a pre-trained θ and an unstructured private corpus D (every email you have written, every meeting transcript your company has ever had), produce θ\* that *knows* D — where "know" is explicitly flagged as the load-bearing, under-defined term that gives the field its leeway. Requirements are behavioural, not loss-based: answer questions about D, generate new artifacts like those in D, generalize beyond exact matches

data.name: The synthetic data wall
data.brief: Why every surveyed method saturates. Whatever you do — KV compaction, on-policy distillation, self-study QA pairs from the cartridges line of work, synthetic continued pre-training, unsupervised RL environments — you must first *define a dataset*, and "unless your model is under-parameterized, eventually it will learn all the data." That yields a bounded curve rather than pre-training's beautiful scaling: you fit the synthetic data, you know some of D but not all of it, and adding compute stops helping. The naive baseline is worse still — next-token training directly on D reaches a loss of ~0.0001 and then collapses on generation, memorizing without acquiring any generalization

data.name: Training that makes itself harder
data.brief: The proposed missing ingredient, drawn by analogy to AlphaGo: the reason RL self-play scales is that "AlphaGo makes its own training questions harder by getting better through training." Applied to private corpora, the goal is a technique where the model generates data, improves, and then generates *better* data recursively — converting the flat post-saturation curve into one where compute continues to buy depth. Presented as the company's active research direction and as an honest open problem: their early curves plateaued exactly like everyone else's before "more sophisticated things that make the training gradually harder"

data.name: Scaling only ever touched public data
data.brief: The structural observation the talk is built on: all three scaling axes have only ever been applied to public data — Wikipedia, Reddit, arXiv, GitHub — and even the post-training layer bought from Scale, Surge and Mercor "is still by definition creating publicly available data, because it's something the model could tell to a user." So models keep getting better at public coding and public maths and get no better at your life or your company. Framed not as an academic gap but as "the core problem with the current paradigm in AI." the supply-side leg of the pattern

data.name: Private corpus methods all saturate
data.brief: An unusually candid competitive survey from someone selling the solution: naive next-token training on D collapses at generation; KV compaction only covers what fits in context and forgoes the benefit of gradients; on-policy distillation works but leaves open what data to distil; synthetic continued pre-training overwrites pre-training and is hard to scale, and presumes a base model most teams no longer have. All of them share one defect — you must define a dataset, and once fitted, additional compute buys nothing. A vendor publicly naming the ceiling its own category has not yet cleared

data.name: Fourth scaling axis proposed
data.brief: The positive claim: with data fixed and model size fixed, compute becomes the only remaining axis, and the open research problem is how to spend it without saturating. Named "scaling compute on context" and explicitly identified as one idea wearing eight names across the industry — sleep-time compute, neural memory, write-time compute, note taking, dreaming, studying, machine studying, amortized inference — with the naming disorder itself offered as evidence that the paradigm "hasn't solidified the way pre-training or post-training have." with Su's escape-intelligence claim, the pattern's second anchor

data.name: Self improvement is the missing ingredient
data.brief: The proposed way past the wall, argued from AlphaGo: scaling worked there because the system's own improvement made its training questions harder, so the curve never flattened. The equivalent for private corpora is a loop where the model generates training data, improves, and generates harder data — "everyone is looking for a technique that can make models better, which makes them train themselves better." Reported honestly as partially solved: the company's initial curves plateaued like everyone else's until they found methods that gradually raise difficulty

data.name: Depth is the unclaimed capability
data.brief: The market read behind the research: models have breadth no human can match and none of the depth a specialist accumulates, and the three visible symptoms are the training cutoff, thin long-tail skills like AMD kernel authoring, and the total absence of personal or company knowledge. The Terence Tao exhibit sharpens it — the world's most famous mathematician values AI for cross-literature connections while noting it lacks a graduate student's five-year intuition. Depth, not breadth, is framed as the unclaimed axis

data.name: Public data ceiling is structural
data.brief: The reason scaling has never touched private data is not neglect but definition: a data vendor can only sell what a model is allowed to say back to a user, so the entire commercial data-acquisition layer reproduces the public/private boundary rather than crossing it. That makes the private-corpus problem structurally immune to the industry's current fix for data scarcity — you cannot buy your way past it, because the buying mechanism is what enforces the limit. Any method that works has to spend compute rather than acquire data

data.name: Saturation is the real benchmark
data.brief: Every method in this space can be made to look good on a single pass and they differ only in where they stop, so the honest evaluation is not "does it learn D" but "does adding compute keep helping." Under that test the field's current toolkit is uniformly bounded, and the one existence proof of an unbounded curve — self-play — worked because improvement fed back into problem difficulty. The practical filter for anyone assessing continual-learning vendors is therefore to ask what happens on the second and third pass, not the first

data.name: Judge private-corpus training by whether compute keeps paying
guidelines: State the problem precisely before choosing a method — a fixed pre-trained model, a fixed unstructured corpus, and a behavioural definition of "knows" that covers answering, generating and generalizing, since that word is where most vendor claims hide
do not train next-token directly on your corpus expecting knowledge, because loss will go to ~0.0001 while generation collapses and nothing generalizes beyond exact matches
treat KV compaction as limited to what fits in context and as forgoing what gradients give you
when using on-policy distillation, recognize that the hard question is *what data* you distil, since raw documents do not work and QA-pair generation changes the objective
expect synthetic continued pre-training to overwrite some pre-training and to assume a base model you may not have

and above all test the second pass — every dataset-defining method saturates once fitted, so the question that separates approaches is whether additional compute still buys depth, which today requires a loop that makes its own training progressively harder
finally, remember the data budget is softer than the idealized problem implies, since a real learner also seeks out adjacent textbooks, searches the internet, and asks practitioners

data.name: Scaling up Continual Learning (Ronak Malde, Trajectory — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Ronak Malde
Trajectory
data.brief: Continual-learning platform: ingests production agent traces, optimizes them as a self-served loop, redeploys as a continually-learning system, with a control plane over the whole thing. Team drawn from DeepMind, Meta Superintelligence Labs and OpenAI. Early access customers named: Harvey, Decagon, Rogo

data.name: Windsurf
data.brief: Speaker's prior employer; trained SWE-1; ⚠ the acquisition is described as "the two billion acquisition at DeepMind" — the captions conflate acquirer and destination, see review note 5

data.name: The four criteria for post-training
data.brief: The evaluative frame that organizes the talk: a learning algorithm should have an online task distribution (tied to what users actually do, not a curated benchmark), on-policy sampling, parallelism of one (no fleet of rollouts, hence no environment infrastructure), and per-token dense reward. Applied historically: SFT gets parallelism and per-token reward but is off-policy on a curated distribution; DPO/RLHF gains online task distributions but reverts to sequence-level reward and pairwise infrastructure; GRPO is "a Faustian bargain" — maximal on-policy power at the cost of off-policy task distributions, exploded parallelism demanding one-to-one environment replicas, and whole-sequence reward

data.name: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD)
data.brief: The proposed algorithm, derived in three steps. Classical distillation fits a student's log-probs to a *smarter teacher's* on fixed data; on-policy distillation swaps the fixed data for the student's own rollout; self-distillation resolves the remaining problem — at the frontier there is no smarter teacher — by making the teacher *the same model given privileged information*. A hint (in the simplest case a golden solution, more generally environment information or guidance) is prepended to the teacher's prompt, and the student without the hint is trained to match the teacher with it. Satisfies all four criteria at once. Because it matches the full distribution rather than sharpening a sampled token, it "shifts entire distributions" across a ~65k vocabulary per token rather than nudging the top choice

data.name: Hint leakage
data.brief: OPSD's structural analogue of reward hacking, and the talk's most transferable warning: "with RL the number one problem is reward hacking… there is an equivalent for OPSD, and that is hint leakage." If the hint contains information the student could never have derived, the model learns to skip the reasoning that would have produced it — the worked example being a maths task where the hint states the answer and the rollout becomes "I know the solution is 000, so let me go back and put that into my reasoning trace." Two fixes offered: an LLM filter that rewrites hints into *what the model should reasonably have known* (e.g. "look through the logs" instead of "the SSO token is expired"), and the algorithmic residual guidance below

data.name: Step-level divergence weighting
data.brief: The fix for the long-horizon failure mode. On long tool-calling trajectories the student drifts far from the teacher, so the teacher course-corrects at every opportunity and the model collapses into hedging — the "but/wait" problem, visible as *wait*, *but* and *maybe* dominating a token cloud as steps progress, and as the model settling between two divergent distributions. The fix computes student-teacher KL divergence per step and uses it as a multiplicative token weight rather than as the usual KL penalty, so a diverged step is down-weighted while later steps that come back on track are still learned from

data.name: Residual guidance
data.brief: The more principled anti-leakage method. Run a partial hint (e.g. half of it) to get a slightly-smarter teacher alongside the full-hint teacher, then train against a linear combination of the two. The combination measures how strong and how out-of-distribution the hint is, keeping the student from being shifted into territory with no overlap with its own distribution — the failure the talk illustrates as "entirely shifting distributions with almost no overlap between your model and the original solution"

data.name: Rl environments decoupled from reality
data.brief: The indictment of the current paradigm from someone who trained a frontier coding model: benchmarks are saturating within months, each new one takes 4, 6, 24 hours or days to build, labs are pouring enormous sums into RL environments — "and perhaps more concerningly they're not tied to real-world use cases where people are using AI." Against that, "we are spending hundreds of trillions of tokens every single day on inference," generating exactly the failure and success signal that should be trained on. The trillion-token problem: the industry is manufacturing synthetic task distributions while discarding the real one

data.name: Opsd satisfies all four criteria
data.brief: The algorithmic claim: by making the teacher the same model with a hint, OPSD gets an online task distribution, on-policy sampling, parallelism of one, and per-token dense reward simultaneously — where SFT, DPO/RLHF and GRPO each sacrificed at least two. The parallelism collapse is the operationally significant part: "we don't need a group of eight to roll out, just a single example," which removes the environment-replica infrastructure that makes RL expensive. Reward density is the other: matching log-probs across a ~65k vocabulary per token instead of "drinking through a straw" from one end-state scalar, likened to being graded 87/100 on an essay with no other feedback

data.name: Opsd beats grpo past saturation
data.brief: Reported results: on LiveCodeBench, GRPO "saturates around Sonnet-level performance and doesn't really push the frontier," while OPSD reaches new territory because it shifts distributions rather than sharpening them. A second, counter-intuitive result on cost — where RL trains models to think longer for better scores, OPSD collapses the tokens needed on hard problems, which the speaker calls the exciting part for token efficiency. Scaled at Trajectory to 120B, 500B and one-trillion-parameter models, and to a 12B model on Mercor APEX agents requiring 100+ tool calls, where it "has even surpassed RL"

data.name: Hint leakage is the new reward hacking
data.brief: A named failure class for the emerging method, offered by its own author: hints containing underivable information teach the model to skip vital reasoning, producing rollouts that announce the answer and then reverse-engineer a justification — "you can imagine this is not going to occur whatsoever in the real world." That an algorithm's first serious adopter publishes its exploitation mode alongside its results is itself the signal; the mitigations (LLM hint-rewriting toward what the model should have known, and residual guidance via partial-hint interpolation) are second-order

data.name: Long horizon breaks distillation
data.brief: The honest scaling report: everything works for small models and short horizons — "this is where academic papers kind of end" — and at 120B with 50 or 100 tool calls it degrades. Eval accuracy swings wildly, run-to-run variance is high, tool calls stop matching the format the model was instruction-tuned on, and the model collapses into hedging as the teacher course-corrects a diverged student at every step (the but/wait problem, with *wait*, *but* and *maybe* taking over the token cloud). Fixed with per-step KL used as a token weight rather than a penalty

data.name: Software that improves every use
data.brief: The thesis statement: Trajectory is "building the platform that turns every interaction into model improvement, harness improvement, and the entire agentic loop just getting smarter over time," with production traces optimized as a self-served loop and redeployed under a control plane — toward "a world where software in general just gets smarter every single time it's used… the most exciting unlock in 2026–2027." Tempered in Q&A: the field is in pseudo continual learning, still doing batch updates offline and re-uploading, with merging 10,000 concurrent production rollouts an open infrastructure *and* algorithmic problem. the algorithm-leg statement of the pattern

data.name: Privileged information replaces the teacher
data.brief: The move that makes self-distillation work is recognizing that a teacher's only necessary property is being *better on this instance*, not being a bigger model — so privileged information substitutes for capability. That is what lets the technique survive at the frontier, where no larger teacher exists, and it reframes distillation from a compression technique into a general mechanism for converting hindsight into policy. It also explains the failure mode exactly: if the privilege cannot be earned by reasoning, the student learns to fake having earned it, which is why hint design becomes the discipline that reward design was for RL

data.name: Real token flow is the untapped distribution
data.brief: Hundreds of trillions of inference tokens a day constitute the largest and most task-relevant distribution in existence, and the industry is spending heavily to manufacture synthetic substitutes for it while that stream goes unused. The bottleneck was never availability but algorithmic: previous methods needed curated tasks, parallel rollouts and replayable environments, none of which production traffic provides. An algorithm requiring only one on-policy rollout and a hint is what makes the real distribution trainable, which is why the method and the trace-mining business model arrive together

data.name: Run on-policy self-distillation without leaking the answer
guidelines: Score any post-training method against four axes before adopting it — is the task distribution online, is sampling on-policy, how much parallelism does it force, and is the reward per-token or per-sequence — since most methods trade two of these for the others
build the teacher by giving the *same* model privileged information rather than reaching for a larger one, so the technique still applies at the frontier

design hints as what the model should reasonably have known, not as the answer, and use an LLM pass to rewrite leaky hints (turn "the SSO token is expired" into "look through the logs"), because a hint the student could never have derived teaches it to skip reasoning and back-fill a justification

where you need a principled control, run a partial hint alongside the full hint and train against a linear combination, which measures how far out of distribution the guidance is and keeps the student from being pushed somewhere it has no overlap

expect long-horizon tool-calling to break naive implementations into hedging — watch for *wait*, *but* and *maybe* taking over your token distribution — and fix it by computing per-step KL divergence and applying it as a multiplicative token weight rather than a penalty, so diverged steps are down-weighted while recoveries still teach
and be honest that eval variance, format drift on tool calls and run-to-run instability all appear between the short-horizon regime where papers stop and the 100-tool-call regime where products live

data.name: Beyond Static Intelligence: Evaluating Continual Learning (Parth Asawa, UC Berkeley — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Parth Asawa
Continual Learning Bench 1.0
data.brief: Benchmark for learning ability rather than point capability. Six task domains — blind spectrum monitoring (signal processing), codebase adaptation (software-engineering efficiency), cohort studies (epidemiology), exploitable poker (strategic play), database exploration, and sales prediction — each built as a sequence of instances with per-instance reward, validated with domain experts for learnability and realism. Deliberately includes concept drift (e.g. a database migration mid-sequence that drops columns and renames others) to test whether a system can discard stale experience while still updating from new. Collaboration across Berkeley, Snorkel, UW and UW–Madison; funded by Snorkel's open benchmarks grant and Laude Slingshots

data.name: Gain (stateful minus stateless)
data.brief: The metric that makes learning measurable rather than inferred. Every system is run through the benchmark twice: once normally, allowed to maintain state across instances (updating a policy, its notes, or just growing context), and once as a stateless baseline reset between every instance. Gain is the difference. It answers "how much did my prior experience on the first four tasks actually improve performance on the fifth," isolating learning from base-model strength — the confound that cumulative reward alone cannot separate, where a stronger model that learns nothing outscores a weaker one that learns well

data.name: Three criteria for a continual-learning benchmark
data.brief: Why existing benchmarks cannot simply be chained. Headroom — the task must actually require online adaptation; if a model could improve by offline training on that data, it does not measure continual learning, which rules out most benchmarks for frontier models trained on "almost everything on the internet." Shared structure — instances must have shared latent structure to exploit, whereas traditional benchmark instances are *designed to be independent*, which is the fundamental reason chaining AIME problems into a sequence cannot work. A learning mechanism — the environment must return signal (scalar reward, error messages, textual feedback) that makes improvement realistically possible

data.name: Stability and plasticity failure modes
data.brief: The observed taxonomy: nearly every continual-learning failure lands on one side of the stability/plasticity trade-off. Stability failure, from the sales-prediction task — the model is told it over-predicted, revises down, is told it under-predicted, and instead of converging to the middle as a human would, jumps straight back to the original over-prediction, having failed to retain the first correction. Plasticity failure, from the epidemiology task — a notepad-equipped system dismisses genuinely applicable material with "these seem to be cohort definitions from a different study schema that doesn't apply here," refusing to update priors from new information it does not recognize as relevant

data.name: Continual learning as a first-order design requirement
data.brief: The closing argument, framed as a sunk-cost critique. Today's stack — pre-training, mid-training, RL against teacher models, finishing with multi-tier on-policy distillation — produces a frozen checkpoint, and continual-learning research then tries to bolt learning onto models "never designed to be continual learners to begin with." If it were a first-order requirement, the architecture might look nothing like this: "in the purest sense, continual learning might just be one phase of training, and everything after that is deployment" — one learning phase, then a model updating its weights in the environment indefinitely

data.name: Benchmarks assume amnesia
data.brief: The framing indictment: every leaderboard is built from independent single-task scores, which means "we've told the models: imagine that every time you do something, you completely forget your memory. Imagine if your life was like that." Learning ability is therefore invisible to the entire measurement apparatus the field steers by, and the closing claim makes the stakes explicit — "continual learning doesn't look like point capabilities; we need to measure it the right way to optimize for the right objective as a field, because that's the history of how machine learning has progressed." A measurement critique aimed at the industry's dominant scoreboard

data.name: Benchmarks cannot be chained
data.brief: The technical result that closes the obvious shortcut. Asked repeatedly why one cannot simply sequence existing benchmarks, the answer is that traditional instances "are designed to be independent" — no shared latent structure, therefore no mechanism by which earlier instances could improve later ones. Combined with the headroom problem (frontier models are pre-trained on nearly everything, so improvement from online adaptation is hard to elicit at all), this means continual-learning evaluation requires purpose-built environments, not a re-packaging of existing ones. HELD PATTERN-LESS — a construction-methodology data point for the uncoined pat-benchmark-trust-crisis ledger (see review note 2)

data.name: Gain metric isolates learning
data.brief: The methodological contribution: measure each system twice, once stateful and once with state wiped between instances, and report the difference. Cumulative reward alone "confounds continual learning ability with base model strength" — the talk's diagram shows a stronger system topping the leaderboard while improving not at all over its own stateless baseline, next to a weaker one that genuinely learns. Reward, gain and cost are then reported on Pareto frontiers rather than collapsed to a single number, on the argument that base capability, learning and expense all matter independently

data.name: Vanilla icl tops the leaderboard
data.brief: The surprising empirical result: across the first release, plain in-context learning — just putting experience in the context with no context-management machinery — tops the leaderboard, and not only on raw reward but across the reward-versus-cost and gain-versus-cost Pareto frontiers. The more elaborate (and more expensive) context-management systems performed notably worse on tasks requiring real learning. Reported with its own caveat: these were medium-horizon tasks that may not have stressed in-context learning enough, and longer horizons are on the roadmap. The most falsifiable claim in the track, and it cuts against the memory-product category

data.name: Cl failures split stability plasticity
data.brief: The failure taxonomy with worked examples from the benchmark: a sales-forecasting model that, told it over-predicted then under-predicted, discards the first correction and jumps back to over-prediction (stability failure), and a notepad-based system that dismisses applicable epidemiological material as belonging to "a different study schema that doesn't apply here" (plasticity failure). The environments deliberately induce this by injecting concept drift — database migrations that drop and rename columns — because handling drift requires learning what to forget as well as what to keep. the empirical counterpart to Su's stability/plasticity claim in the same batch

data.name: A stateless control arm for memory
data.brief: Gain generalizes past this benchmark into the discipline the memory-product category currently lacks: run the system twice, once with state and once with state wiped, and report the delta. Almost no memory or context-management product is evaluated this way, which is precisely why a category can grow without demonstrating that its machinery beats simply putting the experience in the context. The stateless control arm is cheap, obvious in retrospect, and would settle most vendor claims in this space — which is a reasonable definition of a good metric

data.name: Independence was designed in
data.brief: The reason continual learning cannot be evaluated with existing benchmarks is not an oversight but a design commitment: instance independence was deliberately engineered into evaluation to make scores clean, comparable and unconfounded. That choice, sensible for measuring capability, structurally forbids measuring accumulation — and since the field optimizes what it measures, an entire dimension of progress has been invisible by construction. Fixing it requires building environments with shared latent structure and drift, which is expensive in exactly the way independent benchmarks were designed to avoid

data.name: Measure learning with a stateless control arm
guidelines: Do not chain existing benchmarks and call it continual learning — their instances are designed to be independent, so there is no shared structure for earlier experience to exploit

build or select environments against three criteria instead: headroom (if offline training on that data would produce the same improvement, the task cannot measure online learning, which rules out most public benchmarks for frontier models), shared latent structure across instances, and an explicit learning mechanism in the environment — scalar reward, error messages or textual feedback — so improvement is realistically achievable

run every system twice, once maintaining state and once reset between instances, and report the gain between them, because cumulative reward confounds learning ability with base-model strength and will rank a strong non-learner above a weak learner
report reward, gain and cost on Pareto frontiers rather than collapsing to one number
inject concept drift deliberately, since handling it requires discarding stale experience as well as absorbing new, and that is where the stability/plasticity failures surface
and validate task sequences with domain experts for learnability and realism before trusting any number they produce

data.name: Bringing Continual Learning into Enterprises (Samuel Denton, Applied Compute — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Samuel Denton
The offline–online distillation spectrum
data.brief: The first axis. At the offline end, a single batch of production traces from an agent in the wild that you must learn from by hindsight. In the middle, a daily batch collected from a deployed model. At the online end, "the holy grail of continual learning" — a unified engine where serving and training collapse together: the model serves production traffic, produces a trace, learns from it, and serves the next request. Positioned commercially rather than aspirationally: most enterprises sit at the offline end today, some are willing to run the full flywheel, and the stated goal is to provide value across the whole spectrum

data.name: Offline versus online hints
data.brief: The second axis, and the file's genuine contribution to the batch's distillation thread. Distillation needs a teacher smarter than the on-policy student, which requires privileged information — a hint; the question is where the hint comes from. Offline hints derive from static data: known rubrics, general behavioural priors ("a customer-support agent too willing to give refunds"), or aggregate loss reports — independent of any particular rollout. Online hints are constructed dynamically *from* the online rollout, so the guidance is conditioned on what the model actually just did

data.name: The four distillation quadrants
