data.brief: Crossing the two axes. Q1 offline hint + offline trace: apply a behavioural prior across a batch of production traces. Q2 offline hint + online rollout. Q3 offline trace with a single on-policy step — replay a production trace to a chosen moment, roll out one step from the current model without touching the environment, and hint against that step. Q4 online hint + online trace: let the on-policy model finish, construct a hint from the full rollout, distil against it. Applied Compute focuses on Q1 and Q4 — Q1 as day-one value requiring no replayable environment, Q4 as "our most scalable solution" and the complete flywheel. Framed with the caveat that these are spectrums drawn as boxes

data.name: Per-step hint injection
data.brief: The first of two techniques presented as what makes distillation actually work: rather than prepending a hint to the whole rollout, use a judge to choose where in the rollout to inject it, then distil on the next step or few steps rather than the entire trajectory — "that's really the moment in time you want the teacher to teach something to the student." Supported by the observation that the KL learning signal decays with distance from the hint

data.name: Relevance-masked self-distillation
data.brief: The second technique, with a published write-up on the company's site: use an LLM judge to select which tokens to learn from in the teacher's output, because "the teacher model has preferences of certain connector words that are not really relevant to what we're trying to teach the student." Reported to improve learning of very out-of-distribution behaviour while reducing catastrophic degradation — i.e. it attacks the plasticity and stability sides simultaneously

data.name: Enterprises start at offline traces
data.brief: The market read from a vendor selling into it: "this is sort of where a lot of enterprises are today" — they have production traffic and a pile of traces and say "figure out a way to make our agent better. It's clearly doing something, but it clearly can be better." The commercial framing is a spectrum rather than a product: improve for free today from a dump of offline production data, and raise all ceilings tomorrow once an online policy model is deployed and updating while serving. Some enterprises are already willing to run the fully online flywheel. A concrete picture of where continual learning actually sits in enterprise adoption, against a track full of frontier claims

data.name: Hint provenance is the second axis
data.brief: The conceptual contribution: distillation's teacher must be smarter than the student, which requires privileged information, so where the hint comes from is a design axis independent of how online the traces are. Offline hints encode static behavioural priors and target specific known problems; online hints are constructed from what the model just did and therefore "can cater to a bunch of different behaviours" without enumerating them in advance. Crossing hint provenance with trace recency yields four working regimes rather than one method

data.name: Offline distillation shifts behaviour
data.brief: The Q1 measured result, and the surprising one. Goal: get a Qwen 3.5 thinking model on SWE-bench to stop taking up to 80 turns and call its submit tool before turn 40. Task-complete call rate rose from ~22% to ~60% with the test pass rate flat (in fact slightly up), so the behaviour was added without regression. The surprise is mechanical: the rollout is conditioned on a production trace that never called the tool, so "the teacher doesn't force the tool call — it just starts to force the reasoning path towards the tool call without ever actually changing the tool call." Adding one on-policy step to an otherwise offline setup raised SWE-bench pass rate further

data.name: Online hinting beats offline on ood
data.brief: The Q4 measured result, on a real customer constraint: a coding agent had to emit a hyperlink format dictated by a customer's harness, a format "very very out of distribution for previously post-trained models." Adding a format reward degraded overall coding performance; SFT on correctly-formatted traces did too. Online hinting — roll out, then inject a hint referencing *that* rollout ("in your prior rollout you formatted hyperlinks like this; next time format them this way") — moved correct formatting from ~15% to ~80%, while applying the same static hint to every rollout climbed "far less." Direct A/B evidence that hint provenance, not hint content, carries the gain

data.name: Distillation without golden answers
data.brief: The methodological stance, offered as a standing frustration with the field: "a lot of distillation work is done assuming you have some kind of golden answer that you can distil into the model, and this is often not the case." Applied Compute's whole taxonomy is built to work without a golden rubric per task — behavioural priors and rollout-derived hints substitute for ground truth. Paired with the infrastructure prediction that closes the loop: "as the infra collapses between serving and training, we're automatically going to raise the ceiling continuously via online distillation"

data.name: Privileged information is the real axis
data.brief: Read alongside the OPSD talk earlier in the same track, this file completes a shift in what distillation *is*: not compression of a larger model into a smaller one, but a general mechanism for converting privileged information into policy. Once that is the frame, the design questions become where privilege comes from, how much of it the student could plausibly have derived, and where in a trajectory to apply it — which is why both talks independently identify hint construction as the discipline that reward design was for RL. The 15%→80% online-versus-offline gap is the cleanest available evidence that *provenance* of the hint, not its content, carries the learning

data.name: Behaviour can be installed from hindsight
data.brief: The SWE-bench result shows a model being taught to take an action it never took in any training trace, because the teacher shaped the reasoning path leading toward the action rather than the action token itself. That decouples behaviour change from demonstration data and makes a large class of enterprise asks tractable from logs alone — no replayable environment, no golden answers, no new labelling. It also sets the boundary condition: what can be installed this way is behaviour reachable by reasoning the model already has, which is the same limit hint leakage describes from the failure side

data.name: Run enterprise distillation from production traces
guidelines: Locate your situation on two axes before choosing a method — how online your traces are (a one-time dump, a daily batch, or a live serving loop) and where your hints come from (static behavioural priors versus guidance constructed from the rollout just observed) — because the four combinations have genuinely different requirements and pay-offs
start in the offline-trace, offline-hint quadrant if you have nothing but logs, since it needs no replayable environment and can still install targeted behaviour changes
do not assume golden answers, as most real tasks have no per-task rubric — encode what good looks like as a behavioural prior instead

when you need broad improvement rather than one targeted behaviour, move to online hints constructed from each rollout, which adapt to whatever the model actually did and in measured comparison outperform applying one static hint to every rollout by a wide margin
cheat toward on-policy where you can — replaying an offline trace and rolling out a single on-policy step before hinting measurably beats the fully offline setup at almost no infrastructure cost
use a judge to pick where in the rollout to inject the hint and distil on the next step or few rather than the whole trajectory, since the KL learning signal decays with distance from the hint

mask irrelevant tokens with an LLM judge so you learn the behaviour rather than the teacher's connector-word habits, which improves out-of-distribution learning while limiting catastrophic degradation

and always track a non-regression metric alongside your target behaviour, since format rewards and naive SFT both degrade base capability in exactly the cases where the target behaviour is most out of distribution

data.name: Adaption Labs: Gradient-Free Continual Learning (Sara Hooker, Adaption Labs — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Sara Hooker
Adaption Labs
data.brief: The speaker's lab. Mandate stated as building "intelligence that continuously adapts" with control in builders' hands. Shipped Auto Scientist in beta ~4 weeks before the talk, covering 242 languages from day one, with a stated focus on non-verifiable tasks, and offering free GPUs during the beta

data.name: The unreasonably narrow path
data.brief: The talk's diagnosis of who gets to work at the frontier, credited to Rosanne Liu. Science's professionalization moved discovery from independent "gentleman scientists" to institutions, and in AI it compressed into one route: the right PhD programme, the right industry lab, sufficiently interesting work, and only then a contribution to the frontier — "a very aggressively filtered system" where being uncurious about the right problem at the right time excluded you entirely. Double-compounded in AI by compute, producing the GPU-poor/GPU-rich split and a handful of labs building the technology everyone uses. Illustrated with a Stanford map of significant breakthroughs showing whole regions of the world absent

data.name: Auto Scientist
data.brief: Adaption Labs' system for automating the training of models. Distinguishing claim: it co-optimizes the entire loop from data to alignment and self-evolves per domain and data type, rather than treating data as something the agent merely decides whether to generate — "we did not get the returns until we controlled for data quality; we co-optimized the data exactly as we would the model." Reported to outperform research staff, attributed to the search space being broader than any individual's experience across model types, sizes, and dense-versus-MoE architectures, and to its willingness to change many hyperparameters at once "that humans are much more wary about changing." Win rates cluster just above 60% because a budget-stopping rule exited at 60; with that removed, performance continues climbing. Beta uptake most acute in medical, sciences, legal and code — domains where models fall short and last-mile customization is acute

data.name: The death of pre-training scale
data.brief: The empirical claim underpinning the optimism: pre-training size is no longer the most lucrative axis of scale, because "our architecture is saturated." Evidence offered is the Open LLM Leaderboard's daily best sub-13B model versus all larger models, where the ratio "totally flips" over time, plus the observation that recent size-maximizing releases have not delivered the stepwise gains their predecessors did. Carefully bounded in Q&A: architecture determines the ceiling and a new architecture changes everything; the argument is that we are at *this* architecture's size ceiling, not that small models are sufficient — "I'm not advocating everyone use a 0.8B"

data.name: Distributed compute returns
data.brief: Why the scaling claim is a governance claim. Pre-training compute must be co-located and provisioned in bulk for redundancy; inference, post-training and agentic compute can be far more distributed and return more per FLOP. So if returns have moved off the pre-training axis, they have moved onto compute shapes that do not require "hoarding of GPUs" — "it's very different compute purchasing dynamics, and again it means the person with the best idea has a higher chance of winning." Paired with the observation that the industry ships one model to everyone, which is both intuitively wrong for billions of users and a poor allocation, since easy and hard problems receive identical compute

data.name: Frontier participation is filtered
data.brief: A frontier-lab veteran describes the filter from inside it: AI research access runs through one narrow funnel — right PhD, right lab, right problem at the right moment — compounded by compute, so "a handful of frontier labs have been able to build the technology we use," with a Stanford breakthrough map showing entire regions absent. The consequence named is product-level, not only equitable: "we ship the same model to everyone," which most people intuitively understand is wrong for billions of users and is also a poor use of compute, since easy and hard problems consume the same amount

data.name: Auto scientist outperforms research staff
data.brief: The product claim, and the batch's strongest auto-research data point: a system that automates model training end-to-end outperforms the lab's own research staff, because staff specialize in particular model types while the search covers architectures, sizes and dense-versus-MoE jointly, and because it changes many hyperparameters at once where humans are cautious. Reported win rates sit just above 60% only because a budget-stopping rule exited there; removed, the curve keeps climbing. The load-bearing methodological detail is that it only worked once data was co-optimized with the model — the speaker's explicit differentiation from auto-research projects that leave data to agent discretion

data.name: Pretraining scale exhausted
data.brief: The empirical claim from someone whose research career was efficiency at scale: pre-training size is no longer the most lucrative axis, because the architecture is saturated. Evidence is the Open LLM Leaderboard's daily best sub-13B model versus all larger models, a ratio that "totally flips" over time, plus recent size-maximizing releases failing to deliver stepwise gains. Sharpened in Q&A into a prediction rather than a preference: "no frontier AI lab is going to re-run their model again for pre-training… we are probably at the ceiling of size" — with the explicit caveat that a new architecture resets the ceiling, and that this is not an argument for tiny models

data.name: Compute shape shifts who competes
data.brief: The structural consequence: pre-training compute must be co-located and over-provisioned, while inference, post-training and agentic compute distribute well and return more per FLOP — so returns moving off the pre-training axis means they move onto compute that "does not require the same hoarding of GPUs… it's very different compute purchasing dynamics, and the person with the best idea has a higher chance of winning." A frontier-lab insider arguing the capital barrier to frontier participation is falling for structural rather than charitable reasons

data.name: Training knowledge is tacit and scarce
data.brief: The scarcity claim that makes automation valuable: "there are very few people who know how to train frontier models — realistically probably fewer than 5,000 in the world at scale," and that knowledge is "kind of secret knowledge we pass as if we're apprentices," which makes it "a very exploitable search space" precisely because humans are bad at those configuration choices. The second-order argument is the interesting one: automating it lowers the cost of asking, and "the cost of asking something informs what is asked — if you make it cheaper to ask, you change the volume of things that are asked"

data.name: Saturation redistributes participation
data.brief: The argument that makes this more than an equity talk: if the dominant axis of progress required co-located capital-intensive compute, then participation was decided by balance sheets regardless of ideas — and if that axis has saturated, the redistribution follows mechanically rather than as a favour. Post-training and agentic compute are distributable, higher-return per FLOP, and purchasable in different quantities, so the field's competitive question shifts from who can hoard GPUs to who has the better recipe. That is a falsifiable claim about compute economics, and it is what a new architecture would reverse

data.name: Automating tacit craft changes the questions
data.brief: Frontier training knowledge is apprenticeship-transmitted, held by a few thousand people, and consists largely of configuration choices humans make badly — an unusually good automation target, since the expertise is tacit but the search space is mechanical. The consequence the speaker emphasizes is not cheaper training but a different question distribution: when asking costs less, more and stranger things get asked, and the innovation cycle rather than any single result is what accelerates. That reframes auto-research from a productivity tool into a change in what gets investigated at all

data.name: Automate the training search, but co-optimize the data
guidelines: Treat frontier training configuration as a search problem rather than craft knowledge, since the expertise is tacit, held by very few people, and consists mostly of choices humans make conservatively — an automated search will change many hyperparameters at once where a human changes one, and will cover architectures, model sizes and dense-versus-MoE jointly where a researcher specializes

co-optimize data with the model, because treating data as something the agent merely decides whether to generate leaves most of the available gain unrealized — control for data quality and adapt the data exactly as you adapt the model
watch your stopping rules before reading your own results, since a budget-stopping threshold will make every win rate cluster just above it and hide the real curve
expect the strongest demand in domains where general models fall short and last-mile customization is acute (medical, sciences, legal, code)
plan for non-verifiable tasks rather than only the verifiable ones, since that is where most everyday work sits

and evaluate the pay-off as innovation cycle rate and probability that a compute spend succeeds, not as a single benchmark delta — the reason automation matters is that it lowers the cost of asking, which changes what gets asked

data.name: Lessons from Studying Every Memory System (Shlok Khemani — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Shlok Khemani
The Agent Memory Layer
data.brief: Persistent memory is becoming a first-class layer of the agent stack rather than a feature of individual products: systems that accumulate, synthesize and re-inject what they learn about a user, a team or an environment, maintained on a compute budget and updated outside the model's weights. Evidenced across ~15 corpus data points from batch 9 onward — graph-native memory products (Zep/Graphiti, CrabRAG, BabyAGI 4, TwelveLabs, monday.com), the convergent running-profile architecture of the leading consumer assistants, and frontier-lab productization (Anthropic's memory + dreaming). Contested from birth, deliberately: three independent counters hold that the layer is often unnecessary (memory adds cost and no capability when the task fits in context), that it is a convention over existing infrastructure rather than a product (markdown in git; SLA budgets ruling it out), and that it cannot be outsourced at all — the converged part is cheap to reimplement and the divergent part is product-specific. Scope note: the no-outsourcing finding is drawn from consumer personalization; most vendors in this space sell into enterprise, where the economics amortize differently

data.name: The running profile
data.brief: The architecture both leading assistants converged on. Every few days (ChatGPT) or every 24 hours (Claude), a background process reads recent conversations, extracts what matters, and rewrites a persistent profile that is then injected into the context window of every new conversation. ChatGPT's is ~4,000 tokens across 16 sections and written as extremely dense keyword clusters — "almost like clues," relying on frontier models' ability to infer context from limited information. Claude's is ~1,000 tokens of complete sentences. Introduced in ChatGPT V2 (April 2025) and Claude V2 (September 2025)

data.name: The user-editable fact list
data.brief: The first serious memory implementation (ChatGPT V1, February 2024): the user asks the model to remember something, it extracts a fact ("the user is vegetarian"), stores it in a visible list, and injects the list into every conversation. Two structural flaws named: the burden of memory management fell on the user, who had to curate memories while trying to have a conversation; and staleness — facts true when written ("Shlok is going to Bengaluru") persist indefinitely. Deprecated by ChatGPT in mid-2026 once the running profile and conversation-search tools superseded it

data.name: Conversation-search tools
data.brief: Claude's V1 (August 2025) approach, and the architectural opposite of a profile: no stored profile and no fact list, but two tools — search past conversations by keyword or topic, and search by time period ("what did we discuss last week"). Every conversation starts fresh with no user context, and the model retrieves on demand when it judges it needs to. ChatGPT later added an equivalent tool, completing the convergence from both directions

data.name: The memory convergence
data.brief: The survey's central finding: after three years of independent evolution from opposite starting points — ChatGPT from stored facts toward retrieval, Claude from retrieval toward a stored profile — both now have a running profile that is visible and editable, plus tools to search past conversations. Gemini has a running profile too, but with detailed per-memory timing logs. The general architecture converged; the implementation details did not. Notably, neither uses the RAG-chunk-and-embed approach the industry assumed was the answer: "it wasn't too long ago that everyone, including me, assumed that RAG was the way to go about memory"

data.name: Memory as a function of compute
data.brief: The economic frame that explains the design differences. A running profile has two costs: maintenance (how often you update it × how much compute per update) and serving (it sits in every context window, so length is a per-conversation tax). The ideal system — update after every conversation, spawn subagents for the update, store 400,000 tokens instead of 4,000 — is unavailable "because we live in a GPU-constrained world." The two vendors take exactly opposite trade-offs: ChatGPT 4,000 tokens updated every few days (high serving, low update), Claude 1,000 tokens updated every 24 hours (low serving, high update)

data.name: The context acquisition gap
data.brief: The closing argument, and the one the speaker calls a rant: memory quality is capped not by architecture or compute but by how much context the system can gather. The worked example — a profile records travel to both Thailand and Turkey with overlapping dates, because the source was a conversation *deciding between them*; the actual decision was made in person, and the corroborating evidence (flight and hotel bookings) sat in connected email the assistant does not reason over. The sharper complaint is not the missing data but the missing curiosity: "what really bothers me is that it doesn't realize there is a conflict. It's not curious about trying to fill in gaps." Diagnosed explicitly as "not a technology problem, it's a product problem," compounded by fragmentation — every chatbot, vertical app, agent and hardware device builds its own private memory, none shared, all rebuilt from scratch

data.name: Memory architectures converged
data.brief: The survey result: three years of independent evolution produced the same architecture from opposite directions. ChatGPT started with a user-curated fact list and moved toward background profile synthesis plus retrieval tools; Claude started with retrieval-only tools and no profile, then added one. Both now run a profile that is visible and editable with search over past conversations; Gemini matches with per-memory timing logs. And neither converged on RAG — the chunk-embed-retrieve approach the industry assumed was the answer is used by neither leading assistant. Convergent evolution on architecture, persistent divergence on implementation

data.name: Memory cannot be outsourced
data.brief: The strongest commercial claim in the talk, from someone with no product to sell: "if you're a serious team, you do not outsource memory. It is something you build alongside your product — your memory system evolves with your product and cannot be an afterthought." Evidence offered is a market scan: every top consumer AI product across categories has memory, and none of them outsource it. A direct challenge to the memory-as-a-service vendor category, arriving in the same track as several of those vendors

data.name: Memory budget is a compute decision
data.brief: Memory design reduced to an economics problem with published numbers: maintenance cost (update frequency × compute per update) versus serving cost (profile length × every conversation). The two leading vendors sit at opposite corners — ChatGPT 4,000 tokens every few days, Claude 1,000 tokens every 24 hours — which is presented not as one being right but as the same constraint resolved differently. The unconstrained design (hourly updates, subagent-driven synthesis, 400,000-token profiles) is named and dismissed as GPU-unaffordable

data.name: Continual learning already shipping
data.brief: The claim that reframes the whole track: "continual learning is already here." A running profile *is* a learning loop — profile conditions the conversation, conversation produces new information, background synthesis folds it back into the profile, repeat — running today at consumer scale. The qualifier is where it happens: outside the weights. The open question is posed as economic rather than technical: weight updates amortize across employees and customers at enterprise scale but not for an individual, so "will each of us get our own self-learning model, what data kicks the process off, and who pays for it?"

data.name: Context acquisition is the real cap
data.brief: The rant, and the most product-relevant finding: perfect architecture and infinite compute would still leave memory capped by what the system can observe. Demonstrated by a profile that records two mutually exclusive trips because it read a *decision-making* conversation and never saw the decision, which happened in person and left traces in connected email the assistant does not reason over. The indictment is the absence of curiosity — the system does not notice the contradiction or try to resolve it — and the diagnosis is explicit: "it's not a technology problem, it's a product problem." Compounded by fragmentation: every product builds a private memory, none shared, each rebuilt from scratch, all updated by hand when life changes

data.name: Convergence without consolidation
data.brief: Two teams solving the same problem in isolation reached the same architecture, which is the strongest available evidence that the running profile plus retrieval tools is a genuine attractor rather than a fashion — and simultaneously that the details where they still differ (density versus prose, update cadence, what the user may see and edit) are the real product surface. That combination is bad news for anyone selling memory as a horizontal component: the converged part is cheap to reimplement and the divergent part is exactly what has to be tuned against a specific product, which is the mechanism behind the no-outsourcing finding

data.name: The scarce input is observation
data.brief: The memory field has been optimizing the wrong end of the pipeline. Enormous effort goes into synthesis, storage and retrieval, while the binding constraint is how much of a user's life the system ever gets to observe — and the fix requires no research breakthrough, only products willing to reason across the sources users already connected and to notice their own contradictions. That a system can hold two incompatible facts without registering the conflict is a product-design failure, not a model limitation, and it is the clearest statement in the corpus of why personal AI still does not feel personal

data.name: Design memory as a compute budget, and build it in-house
guidelines: Do not reach for RAG by default — neither leading assistant chunks-and-embeds conversations, and the architecture both converged on is a running profile synthesized in the background plus tools to search past conversations on demand
keep memory synthesis asynchronous so the user is never made responsible for curating memories while trying to have a conversation, which was the flaw that sank the first-generation fact list

budget memory explicitly as compute, trading update frequency against profile length, since the profile is injected into every conversation and its length is a per-conversation tax while its freshness is an update-cost tax — the two leading vendors sit at opposite corners of that trade-off and both are defensible
decide deliberately how dense the writing is, since keyword-cluster profiles pack more per token and lean on the model's inference while prose profiles are more legible to users
make the profile visible and editable, and treat an edit as triggering a resynthesis rather than a patch
design for staleness from the start, because facts true when written stop being true and the corpus of failures here is mostly stale-fact failures
build memory in-house alongside the product rather than outsourcing it, because the converged part is easy and the divergent part is product-specific

and invest in context acquisition and conflict detection — reason over the sources the user has already connected, and make the system notice and try to resolve contradictions rather than storing both

data.name: Memory Harnesses for Long-Running Research Agents (Stefania Druga, Sakana AI — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Stefania Druga
Sakana AI
data.brief: Tokyo-based AI research lab; the talk's sovereignty framing ("we believe in the importance of sovereign AI today more than ever") is stated as an institutional position, not a personal one. Hiring in Japan

data.name: Coinbase
data.brief: Coined on reference to carry one signal: publicly reported reducing AI spend while increasing AI usage, by shifting to local models plus better routing, caching, context hygiene and per-task visibility

data.name: Memory as a write-manage-read loop
data.brief: The mental model the talk asks the audience to adopt: memory is "not just a database store — it's actually a control loop around the model," with distinct write, manage and read stages. Instantiated as a harness with three blocks: a core of traces always shown to the agent, a recall block where retrieval policy varies, and an archival block tracking information across sessions. Deliberately built over research agents with *zero durable memory* so that all memory behaviour comes from the harness and can be ablated

data.name: The recall-policy ladder
data.brief: The experimental design, and the file's most reusable artifact: hold the model fixed and vary only the recall policy across four rungs — (1) no recall baseline, (2) vector RAG, pulling on similarity alone, (3) a decisions ledger recording what was decided each turn, so entries can be ranked and prioritized, and (4) an oracle that is handed the ground-truth memory for each loop. The oracle is the ceiling estimate, and the finding that it does *not* reach maximum performance is itself a result

data.name: Ranked decisions ledger
data.brief: The winning recall policy. Rather than embedding and retrieving by similarity, record the decisions made at each turn and rank them for retrieval. On xbench long-horizon questions it outperformed vector RAG, no-recall, and a gated policy that merely asks the model whether it needs memory at all — and reproduced across two models (Qwen 27B 4-bit and DeepSeek V4 Flash) and a second benchmark (Spider V2). Its second property is economic: it retrieves the right thing *and* spends fewer tokens

data.name: Recall policy as a first-class metric
data.brief: The call to action: treat the recall function as something you design, measure and report — "what type of memories do you want to store, how do you rank them, how do you design your recall function, and what survives across multiple sessions and runs?" Backed by the cost heuristic the experiments produced: bad memory is expensive, because it burns tokens *and* sends the agent the wrong way, while a good structural recall policy saves both budget and error

data.name: Memory adds nothing when context fits
data.brief: The negative result, reported first and unusually plainly: on a literature-review task where all papers and relevant context fit in the window, "the memory actually didn't add more capability — it was the same performance with memory and without, and it only added more cost." The test case was deliberately adversarial for retrieval (a retracted Nature claim about 742,000 discovered materials, where the retraction is a far smaller needle than the headlines and citations), and memory still bought nothing. A vendor-neutral finding that cuts against reflexive memory adoption

data.name: Ranked ledger beats vector rag
data.brief: The positive result: on xbench long-horizon tasks — where the answer sits at step 124 and the question is asked at step 500, entirely outside the context window — a ranked decisions ledger beat vector RAG, no-recall, and a gated policy that just asks whether memory is needed. Across 68 questions with multiple cells and seeds, reproduced on two models and on Spider V2. The structure of *what* is stored and *how it is ranked* mattered more than retrieval sophistication

data.name: Oracle does not saturate
data.brief: The subtlest finding, and the one most useful to anyone building evaluations: even the oracle condition — handed the correct memory for every loop — does not reach maximum performance, "because the Oracle provides the right memory but doesn't force the model to use it. The model can get the right memory and still retrieve the wrong information, or choose to ignore it, or be confused." Retrieval quality therefore has a hard ceiling below perfect, and a measurable share of memory-system failure is *utilization* failure rather than retrieval failure. Ablations with arbitrary, wrong-step and most-recent-step memories all confirmed the ranked policy as best

data.name: Bad memory is expensive
data.brief: The cost inversion: better recall was also cheaper. "Bad memory is expensive because it spends more tokens and it can send the agent the wrong way, but a good structural policy for recall can save you a lot of tokens and budget." Turns recall-policy design from a quality knob into a cost lever, and supplies the argument for the talk's ask — treat recall policy as a first-class metric you design and report rather than a library you install

data.name: Local models cross the agentic line
data.brief: The enabling condition, and the sovereignty argument. Local models are now usable for agentic tool-use work — DeepSeek V4 Flash runs on an M3 Ultra, GLM is "on everyone's minds especially with Fable going away," RAM remains the bottleneck — and the whole study ran on one 96GB/28-core desktop in Tokyo, controlled from a phone, with household fans stacked around it. Corroborated externally by Coinbase reporting lower AI spend with higher AI usage after moving to local models plus routing, caching and context hygiene. The research payoff is stated as control: "I got to control the data, the entire traces of compute and evaluations — I see that as an example of sovereignty." Cost admitted: serial-only evaluation, no batch querying on DeepSeek V4 Flash

data.name: Memory earns its keep only past the window
data.brief: The two headline results form a decision rule that most memory adoption skips: below the context window, memory is pure overhead — same accuracy, higher cost — and above it, the *policy* rather than the machinery decides the outcome. Teams reaching for a memory system should first establish which regime they are in, because the honest answer for a large share of production tasks is that the task fits and the memory layer is buying nothing but tokens. That framing also explains why memory benchmarks disagree so violently: they are sampling different sides of the same threshold

data.name: Retrieval ceiling is utilization
data.brief: An oracle that hands the model exactly the right memory and still misses the maximum relocates a chunk of the memory problem from retrieval to use: the model can hold the correct evidence and still ignore, misread or be confused by it. Any memory evaluation that stops at retrieval precision is therefore measuring the easier half, and any memory product claiming wins on recall metrics has not yet shown the wins survive to task outcome. The oracle condition is cheap to add and belongs in every memory evaluation as the ceiling estimate it turns out not to be

data.name: Ablate the recall policy before buying a memory system
guidelines: Model memory as a write-manage-read control loop around the model rather than as a store, and separate the always-present core, the recall block and the cross-session archive so each can be varied independently
build over agents with no durable memory of their own so every memory effect is attributable to the harness

first check whether your task fits in context, because below that threshold memory reliably adds cost without adding capability, and the interesting regime only begins where the relevant evidence sits outside the window

then hold the model fixed and climb a recall-policy ladder — no recall, vector similarity, a ranked decisions ledger, and an oracle handed the ground truth — since this isolates policy from model quality
expect the ledger of decisions to beat similarity retrieval and to beat merely gating on "do I need memory," and expect it to be cheaper, because bad memory both burns tokens and misdirects the agent
always include the oracle arm, and treat the gap between oracle and maximum as your utilization failure rather than assuming perfect retrieval implies perfect outcomes
run ablations that feed arbitrary, wrong-step and merely-most-recent memories to confirm the policy is doing the work
and reproduce across at least two models and two benchmarks before believing the ranking

data.name: LLM Knowledge Bases: a practical guide (Ben Holmes, Warp — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Ben Holmes
Warp
data.brief: Terminal built for developers and their coding agents, positioned also as "a cloud platform that helps you build out software factories"; gives access to any model including open-weight. Ships oz.dev (warp.dev/oz), the cloud automation platform used for the scheduled runs in this talk

data.name: LLM knowledge base
data.brief: The talk's organizing artifact, credited to a Karpathy gist: take a raw directory of unstructured personal notes and have an agent compile it into a navigable, interconnected knowledge base scoped to a focus area. Four stages — raw capture, enrichment, wiki generation, visualization — with markdown as the substrate throughout so any viewer (Warp, Obsidian, a custom app) works. Framed as the antidote to "an Apple Notes folder that's a complete disorganized mess," and as making forgotten ideas rediscoverable rather than merely stored

data.name: Voice-first raw capture
data.brief: The input stage, argued as the load-bearing one: dictation runs ~200 words per minute and "will be faster than any other method unless you're an absolute Olympic typist," so it is how you generate the volume of raw material the later stages need. Explicitly permissive about quality — scrappy, rambly, unformatted is fine, because the agent does the structuring. Local, on-device options named (Handy, open source; VoiceInk, one-off fee) as removing the subscription barrier

data.name: The enrich-note skill
data.brief: The enrichment stage as a reusable agent skill, and the file's most transferable artifact. For each note it: writes an enrichment timestamp so later passes can skip already-processed notes; generates tags drawn from a fixed reference folder rather than inventing new ones ("I actually instruct the agent to be reluctant to add new tags, because Claude loves to get creative" — with permission to add only on a genuine pattern); researches and attaches the source via web tools; and finds backlinks to related notes by key-term search. The timestamp is what makes the skill idempotent and therefore schedulable

data.name: Agent-generated wiki
data.brief: The synthesis stage: over the enriched corpus, an agent generates a browsable wiki per focus area, structured as people, concepts, organizations and sources, with entries and backlinks to the raw notes. Demonstrated on two corpora (an AI-news wiki and a religious-texts study wiki) and pitched for workplace use — a people section built from meeting notes, with backlinks to every related meeting, useful for customer-success and client work. The point of the structure is that entity extraction turns a pile of notes into something with an index

data.name: Nightly knowledge-base automation
data.brief: The operational stage that makes the rest compound: sync the markdown folder into a cloud sandbox, run the skills against unenriched notes, sync back. Implemented with the Obsidian headless CLI for two-way sync (a git clone is the low-tech alternative) inside a Docker-backed cloud sandbox on oz.dev, triggered on a daily or weekly schedule or by events like a Slack or iMessage. Contrasted explicitly with local automations such as the Codex app's, which "means your laptop has to be cracked open when it runs." The payoff framing: "I wake up to a perfectly fresh wiki — it's like the daily paper, but it's your own"

data.name: Personal knowledge base as agent output
data.brief: The practical thesis of the track's most accessible talk: the interconnected knowledge base people have wanted from personal-wiki tools for two decades is now generated rather than maintained — tags, sources, backlinks, entity indexes and browsable wikis all produced by agents over a raw markdown folder, with the human contributing only unstructured capture. "All of that is generated programmatically. I didn't write any of this, because all I have time to do is generate the raw ingredients, not connect it all together myself." Credited to a Karpathy gist and shown working over two unrelated personal corpora

data.name: Capture bandwidth is the input constraint
data.brief: The input-side argument that mirrors Khemani's finding from the opposite direction: the binding constraint on a personal knowledge system is how much raw material you actually capture, so the highest-leverage intervention is dictation at ~200 wpm rather than better organization. Quality standards are deliberately abandoned at capture time — scrappy and rambly is fine because the agent structures it later — and the tooling barrier has fallen, with on-device local models (Handy, VoiceInk) replacing subscription transcription

data.name: Skills need fixed vocabularies
data.brief: A small, concrete authoring finding with wide applicability: agents generating metadata will invent new categories unless constrained, so the enrich-note skill keeps tags in a fixed reference folder and instructs the agent to be reluctant to add to it — "Claude loves to get creative, so just telling it please don't do that" — with permission to extend only on a genuine pattern. Paired with an enrichment timestamp per note, which makes the skill idempotent and therefore safe to run repeatedly and on a schedule. Vocabulary control and idempotence as the two properties that turn a prompt into infrastructure

data.name: Knowledge work moves to nightly cloud
data.brief: The operational shift: the enrichment and wiki-generation skills run unattended in a cloud sandbox on a schedule, syncing a markdown folder down via the Obsidian headless CLI, running the agent, and syncing back — so the user wakes to an updated knowledge base. Explicitly contrasted with local automation (the Codex app's scheduled tasks) which requires the laptop open. The framing is that background compounding, not interactive speed, is what makes the knowledge base worth having: "it's like the daily paper, but it's your own"

data.name: Visualizations are now disposable
data.brief: The closing demonstration and its economic point: a force-directed graph view over the note corpus, clickable nodes, a GitHub-style habit chart, and an on-request restyle into a starfield — none of it installed, all of it generated. "This is not a tool that you have to install. I told an agent: build this for me. So you can do that now." Bespoke visualization drops from a tooling decision to a throwaway prompt, which changes what personal software is worth building versus asking for

data.name: Capture cheap structure later
data.brief: Personal knowledge management historically failed because it demanded structure at capture time — tags, folders, links — precisely when the user has the least patience and the most to say. Inverting the order removes the failure mode: make capture as close to free as speech, then spend agent compute on the structuring nobody was ever going to do by hand. The corollary for tool design is that the valuable interface is a very fast unstructured inbox plus a scheduled enrichment loop, and that almost every feature between those two is now something an agent generates on request

data.name: Idempotence makes skills schedulable
data.brief: The two unglamorous details in the enrich-note skill — a fixed tag vocabulary and a per-note enrichment timestamp — are what let a prompt become a nightly job. The timestamp makes reruns cheap and safe by scoping work to unprocessed items; the fixed vocabulary keeps repeated passes from drifting into an ever-growing taxonomy. Any agent skill intended to run unattended and repeatedly needs both properties, and most published skills have neither, which is why they demo well and degrade under schedule

data.name: Build a knowledge base agents maintain for you
guidelines: Optimize the capture step first, because raw volume is what every later stage feeds on — use voice dictation (~200 wpm, faster than typing for almost everyone) with a hotkey on desktop and phone, and accept scrappy, rambly, unformatted output since structuring is the agent's job
keep everything as markdown in a plain folder so any viewer works and any agent can read it

write enrichment as a skill, not a prompt, and give it two properties that make it schedulable — a per-note enrichment timestamp so reruns only touch unprocessed notes, and a fixed tag vocabulary in a reference folder with explicit instructions to be reluctant to add to it, because agents will otherwise invent a new taxonomy on every pass
have the skill attach sources via web search and generate backlinks by key-term search, so the corpus grows more interconnected with each run

generate wikis over the enriched corpus structured as people, concepts, organizations and sources, which is what turns a pile of notes into something with an index — this works as well for meeting notes and client histories as for personal research

then move the whole loop to a cloud schedule rather than a local one, syncing the folder down (Obsidian headless CLI, or just a git clone), running the skills, and syncing back, so it compounds nightly without your laptop being open
and treat visualizations as disposable — ask an agent for the graph view or the habit chart rather than adopting a tool for it

data.name: Improving Agents is a Data Mining Problem (Vivek Trivedy, LangChain — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Vivek Trivedy
Agent trace mining
data.brief: The talk's central practice: point agents at other agents' traces at scale to answer questions no dashboard can. Worked examples given — find interactions where users got upset or delighted; determine whether "the agent gets really dumb after the first compaction, after the second, or never"; and test counterfactuals across models ("I ran GPT 5.5 for this and heard GLM is really good — what happens if I run GLM 5.2 and how do I compare them?"). The argument for traces over metrics is that "the trace level captures the actual behaviour that users see," at a granularity aggregate metrics erase

data.name: The trace-scale problem
data.brief: Two constraints that make naive trace reading impossible. Cost: input-token cost × number of traces × average trace size, which at millions of traces of millions of tokens is prohibitive. Capacity: a long coding-agent interaction "can't even be read with another agent because that context doesn't fit in memory," so the trace must be treated as an external object you query into rather than material you load. Framed against a forecast — "the data we see today is going to be the smallest that humans have ever seen," as agent-generated data outpaces the human total on shrinking timescales

data.name: Model × harness × task fit
data.brief: The talk's unifying abstraction, drawn from classical ML: scikit-learn was "a bunch of helpers to fit learning systems to data," and the same fit function survives in the agent world with three arguments — take your data, take a harness, take a model, and fit them so the tasks pass. "The algorithms look slightly different, but the overall process of machine learning doesn't really look that different." The job then decomposes into two research questions every team faces: find good fit functions (auto-research, OPD/OPSD, rejection-sampling SFT) and find good data

data.name: The harness–finetune–harness sandwich
data.brief: The practical ordering, argued from feedback latency: do whatever gives you feedback fastest. Harness engineering returns signal in about two minutes, so exhaust it first; once you hit the point where "if I keep tweaking this prompt I'm not going to get much more out of it," fine-tune to break through that ceiling; then harness-engineer again on top. The observed reality is that "a lot of teams are happy with harness engineering and it solves their customer use case," so the sandwich's later layers are optional rather than aspirational

data.name: Densifying feedback
data.brief: The lever that makes auto-research work: a terminal-style benchmark returns only pass/fail, which "is kind of helpful, but if I gave you a super random task and just said you failed, you wouldn't really have a good signal to figure out what to do next." Traces are named as the substrate that holds dense feedback, and agents as unusually good at reading them and deciding what to change. Paired with the honest caveat about auto-research generally: "agents are pretty good at making that number go up — they might cheat a little bit and you need to check them on some stuff"

data.name: Observability and continual learning converge
data.brief: The bridging claim, stated as a hot take by a vendor sitting on both sides: "there's a very tight coupling between what observability is and what continual learning is" — agents act in environments and produce traces; learning is reading those traces and updating. The commercial corollary is blunt: "if you're a continual-learning company, you need traces, and if you have traces, you can try to do continual learning over your agents." A structural claim that the observability category and the continual-learning category are converging on the same asset

data.name: Agents are unreadable without agents
data.brief: Why the practice is necessary rather than merely convenient: source code can be reasoned about by reading it, but agents have "prompts, tools, skills, hooks, middlewares, some agents call other agents and I orchestrate them in swarms," and a prompt change behaves differently in the medical domain than the legal one — "it's really really hard for humans to reason about how certain prompts they change are actually going to affect agent behaviour at scale." Placed in a four-year arc: "since the ChatGPT moment we've started trading determinism for autonomy," and the tools to understand autonomous systems have to be rebuilt

data.name: Trace volume outgrows reading
data.brief: The scale wall with its arithmetic stated: cost is input-token price × trace count × trace size, and a long coding-agent trace "can't even be read with another agent because that context doesn't fit in memory," forcing traces to be treated as external objects queried into rather than loaded. Set against a forecast that agent-generated data will eclipse humanity's lifetime output on year, then six-month, then three-month, then daily timescales — "the data we see today is going to be the smallest that humans have ever seen in their entire lives"

data.name: Open models hit the intelligence waterline
data.brief: A practitioner data point on open-model viability: "in the last 6 months open models have basically hit an inflection point in intelligence" such that LangChain no longer reaches for frontier models by default. The stated method is a waterline test — start with Opus or GPT-5.5 to establish the task is possible at all, then look back at those traces and ask whether an open model can match it. On the Harvey legal benchmark they matched Opus's trace-judging capability with an open model at roughly one to two orders of magnitude lower cost, closing the gap through harness engineering informed by reading Opus's traces. A second economic note: high-volume inference can shift from token costs to hardware costs — "run a cluster and I get unlimited inference, then spin it down"

data.name: Harness first then finetune
data.brief: The ordering advice, argued from feedback latency rather than ideology: harness engineering returns signal in ~2 minutes, so exhaust it first; fine-tune only to break the ceiling where further prompt tweaking stops paying; then harness-engineer again — a sandwich. Reported reality is that most teams never leave the first layer: "a lot of teams are happy with harness engineering and it solves their customer use case, so we always recommend it." Where teams do fine-tune, the observed win is narrow verticals — customers "don't care about the entire variance of tasks, they care about what their customers care about," and base models tuned on that narrow set "reach and then also go beyond frontier performance"

data.name: Traces are the shared substrate
data.brief: Every approach in the continual-learning track needs the same input and few of them say so: on-policy self-distillation needs on-policy rollouts, enterprise distillation needs production traces, memory synthesis needs conversation history, and auto-research needs dense feedback. Traces are that substrate, which means observability infrastructure is quietly the precondition for the entire category — and explains why a tracing vendor, a continual-learning startup and an enterprise distillation lab all arrive at the same business shape from different directions. The competitive question becomes who owns the trace stream, not who has the better algorithm

data.name: Optimize for feedback latency
data.brief: The harness-then-finetune ordering is really a rule about feedback latency: prefer whatever closes the loop fastest, because iteration count dominates per-iteration quality until you hit a ceiling. That explains why most teams stop at harness engineering and are right to — two-minute feedback beats a training run for almost every problem — and it reframes fine-tuning not as the mature endpoint but as the thing you do specifically when your ceiling is provably reached and your task distribution is narrow enough that a small model can be pushed past a frontier one on it

data.name: Mine agent traces to improve agents
guidelines: Ship the agent first — it cannot generate the data you need to improve it until it operates in a real environment — then centralize traces in one project, per-agent or across agents, and point agents at those traces rather than trying to read them yourself, because prompts, tools, skills, hooks, middlewares and agent-to-agent orchestration make behaviour effectively unreadable by inspection

ask trace-level questions a dashboard cannot answer, such as which interactions delighted or upset users, whether quality degrades after the first or second compaction, and how a candidate model would have handled the same task

budget for scale, since cost is input-token price × traces × trace size and long agent traces will not fit in another agent's context — treat a trace as an external object you query into, not material you load
use traces to establish a waterline by starting with a frontier model to prove the task is possible, then reading those traces to work out what guidance a cheaper open model needs to match it
densify your feedback, because a pass/fail number gives an agent almost nothing to act on and traces are the substrate that holds richer signal

and order your work by feedback latency — exhaust harness engineering first at roughly two-minute iterations, fine-tune only to break a demonstrated ceiling and only where the task distribution is narrow, then return to harness engineering
finally, keep humans in the loop for high-trust domains such as legal and medical by preparing trace summaries for review rather than expecting anyone to read it all

data.name: Evolution of Agentic Surfaces (Gagan Bhat & Isabella Kai He, Anthropic — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Gagan Bhat
Isabella Kai He
The three agentic surfaces
data.brief: The lineage the talk is built on. Messages API (with Claude 3): tokens in, tokens out. Claude Agent SDK: packages the Claude Code harness with a built-in agentic loop, file-system access, tools and sandboxing — but leaves credentials, hosting and scaling to be hand-rolled. Claude managed agents: the loop, the sandbox, credentials, session management, observability and hosting all operated by Anthropic, leaving the developer "your product, your task, your context, and your domain knowledge." The driver named is task complexity climbing from questions → delegated tasks → "agents own entire outcomes"

data.name: Harnesses encode assumptions that go stale
data.brief: The talk's core principle, and the sharpest statement of it in the corpus: "harnesses encode assumptions about what Claude cannot do on its own" — context resets, compaction, and similar primitives — and "they have to be questioned frequently because they go stale as models improve." The worked example is context anxiety: Sonnet 4.5 wrapped up tasks early as it neared its context limit, so the team built context resets into the harness; Opus 4.5 no longer exhibited the behaviour, and the fix "became dead weight… pure overhead, adding latency and causing issues with the cache being discarded incorrectly." Generalized as: when the model moves and the harness doesn't, it degrades the agent

data.name: Decoupling the brain from the hands
data.brief: The load-bearing architectural decision. The first implementation put the agent loop and tool execution in one container, which meant the model could not begin reasoning until the container finished setting up, and one component failing took the whole agent down. Separating them yields three benefits: sandboxes spin up just in time and only when needed; a dead sandbox can be replaced while the loop continues; and — the measured payoff — the model reasons immediately while container setup runs in parallel, or is skipped entirely when the task needs no container

data.name: Agent, environment, session
data.brief: The three primitives managed agents is designed around. Agent — model, prompts, tools and skills defining what it does. Environment — the container it runs in, reusable across sessions with isolated instances, and the place network boundaries are set. Session — the combination, persisted as a durable cloud resource recording every interaction, with four states: *idle*, *running*, *rescheduling* on a retryable error, and *terminated* when unrecoverable. Durability is what makes long-horizon reliability possible: the agent can always return to a session and resume

data.name: The durable session log
data.brief: The single mechanism three separate capabilities are built on. Every event — user message, model response, tool execution, result — is written play-by-play to a persisted log. Surfaced in a UI it becomes observability; read back in slices it becomes context recovery, solving the problem that in traditional harnesses "the context window and the session are one and the same," so discarded context is unrecoverable — here Claude can re-read what it dropped; and fed to a batch process it becomes the substrate for memory and self-improvement

data.name: Dreaming
data.brief: The frontier feature, and the batch's fourth independent use of the term: take the agent's daily session transcripts plus its current memory state, run a periodic batch process over them, and extract new insights and organized structures that edit the memory — "to make the next day's agent sessions automatically much more intelligent. This is how we're seeing self-improving agents as they execute more and more over time." Positioned alongside memory as "two cornerstones of a new frontier unified memory system," with a third form flagged as emerging: organizational-scale memory storing a team's runbooks and details

data.name: Outcomes (rubric-graded retry)
data.brief: The second frontier feature: the developer defines success criteria and failure cases as a rubric, and a separate grader agent runs alongside the agent loop, checking whether the task was actually accomplished. If the grader says no, the agent keeps trying until the criteria are met. Framed as moving toward "a world where we can have an agent understand what success actually means for a task and have a mechanism to keep iterating," unlocking tasks that were not possible months earlier

data.name: Harness is now the limiting factor
data.brief: The closing thesis, from the vendor whose harness the industry copies: "harnesses have become the limiting factor to what models can achieve," and managed agents exists "to close the gap between what products offer today on many surfaces with static harnesses and what models can actually do." A frontier lab stating that the constraint on deployed capability sits in the scaffolding rather than the weights — the strongest first-party support the harness thesis has received, from the same lab whose prompt-shrink arc supplied one of its counter-edges

data.name: Harness fixes become dead weight
data.brief: The counter-current inside the same talk, and the most falsifiable claim in it. Sonnet 4.5 exhibited context anxiety — terminating work early as it approached its context limit — so the team built context resets into the harness. Opus 4.5 did not exhibit it, and the fix "became dead weight, in fact pure overhead, adding latency and causing issues with the cache being discarded incorrectly at times." Generalized into a maintenance warning: customer harnesses "built around older Claude models" are rigid, and "you don't want a stale harness that takes weeks or months to migrate to a new model, especially with release cycles coming out shorter and shorter." Harness engineering as a depreciating asset

data.name: Brain hands split cuts latency
data.brief: The measured engineering result: decoupling the agent loop from the tool-execution container removed container setup from the critical path, giving ~60% faster time-to-first-token at P50 and over 90% improvement at P95, because the model starts reasoning immediately while setup runs in parallel — or the container is skipped entirely when unnecessary. The same split also supplies fault isolation (a dead sandbox is replaced while the loop continues) and the security property below

data.name: Credentials kept from the model
data.brief: The first field lesson, answering a question customers ask repeatedly — how to stop the agent reading the environment file with the security tokens. Two mechanisms: the brain/hands split already separates the loop from where tools execute, and vaults store credentials so they are "decrypted only when needed at tool execution runtime," so "the model never sees your security tokens." Extended by two enterprise features: self-hosted sandboxes, letting customers run the hands inside their own VPC under their own policies, and MCP tunnels, so MCP servers stay on a private network making only outbound calls to the Claude agent loop

data.name: Session log powers memory and dreaming
data.brief: The architectural payoff and the batch's frontier-lab memory data point: one durable session log yields observability when surfaced in a UI, context recovery when read back in slices (fixing the traditional harness problem that context window and session are the same thing, so discarded context is gone), and — combined with dreaming, a periodic batch over transcripts plus memory state — a self-improving loop where "the next day's agent sessions are automatically much more intelligent." Anthropic names memory and dreaming "two cornerstones of a new frontier unified memory system," with organizational-scale memory holding team runbooks flagged as an emerging third form

data.name: Rubric grader loops until success
data.brief: The outcomes feature: developers define success criteria and failure cases as a rubric, and a separate grader agent runs alongside the loop and sends the agent back to work until the criteria are met. Presented as moving toward "a world where we can have an agent understand what success actually means for a task and have a mechanism to keep iterating," unlocking tasks impossible months earlier. A frontier lab shipping verification-by-second-agent as a platform primitive rather than a customer responsibility — the same shape as OpenAI's auto-review in b18, arriving within two days of it

data.name: Harness code is a depreciating asset
data.brief: The context-anxiety story is the cleanest statement anyone has given of why harness engineering is structurally unlike ordinary infrastructure work: every workaround is a bet about a model deficiency, and the bet expires when the deficiency does — silently, while continuing to cost latency and cache efficiency. That makes harness code a depreciating asset requiring scheduled re-examination rather than a foundation that accrues value, and it explains why the vendor's own answer is to sell the harness as a managed service. It also sets the design rule the talk states outright: build for the model capabilities of *tomorrow*, and keep components independently swappable so the architecture survives what the model stops needing

data.name: One log three capabilities
data.brief: Persisting every agent event to a durable log is a single decision that pays out three times — observability for humans, context recovery for the model, and a training substrate for memory and dreaming — which is why several independent teams keep converging on it from different motivations. The non-obvious part is the second: decoupling the session record from the context window means discarded context is retrievable, converting compaction from a lossy one-way operation into a reversible view over a complete record. Any harness that treats the context window as the session has foreclosed both the recovery and the self-improvement capability without realizing it

data.name: Build harnesses that expect the model to change
guidelines: Treat every harness feature as an encoded assumption about what the model cannot do, write down what that assumption is, and re-test it on each model release — the context-anxiety fix that helped one generation became pure latency and cache overhead on the next, and stale harnesses take weeks or months to migrate precisely when release cycles are shortening

design around a small set of independent primitives so individual components can be swapped without destabilizing the architecture, and aim at the capabilities of the *next* model rather than the current one

decouple the agent loop from the tool-execution environment, which removes container setup from the critical path (measured at ~60% faster time-to-first-token at P50 and >90% at P95), lets sandboxes spin up just in time or be skipped entirely, and isolates faults so a dead sandbox is replaced without killing the run
separate agent, environment and session as distinct resources, and give sessions explicit states including a retry state, so long-running work can always resume where it stopped

persist every event to a durable session log rather than treating the context window as the session — that one decision buys observability, the ability for the model to re-read context it discarded, and the substrate for memory

keep credentials out of the model entirely by decrypting them only at tool-execution time, and offer private execution (self-hosted sandboxes, tunnelled MCP servers) for security-conscious deployments
and define success criteria as a rubric graded by a separate agent so the loop can iterate until the outcome is actually met rather than until the model decides it is finished

data.name: Agents, codebases, and teams (Aditya Khandelwal, Amazon AGI Lab — AI Engineer World's Fair)
Aditya Khandelwal
The fear × utilization map
data.brief: The framing device for adoption as a human problem. Plot each developer on two axes — fear (is this coming for my job, or is it a handy tool?) and utilization (how much are they actually using it?) — and trace the arc: at first fear high and utilization low; then early adopters get outsized leverage and others try harder ("it looks like I'm still needed if I figure out how to use this thing"); then mandates and token-maxxing raise utilization without confidence; then slop and sev-2s lower fear but leave confidence flat. The goal is to move everyone toward low fear and high utilization, and the explicit instruction is that "fear is real, human emotions are real, we should recognize it"

data.name: Symptoms of a bad agent setup
data.brief: A diagnostic list, offered as things that *indicate* the setup is wrong rather than that the model is bad. Babysitting agents at all is the first tell. "The model is being really dumb today" — the model did not change; the harness may have, and a setup that cannot absorb small harness changes is not set up well. Silently burning context and money — blowing through 500k, 750k or a million tokens and hitting auto-compact on tasks that do not warrant it. Long sessions needing constant intervention. A constant slop factory. And asking how other companies ship so fast when model labs release on a six-to-eight-week cadence — "clearly they have something which we don't"

data.name: Harness engineering as a team function
data.brief: The reframing the talk exists to argue: "it isn't really an IC's job. It's a job for leadership. It's a job for the company." The mechanism is that the highest-leverage changes — how the codebase is organized for agent navigation — require team buy-in and cannot be done by an individual. The cost of not doing it is distributional: people who figure it out ship 10 PRs a day and look like gods, the one-to-two-PR people inherit the review burden, "and that's actually a really, really bad thing, because now not only can they not ship, they're going to see bad code and then curse the agents." Three principles: smart prompt injection (treat the whole codebase as a map so the right context arrives at the right time), close the loop (a self-healing pipeline, because "slop is inevitable"), and iterate continuously

data.name: Progressive disclosure at codebase scale
data.brief: The concrete technique behind smart prompt injection, expanded in Q&A. Keep CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md as a thin index that points to the right files, not one big overloaded document, because that is what loads on the agent's first prompt. Cap SKILL.md files at ~100 lines on the reasoning that "your skill is really a folder." Put runbook-style documentation in the code comments, so an agent that greps its way into a file finds the pointer to everything relevant. The measurable test: watch what the first prompt costs — "I think like 20, 25K tokens get taken anyway, but if you're coming to 40K, 50K, something's wrong. That's not really progressive disclosure"

data.name: The "ship it" skill
data.brief: The single high-value shared skill the team invested in, and their adoption lever: it takes over everything "from code done to PR ready for review" — opening the PR, writing the description, handling review comments and merge comments, and working through CI failures in a loop. Often runs over an hour, which initially scared people, "but once they saw the value they get invested, because it's one skill which tells them: this AI thing can actually work for me, I don't need to constantly babysit it, I can trust it." Paired with a code gardener that runs nightly over the repo checking organization against the codebase's own standards

data.name: Individual agent setups dont survive teams
data.brief: The gap the talk names: an enormous body of content exists on configuring a personal repo for agents, "but it all seems to break the moment you actually try to use it with your team in your actual production setup." For individual repos the advice holds; at team scale it does not, because the highest-leverage changes are to shared codebase organization and cannot be made by an individual contributor. Reported from ~10 engineers over several months of iteration

data.name: Harness engineering is a leadership job
data.brief: The central claim: "making engineers work well with their agents is truly the most impactful thing you could do as an organization," and it belongs to leadership rather than to ICs. The argument against the figure-it-out-yourself default is distributional rather than moral — uneven adoption produces a class shipping 10 PRs a day and a class inheriting their review burden, who then "can't ship, are going to see bad code, and curse the agents," entrenching the gap. Practical corollaries include budgeting a standing percentage of IC time for shared-setup work that produces no PRs, and treating winning over skeptics — measured by whether they will edit the shared setup — as the real adoption signal

data.name: Adoption arc fear then slop
data.brief: The enterprise arc traced from the inside: coding agents land, a few people get outsized leverage, "is this AGI?"; companies generalize it into mandates and token-maxxing, "clearly a galaxy-brain moment"; then "the inevitable happened — AI slop shipped, and there's a bunch of sev-2s," people retract, prices climb, "people figured out that tokens have to be paid for — you just can't token-max your way through life," and budgets get bolted on because "money is being lit on fire and the money has to come from somewhere." An unusually candid adoption post-mortem from a frontier-lab engineering org. HELD PATTERN-LESS — pat-ai-native-org ledger, dysfunction side

data.name: Progressive disclosure is measurable
data.brief: The most immediately usable content: progressive disclosure has a number attached. Keep the agent-instruction file a thin index pointing to files rather than one loaded document, cap skill files at ~100 lines because "your skill is really a folder," and push runbook documentation into code comments so a grepping agent finds it in place. Then measure the first prompt — "20, 25K tokens get taken anyway, but if you're coming to 40K, 50K, something's wrong." Context discipline stated as an observable threshold rather than an aspiration

data.name: One trusted skill converts skeptics
data.brief: The adoption mechanism that worked: rather than broad mandates, invest in one high-value skill — here "ship it," covering everything from code-complete to PR-ready including CI failure loops — and let its reliability do the persuading. That it often runs over an hour initially scared people and became the point: "once they saw the value they get invested, because it's one skill which tells them this AI thing can actually work for me, I don't need to constantly babysit it, I can trust it." Reframed explicitly as expectation-setting — "it's good if agents take too long, that means you can go off and do other things and you have confidence they're doing the right thing"

data.name: Agent adoption is a distribution problem
data.brief: The damage from uneven agent adoption is not that some people are slower but that the fast and slow are coupled through review: high-throughput adopters generate PRs that low-throughput colleagues must review, so the cost of one group's leverage lands on the other, who then have less time to adopt and more reason to distrust the tools. That feedback loop makes "figure it out yourself" actively harmful rather than merely suboptimal, and it is why the intervention has to be organizational — a shared setup, shared skills, and protected time — rather than individual enablement

data.name: Trust is bought with one long skill
data.brief: The counter-intuitive adoption lesson is that a skill running for an hour converts skeptics better than one running for a minute, because duration is what forces the question of whether the agent can be left alone — and answering that question affirmatively once is what ends babysitting. Teams optimizing agent adoption for responsiveness are optimizing the wrong variable; the thing that changes behaviour is a single end-to-end task the engineer is willing to walk away from, which means the highest-value shared skill is whichever one spans the most of a workflow, not the one used most often

data.name: Roll agents out as a leadership programme, not an IC exercise
guidelines: Treat making engineers work well with agents as an organizational responsibility, since the highest-leverage changes are to shared codebase organization and no individual can make them — and because uneven adoption is self-entrenching, with fast adopters' PR volume landing as review burden on slower colleagues who then have less time and more reason to distrust the tools

diagnose the setup rather than the model when things go wrong — babysitting, "the model is dumb today" (the model did not change), silently burning 500k–1M tokens and hitting auto-compact on simple tasks, long sessions needing constant intervention, and a steady slop output are all setup symptoms

do progressive disclosure properly and measure it — keep the agent instruction file a thin index that points to files rather than one loaded document, cap skill files around 100 lines since a skill is really a folder, put runbook documentation in code comments so a grepping agent finds it in place, then watch the first prompt's context cost and treat 40–50K where 20–25K is baseline as a failure
harvest your best ICs' practices and ship them as the shared setup, accepting that engineers dislike being told their personal setup is imperfect

invest in one high-value end-to-end skill rather than broad mandates, and expect a long-running one (code-done to PR-ready, including CI failure loops) to convert skeptics precisely because it proves the agent can be left alone
close the loop with CI, agentic reviews and a nightly code-gardener, because slop is inevitable and needs a detection-and-repair path
budget a standing percentage of IC time for setup work that produces no PRs
give experiments and prototypes an explicit opt-out from your production standards rather than letting them drag the bar down
and treat winning over skeptics as the real measure — you know they are bought in when they edit the shared setup themselves
